They have different languages, ceremonies, and religious concepts. Inheriting the culture of both nations is certainly possible, but the “Great Spirit” is not some uniform concept across indigenous nations. The first clue is that “Great Spirit” is an English phrase, so it’s necessarily a catch-all term imposed on other belief systems, although indigenous interpreters do use the term now too.
For instance, the Lakota had the concept of Wakhan Thanka, which meant something closer to the total reality being produced from mysterious sacred power. That’s not the same as God according to the Christian missionaries working in America. The Niitsitapi’s concept of Ihtsipatapiyopa comes closer to “source of life” than God, and the distinction matters because “source of life” implies a first cause without omnipotence or personal intervention instead of a foundation for a highly relational lifestyle.
Consider what it would sound like if someone said “I am a Scottish-Turkish woman. Many of us believe in God.” Scotland has had Presybterians, Catholics, Episcopalians, Quakers, Baptists, Gaelic traditions, etc. Turkey has had Sunni Islam, Alevi Islam, Sufi communities, Greek Orthodox, and Jewish communities. Also, Scotland and Turkey are very different countries with different languages, backgrounds, and sociopolitical regimes. Who exactly is “us”? You could ostensibly cast the word “God” out and each faith’s members could use the term, but it would seem very difficult to imagine they actually agree on how the God of their understanding can be mapped to the Higher Power described by the 12 Steps and surrounding A.A. literature.
“I’m a devout, lifelong Catholic. That is an integral part of my experience, strength and hope. I call my higher power God and do not feel I should have to qualify that every time I speak at a meeting. I’m perfectly okay with others referring to Buddha, Mohammed, Yahweh, or whatever name they call their higher power. “I’m uncomfortable, though, with anyone citing the Bible, the Koran, the Talmud, or any non-A.A. literature as the truth in an A.A. meeting. But I certainly give them the right to refer to or even quote (briefly) from any of these texts if it’s part of their A.A. experience.
Calling the Buddha a Higher Power on the same shelf as Yahweh or God is actually one of the quickest ways to confirm you don’t know much about Buddhism. The Buddha is not a prophet or a deity with powers from a higher independent reality. He was a human named Siddhartha Gautama who was awakened to the nature of reality through human actions and sought to teach others to pursue those actions while also questioning his every step. He is valued for his teachings, not as an entity unto himself.
The impermanence of all things means that the Buddha too is impermanent. Or, bluntly, he has died as a matter of having been a human born over a couple centuries ago, and he is not a permanent soul looking down on us from the heavens or another higher independent reality. I genuinely wonder if they consulted a Buddhist of any stripe before writing this, because there are Buddhists who do devotional worship to entities that can be construed as prayer to a personal deity for intervention, but even they would have clarified that the Buddha himself doesn’t make much sense as a Higher Power.
The Buddha more or less regarded questioning the existence of God as an intellectual exercise compared to the practical problem of resolving human suffering, and he was pretty negative on the concept of a Supreme Creator in making humans complacent with both their own actions and those of others:
“So, then, owing to the creation of a supreme deity men will become murderers, thieves, unchaste, liars, slanderers, abusive babblers, covetous, malicious, and perverse in view. Thus for those who fall back on the creation of a god as the essential reason, there is neither desire nor effort nor necessity to do this deed or abstain from that deed”
Would you quote this in the same meeting as the Serenity Prayer, where God is asked for serenity to accept the things you cannot change? Could you use someone as a Higher Power if they are depicted questioning gods who claim to be higher powers?
In my personal experience, I have yet to hear anyone quote the Koran, Talmud, or Buddha at an A.A. meeting, but I’ve heard many times that you cannot get sober without accepting God from someone who cites the Bible. The lack of consistency is part of the problem with decentralized anonymous peer-facilitated mutual-aid organizations. This testimony could be absolutely true while also not being an experience many of us can relate to in recovery. The same applies to every other type of meeting too.
I’ve been in Recovery Dharma meetings that got quite uncomfortable as some people called out systemic biases they observed in Buddhist institutions or threw some fuel on the flaming schism between RD and Refuge Recovery (I’ll dig into that elsewhere). The notable difference is that SMART, Recovery Dharma, and Refuge Recovery explicitly mention you can do A.A. and the Steps alongside their program and that many members successfully do. A.A. literature tends to put things in more binary terms: you’re doing the Steps or you’re heading for relapse.
From the next testimony:
I’m still an agnostic. But I have discovered that the program will work for anyone who will let it. I didn’t have to find a way to make it work. It will work perfectly well on its own, provided I’m willing to do some work myself.
I genuinely am not sure what this means, but I feel a lot of whiplash.
I saw that whatever else spirituality might consist of, it had to include being of maximum service to my fellow alcoholics, whether or not they were still suffering
When I first came to A.A., I thought that religion and spirituality were the same thing. But I’ve come to realize that religion means being committed to a practice of belief, and being spiritual means actively living life through a life-giving force. I believe this is any power greater than myself, whether I choose to call it God, Allah, Higher Power, Creative Intelligence, or the Power of Good.
This is one of the rare instances I’ve seen of A.A. literature delineating religion from spirituality with definitions. It also gives away how particularly religious their perspective is: the emphasis on belief before understanding, personal awakenings, and Creator worship over ritual schedules, kinship networks, and communal resources.
Also, where does a “practice of belief” end and “actively living life” begin? Do we not practice our beliefs actively while living life? If not then they aren’t really beliefs, they’re partially-internalized aspirations. Someone tried to explain this difference to me as “religion is something you study, spirituality is for your soul.”
That confused me a lot more, because you can absolutely find thousands of texts throughout history attempting to study human psychology and identity through the concept of a soul. Some cultures frame trauma and its aftermath in terms of a disturbed soul that cannot maintain functional harmony within a body and its mind after some kind of event, and they address it with community rituals that use interconnectedness as a premise in healing rituals. I have no clue how you could separate that into religion and spirituality, or “practicing beliefs” and “actively living life.” A.A. itself says to practice its principles “in all our affairs.”
From Nancy Ammerman, a 2013 abstract I found useful:
“Spirituality” often has been framed in social science research as an alternative to organized “religion,” implicitly or explicitly extending theoretical arguments about the privatization of religion. This article uses in-depth qualitative data from a religiously diverse U.S. sample to argue that this either/or distinction not only fails to capture the empirical reality of American religion, it does no justice to the complexity of spirituality. An inductive discursive analysis reveals four primary cultural “packages,” or ways in which people construct the meaning of spirituality in conversation: a Theistic Package tying spirituality to personal deities, an Extra-Theistic Package locating spirituality in various naturalistic forms of transcendence, an Ethical Spirituality focusing on everyday compassion, and a contested Belief and Belonging Spirituality tied to cultural notions of religiosity. Spirituality, then, is neither a diffuse individualized phenomenon nor a single cultural alternative to “religion.” Analysis of the contested evaluations of Belief and Belonging Spirituality allows a window on the “moral boundary work” being done through identifying as “spiritual but not religious.” The empirical boundary between spirituality and religion is far more orous than is the moral and political one.
From Linda Mercadante’s 2014 book Belief without Borders:
The dramatic rise in the number of religiously unaffiliated, who nevertheless claim to be “spiritual but not religious,” suggests the need to rethink the categories of spirituality and religion. Although more a rhetorical device than true divorce, this important shift demands the study of the beliefs of “nones.” The “why” of this and the interview process are explained. The book asks whether this is a spiritual crisis or revolution, and whether the situation is really spirituality versus religion. It also explains why the study of belief, although often neglected by the social sciences, is critical. The interview process and the interviewees are discussed, showing that qualitative research is an appropriate method to elicit SBNR beliefs. A main contention is that SBNRs need to be heard in their own voices.
I would have a hard time disagreeing with the bold part. I agree that it means something that we have people identifying as “spiritual but not religious.” I do think they’re sincerely conveying a real pattern we can identify and study in people who are unhappy with dissociating from life through radical materialism and hyperindividualism, and they’re seeking a real aspect of human experience that our modern social institutions systematically denigrate.
But I also remember the Oxford Group literature. The community called themselves “not a religion” while also calling themselves Holy Crusaders bringing about a New World Order for Jesus Christ the King. They wanted to separate themselves from “religious bores” or those who emphasize practice and study in ways that can come across as boring and disciplined. Remember that the Oxford Group was trying to spread by appealing to wealthy elite students and inviting them to lavish parties at hotels and estates. I would argue that there’s definitely a rhetorical angle at work here, even if completely sincere or unplanned, that moves religious beliefs under the aesthetics of general spirituality.
When I finally admitted I was an alcoholic and came into the program four years ago, I thought, ‘Oh God, why me?’ We Jews were supposed to be immune to alcoholism, we were the ‘Chosen Ones’ — or so my denial told me. Yet today I am doubly blessed; I am a grateful, recovering, Jewish alcoholic.
“It took me a long time to separate Judaism from alcoholism, to accept that spirituality did not affect or change my religious beliefs, but enhanced them, that my higher power was not the same as yours, that praying and the posture I use to pray does not alter my Jewishness but is necessary for my recovery.
I asked a couple Jewish friends about this part. They’ve said that there is really something comparable to the “model minority” concept for Asians where holding oneself to higher standards is both an internally generated and externally imposed expectation of their identity. Throughout American history, certain European groups like the Irish, German, and Eastern European peoples were stereotyped as having a heavy “working-class” drinking culture, so it became socially advantageous for Jewish communities to separate themselves by downplaying their own. It’s in the same vein of saying “we’re Asians: we don’t get divorced, we’re good at school, and we get ahead by following rules.” It’s also very real for denial to use this identity as an excuse to ignore real problems.
My friends also said that the “Chosen Ones” reference was weird though because they’ve heard it in the context of an association with struggle, as in being chosen by God through a covenant to fulfill obligations that involve trials and tribulations. Between this and the earlier reference to “white man’s world” from the Sioux/Blackfoot woman, I’m getting a vibe. I’m not saying the testimony is made up, but I am saying that it feels this testimony was chosen in an attempt to be culturally sensitive only to end up projecting stereotypes. I say this as someone who has met many kind and genuine people in non-recovery spaces who have done exactly that to my face with the best possible intentions, often to my benefit by assuming better things about me than I would have said. Still, it’s going to come across as stereotypical and throw readers off.
Today I can even recite the Lord’s Prayer without feeling guilty since it was pointed out to me in ‘How it Works’ that I have to go to any length to get and stay sober.
This is one of those things you can’t help but notice once it’s been pointed out to you, as it was to me. Notice how the spiritual and religious compatibility discussion is being sidestepped into a discussion about desperation, as if trying to brute force past a complex discussion that requires time and energy.
More than once, the response to my hesitance or questions about the Higher Power has been some variation of “this disease wants you dead” (I’m aware, which is why I’m asking how this program works to prevent that outcome) or “can you really say you’re willing to go to any lengths to stay sober if you won’t even try this free step” (nothing is free, I have finite time and resources, so I would like to know if another program might be more compatible for me).
This is one of the practical ways in which the strong claims in How It Works can manifest as an obstacle. If you accept that only dishonesty or ego keeps people from working the “simple” program and that God is the only one capable of curing you of the defects of your “self-will run riot”, then it makes sense that you would want to apply some type of “tough love” or “reality check” to deflate that ego.
My sponsor was well versed in A.A.’s Twelve Steps, Traditions and Concepts. He had a substantial service history and talked to me about the 36 principles upon which A.A. was founded. It is these principles that I would ultimately turn my life and my will over to. “This God — ‘good orderly direction’ — as represented by the two million or so alcoholics who are members of this global Fellowship, is what I have accepted.
“In reading Appendix II in the Big Book, Alcoholics Anonymous, I have come to understand the profound changes that come from spirituality. The appendix says, ‘With few exceptions our members find that they have tapped an unsuspected inner resource which they presently identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves. Most of us think this awareness… is the essence of spiritual experience.
We’re rapidly reapproaching something like the Oxford Group’s claims of not being religious while also claiming monotheism, dualism, and personal awakenings characteristic of certain religions and not others. Kind of like how being a Holy Crusader spreading the word of Jesus Christ is characteristic of certain religions and not others, even if you say you’re not aiming to be a religion.
I am proof that it is possible to be an atheist on matters of the supernatural but still have a spiritual awakening and reap the rewards of the A.A. program of recovery.”
This is, again, a stereotype but of atheists. Atheism is not a belief system. Atheists are not materialists who deny the immaterial world. Atheism doesn’t even have a consistent meaning, because those who advocate for radical materialism, those who don’t have any specific belief in a God, and those who think theism is an irrelevant question are all lumped together as “atheists.” Many argue a distinction must be drawn between non-theists and atheists, between the indifferent and the actively opposed. The mainstream Buddhist perspective is arguably non-theistic, as are many Hindu perspectives. There are atheist Hindus. Atheism in Hinduism is as old and respectable as any other tradition, not a modern trend as the result of living in a post-Enlightenment industrialized age of radical materialism and hyperindividualism.
The Rig Veda doesn’t actually command any kind of belief in an ultimate Creator to be worshipped. Almost the opposite, in fact. Lots of Hindu texts explicitly engage with skepticism and the value of realizing the divinity of your true self in the face of gods who selfishly seek worship for their intrinsic divinity. Some schools go further and say gods only have power through the mantras that name them and the concepts they invoke within ourselves, so to separate oneself from divinity is to attempt to surrender to the concepts within yourself. It’s shying away from your own autonomy. None of this rules out the ideas of karma and dharma as principles of the universe, which you might very well call supernatural. A lack of theism doesn’t mean disorder.

Personal Experiences
I hate bringing up unverifiable personal experiences, but when they form a pattern and they’ve been validated by someone else, I feel compelled to share them tentatively as a warning.
A lot of people in AA frown upon having an understanding of religion and spirituality that doesn’t work with the 12 steps. Sometimes it’s as explicit as “if God scares you out of these rooms, your addiction will bring you back” or “I don’t know how anyone can do this without praying for strength from God” or “I don’t care if it offends you, God is the reason I’m here today.” This can be framed as “tough love” but I would say it’s closer to bordering on “proselytizing.”
The organizations around AA will tell you that there’s no central authoritative governing body that can vet safety or quality of meetings. By design, they are not intended to be institutional or professional, which is fine. When you roll the dice, you might have some truly great inclusive groups, and you might have some that make you feel a little on edge for not sharing in their zeal. Each meeting ends up having regulars that form a subculture out of the lives they inhabit outside of the meeting.
Don’t get me wrong though, there are plenty of excellent mentors and peers you can find in AA. It remains an accessible way to meet others struggling with substance abuse, and there are plenty who just use it to have a place to share in a group that feels safe rather than work any of the Steps. If you have trouble at one, any town or city that has one group will almost certainly have another, or another that will pop up soon.
Really good AA groups will also provide access to all kinds of recovery capital, including employment opportunities dedicated for those in recovery, rental assistance to secure safe and stable housing, transportation for meetings and sober outings, directories of local nonprofits, clothes, meals, help navigating the medical system, and just some swell friends you can talk about deep traumas with. Even if you don’t work a single step, those resources alone can dramatically increase your quality of life and sustained abstinence.
I just think people should know that it’s a religious program. I wouldn’t say you should stop going to gurudwaras for free meals, but I’d definitely let you know it’s a sacred place of worship for Sikhs. I wouldn’t tell you to skip Diwali celebrations, but I would let you know it’s a festival that’s part of a religious calendar rooted in Hindu cosmology and epics. I wouldn’t recommend to anyone that they should never try AA and 12 step programs, but I would say it’s religious and not everyone’s Higher Power, if they have one, will be compatible with it.
Some Nuances
These are less direct points, but they’re worth mentioning.
Creator Worship is Not Universal
Not every religion follows the idea that the Creator figure, if they even have one, is an ultimate authority. In fact, not every Christian sect even believes that praying to God would lead to any kind of intervention, that the universe was set in motion a long time ago and the laws of physics and logic are God’s laws. There are really cool arguments made by religious scientists positing exactly that throughout history.
Many Hindu belief systems see the Creator as the least significant part of their pantheons or trinities. I mean, you’ve already been created through no volition of your own, for better or for worse. Venerating the Creator is often seen as an act of looking to the past rather than the future before you in which you have a purpose to fulfill. Krishna, Shiva, and Vishnu are all actively worshipped while worshipping or building temples for Brahma is discouraged.
Buddhists often dispense with the idea of gods altogether. Although there are branches that maintain theistic or supernatural beliefs, deities are not assumed to be a primordial Creator or avatars of a single universal consciousness. They’re understood to be sentient beings bound by the laws of reincarnation, karma, and dharma like humans. The concept of dependent origination for all things makes an absolute uncaused first cause represented by a Creator God virtually impossible.
God is not necessarily a Him or a Father
To many, God sits above human constructs like gender roles or sex as determined by physical genitalia. To others, God can manifest in any gender or sex if so desired. In some Hindu traditions, the personification of the trinity of male deities can be a supreme female deity like Durga. Framing a Higher Power as a necessarily masculine Father can be an intersection of Creator worship and particular gender dynamics, which is very far from neutral or universally applicable. I’ve read arguments claiming that it’s proper to refer to God as masculine because God plays the active role in creation just as a man does. I imagine that will resonate with some and definitely not resonate with others.
It Really is Okay to Be Religious
Seriously, I’m not complaining about the efficacy of AA in this page. It clearly does work to keep lots of people sober. What motivates me to spend this much time establishing the religiosity of AA is that it doesn’t work for everyone, and AA principles can set up a framework to blame you for that. From How It Works:
Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path. Those who do not recover are people who cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program, usually men and women who are constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves. There are such unfortunates. They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way. They are naturally incapable of grasping and developing a manner of living which demands rigorous honesty. Their chances are less than average. There are those, too, who suffer from grave emotional and mental disorders, but many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest.
If you have decided you want what we have and are willing to go to any length to get it — then you are ready to take certain steps. At some of these we balked. We thought we could find an easier, softer way. But we could not. With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start. Some of us have tried to hold on to our old ideas and the result was nil until we let go absolutely.
Remember that we deal with alcohol — cunning, baffling, powerful! Without help it is too much for us. But there is One who has all power — that One is God. May you find Him now! Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point. We asked His protection and care with complete abandon.
Taken in sum, you are to blame if you have not chosen to surrender to a benevolent and omnipotent God as the sole Power to solve the Powerlessness you have to admit to in Step 1. You have been born in a way that has left you “constitutionally incapable of being honest” enough to address your health and well-being. If you don’t pray for God and His protection (capital G, capital H) “with complete abandon,” you’re seeking a softer and easier way than the difficulty of a spiritual awakening through a conversion from the 12 Steps. You are one of the “unfortunates.”
I’m not going to say this is right or wrong as theology or metaphysics or ethics. I’ll reiterate this constantly just as I did at the top: if this program works for you, great. If this method works for you and you want to share it with people, that’s fine. It’s free and anonymous, you never have to come back if you hate it. You don’t need to sign a waiver or join an email list or anything. No blood pacts with demons or timeshare salesmen. Others have called it a cult, and if so, it’s the easiest cult to walk away from if you decide it’s not for you. They don’t take your keys or back account information or the deed to your house.
The method might be great for the ones it works for, just like medications can be great, but you would never blame someone if the medication didn’t work. If they stopped taking it because it wasn’t working and produced unwelcome side effects, we would think it rational to see a professional to chart a new course of action for your unique self.
So my problem is when A.A. is presented as the baseline default option everyone should start at without any mention of alternatives, because the program’s literature will blame you and most members are told to remind each other of their desperation to power through a lack of understanding. I am as green as they come in recovery communities, but I’ve had doctors ask me to explain Recovery Dharma to them because they didn’t know A.A. wasn’t the only support group for recovery. I’ve had over a dozen people thank me for introducing them to it, even devout Christians who said they felt more comfortable sharing in RD meetings than A.A. meetings- people who have battled substance abuse longer than I’ve been alive.
I can’t ignore that just to avoid ruffling feathers. I think someone should tell you that the problem isn’t you. You are not an “unfortunate.” You are not “constitutionally incapable of being honest” or having the self-awareness to make meaningful progress in your life. You are not “born that way” or in any way that makes your doom inevitable as a fact of your birth. You do not have to surrender yourself into Powerlessness and seek a Higher Power in order to make progress on your recovery. Seeking self-empowerment is a completely valid approach to regaining control of your life as an alternative to surrendering to something you don’t understand. There are multiple ways to tackle this “self-will run riot” or “misidentification with an impermanent ego.”
Everyone’s body, mind, and soul are different, so everyone’s recovery is going to be different in spite of the similarities. That has to be acknowledged if we want to really be inclusive about recovery. Chances are you’ll probably still end up going to an AA meeting since that’s the default option people are aware of, but know that you have other recovery options too that don’t reflect poorly on you if you choose to try them. Take what works, leave what doesn’t.

rants/animal-addiction.title: Animal Addiction
rants/animal-addiction.content:
Humans are far from the only animals that can experience addictive compulsions and behaviors.
Bats
Bats eat fermented fruit but can maintain their echolocation abilities and coordination in concentrations that would exceed legal limits if given to a human.
Bees
Some studies suggest that bees prefer nectars that have stimulants like nicotine and caffeine.
Birds
The primary way birds come across alcohol is through fermented fruits that have natural ethanol. Cedar waxwings are perhaps the most famous bird known for this, but many species are capable of consuming fermented fruits unwittingly. Unfortunately, flying drunk does not go well, and many of these birds end up crashing to an early death.
Cedar waxwings and American robins have large livers relative to other birds, which means they have a better chance of processing the ethanol from the berries they eat. Ethanol functions more like a high-calorie substance than a toxin. The pen-tailed tree shrew from Malaysia developed resistance to the nectar of bertam palm trees.
European Starlings have a special enzyme that breaks down ethanol 14 times faster than a human liver. Some birds have throats that expand to hold collected fruit, which slows down the rate of ethanol entering the bloodstream.
Red-collared lorikeets have been noted to regularly get intoxicated from the fermenting fruit in northern Australia in certain times of the year, leading to a “drunken parrot season.”
Songbirds have been noted to quickly consume berries and become intoxicated.
Caterpillars
Certain caterpillars like the Eloria noyesi larvae can eat coca because their dopamine receptors are apparently completely resistant to it. This is being explored by Colombian policymakers and researchers who aim to destroy illegal coca plantations.
Cats
Catnip, of course.
Dogs
Here’s a study about “excessive toy motivation” in dogs as a parallel to process addictions in humans like gambling. “Our results highlight parallels between excessive toy motivation in dogs and human behavioral addictions, with dogs as the only non-human species so far that appears to develop addictive-like behaviours spontaneously without artificial induction.” Man’s best friend, truly. www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-18636-0 Some have taken to calling these dogs “ball junkies.”
Seriously though, it’s interesting that the animal we’ve domesticated to be most compatible with our understanding of reinforcement-based training also presents with “addiction-like behavior.” Dog brains also use dopamine reward pathways that can be disrupted by addictive stimulus.
It’s also seriously dangerous for the dogs in question. It’s not an exaggeration.
The conventional criteria observed in human addiction (craving, salience, and loss of self-control) are also observed in these dogs. It’s possible for dogs to prioritize the toy over food, rest, and socialization. In extreme cases, dogs can chase toys to the point of exhaustion, joint injury, or heat stroke. When the toy is taken away, the dogs show measurable distress like elevated heart rates and persistent vigiliance. There are even genetic components. Working breeds like Border Collies and Belgian Malinois are more prone to developing these addictive-like behaviors.
Dogs can develop chemical dependencies too, though usually they aren’t exposed to addictive chemicals regularly in a domestic context. If they are, they can also go through withdrawal with symptoms like tremors, agitation, and vomiting.
In some places where toxic wildlife is common, dogs can end up using them for psychoactive effects. Dogs that lick certain cane toads ingest bufotenine, which can cause hallucinations, and they can end up compulsively hunting for these toads even after feeling sick. Dropped fruit that ferments can produce alcohol that wild dogs are known to return to.
Prescription medication can impact dogs just like humans. Benzodiazepines prescribed for separation anxiety or phenobarbital prescribed for epilepsy can induce dependency. If they’re abruptly stopped, digs can experience fatal withdrawals with tremors and seizures.
Although arguably closer to OCD than addiction, compulsive behaviors even extend to self-harm. Some dogs with Canine Compulsive Disorder (CCD) can cause serious self-injury by repeatedly chewing at themselves, swallowing inedible items, or skipping meals and sleep to continue the behavior.
Dolphins
There’s some controversy over whether dolphins use toxins from puffer fish as an intoxicant, but tetrodoxin isn’t really psychoactive or euphoric. In high doses, fatal.
Elephants
This one is also controversial since it became a popular myth that media figures tried to cash in on, not unlike the elephant art crowd. It’s possible elephants consume some bark because it is likely to have toxic bugs that might produce an intoxicating influence, but this seems far from settled. Some elephant stampedes in India have been attributed to intoxicated elephants that binged rice beer.
Jaguars
After chewing on the bark of Yage vines, which are known for being hallucinogenic, jaguars apparently behave similarly to cats who have catnip.
Lemurs
Black lemurs use the toxins from millipedes to produce an effect similar to narcotics, though it also has the practical use of repelling insects that might transmit diseases like malaria.
Monkeys
Vervet monkeys, found in the Caribbean, consistently prefer alcoholic beverages over non-alcoholic beverages likely as a result of acquiring a taste for it through fermented sugar cane juice commonly found in plantations. They even show distributions of moderation, excessive consumption, and teetotalers, and younger monkeys drink more than matured adults.
Reindeer
Reindeer forage for Amanita muscaria, a highly toxic mushroom that is considered unsafe for human consumption. So instead, humans collect urine from deer that eat the magic mushrooms as an intoxicating drink.
Sheep
Wild bighorn sheep will take very risky chances alone to find narcotic lichen, even as it goes against their social inclinations to stick near their heard.
Wallabies
In 2009, the state attorney general of Tasmania, Lara Giddins, remarked to a Parliamentary hearing that “we have a problem with wallabies entering poppy fields, getting as high as a kite and going around in circles.”
Links

www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-18636-0
royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/13/7/rsos252252/482506/The-high-end-of-toy-motivation-in-dogs
www.theguardian.com/science/2025/oct/09/some-dogs-may-be-addicted-toys-study
www.petmd.com/dog/behavior/canine-compulsive-disorder

rants/drugs-on-war.title: Drugs On War
rants/drugs-on-war.content:
Drugs and war have gone hand-in-hand well before the War on Drugs.
Ancient Mesopotamian soldiers were paid in beer.
Ancient Greeks treated wine as a masculine drink for those who face down the dangers of war.
Benjamin Rush notably complained about excessive rum being given to American soldiers.
In 1846, George K. Smith & Co, which would later become the major pharmaceutical company GlaxoSmithKline by 2000, sold quinine to US troops for the war against Mexico.
Bavarian soliders were issued cocaine in the late 1800s.
Nazi Germany was very prolific in using drugs to sustain their morale.


They used amphetamines to hype up their soldiers in Blitzkrieg strategies and keep dive-bombers from fainting.


Over 35 million tablets of methamphetamine were ordered by the German military for the invasions of France and Poland


A chewing gum laced with cocaine was given to frontline soldiers and pilots who faced exhaustion


Chocolate spiked with caffeine. That one isn’t so bad.


Benzedrine, an amphetamine, was tested against Pervitin, methamphetamine, to see which gave pilots faster reaction times and minimal hallucinations


D-IX, a combination of oxycodone, cocaine, and methamphetamine was given to pilots of single-man mini-submarines who would have to stay awake for up to 72 hours as there was no one to take shifts with.


Morphine, used almost universally as an analgesic, was administered to injured soldiers with severe trauma and wounds, like amputation.


Barbiturates were given out as sedatives for soldiers who had taken too many stimulants to fall asleep on their own.


Steroids, like synthetic testosterone, were injected into soldiers with the goal of rebuilding muscles in fatigued troops while increasing aggression in battle.


Hitler himself had personal physician Theodor Morell load him up with about 80 substances, including oxycodone injections, cocaine eye drops, bull testicle extract injections, antigaspills to reduce chronic farting through compounds derived from rat poison, Brom-Nervacit to force sleep after stimulant use, cardiazol to manage panic attacks, straight glucose solutions for energy spikes, glyconorm to manage high blood sugar levels, aloe laxatives and castor oil to force poops, muscle relaxants to handle severe cramping, vitamin complexes for nerve issues, camphor-infused alcohol solutions for skin irritation, arsenic-based compounds just in case of syphilis, and many more.

rants/elitism-is-anti-intellectualism.title: Elitism is Anti-Intellectualism
rants/elitism-is-anti-intellectualism.content:
The San Francisco Bay Area is one of the most competitive places in the world. Singapore, Seoul, Shanghai, Delhi-NCR, and other regions also rank highly, but the Bay Area is unique in that American higher education applies holistic evaluation that goes beyond standardized testing with defined material to study. Across these regions, the average high school (or equivalent) student gets fewer than 6 hours of sleep per night. Students in these areas are competing to be in the top 0.1% of scorers for institutions to pick from. Private education industries have popped up around these areas. I’ve seen families pay over 50k to hire college counselors to map every aspect of a high school student's education out to maximize their competitive profile. Specialized tutors for standardized testing can easily clear 100/hr.
So it’s quite surprising to me, having grown up in the SF Bay Area, how utterly stupid many of these students are.
Academic vs Intellectual
Let’s get some basic terminology out of the way. Something being “academic” does not mean anything other than affiliation with an institution that claims to train and educate people. In an institution designed to train people to perform icepick lobotomies, a successful academic is one who passes an exam about the history of icepicks to obtain a paper that says the institution vouches for their ability to recite knowledge about icepick lobotomies.
In this sense, academic institutions function like localized oral storytelling traditions. Ostensibly, attaching education and training to research can inject patterns of discovering new knowledge into the traditions, but these researchers first have to pass through standardized evaluation methods. Much like politicians, academics are not in the habit of questioning the system that vouches for their authority or legitimacy. If you were to look for intellectualism, academia is a reasonable starting point, but only that - a starting point.
Institutions, by definition, are finite constructs that have borders and traditions of patterns. An institution that says “our members can do whatever they want” quickly runs into the problem of its members questioning the institution’s legitimacy and existence. A school cannot grade students if they pursue subjects or projects that its evaluators cannot place a rubric on. One student may want to dedicate themselves entirely to the history of the economics of rope, one student might want to become an expert on the process of caramelizing foods, and another student might want to hyperoptimize video game engines. If evaluating students on their capacity to develop expertise and demonstrate resilience, this is tenable. If evaluating the specific information internalized by each student upon graduation, this is intractable.
Or take a more grounded example: if a prompt asks the student to compare Eastern and Western cultures, and the student argues that the terms Eastern and Western are too generally reductive to be coherent, how could the institution actually accept this paper? If it grants an A, the institution is admitting that rejecting its ability to ascertain truth is a valid option in the course of its training. It might pass the student, but the student’s takeaway is that the institution has unrectifiable incoherence. If the institution fails the student, the student learns that questioning is futile and compliance is the only option for advancement; this learned helplessness works just fine for an institution looking to generate proof of its efficacy in getting students to meet standards.
As such, institutions require some standards or culture of norms that are maintained internally in order to justify their existence through utility. A school that allowed students to learn anything they wanted could not reliably calculate and report progress to satisfy demands for a return-on-investment. A school that uses standardized evaluation methods, such as the SAT or a GPA system, can at least present metrics that map something like budget increases to score increases or college acceptance rates. For the managers of these institution, this is a godsend. It doesn’t even take someone with any subject matter expertise to examine a list of manualized best practices and choose the ones that time and budget constraints allow for.
If they fail, well, they were best practices right? How could anyone hope to do better than the best practices? The problem must of course lie outside management, as usual. Either the kids these days require more discipline or research simply hasn’t come out that allows for the problem to be solved.
The consequences of generating homogeneity are, predictably, a loss of heterogeneity. In other words, standardization and specialization operate on tradeoffs. Time spent conforming to a standard is time lost for developing unique talents. Even worse, time spent marketing conformity to a standard is time spent atrophying compliance to it. None of this is a novel perspective either. You can go back to Adam Smith and Alexis de Tocqueville to find this exact tension described in more eloquent terms than I could.
Smith posited that specialization in factories drives massive production of wealth by allowing one process to be distributed among individuals who focus on one component of a widget rather than a master who designs and creates the widget end-to-end. When broken into simple and standard tasks, the work can be done by individuals who are interchangeable without much friction. Smith also said that a human bound to repetitive standardized tasks would suffer from a much narrower mental state as well, struggling to exercise their creative capacities in novel and unstructured ways. Consequently, Smith argued for universal state-sponsored education systems for the purpose of providing a broad humanist education that instilled a general sense of literacy and civic awareness, so that individuals could meaningfully participate in the world around them outside of the factory floor. It was taken for granted that a workplace that wanted someone to do job would actually train a worker to do that job in the way that workplace asks.
Modern academic institutions have completely abandoned these aspirations, and I use “aspirations” here deliberately, as it would be too generous to imply we abandoned a tradition that we never cultivated.
Harvard University, founded in 1636, was designed to train the sons of Puritan ministers and landed nobility to manage the institutions of colonial society. MIT, founded in 1861, was the product of Harvard gatekeeping educational and financial resources for classical studies at a time when there was a shortage of experts who could work on industrializing sectors like railroads and textile factories. Harvard Business School, founded in 1908, was in part a response to fears that wealthy families would prefer polytechnic universities like MIT to an outdated classical education; a business school enabled students to choose corporate law and finance to retain relevance in managerial positions.
The centralized public school system as we know it today emerged out of the early 1800s to instill a factory or military work ethic in students. Wealthy families funded the Lancasterian System that placed a single educator in front of several hundred children who were expected to sit silently in rows until given repetitive tasks to complete. It was considered effective at building the stamina needed to work long shifts in a factory’s assembly line. Horace Mann, who pushed for a state-sponsored version of this system, explicitly argued to wealthy families that raising their taxes for working-class education would be profitable in the long run. Specifically, he argued that education would make workers more obedient, curbing labor strikes, radical political movements, and property crimes. It also shifted the burden of basic education and training from their private corporations to public taxpayers, though they were against education past what we would consider elementary or grade school now. They actually launched lawsuits against initiatives to establish high schools, and they were not shy about stating that they didn’t want workers who might reject the manual labor their factories demanded.
By 1910, child labor laws suddenly led to millions of students entering school systems that were never built with the intention of educating or evaluating the general public. Enter standardized testing. American psychologists like James McKeen Cattell, the first psychology professor in America and fourth President of the American Psychological Association, were leaning heavily into eugenics to justify their own success in the face of demographic and cultural shifts that provoked anxiety about their social status. Cattell clashed with his German doctoral supervisor Wilhelm Wundt over intelligence as a hereditary trait that could be used to compare individuals or ethnicities, and in fact, he argued that the purpose of education in a democracy was not to grow the capacity of its citizens but to slot them into roles suited to their natural capacities. Sir Francis Galton, Darwin’s half-cousin who was eager to apply the concepts of evolution to human talent, collaborated with and inspired Cattell into a fixation on ranking humans.
Cattell’s victory was paved through ownership of academic infrastructure more than research. His own graduate student found no correlation between Cattell’s “mental tests” and college grades, or even between the performance on one “mental test” and another. The Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale that established IQ testing displaced Cattell’s mental tests pretty quickly. Following his dismissal from Columbia for his protest against the WWI draft, he founded The Psychological Corporation to advocate for his ideas through corporate and government clients and publishing psychological assessment materials rather than continuing to do research.
Cattell had become something of a powerful if controversial giant by this point, and his solutions to the sorting and ranking of people were in high demand from White Anglo-Saxon Protestant (WASP) elites who feared losing control of their institutions to immigrants and minorities. Pre-packaged assessments gave a pseudoscientific justification to sort children by their pedigrees, since children whose parents weren’t educated were likely to do worse on these assessments than the parents who had greater capital. Following WWII, Harvard President James Bryant Conant was among many calling for the national adoption of the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT), which was derived from early military IQ tests that were used to quickly sort millions of soldiers. Even though elite families could afford to live in the best neighborhoods with the best schooling and afford better resources for their children, the testing apparatus provided an illusion of meritocracy and equal opportunity.
Until the 1980s, the computers required to analyze the massive influx of student assessments were not accessible to organizations outside of governments, corporations, and the testing agencies. There was no legal requirement to disclose test questions, score distributions, or demographic breakdowns under the argument that these were trade secrets. Then, microcomputers and statistical software packages made their way into university labs during this decade. Governments began enforcing transparency requirements against these agencies, allowing researchers to finally examine the outcomes and mechanics of mass standardized testing.
It is at this point that we can begin to see how academic institutions had a momentum divorced from the direction of research and truth. Studies began to show that when we control for family income status and other socioeconomic conditions, the predictive power of the SAT collapses dramatically, with some studies suggesting essentially no predictive power. In fact, one-third of high-income students achieve over a 1300 while less than 5% of middle-class students do so.
In Washington v. David (1976), the Supreme Court had ruled that so long as the tests weren’t intentionally discriminatory, the disparity across protected classes or socioeconomic groups was legally valid. Testing agencies, no longer able to claim they measured intelligence any more than cigarette companies could claim their product didn’t cause cancer or addiction, rebranded into claiming they measured “college readiness” or “achievement.” Rather than acknowledging the biases of the test, they argued that their tests reflected disparities that should be used as a basis to improve schools.
Yet, pivoting to holistic admissions without standardized testing also just changes the nature of the problem. Affluent families can just as easily apply their capital to boosting extracurricular achievements or application essays as they applied to elite tutors and bootcamps. They still live in wealthier neighborhoods with more opportunities and support for their success.
But remember, this doesn’t mean empowering students to develop their intellectual capacity independently. This means conditioning students towards academic achievements that adhere to the ideals of a knowledge economy rather than a factory floor. Everything discussed so far is about the way academic achievements have derived their legitimacy from claiming to be built on some combination of work ethic, attitude, upbringing, and innate cognitive abilities referred to with “intelligence.” In reality, academic institutions have been as susceptible to the power dynamics, personal career ambitions, and outdated American management philosophy as any other institution suffering from a trust crisis today. Is it hard to see why?
Ignore academic achievements for a brief moment. Consider mental health. Affluent suburban high school students in these competitive districts have a two to three times higher chance, over 20%, of meeting the criteria for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and clinically significant anxiety than the national average. This include physiological symptoms like nausea, hyperventilation, migraines, chest pains and difficulty breathing, etc. 1 in 5 “high-achieving students” show escalating substance use between sophomore year of high school and turning 18. Biological studies that examine cortisol levels show that hyper-competitive students operate with stress hormone profiles comparable to children growing up in war zones. From 2003-2015, Palo Alto had a teen suicide rate rate that was four times the national average. Over 80% report constant exhaustion or burnout.
So, to recap, this is a system that fails to measure intelligence, fails to produce healthy childhoods, and fails to preserve financial security when that remains contingent on the loyalty of for-profit corporations.
Then, who is this for? What kind of person would continue to participate in this system?
I have found that the answer is prodigiously stupid people.
Well, that’s harsh. It’s not as if I have any metric of my own to propose that measures intelligence. I use “stupid” as a shorthand, but I’ll elaborate on what I mean.
Studies have shown that  GPA has negative to zero correlation with high-level divergent thinking. Big Five Personality metrics show that Conscientiousness (measuring compliance and sense of duty) correlates positivity with GPA, but Openness to Experience (measuring autonomy and curious questioning) correlates weakly and sometimes negatively with GPA. An analysis of over 270,000 Americans from 1990 to 2008 showed that metrics for “Creative Fluency” dropped by 0.6 standard deviations and “Elaboration” dropped by an entire standard deviation. In other words, the average student in the 2000s performed worse than 84% of students in the pre-1990 era.
William Deresiewics, a former associate English professor at Yale, coined the term “Excellent Sheep” in reference to the ideal student shaped by academic institutions: absolutely brilliant at performing tasks with a sense of perfectionism, but terrified of establishing their own direction away from the hurdles designed by authority figures. If there were a train running off a cliff, the Excellent Sheep will having the engineering and design skills to ensure it drives at optimal speed off that cliff.
Robert Sternberg, a former President of the American Psychological Association just like Cattell once was, has published decades of literature detailing the evidence behind standardized evaluation systems, like the SAT and GPA scores, measuring a very narrow band of analytical compliance and memory retrieval. Rather than “Excellent Sheep,” he uses the term “analytical bureaucrats.”
I use the term “prodigiously stupid”, a phrase found in Jane Austen when Maria and Julia Bertram mock their poorer cousin Fanny Price for failing to regurgitate the information they memorized rotely:
“Fanny could read, work, and write, but she had been taught nothing more; and as her cousins found her ignorant of many things with which they had been long familiar, they thought her prodigiously stupid, and for the first two or three weeks were continually bringing some fresh report of it into the drawing-room. ‘Dear mama, only think, my cousin cannot put the map of Europe together— or my cousin cannot tell the principal rivers in Russia— or, she never heard of Asia Minor—or she does not know the difference between water-colours and crayons!— How strange!—Did you ever hear anything so stupid?’
“…it is not very wonderful that, with all their promising talents and early information, they should be entirely deficient in the less common acquirements of self-knowledge, generosity and humility. In everything but disposition they were admirably taught. Sir Thomas did not know what was wanting, because, though a truly anxious father, he was not outwardly affectionate, and the reserve of his manner repressed all the flow of their spirits before him.”
The irony being, of course, that the sisters are prodigiously stupid. Their social etiquette and memorized knowledge only indicate that they’ve conformed to the expectations of their position as upper-class women. They fail to develop the independent reflective capacity that allows them to navigate the world or self-actualize.
So, where do the truly prodigious end up in institutions that are designed to be managed and operated by the prodigiously stupid? They leave.
Studies show that those between 1.5-2 standard deviations above average in g-score assessments leave traditional jobs at 1.5-2 times higher as well. Those with the highest scores in Openness to Experience and Fluid Intelligence are heavily concentrated in entry-level roles rather than corporate leadership. Top-scorers are far more likely to cite a lack of autonomy or excessive bureaucracy as a reason for leaving roles too. Data from platforms like Toptal and Upwork show that the fastest-growing section of independent contractors are hyper-specialized technical workers and strategists who left FAANG and consulting companies; 85% of them report being significantly happier despite the instability of their income.
East Asian countries are further along than America in achieving this burnout. Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare tracks over 1 million individuals out of its 74 million working-age population who classify as “Hikikomori”, referring to a lifestyle that rejects consumerism, status symbols, and external social validation in favor of part-time jobs with lower stress. The “Satori Generation” refers specifically to highly-educated young adults following in these footsteps. China reported a youth unemployment spike crossing 20%, with a large proportion being voluntary from credentialed university graduates opting for minimalist gig work (Tangping, or “Lying Flat”) rather than a 996 schedule for a corporation.
There are many who are all too aware of this game, but they play anyways with a sense of detachment since it’s preferable to the volatility of an independent practice. The very worst outcomes don’t come from this group, but the elitists who are unable to accept that their success has been highly contingent on their compatibility with institutions that fail to reward merit or talent. In fact, the more evidence comes out about the role of social and other factors that are out of our control, the stronger elitist attitudes can become entrenched as a defense mechanism for the legitimacy of the hierarchy in which they are embedded. All the flaws about institutions as limited, standardized, and hierarchical are celebrated instead with the aesthetics of intellectualism, even when using psuedoscience and relying on managerial marketing to ascertain truth.
Taken to extremes, we arrive at eugenics, in which elites throw a Hail Mary through the fog of biological complexity to hope some metric arises to justify their socioeconomic outcomes and political influence. In the worst case scenario, if they do lose their status, they can rationalize the change as the result of dirty tricks or a decaying world that throws the rightful rulers out of their thrones. H.P. Lovecraft is a testament to how powerful these anxieties can be, as his whole pantheon and theory of horror is built on his fears of being part of a degenerating world where superior “Aryan” families like his lost wealth and power to unknown arrivals with unfamiliar practices.
Intellectualism in the sense of creative, critical thinking that can both design and adapt to new systems, that develops problem-solving skills as a result of facing problems, that challenges the paradigms of existing institutions, is simply not something that can be mass produced or commodified.
Institutions are only capable of moving around external sources of motivation, not instilling intrinstic motivation that segues curiosity into learning. They can design rubrics, but not teach the habit of rejecting a rubric’s premises to build something new. They can fund training and research projects, but not the humility it takes to be prepared for blowback if they admit something went wrong. They can ask their members to follow a code of ethics, but not engender moral responsibility or courage through manuals or training. As Edward Said said in 1993, the duty of the intellectual is “speaking truth to power,” and institutions are necessarily defined in part by their power dynamics. To speak truth to power requires not having the power stifle your ability to speak, which necessarily puts the intellectual’s duty outside the compliance and comfort of institutional validation.

rants/goofy-shit.title: Goofy Shit
rants/goofy-shit.content:
Life is absurd. Sometimes, it’s goofy and absurd. Here is a series of cases where recovery has .
Case Zero
The specific incident that motivated me to start sharing some of the goofy shit is when I had to roleplay as someone’s rapist while writing a passive-aggressive postcard to them as part of a group exercise.
Within the confluence of events that led to this moment, not a single person must have imagined that this would be the outcome:


The idea of using group sessions to build a sense of community and mutual support among those in recovery is a good instinct.


The idea of writing a letter to someone you’re angry at or sad about just to vent is one that works for a lot of people; almost everyone who goes through treatment will end up writing or reading the goodbye letters to a personification of an addictive substance or process.


Someone using this opportunity to vent anonymously about someone who deeply traumatized them in the past is engaging entirely in the spirit of the exercise. They did also write that they wanted to kill me, but I didn’t take that personally.


The two-step process of first writing the letter and then getting a response back through roleplay might be a little tricky, but it might be able to bring closure to people who would never (or can’t) voice the letter to the actual person.


The exercise’s stipulation that we use a communication style we try to avoid led to me being “passive-aggressive” (if you think I actually am passive-aggressive, well, everyone’s entitled to whatever opinion makes them feel good). In any case, it can definitely push someone into the headspace of a different style of communication which is helpful.


All of this in combination led to me writing a passive-aggressive postcard while roleplaying as someone’s rapist. It reminds me of a software project where each module is doing exactly what it was intended to do, but the way they operate together at scale can produce some unforeseen and bizarre events. In this case, I have no idea if the author of the postcard found it helpful or not.
I will say though that roleplays seem to be a real hit or miss. Someone once shared that in one group roleplay session, a facilitator assumed the role of her deceased grandfather and tried to hug out the pain. It did not help.
Case One
I once called comedian Mark Lundholm a “fucktard” to his face, and then I got a free copy of his book Shortcuts: Better Ways to Better Days.
Case Two
I’m not taking advice about ambivalence from someone who spells it “ambivalance.” I’m sorry, but if you’re standing in front of a whiteboard ready to lecture me for an hour and cannot spell the topic, I am mentally checking out at best. At worst, I’m questioning the credentialing processes that allowed you to be lecturing. I’m not saying this to nitpick spelling or grammar as I make plenty of mistakes myself on this site alone, but if you’re lecturing on a subject, you have to at least care enough to spell it right.
Case Three
“I’m angry that my government is ignoring people’s rights and just pulling people out of their homes and off the streets.”
“But how does that affect you though?”
A group facilitator and a client got into a long argument over this point, and though they didn’t express the disagreement in philosophical terms, they were having a deeply philosophical disagreement that I’ve touched on through this site before.
What happens when “you can control nothing except yourself and your faith that a Higher Power will shape the world outside of you” meets “democracy requires a deliberative collective of citizens willing to think critically to hold their leaders and systems accountable?”
By the end of the conversation, I was fairly fucking horrified, because “I can’t control anything except myself” ends up being a wiser-sounding version of “I was just doing my job.” This isn’t a new revelation; psychologists, political theorists, and commentary from the recovery community have all connected this strand of hyperindividualism to complicity with authoritarian structures. What was really horrifying though was seeing how an enormous philosophical gap between authoritarianism and self-empowerment was condensed into a group facilitator yelling at a client that they wouldn’t be sober if they kept their beliefs, all started by a disagreement about a 10-minute motivational video off YouTube.
By the end, both were only more entrenched in their worldviews. The facilitator took the exchange as confirmation that clients have to be made to doubt their self-will more in order to humble themselves to receive the serenity from their Higher Power. The client, while still motivated to find recovery, grew more skeptical of institutional interventions and their capacity to understand the real world outside the facilities they maintained.
Once again, if AA works for you, great, but taking the AA philosophy as a baseline framework for recovery is inherently a sociopolitical stance, not just a spiritual one. The author of the Serenity Prayer, Reinhold Niebuhr, was famously a pro-union Socialist Party of America leader who collaborated with Martin Luther King Jr. on the issues of class warfare, international relations, and civil rights. He also hated the premises of the Oxford Group as being fundamentally fascist and delusional about producing change in the world in a way that only the most privileged people in society could embrace. William Wilson (Bill W.), the founder of AA, credits the Oxford Groups for directly inspiring the 12 steps.
So, you cannot take the political out of the spiritual or the religious. Even the distinction between “spiritual” and “religious” is fundamentally a political phenomenon. If you mean to introduce that premise into a psychoeducation class or facilitated discussion session, you’re going to run into absurd political conversations.
Case Four
I have had multiple classes in which the facilitator turns on a soundbowl ASMR for an hour and takes a paid nap. I have had others where we watch a Ted Talk, go around the room to answer how we felt about it, and then watch another Ted Talk. I cannot see the therapeutic value in this process, and I do not blame half the class for ignoring the rules about not being on their phones. An hour of Sudoku or texting a friend seems more therapeutic than being lectured by prerecorded “happiness coaches” rehashing corporate propaganda from a decade ago.
Case Five
I walked into a doctor’s office and explained how I had been managing recovery, medication, and other health issues, hoping to get advice on what works in the long-term. Instead, after telling the doctor about my recovery approach, they took out a notepad and asked me to repeat it so that they could recommend it to other patients. I came to get an expert’s evaluation, and I left having given the expert my self-evaluation. It is in that moment I truly felt the old adage, “No one is coming to save you.”
Case Six
I once had a therapist attempt to be culturally sensitive by handing me a worksheet describing “Indian-American values” to, supposedly, help me discover the value system from which I could find the strength to apply coping skills. I, an actual Indian-American, am sitting in front of this person and can answer questions about my relation with my culture and the negotiation of values involved in applying those to a changing world. I have no idea what therapeutic manual recommended that was a good way to go. Admittedly, it’s not a reasonable expectation for a therapist to know about cultures around the world, but neither is it reasonable for me to explain air to a fish that’s only known water.
Case Seven
If you didn’t walk into a treatment facility using nicotine, you almost certainly will walk out using it. You might as well with all the secondhand exposure you’re guaranteed to inhale. I have been given an absurd amount of free vapes.
Case Eight
Someone named their kid Justin. Middle name Hale. Justin Hale. Just inhale. I know I’ve brought up the “No True Scotsman” fallacy when it comes to discussions about being a “True Addict”, but this is one of those incidents that makes me reconsider that position.
Case Nine
If you’ve seen Better Call Saul, you might recall that there’s a story beat where Mike Ehrmantraut attends a support group for people who lost loved ones at the request of his daughter-in-law. While it represents a turning point for Mike when he turns away from the group and the prospect of processing his grief, the scene also depicts a real phenomenon of someone faking stories in peer support circles to elicit sympathy, compassion, and attention. Sometimes this is through a clinically-recognized Factitious Disorder, historically referred to as Munchausen syndrome, though the show doesn’t explicitly use this label. Many peer recovery groups begin with a premise of unconditional support rather than cross-talk and questioning in order to create a safe space to share their stories. Anonymity and rigorous honesty form a complex paradox, a fine line of enabling or disabling each other. People who seek attention can readily get it from these groups without the years of gradual intimacy it can take to share deeply personal traumas.
Anyways, it was surreal the first time I saw someone fake stories in a real support group. I didn’t notice it at first because you hear a lot of genuinely crazy stories when you put a group of people who live in subcultures on the margins of broader society into a single room. Also, I just struggle to pay attention when people who are not me are talking longer than 15 seconds. Over time though, I begin to notice details that don’t add up, that don’t seem like they can just be chalked up to the ordinary messy process of memory retrieval and reconsolidation that people always undergo.
Their cadence seems rehearsed, not in the way that someone with social anxiety might try to prepare their thoughts before speaking, but in the way that a standup comedian plans to pause for audience feedback. If and when it doesn’t come on some nights with a tougher crowd, an expression flickers across their face as if they missed a step walking down the stairs. If they try nervously to recover, they can end up slipping between associated concepts. An ex-girlfriend becomes a fiance becomes an ex-wife, who cheated with a best friend who becomes a random Tinder hookup who becomes a sugar daddy after driving her away through a DOC that changes each time the story is recounted. One gets the impression that the speaker is giving a new improvisation of the same rejected mad libs script.
But creating and remembering stories is exhausting, so lies and sarcastic jokes are often wrapped around kernels of truth. The most sincere part of the story this person expressed was their repeated ostracization from groups they joined, oblivious to how they were the common denominator in each of these instances, but especially oblivious to the way even their own description of events raised eyebrows. Complaining that people don’t get your sense of humor, especially when we’re talking about people in recovery who have an unusually high tolerance for dark humor, edgy jokes, and tough love, is a major red flag.
An interesting contradiction I noticed though is that this person, despite their vocal and enthusiastic sharing in the context of group, had almost no interpersonal dynamics outside of the meeting structure unless it was part of an emotional rollercoaster that factored into the stories of trauma they shared at meetings. In fact, they seemed to keep to themselves when the spotlight was off, so to speak. I wouldn’t make this claim if I was the only one who felt this way. It was echoed numerous times by others in private conversations, yet no one dared to break the trust and culture of the recovery group by suddenly accusing someone else of making up their story. To do so would be to put everyone on their toes for an accusation as if giving testimony on a witness stand. So we all carry on agreeing to the polite fiction that we’re all practicing rigorous honesty underneath the anonymity.
