rants/kill-the-new-age-spirit.title: Kill the New Age Spirit
rants/kill-the-new-age-spirit.content:
Hindus and Don’ts
I come from a Hindu background.
“Hindu” is a practically meaningless label except as a general reference to belief systems and traditions of the network of cultures originating across South Asia. There are some groups that will argue for a nationalist identity behind “Hindu” but this will necessarily be a modern reclamation of the world. Practically speaking, all I know if someone says they’re Hindu is that they look at the world through a metaphysics interpreted out of the Vedic texts and the lineages of literature and traditions that evolved in the thousands of years after.
I do not think a lifetime of study would be sufficient to appreciate the diversity and depth of ideas developed in these traditions. Much of it cannot be understood without direct experience between oneself and the world around them, which is where the impetus behind yoga and meditation come from; sure, they have physical benefits as somatic exercises, but they’re embedded in broader frameworks about understanding one’s psychology.
Personally, I draw a lot of my beliefs out of Kashmir Shaivism, which posits that a single universal consciousness defines all of existence, and material reality is a finite contraction of an infinite reality with creative experience as an end into itself. An infinite being can never experience beind told a story, so it requires a finite version of its existence to experience hope and suspense, comedy and tragedy. Ultimately we are all drops in an ocean, and our ego is both a necessity to see the gift of being a finite drop and a barrier to recognizing our true nature as the ocean itself. Within the microcosm is the macrocosm, as the saying goes.
Note that in the above description, I never once used the words “religion”, “philosophy”, or “spirituality.” If you asked me what religion I identify with, what cultural traditions I inherit, what kind of philosophies I apply to life, and where I derive my spiritual practices from, I would say “Hinduism” to all.
So the question is, what do you mean when you’re asking me to distinguish between a “religious” practice and a “spiritual” practice?


Are you asking if I believe in God? I would ask you if my description of a universal consciousness that forms the substrate from which all finite things emerge satisfies your definition of God.


Are you asking if I believe in souls? I would ask you if the formulation of an impermanent ego that has never left the permanent consciousness from which it emerges satisfies your definition of “soul.”


Are you asking if I believe there’s a rational order to the universe according to some core higher maxims? I would ask if you consider the pattern of things creating other things to be rationally motivated or just a property of a reality in motion.


Are you asking me if there’s some force that evens the scales according to justice, love, or balance? I would say the universe has justice, love, and balance just as it has injustice, hate, and imbalance; if there is a force that evens the scales, it’s the same force that renders them uneven too.


Are you asking me what I do to practice letting go of my attachments and chase a transcendental experience? Pratyabhijna, or the term used in Kashmir Shaivist circles to refer to internalizing the recognition of the individual self as the Universal Self. I approach it similarly to the way Buddhists use koans to break analytical reasoning and force a mode of thinking that deals with the concepts, or non-conceptual processes if you prefer, beyond the descriptive limits of language and material reality. I can go to a Recovery Dharma meeting and get much of the same core practices and teachings that my understanding of Kashmir Shaivism shares.


So, where do these labels like “religion”, “philosophy”, and “spirituality” come in?
Welcome to the New Age
I have a burning passion for the legacy of the New Age movement.
I can acknowledge some very valid tendencies behind wanting to understand new approaches to life, especially to overcome the feeling of something missing in yours in our global society’s hyperindividualistic ratrace to fill a black hole of meaning through one material bucket of dissociation at a time. We as humans seek novelty and experimentation, and I love diversity and trade as the creative engines of human society.
I can sympathize a lot with having limited access to information about another culture, thus forming inaccurate but well-meaning interpretations of their ideas and traditions. Rest assured that if you are someone who actively seeks knowledge to help yourself grow and share it with others in your community, I am not aiming this at you. You’re almost certainly doing the best with what you have to work with, which reflects on the systems around you rather than you as an individual.
What I despise is the attempt by institutions to treat these categories as rigid enough to generalize, manualize, and operationalize.
My first experience with these came through AA literature and The Four Agreements, both of which are treated as “spiritual” rather than “religious” despite drawing on explicitly religious traditions in their history and substance. It’s perfectly fine if these are options presented to people as ways to explore themselves, but it is the norm rather than the exception that literature like this becomes part of a syllabus or curriculum as a starting point for recovery approaches in institutions like treatment centers. I was very vexed about the decision to label these as “spiritual” when it seemed to be pushing a particular hyperindividualistic perennialism that is fundamentally incompatible with the belief systems practiced by billions around the world.
The answer is disappointingly simple: marketing.
That’s it.
Just like “Artificial Intelligence” is used to imply that statistical models are sentient reasoning agents capable of replacing humans instead of requiring even more humans to operate the new machinery.
Just like “evidence-based” is used to imply that a treatment is driven by the latest evidence to be as effective as possible, when it really tends to mean manualized treatment that is easy to produce evidence for in controlled trials.
Just like “Toltec” is used to imply lineage to an ancient mystical Mesoamerican civilization and culture, when actual Mesoamerican scholars point out that celebrity authors of the New Age movement created a version of the Toltecs that does not match the archaeological evidence we now have.
Just like “Eastern” is used to imply something mystical, ancient, and collectivist in contrast to “Western” rationality, industrialism, and individualism even in the works of transcendentalists like Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau (see Edward Said’s Orientalism for a very thorough breakdown of this).
Similarly, “spirituality” has been a rhetorical tool. Sometimes it’s used to market something derived from religion but without the institutional organization. Sometimes it’s used to add exoticism to a philosophy that wouldn’t actually be coherent or digestible without the, pardon the technical term, “woo-woo.”
The New Age gurus, pundits, magicians, diviners, prophets, old wise men, liberated witches, esoteric archivists, alternative healing practitioners, supplement factories, life coaches, wellness lifestyles, publishing houses, influencers, celebrities, online merchandisers, and countless others have formed an industry that never rises to the metaphysics of religion nor the empiricism of science. They’re simply spiritual, no less individualistic and hedonistic than the materialism it claims to address but with a garnish of foreign words to appear transcendental. In short, the New Age spiritual movements encourage dissociating from the world and into your own mental reality even harder in response to materialism.
And again, that might actually work for people. I don’t have to like it in order to acknowledge its efficacy. I have no doubt lots of people have developed coping skills or improved their health through exposure to the industry. When it enters the recovery space through institutional acknowledgement, we have a problem, because we’re leaving the space of consumer choice and entering the space of wellness and health. Something like The Four Agreements goes from a book on a shelf at Barnes & Nobles that you might flick through to standard reading in treatment paid for by insurance companies and administered by healthcare professionals or paraprofessionals. This can lead to really disastrous moments like telling someone living with domestic violence that “no one can abuse you more than you abuse yourself” or claiming the government isn’t taking away your freedom as much as you are for having a part of you that insists on playing The Victim. Real things from real books that reached real people while being marketed as a liberating framework.
But it’s a “spiritual” reading, so it doesn’t have to be evaluated by religious authorities or researchers with expertise. The prescriptions it gives don’t have to be tested through randomized controlled trials or undergo peer-review before it gets published and distributed into treatment. It gets by on the standard of inducing good vibes and a “take what works, leave what doesn’t” approach to coherence. You’ll notice I use that phrase specifically as a disclaimer that I’m not prescribing solutions, only presenting my own analysis. That’s the opposite of what the New Age literature does by creating vast generalizations out of a syncretic piecemeal approach to very intensive philosophical traditions that are then haphazardly synthesized through personal anecedotes.
That’s where we have to start making institutional critiques.
Publish or Perish
The Four Agreements is a thread that I never tire of pulling on.
The publishing company behind The Four Agremeents is Allen & Allen, based out of San Rafael in Southern California. The project that put them on the map of New Age publishing was The Chronicles of Seth by a woman claiming to be possessed by a spirit named Seth who would share the secret to changing reality with your mind.
For those who may not know, Southern California is home to a lot of mental health programs and industries. There’s a strong network of universities like the UCs (Irvine, Los Angeles, San Diego) and private colleges like USC and the Claremont-McKenna group. The entertainment industry has both some of the wealthiest clients and wealthiest proponents of mental health and wellness services. Municipalities like Ojai, Topanga, and Sedona are home to lots of businesses and organizations that spawned out of historical attempts to address tuberculosis with nature retreats. Southern California is very well-structured to amplify countercultural trends, though much of it is born out of a focus on individual self-actualization.
The way The Four Agreements became popular connects these dots. After Ellen DeGeneres came out as gay, she was blacklisted from the entertainment industry and spent time in the spiritual communities in SoCal. [WIP]
To the West
In practice, much of this ends up reinforcing individualism. Yoga and breathwork become personal wellness exercises to relieve stress rather than a set of principles to liberate oneself from an ego that undergoes worldly suffering. Karma is seen as an external force that ensures “what goes around comes around” instead of a principle by which any action done with bad intentions has ongoing consequences. Mindfulness is seen as a self-awareness tool that can help one achieve their goals better when right mindfulness is just one of the parts of the Eightfold Path which are intended to be taken together. A serial killer can be very mindful of their inner self while they cause harm to others after all. Meditation and mindfulness are intended to question the notion of a permanent self and the ego seeking attachments, but they end up becoming coping or self-actualization mechanisms that focus on increasing the self’s wellbeing and strength.

rants/losing-language-models.title: LLMs - Losing Language Models
rants/losing-language-models.content:
Semantic satiation is the term for saying a word so often that it doesn’t sound real or meaningful for a while.
An EEG study from the MIT Media Lab found that people using chatbots to do their work displayed the weakest signs of neural activity for semantic processing, memory load, and creative ideation compared to those using traditional search engines or no tools at all. That means the cognitive offloading provided by a language doesn’t meaningfully activate your brain’s mechanisms for semantic coding, or the process of taking abstract ideas and constructing language that conveys the meaning. Your brain doesn’t perform the work of matching a word and its past context to present concepts, or invoke a theory of mind or human communication since you know the output comes from a program. Instead, your brain slips into a passive pattern recognition state that doesn’t commit the information being processed into long-term memory.
In other words, chatbots are really good at semantic satiation, which means they’re really good at killing the meaning of words. What we’re looking at is a Losing Language Model, where humans are trained not to actually engage with the relationship between abstractions and their symbolic representations, but to quickly scan for key symbols that seem relevant to their task.

rants/on-decency-in-health-policy.title: On Decency in Health Policy
rants/on-decency-in-health-policy.content:
Examining a society’s mental health policies is a really good way to figure out:

how much they blame an individual for being sick and
how much they value a standard human life

People like to believe that the universe is fair. If they do good things, they get good things, whether it comes from God or karma or organizational leaders. If someone is mentally unwell, we like to think there was a sequence of choices they made to get there. They failed to make themselves resilient enough to handle stress; they chose to put themselves in a dangerous situation like signing up to a career that’s exposed to trauma or violence; they neglected to form a balanced diet and exercise routine or practice basic self-care. After all, how hard can it be to just… not do all that?
Eventually though, we observe things like children getting cancer or global pandemics, and we might concede the universe isn’t always entirely fair, but that the inequality still happens for a reason. Perhaps evolution requires that we have ten mediocre men for each great man but we all benefit so long as we know our place; mental illness is often genetic so perhaps some families are simply doomed at birth to live on the margins; many people think that a progressive perspective on mental illness means framing it as another challenge to be overcome through willpower, grit, and ingenuity; others see mentally unwell people as props for their resumes. “I know the real you is still in there!” we’ve seen countless characters scream on screen to a loved one with a mental illness personified by spiritual or supernatural possession. “Here’s an app for your mental health” we’ve seen countless high schoolers vibe code without any professional input.
Many people can’t find the stomach to hold all the rationalizations required for that perspective. A lot of horrible things happen for no clear reason, or if there is a reason, it’s so beyond their understanding that the universe begins to appear much more random than they thought. They have far less control than they imagined. I find that people split into two main personal reactions: they either adopt the mentality of a zero-sum game characterized by “fuck you, I got mine” hyperindividualism or they feel a need to build a strong social safety net with others to at least provide comfort for the suffering that can’t be addressed. The first camp tends to
declare war on the second camp because they have no need for anyone preaching the values of redistribution. The second camp tends to keep trying to reconcile with the first camp as part of empathy for the human condition. After a while, the first camp selects for leaders who declare war on the second camp the best, usually through a combination of addicts and psychopaths who can set aside any conscience and concern for rules, while relying on people’s bias towards short-term problem-solving. Give the bully what they want, and they go away. They might come back tomorrow and ask for double, but today you’re safe. You can just keep “doing your job.” So all’s well that procrastinates well, right?
The way this breaks down long-term is that individual health issues compound into systemic public health crises. The burnout of healthcare workers during COVID-19 is a great example that’s still in our living memory. Prior to the pandemic, we already had issues with worker burnout. Researchers like Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter found that burnout varied enormously between organizations rather than individuals, which is in line with the work of those like William Edward Demings who notably said “a bad system beats a good person every time.” Consistently, institutions and their managers seem incapable of moving past the idea that individual performance is the primary determinant of outcomes when most factors determining an individual’s capacity have nothing to do with the individual’s choices. After all, that ends up putting a lot of accountability for a lot of failures in their court, and the solutions end up being more complex than adding resilience, stress management, or work-life balance classes as if the problem people have is being too stupid to assess their own needs. Of course, this mentality trickles down to the rest of society as the required mentality for success.
It’s at this intersection of individual health, systemic policy, and social ideology that you can see a society’s values. Do we care that some people don’t have the agency that others do to live a healthy and fulfilled life? Do we care about trying to make changes in the world that could improve that outcome? Do we foolishly believe that it could never happen to us, so we have no reason to care about it? Do we have the arrogance to think that it’s everyone else’s kid that will get offered and try drugs, but we will be
the sole exception as guardians who can enforce a “Just Say No” policy? President Obama’s own drug czar struggled to navigate the mental healthcare system when his son struggled with drugs. President Trump’s brother died of alcoholism which he cites in his motivation to swear off drinking for good.
So given all that, I have given up on trying to make arguments from the position of morality or compassion, or even asking people to think of their kids. It simply isn’t happening, whether it’s because of greed, complacency, or ignorance. I now make arguments from the perspective of effectiveness and cost-savings, because when you point out how someone fumbled those within an organization, jobs might actually be lost. No one likes knowing that they hired someone who cost them money. Not taxpayers or managers.

rants/the-reality-based-community.title: The Reality-Based Community
rants/the-reality-based-community.content:
Reality-Based Community
“People like you are still living in what we call the reality-based community. You believe that solutions emerge from your judicious study of discernible reality.”
“That’s not the way the world really works anymore. We’re an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality.”
“And while you are studying that reality—judiciously, as you will—we’ll act again, creating other new realities, which you can study too, and that’s how things will sort out.”
“We’re history’s actors, and you, all of you, will be left to just study what we do.”
This quote from Karl Rove is one of the best encapsulations of what America’s governing philosophy has been for a while. It played off an awe for the Presidency and its surrounding administration for a public whose political imaginations were built by The West Wing, Harry Potter, and The X-Files. Either we had super competent and ruthless political actors who strove for the perfection of their statesmanship, students who used the power of friendship and love to defeat a fascist uprising, or the lone wolves nibbling at an elaborate conspiracy that would change the world if revealed. Needless to say, all three interpretations of the institutions of power have collapsed for a far more disappointing reality.
No one actually knew what they were doing this whole time. Ignorance, incompetence, and insatiable greed: it turns out these three factors have both explanatory and predictive power. In a world that is too overwhelmingly complex for any empire to control except through a violent and totalitarian imposition of monopolies, reality cannot be determined by on-the-ground facts. There are simply too many details to be transmitted through too many layers of bureaucracy for a centrally-planned organization to have the ambition of infinite growth.
Between accepting that reality is too complex to be deterministically controlled and inventing a new reality where ignorance is bliss, social institutions and their constituencies have largely chosen the latter. Eventually, ignorance goes from bliss to virtue. The popularity of the positive psychology movement is little more than blissful ignorance and feel-good slogans detached from empirical reality, trickling-down from executives and managers who hope TED Talks deter conversations about collective action, like unionization. As Barbara Ehrenreich has said:
“The ideology of positive thinking is not just a matter of attitude. It is a way of coping with a world that has become increasingly difficult to control.”
“Hard-headed corporate culture is becoming interested in how to get more work out of fewer workers. They’re realizing that if their workers are happy, they will work harder and more productively. So they’re leading the charge.”
“The flip side of positivity is thus a harsh insistence on personal responsibility: if your business fails or your job is eliminated, it must be because you didn’t try hard enough, didn’t believe firmly enough in the inevitability of your success.”
“Breast cancer, I can now report, did not make prettier or stronger, more feminine or spiritual. What it gave me, if you want to call this a ‘gift,’ was a very personal, agonizing encounter with an ideological force in American culture that I had not been aware of before - one that encourages us to deny reality, submit cheerfully to misfortune, and blame only ourselves for our fate.”
I can now report, too, that this force is alive and well in the recovery community for all types of mental health protocols. You repeatedly hear the concepts of accountability and responsibility, but there’s next to no discussion about the actual models of health or wellbeing unless some New Age nonsense is used with the aesthetics of exotic and ancient mysticism in the place of evidence and common sense. There is next to no discussion, for example, of the concept of recovery capital. Perhaps because, inconveniently, studies show that community recovery capital has a greater bearing on someone’s sustained abstinence than individual recovery capital. In other words, our institutions are unwilling to discuss collective action or community resilience when personal coping skills and positive psychology tools can be thrown at you through manualized protocols. “You can’t change anyone except yourself” says the institution trying to change you into accepting an inability to change the world around you.
No book captures this better than The Four Agreements, which explicitly discourages you from blaming the government for restricting freedoms while telling you that no one can abuse you more than you abuse yourself. I’ve ranted at length about how repugnant the book is to me for its advice alone, setting aside the bastardization of other cultures to fit the author’s preconceived framework. Supposedly, everyone is inside their own dream that is composed entirely of things they agree to, and by simply not agreeing to external conditions. The fact that this book made its way into treatment centers as a basis for psychoeducation classes is beyond my understanding. It moves firmly beyond positive attitudes and into magical thinking about taking 100% control of your life.
It gets even worse through TED Talks and motivational speakers with YouTube channels who repeat truisms divorced from both scientific consensus and complex lived experiences. As Edgar Cabanas and Eva Illouz point out in Manufacturing Happy Citizens  (2019):
“Positive psychology has helped to transform happiness into a commodity, a lifestyle, and a form of social control.”
To Succeed Reality
“Everything changes. The studio was gonna tank when I bought it, everyone was gonna stay home with video tapes. But guess what? No! They wanna go out. No one was gonna watch network except you give it zing, and they do. You make your own reality. And once you’ve done it, apparently, everyone’s of the opinion it was all so fucking obvious.”
Succession is one of my favorite shows just under The Sopranos and Twin Peaks.
I binged The West Wing during my high school years when my career aspirations included law and policy, but House of Cards was being released at the same time. The two had very different premises for what politics at its core was, and radically different premises for what people at their cores are. Reportedly, Veep is the show that political staffers say comes closest to their experiences, but there’s also a fascinating podcast that was released alongside Succession that interviewed real political figures about their feelings about the show. Most notably, the actual Murdoch family saw the show and considered new possibilities about the cahos that would ensue about the succession planning of Murdoch’s businesses, leading to Mark Devereux drafting a real document as a representative of Elisabeth Murdoch to the family trust, termed “the Succession memo.”
What the show nails is the ambiguity found in the way power and reality interact. Where do the people who run the news get their news? How much of reality changes based on the news, and how much does the news change to reflect reality? How do impersonal systems that are bigger than any individual still end up shaped by each individual acting within it? Some say a bad system beats a good person every time. Others say every institution is the shadow of a single person.
In one episode, a Republican meeting to decide which nominee to support for President is described as a place where you don’t have to pretend to like Hamilton. It’s a clever nod to The Room Where It Happens, a song in which negotiations between Hamilton and Jefferson happen behind closed doors over dinner, rather than out in some public forum as he used to when he was young and looking for opportunity. In the course of my very short foray into that world, I’ve felt Succession comes closest to nailing the philosophy the world seems to run on.
“Oh, oh! There are rules? Do you know something Greg? There are no fucking rules.”
“Nothing is a line. Everything, everywhere is always moving. Forever. Get used to it.”
“Life’s not knights on horseback. It’s a number on a piece of paper. It’s a fight for a knife in the mud.”
“The future is real. The past is all made up.”
Though incredibly cynical and nihilistic, there is nonetheless something that reminds me of Eastern concepts of impermanence and detachment. Once we let go of the need to impose a moral righteousness onto the world, and once we accept that everything about reality changes, where does that leave us? Being radically free through being radically untethered? Are we empowered or powerless in the face of that realization, that the absurd universe provides no stable rules to learn and protect oneself through?
And what does it mean when the core of our information and investment infrastructure runs on some perverse version of this principle? If finance is driven by the management of risk and return, and risk relies on the expectations others have of what reality will be, and everyone is gaming everyone else’s expectations to get ahead in their own reality, have we short-circuited the entire process of informed judgment? Are we in control of our succession planning at all? Is it just might makes right in the end, big eats small, winners writing the history over the corpses of the losers?
Or can a David with a nugget of truth take down a Goliath whose blind spot has been misconstrued as an asset? Does the truth eventually win out in the end if only because it can be independently approached through innate human curiosity? Is our desire for stable codes and principles, continuity and legacy, something greater than ourselves, all indicative that we’ve lost our way from some state of affairs that our limited, finite selves could manage? Is our present state cynicism and nihilism, even embrace of absurdism, just an adaptation to a world that’s constantly changing, and to resist it is to have the currents turn against you?
“That’s it! We don’t know. We can’t know. But I’ve got my suspicions. I’ve got my fucking supsicions.”

rants/wikipedia-is-not-a-good-source.title: Wikipedia is Not a Good Source
rants/wikipedia-is-not-a-good-source.content:
Wikipedia is not a good source. It is a better source than ChatGPT or Gemini or any LLM, and it is better than a blog run by someone using their professional credentials to promote snake oil. It is definitely better than Facebook and Whatsapp memes, which are just the modern-day equivalent of email chains claiming Satanists in government are turning frogs gay in preparation for human trials and we can only stop it by writing checks to a campaign to draft Ralph Nader.
To be fair though, Wikipedia isn’t a source. It doesn’t market itself as a source. It’s an encyclopedia comprised of incomplete references that are skewed by its close connection to Western academia and historical archives. That’s not the same as saying it’s full of factual inaccuracies either. It means that you can walk away from Wikipedia with a completely different understanding of reality than if you had a different set of references that were equally factual.
My go-to example of this has to do with the Portuguese invasion of India in the 15th century. If you read the Wikipedia page, you will walk away thinking the two parties had misunderstandings that led to conflicts over trade because the references come almost entirely from outdated and skewed materials from European state archives. I hope we can all agree that European state archives are probably not going to give a balanced perspective of European colonialism. If we take a look at other sources, we come to a very horrifying set of interactions that include setting entire ships of families on fire for refusing to grant a random foreign power a practical monopoly over their domestic markets. That history matters, because it impacts how you might interpret the behaviors of countries today.
When you see Indian nationalism or consolidation around a Hindu identity driven by Hindutva groups, it’s tempting to compare it to the authoritarian and fascist movements that the West is familiar with since WWII. What’s often missing is the context of centuries of European powers playing regional Asian powers against each other, the same divide and conquer strategy they used with indigenous American nations. If these nations had a glimpse into the future of Manifest Destiny, they perhaps would’ve played their political hands very differently. Indian nationalism has to be understood in this context of trying to form a political coalition of a billion people arbitrarily grouped together by those European nations. To quote Sir David Gore-Boothe, High Commissioner to India from 1996 to 1998: “We didn’t promise to leave a perfect world, and we didn’t. We fucked up.”
It also recontextualizes how you might perceive European powers. Is their success really built on post-Enlightenment ideals about liberal marketplaces, rational discourse, individual liberties, democratic foundations, and unparalleled breakthroughs in material sciences? Or does it come from the unapologetic cruelty of refusing to recognize the humanity of anyone who didn’t follow the paths laid out by their social institutions? How much of America’s success is just inertia from being a relative island after a couple of wars that destroyed the former superpowers and a policy of continuing to destabilize any political structure that wasn’t compliant with institutional mandates?
Of course it’s not that black-and-white. The world isn’t split into good people and Death Eaters. That’s the point. Wikipedia tends to lean heavily on skewed evidence that leads to skewed perspectives. Even when there is nuance, it’s filtered through the skewed perception of nuance and balance.

recovery/directories/cars-peer-recovery-.title: CARS Peer Recovery Organizations
recovery/directories/cars-peer-recovery-.content:
Peer recovery organizations generally, though not always, refer to an independent center that address mental health and substance use without a clinical or medical intervention. They provide services such as coaching, support groups, resource navigation for housing and employment, social events, etc. They’re typically more involved in everyday life than a treatment center, which mainly delivers government-regulated and approved healthcare services.
The Center for Addiction Recovery Support (CARS) is a program run by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, a U.S. government federal agency. The directory they maintain contains, as of August 2026, centers across the country, including some territories like Guam. There is both an interactive search tool available on their website that allows filtering by organization type and location, as well as a PDF containing a spreadsheet with similar information.
Links

Interactive Website: www.carsrecovery.org/directory-of-peer-recovery-organizations
Downloadable PDF: static1.squarespace.com/static/67017deb9fbcef5ab5aa6989/t/676490cb7cf2ed294d060bd7/1734643916509/CARS+Peer+Recovery+Organizations.pdf

recovery/directories/find-treatment-gov.title: FindTreatment.gov
recovery/directories/find-treatment-gov.content:
Overview
Under the authorization provided by the 21st Century Cures Act, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) launched FindTreatment.gov as a centralized source for finding substance use and mental health treatment. As of a 2023 audit, they had 22,106 facilities listed.
History
While SAMHSA itself has procedures to update the directory when information changes or inaccuracies are reported, these are largely reliant on voluntary survey responses and cooperation with Single State Agencies. The Office of Inspector General (OIG) audited the directory and found that approximately two-thirds of sampled facilities contained some inaccurate information, including addresses or treatment approaches offered. For every 100 sampled facilities, 66 contained inaccurate information with 14 containing inaccurate contact information and 62 containing inaccurate services information. The latter is a lot more concerning than the former. From the audit report:
“SAMHSA officials said that after contact and services information is reported on FindTreatment.gov, SAMHSA and the Contractor do not reach out to a facility to verify its information until the following year’s Survey starts or until being informed of changes by the facility, a Single State Agency, or a consumer.”
Dr. Cara Poland, an assistant professor at Michigan State University, told CNN in 2022: “It’s being treated as a gold-standard tool, but it’s not.” Jonathan Stoltman, directory of the Opioid Policy Institute in Michigan, remarked “we need FindTreatment.gov to be better… it’s crucial to get this right.” Some private and independent alternative directories shut down because they trusted FindTreatment.gov to do what they used to do.
This site emerged in part because gaps don’t just exist in navigating the world of mental health, but are arguably increasing alongside a doubling of the world’s population living with a mental health condition since 1990. The need to step back and comprehensively rebuild recovery perspectives is paramount in addressing substance use and mental health disorders.

recovery/directories/naatp-addiction-ind.title: NAATP Addiction Industry Directory
recovery/directories/naatp-addiction-ind.content:
Overview
The National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP) is a trade association that started in 1978 for private non-profit addiction programs to advocate for regulatory regimes like uniform insurance coverage. In 2016, they launched the Addiction Industry Directory (AID) as an unsponsored database of members in good standing that pledge to follow the NAATP Code of Ethics.
Provider Members are those licensed to provide treatment services, and Accredited Provider Members are those who specifically achieved accreditation through a body the NAATP recognizes. Supporter Members provide support to treatment services though may not be licensed to deliver services themselves. NAATP Members can login to a listing management system to update their information in real-time, which contrasts with services like FindTreatment.gov which rely on voluntary survey reponses which are issued regularly but not in real-time.
Commentary
It should be noted that the AID has a page dedicated to the benefits of being listed in the directory for its members, in which they report nearly 20,000 page views per month and “prestigious” search engine placement. Many are not aware that the online content space for addiction and recovery services is heavily dominated by search engine optimization (SEO) strategies, which is why almost every time you look something up about addiction or recovery, you’re likely to find a blog or information page hosted by a treatment provider marketing their own services. This doesn’t mean the information you might receive is wrong per se, or that there’s anything particularly suspicious about members listed in the directory, but it does speak to the decentralized nature of information and referrals within recovery spaces. The AID markets itself as a cooperative solution to this:
“Not only does the directory help its members; the members help the directory. Through their inclusion in our archives, distinguished members effectively “vouch for” the credibility of the Addiction Industry Directory and reinforce NAATP’s mission to advance the addiction treatment field. In so doing, they ensure the continued high ranking of the service in search results, pushing other, possibly pseudo directories further down in search results.”
So, there’s a little bit of the ol’ “you scratch my back, and I’ll scratch yours” dynamic here.
One of the motivations I had behind this site is to aggregate information about treatment without selling or promoting treatment services, which minimizes the biases that lead some information to be excluded or outdated.
Links

www.naatp.org/resources/addiction-industry-directory
www.naatp.org/resources/news/new-addiction-industry-directory-aid/jul-11-2016

recovery/directories/peergalaxy.title: PeerGalaxy
recovery/directories/peergalaxy.content:
Overview
Peer Galaxy is a platform that aggregates peer-led recovery services and events across the world with a focus on Oregon. From their main page, they maintain peer support, recovery and wellness activities, webinars, consumer input, and special events. They also seem to have an appreciable focus on addressing barriers to participation through accessibility and translation options that are often a secondary consideration for both online and offline recovery groups.

recovery/directories/shatterproof-treatm.title: Shatterproof Treatment Atlas
recovery/directories/shatterproof-treatm.content:
Overview
Shatterproof is a nonprofit founded by Gary Mendell in 2013 to bridge the gap between the latest medical science and community treatment practices. From 2017 to 2019, the organization collaborated with medical experts, state governments, and healthcare payers to develop a data-driven system that monitored facilities for compliance with the National Principles of Care. These principles include routine screenings, personalized treatment plans, long-term disease management, medications, external non-clinical support connections, etc.
In 2020, ATLAS (Addiction Treatment Locator, Assessment, and Standards) was launched as America’s first non-profit quality measurement tool for addiction and recovery services, allowing users to compare treatment providers and services anonymously. It was supported by Arnold Ventures, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and major insurers like Aetna, Anthem, Cigna, United Health, Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Carolina, Beacon Health Options, and Magellan Health.
As of August 2026, the Treatment Atlas platform serves 14 states with plans to expand.
Commentary
Shatterproof is a rising non-profit in the addiction space, and one that I so far have a positive opinion of. They seem to be heavily data-driven such that they don’t expand to a state without significant cooperatiaon from the healthcare infrastructure there. They also have a fair amount of engagement with the press, especially when evidence-backed interventions like harm reduction and medication for disease management are challenged.

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: Presidential Award | ASAM
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Summary
According to the homepage:
“The ASAM Presidential Award honors an individual for outstanding dedication and service in addressing addiction issues or promoting education, training or awareness of the specialty of addiction medicine.”
The award’s name comes from its selection process, which consists entirely of the discretion of the ASAM President. As a general rule of thumb, I look at awards as a signal from an organization about what it values. From the 2026 press release announcing the winner:
“ASAM President Stephen Taylor, MD, MPH, DFAPA, DFASAM, has selected Dr. Athanasiou for this honor in 2026. Dr. Athanasiou is a supervising mental health psychiatrist with the Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health and a health sciences associate clinical professor with the Department of Psychiatry at UCLA. As chair of the ASAM Publications Council and editor in chief of The ASAM Weekly, he has helped keep addiction medicine audiences informed of the latest commentary, news, and research shaping the field”
So I see this award as a nod to those within ASAM who work on their publications and communications.
It seems Brian Hurley, the ASAM President during the 2024 and 2025 award processes, declined to grant it to anyone. It’s possible that the pages are simply not updated or the announcements weren’t archived, so I’ll update this if I find any more information. On the other hand, a discretionary award can be seen as motivated by political or professional ambitions, so it’s possible Hurley just didn’t want to enter that thicket.
The 2023 award went to Anthony P. Albanese, who worked to expand associated health training positions within the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) with an emphasis on shifting to a Whole Health model of car and serving veterans struggling with chronic pain in rural areas. Albanese is also a professor within the University of California system ( Davis). The ASAM President at the time was William F. Haning III.

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: Davida Coady Gorham Medical Professional of the Year Award | NAADAC
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
The Davida Coady Gorham Medical Professional of the Year Award was renamed in 2019 from the NAADAC Medical Professional of the Year Award.
Dr. Davida Coady Gorham practiced medicine internationally before settling on addiction medicine. She was a first responder in humanitarian crises in Bangladesh, Cambodia, and India, where Mother Teresa invited her to be a medical director. Instead, she came back to America, specifically California, and founded Options Recovery Services as a diversion treatment program for the Berkeley Court in 1997, which expanded to provide evidence-based treatment and sober living opportunities to thousands of people. In 2006, Options Recovery Services expanded to work with the California prison system and trained hundreds of incarcerated individuals to become certified addiction treatment counselors.
The award is named in her honor, and eligibility requires a minimum of three years of work in addiction treatment, a medical professional license, a focus on fostering long-term recovery with direct patient contact, and adherence to NAADAC ethical codes.
Past Winners


Javad Mashkuri, former medical director at the University of Vermont Health Network - Central Vermont Medical Center (2024)


Abimbola Farinde, an addiction counselor focusing on treatment disparities from a psychopharmacological perspective (2021)

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: H. Westley Clark Award for Distinguished Service | NAADAC
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
The H. Westley Clark Award for Distinguished Service was established in 2024 in honor of Dr. H Westley Clark.
Clark served as the Director of the Center for Substance Abuse Treatment (CSAT) under the U.S. federal government’s Substance Use and Mental Health Administration (SAMHSA), before which he also served as chief of the Associated Substance Abuse Programs at the U.S. Department of Veteras Affairs Medical Center in San Francisco. His public service record is extension across over 40 years of public service work in addiction and recovery. He also held a B.A. in Chemistry, a Master’s in Public Health, a Medical Degree, and a Law Degree, and he drew from all of these fields in his career.
To be eligible for the award, one must have ten years of addiction counseling or service experience across prevention, research, public policy, administration, education, law, social advocacy, and/or treatment methodologies. Membership with the NAADAC is not required.
Past Winners

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: Lectures
Lifetime Achievement
Nelson Bradley Career Achievement Award | NAATP
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
The Nelson Bradley Career Achievement Award was established in 1983 by the National Association of Addiction Treatment Providers (NAATP) as a lifetime achievement award.
Nelson J. Bradley was a psychiatrist who served as the superintendent of Willmar State Hospital in Minnesota, pioneering an approach that incorporated 12-Step principles and peer counselors into treatment facilities, now called the Minnesota Model or Twelve-Step Facilitation (TSF). A 2020 Cochrane Systematic Review analyzed 27 studies of 10,000 participants and found that manualized TSF programs inspired by the Minnesota Model are more effective for sustained long-term abstinence than clinical interventions like Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
Bradley was instrumental in the scientific community’s shift to seeing addiction as a chronic brain disease than a moral or willpower problem, though other researchers have argued that the brain disease model has pathologized and medicalized an issue rooted in socioeconomic systems.
Others argue that the main value of the Minnesota Model is peer support, which increases recovery capital by introducing people to mutual aid societies that share emotional support, but tangible support as well. Navigating healthcare, employment, housing, culture, and other aspects of daily life are made significantly easier through supportive community networks, which clinical or therapeutic interventions are not necessarily equipped to provide or substitute for. Alternative systems like the Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA) consistently outperform TSF models in reducing drinking, securing employment, and stabilizing households over time, suggesting that the medical intervention aspects of the Minnesota Model (28-days in a treatment facility) are not the real driver of improvement.
There is also substantial criticism that complex cases with co-occurring psychiatric illnesses, such as complex PTSD which the DSM-5 does not list despite up to 40% of individuals with substance use disorders testing positive for trauma-related disorders, are either excluded from the studies or are addressed with far worse results than someone solely struggling with substance use.
Despite these caveats, Bradley’s influence on the field was substantial, and the Minnesota Model remains the most common base for treatment formats used in the United States. Bradley’s legacy did a lot of work to destigmatize addiction away from the untreatable death sentence that medical professionals assumed it was. We can discuss the flaws of the Minnesota Model as a particular protocol or treatment with the advantage of new evidence and hindsight, but the man himself made major changes in the way addiction was perceived by the scientific and medical communities.

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: The Copley Medal
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
The Royal Society, an independent scientific academy based in the UK, awards the Copley Medal to scientists for breakthroughs in physical or biological research. Previous winners include Charles Darwin and Albert Einstein.

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: Lora Roe Memorial Addiction Counselor of the Year Award | NAADAC
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
The Lora Roe Memorial Addiction Counselor of the Year Award was renamed in 1988 (and again in 1998 for brevity) from the NAADAC Counselor of the Year Award.
Not much is easily discoverable about Lora Roe, as is unfortunately the case for many pioneering drug and addiction counselors of the 20th century who worked on the frontlines before media, academics, and historians paid the attention they do today.
To be eligible for the award, one must be a counseling professional actively working for at least ten years, worked directly with patients suffering with substance use disorders, and be an active NAADAC member in good standing with adherence to the NAADAC Code of Ethics.
Past Winners

Melanie Sorensen, for work providing culturally grounded care for youth on the Fort Peck Indian Reservation

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: Mel Schulstad Professional of the Year Award | NAADAC
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
Mel Schulstad was one of the founders of NAADAC, then known as the National Association of Alcoholism Counselors (NAAC). He was a WWII bomber pilot who retired in 1966 to volunteer for the Fairfax Hospital alcohol program. In 1973, he was a paid counselor for Arlington County and elected as the first President of the Virginia Association of Alcoholism Counselors (VAAC), which renamed later to the Virginia Association of Addiction Professionals (VAAP). For some context on the frequent renaming of awards and organizations, addiction wasn’t always a unified field of study, so many of the organizations and programs we have now were initially focused just on alcoholism. As their scope expanded, they thought it prudent to rebrand to reflect that.
The award was established in 1979, and Schulstad personally presented the award at NAADAC’s Annual Conferences until 2008, four years before he passed away.
To be eligible for the award, one needs to have a minimum of 20 years of service in addiction counseling, demonstrate a history of commitment to advancing the profession, and be an active NAADAC voting member in compliance with the NAADAC Code of Ethics.
Past Winners


Yasmin Gay (2025)


Debbie Thomas, CEO of The Walker Center (2024)

recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.title: William F. "Bill" Callahan Leadership Award | NAADAC
recovery/events/awards/excellence-and-me.content:
Overview
William F. Callahan was a detective and councilman who maintained a career in public service until retirement in 1971, after which he pivoted into addressing substance use disorders. He was appointed to the Connecticut Alcohol and Drug Abuse Council and was co-founer of PACES Counseling Associates of East Harford and Avon. He founded the Connecticut Federation of Alcohol and Drug Abuse counselors and helped to introduce the first counselor certification in the state.
To be eligible for the award, one must have had 15 years of addiction counseling experience, demonstrate leadership and activism in awareness projects, demonstrate support for other addiction counselors, and be a NAADAC member in good standing and compliance with the NAADAC Code of Ethics.
Past Winners


Jessica Swan (2025)


Pierluigi Mancini (2024)

recovery/events/awards/social-impact/joh.content:

recovery/events/observances/internationa.title: International Overdose Awareness Day
recovery/events/observances/internationa.content:
Overview
International Overdose Awareness Day (IOAD) was established in 2001 by Sally J. Finn and Peter Streker, who were working at The Salvation Army’s needle exchange program in St. Kilda, Melbourne, Australia. The first event, set for August 31st, was held at the needle exchange facility as a community barbecue. Ultimately, 6000 silver ribbons were distributed across Australia and New Zealand in honor of those who had passed from overdoses.
In 2012, the nonprofit Penington Institute began officially managing the campaign in order to handle the scale of a global movement. In 2014, the Penington Institute expanded IOAD’s mission to focus on distributing overdose prevention tools like Naloxone (Narcan) rather than just a day of remembrance.
As of 2026, IOAD boasts more than 1000 localized events across 40+ countries.

Sally J. Finn, founder of the IOAD campaign

Both were formally acknowledged by federal agencies like the CDC as well as state governments that passed resolutions to officially incorporate the dates into public health calendars.

recovery/events/observances/national-pre.content:
Overview
Led by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the National Prevention Week (NPW) is an annual substance use prevention campaign held in the second week of May, as studies show a spike in first-time drug use around June and July. The campaign gives educators and community leaders an opportunity to educate students before they go off on summer break.

recovery/events/observances/national-rec.title: National Recovery Month
recovery/events/observances/national-rec.content:
Overview
Led by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the National Recovery Month is held every September. Studies have shown spikes in first-time drug use in students over the summer, so September serves as a chance to reach students who might need help at the start of a new school year. Each year has a new theme to give local advocacy groups a common focus point, such as “Recovery is For Everyone.”
