recovery/glossary/a-disease-like-any-oth.title: A Disease Like Any Other
recovery/glossary/a-disease-like-any-oth.content:
Overview
“A disease like any other” is a common phrase used in mental health advocacy as an argument that mental health diagnoses should be treated the same as physical ailments. Marty Mann, one of the earlier female members of Alcoholics Anonymous, founded the National Committee for Education on Alcoholism to launch a public relations campaign that argued alcoholism is a “disease like any other” as well. At the time, stigma from the public and medical community alike made it harder for those struggling with substance use disorders to be seen as patients in need of medical help,  from hospitals and government institutions alike. Ironically, the actual A.A. recovery philosophy assumes that alcohol use disorders are not like other disease and require a spiritual awakening to a Higher Power.
Context
Variations of this phrase go back to Hippocrates coming up with a natural cause to explain epilepsy rather than supernatural causes like divine possession or curses. Around the mid-20th century, medical and advocacy organizations in America began using the phrase as part of PR campaigns to destigmatize mental health conditions, including addiction. Unfortunately, this missed the mark and instead led people to think having mental health conditions meant the brain was fundamentally broken.
The medical community began shifting away from this framing. I myself am guilty of comparing addiction to something like diabetes when explaining the chronic and complex nature of health conditions that can be influenced by personal agency. Research shows that framing mental health issues as entirely physiological or structural can make clients more pessimistic about their chances of recovery, as they feel they might be structurally broken in a way they can’t change.
Most importantly, addiction and substance use have been increasingly seen as having strong relational components. If the problem is simply a chemical imbalance or an issue of willpower, then handling substance use becomes an individual’s burden, even if their environment introduces trauma and stressors that led to using substances for coping in the first place. Philosophers, sociologists, and anthropologists have increasingly added humanistic perspectives that contextualize substance use within a specific set of cultures, traditions, enviornments, and institutions in which a network of people operate.
In these studies and papers though, authors are generally quick to note that some people benefit personally from adopting the perspective that addiction is truly a disease like any other, for instance in the context of AA meetings, and that it’s fine for people to articulate their own experiences in their own words. Issues come up when institutions and norms adopt a perspective and impose it on people who don’t find it helpful or decision-makers losing the full context of the concepts involved.
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20843872/

recovery/glossary/a-priori.title: A Priori
recovery/glossary/a-priori.content:
Overview
“A priori” refers to knowledge or justifications that exist prior to experience or empirical evidence, generally achieved through deductive reasoning.
Those who argue that some knowledge is a priori point to mathematics and logic. If two people were raised in completely empty rooms, incapable of any experience outside of their mind’s wonderings, both could arrive at the same logical conclusions. If a = b and b = c, a = c. Often, those arguing for the existence of a priori knowledge come from philosophical traditions developed by rationalists or idealists. Immanuel Kant is perhaps the most famous figure associated with developing this concept.
Others argue that no knowledge is a priori, a camp sometimes called radical empiricism. John Stuart Mill argued that even math and logic are systems built from empirical observations first. If the universe suddenly changed so that when four equivalent objects are grouped together, they disappear, we would start saying 2 + 2 = 0. In that case, 2 + 2 = 4 was never a fact we knew, just a generalization that was very strongly confirmed.
Quantum physics as a field has begun to challenge long-standing assumptions that logical rules as we’ve been able to derive them are universally true. Those like Willard Van Orman Quine have proposed models of human knowledge that function more like a web where knowledge in the center is difficult to change as it would disrupt the entire system, and the rules of quantum mechanics make it so that basic laws we took for granted are at least questionable.
For instance, with the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, we cannot know both where a particle is or how fast a particle is going. This means if A is a claim about the particle’s location, and B and C are claims about the particle’s speed, we cannot know A AND B or A AND C. This means we run into a problem with the distributive law. Normally, we would say A AND (B OR C) should be equivalent to (A AND B) OR (A AND C). However, with the Uncertainty Principle, the first is True while the second is False. There are some arguments about fixing this without changing our known rules of logic, but it’s likely we won’t have a resolution to this debate for a while.
According to the 2020 PhilPapers Survey that reached out to 1,800 academic philosophers, about 72.8% at least lean towards the existence of a priori knowledge. About 18.5% at least reject its existence or lean towards pure empiricism. About 8.7% are either undecided or have an alternative view.
History and Etymology
“A Priori” is a Latin phrase that translates to “from what comes before.”
In the past, philosophers like Descartes argued that God implanted ideas into our minds the moment as part of our birth. Plato theorized that our souls remember truths from past lives. A priori referred to our ability to make inferences about cause-and-effect; for instance, if you know your house caught on fire, you might reason that it will quickly turn to ashes if left alone.
When the concept of a priori knowledge was reinterpreted by Kant, he defined it as having truths independent of sensory experiences. He argued you don’t have to check whether 2 + 2 = 4 for every single pair of pairs in the entire universe. You can use reason alone to know 2 + 2 = 4.
Commentary
In neuroscience, a common paradigm to understand the brain is to see it as a prediction engine that is constantly making assumptions about the world independent of experience in order to help navigate it. “I am inherently a broken human” is a claim to a priori knowledge. “My Higher Power will cure me of my defects if sough” is another. “An abstinent life is the only one worth pursuing” is yet another. Claims to a priori knowledge can be found in every aspect of life, and that includes mental health and recovery. Our brains often begin with these a priori assumptions when processing information about the world, which means we can easily have a tendency to interpret new information so that it aligns with those assumptions.

recovery/glossary/ableism.title: Ableism
recovery/glossary/ableism.content:
Overview
Ableism is bias or discrimination against people who are labeled or self-identify as having a disability.
History and Etymology
Commentary
Ableism is a complex concept because “disability” is a complex concept. Our norms surrounding the expectations we place on ourselves and others are constantly evolving.
Decades ago, the expectation in American workplaces was that people would work 12 hours a day, every day of the week- children included. If someone was suffering from unresolved health issues or trauma as a result of serving in a war and couldn’t work along those expectations, they might be considered disabled. In 2026, expecting someone to work more than 40 hours a week and forsake their weekends to make ends meet is considered unreasonable, and children aren’t expected to work at all when public education is available. Of course, that doesn’t mean people aren’t working unreasonable amounts to survive, but our norms are constantly evolving.
Because the concept of disability has always been fluid and varied, ableism too is a moving target to define. In the context of addiction and recovery, the forms ableism comes in depends on the model of addiction and health being applied in a particular situation.
For instance, reducing substance use disorders to issues of morality, willpower, and/or denial is a form of ableism. It ignores the measurable changes to the brain and body that occur after long-term substance use. It also ignores findings like the increased chance of someone developing a substance use disorder if they were born to parents who struggled with substance use. Most adults who develop alcohol use disorder report having their first drink between 13 to 17, so it seems a little bizarre that a pattern which was developed before someone had a mature adult brain, and was expected to have been protected by adult guardians, is reduced to a moral and willpower issue.
Often, I’ve heard people express the sentiment, “so what if you’re sober? that’s just the baseline everyone is at who was able to control their substance use.” This is ableist since it very explicitly erases the effort it can take to work against the combination of biological predisposition, intergenerational trauma, socioeconomic barriers, and physiological changes that are real parts of one’s lived experiences. We wouldn’t tell someone who survived cancer, “so what? The baseline expectation for a person in our society is that you don’t have cancer.” At least, I hope not.
Medical Interference
In its most extreme forms, the ableism goes beyond social stigma and directly interferes with recovery and medical treatment. In the early half of the 20th century, American physicians largely had written off substance use disorders as untreatable, or at least, not worth attempting to treat. There was a turning point around the debut of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and the “Disease Like Any Other” campaigns pushed for by advocates like Marty Mann, which argued that substance use disorders were really a disease that followed patterns we could manage. The Minnesota Model emerged as a rehabilitation model that incorporated medical supervision with therapy, counseling, and peer support through groups like AA. Still, no disease can truly be said to be like any other, any more than people themselves can be reduced to stereotypes.
Those with SUD who take medication are often accused of substituting one dependency for another, even if to address something like Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that co-occurs with SUD. Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) involves taking methadone or buprenorphine, which are especially likely to be stigmatized as continued drug dependence. Patients with substance use disorders who visit clinics for other health issues will always have to be conscious of the stigma around drug-seeking behavior when approaching treatment providers, particularly for medical professionals who haven’t had specialized training in SUD. In fact, studies have shown that just changing the term “substance abuse” to “substance use disorder” results in physicians treating patients with less intent to punish them, which shows how easily suggestible everyone, including experts, can be to social stigma.
Reasonable Accommodations
In my experience, the vast majority of people with SUD have no idea that there are reasonable accommodations they can request from their workplace in support of recovery. There’s a major misconception that reasonable accommodations for substance use disorders involves tolerating illicit use in the workplace, when in reality these accommodations apply before a positive drug screen or after a recovery program has been initiated. It’s actually somewhat shocking to me that treatment centers and facilities do not provide any kind of standard pamphlet describing these accommodations, especially when they certainly have the time to do sound bowls, equine therapy, and hour-long playlist-sharing sessions.
Adjusting shift hours to accommodate morning/evening clinic visits for MOUD, eliminating erratic shifts that disrupt the sleep cycles needed for healing, modifying break schedules to practice stress-reduction exercises or call a sponsor are all within scope of reasonable accommodations for the workday. Job-protected leave to attend a rehabilitation program or seek short-term stabilization following a relapse are included too. Some people who work in environments with frequent exposure to triggers or substances can request reassignment to other tasks or departments, at least in early recovery. In other words, these protections exist so that a relapse isn’t automatically a cause to be fired and can be seen as part of a chronic disease.
Even if you were completely aware of these accommodations, there are plenty of other systemic manifestations of ableism against substance use disorders that can trip you.
One of them may have occurred to you while reading the above paragraph: “if someone experiences a relapse and seeks treatment, they’re protected, but between those two points, isn’t someone considered an active user who is eligible for termination or eviction?” Yes, that’s a current loophole in the law. Someone who relapses on Saturday, arranges a rehab stay starting Tuesday due to bed availability limitations, but fails a drug test at work on Monday can be fired on the spot. In comparison, if someone with epilepsy has a seizure at work rather than failing a drug test, that wouldn’t be protected justification to fire them even if the productivity loss to the employer was exactly the same.
Under Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, workers with disabilities can be paid below the federal minimum wage.
Government programs like Supplemental Security Income (SSI) effectively penalize individuals with disabilities for marrying, since the combined assets can put them over the eligibility limits for healthcare and income for survival. Many couples with disabilities are not able to live together or get married without significant risks to their wellbeing.
Many laws, like public intoxication, mean that any individual experiencing a relapse who leaves private view to enter the public space can be criminally institutionalized at the sole discretion of law enforcement, despite no damage to property or life.
In a cultural and social sense, the stigma around substance use disorders is intense. Ableism suffers from the same social patterns as racism and sexism; the few who manage to “overcome” their barriers are elevated as proof that the systems people live in don’t need to change. Instead, others with disadvantages simply need to live up to the standards of the elevated examples. To illustrate the absurdity of this, imagine that someone paralyzed from the waist down manages to climb up a flight of stairs with their upper body alone because the elevators in their building aren’t working. It would be barbaric to celebrate this as a norm anyone should live up to while discarding plans to make buildings more accessible to those in wheelchairs. Similarly, there are people with substance use disorders who go into spontaneous remission without any treatment whatsoever, and there are people who recover because communities like AA provide a network of resources that align with their religious beliefs. It would be barbaric to assume this means we have proven paths for recovery within our current system and simply need to coerce individuals into the treatment process.
Media
Our media is pretty hostile toward substance use disorders too. I have a lot of affection for Thor from God of War: Ragnarok as a much more nuanced depiction of alcoholism than we usually get. Thor’s drinking, and attempts to abstain, is directly related not just to his own childhood growing up, but the ongoing dynamics between his family and a changing world that’s increasingly difficult to navigate with the patterns he knew before. The story paints a portrait of him as a genocidal drunken barbarian well before we encounter him, which is a clever use of the connection between mythology and reputation, but without absolving him of the atrocities he’s responsible for. The very first time we meet him, it’s through a classic patriarchal power move of fathers sending their sons ahead of a negotiation to size up the other side. Succession has a very similar scene to illustrate the relationship between Logan Roy and his son Kendall as an extension of himself. In both cases, the person we meet is borderline submissive and internally lost, clearly disengaged from the present moment while following the motions of a plan laid out by a patriarchal father.
The context we learn over time depicts someone who has been in a constant state of abuse and conflict his whole life, who drinks to avoid thinking about the consequences of the actions he feels obligated to carry out, and is the furthest thing from selfish at the point that we meet him. He’s in mourning over how replicating the parenting he got only led to the loss of his sons, in fear of what it would take to change for the sake of his living daughter and wife, in repressed guilt over the damage he’s caused that he can’t process without drinking, and in confusion through the manipulation of a father whose approval he desperately seeks as a foundation for securing his family’s future. It can’t be said that Thor didn’t take pleasure in his moments of brutality, but neither can it be said that he lives for the sake of a selfish agenda that necessitates brutality. His character is a foil to Kratos, who similarly had a brutal childhood that instilled a sense of brutality in him, but who rebelled against his family after feeling betrayed rather than rationalize that betrayal as necessary for the greater good. Whereas Kratos attempts to cast aside his humanity after he’s been tricked into killing his family, Thor is still mentally working out the sequence of events that led to him killing his son. Litigating the justifications that either character took in response to an impossible situation in some kind of morality play is a futile exercise. The narrative emphasizes that the only thing worth considering is the future: “Don’t you know what I’ve done? / Yes, but what will you do now?”
On the other hand, consider the Saw franchise, which has a Wikipedia page dedicated to the 24 “Drug Addicts” included across all their properties. The themes of Saw are generally that a deranged serial killer thinks he’s helping people appreciate the life they had by asking them to undergo a brutal torture to get it back. This explicitly runs with the narrative that addiction is the result of being ungrateful for everyday life and seeking greater pleasures selfishly at the expense of others, as well as their own best interests. In the case of addiction, Jigsaw seems to think addicts need more trauma in order to be grateful for their lives derailed by substance use.
Or consider Requiem for a Dream, which does treat addiction as a pattern that occurs across different social stratifications in different ways rather than a personal moral failing, but only through a parallel downward spiral. The takeaway isn’t just that addiction is a horrifying experience, but that it’s also an inescapable one that swallows an individual’s agency and identity.
Even Breaking Bad suffers a bit from this in order to be a morality play. Jesse is able to pull out of his struggles with addiction at various points in his life without demonstrating some kind of “truly bad” core and is depicted with a backstory that shows trauma and lack of support, but the show generally fails to do the same for characters who don’t have a middle-class white background. Partly, this is for the narrative tension that comes with casting a sense of enigmatic exoticism over both drugs and the drug trade, something that’s deeply embedded in the fabric of America’s imagination, but the end result is the same.
Capitalism
If we really want to dig into the root causes of these issues, we have to discuss capitalism. In a system designed around short-term profit-seeking at all costs, the concept of addiction is highly desirable to you. An addicted customer will sacrifice everything else past the point of their own expressed preferences in order to continue using your products. They will continually seek faster trades with larger volumes as their tolerance for the current volume builds. When the addiction leads to a destruction of one’s own life, perhaps to the point of breaking laws to maintain the usage patterns, the state comes along to institutionalize these individuals so that they can continue working with far fewer liberties and rights.
Logically, addiction is the ultimate goal of capitalism, and one that behavioral economists have historically overlooked with their emphasis on utility and rational choice.
Consider the absurdity of corporate and political leaders panicking about declining birth rates; what exactly is the social problem if people look at themselves and the world, and then decide that they don’t want to pursue parenthood in these conditions? The problem is that once everyone has been put as close to a track of addiction as possible, the only way to generate more capital is to have more labor that can be inserted into the tracks above. The systemic hostility to working-class families is papered over with propaganda about the happiness that’s just one more consumption away. The fundamental problem of modern advertising is convincing people they have an unmet need that only their product can satisfy.

recovery/glossary/aboulia.title: Aboulia
recovery/glossary/aboulia.content:
Overview
Aboulia is a medical condition where someone has a severe lack of will or drive that impacts their ability to act, speak, or even make independent choices. Causes can include brain injuries or strokes, neurodegenerative diseases like frontotemporal dementia, or other anomalies like tumors.
History and Etymology
Commentary
Addiction and aboulia have a bidirectional relationship. Both chronic substance use and aboulia are physiologically linked to a lack of dopmaine in out mesocorticolimbic pathways. The damage directly caused by prolonged substance use can alter the prefrontal cortext and basal ganglia in ways that trigger aboulia. Those with pre-existing aboulia who struggle with feeling rewarded by daily tasks may develop substance use disorders as a way to feel something they otherwise can’t.
Ironically, addiction is referred to often as a “disease of the will” or “spiritual sickness”, but aboulia is literally a condition referring to low drive to act in ways that one desires. Addiction has much more to do with executive function and compulsions that exist even if an individual has an enormously strong drive to do everything they can to stay sober. During relapses or active addiction, that same individual can also be enormously motivated to obtain and consume a substance or initiate an addictive process.

recovery/glossary/abstinence-violation-e.title: Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE)
recovery/glossary/abstinence-violation-e.content:
Overview
An Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE) refers to the negative emotions someone feels after they’ve been inconsistent with some rule, goal, or commitment.
For instance, if you’re on a diet but you decide to cheat with one Oreo, you might feel that you already failed the diet so eating ten more is no big deal, or even inevitable. If you decide to hit the gym every day, and you skip one because you just weren’t feeling it, you might decide that you don’t have the willpower to get the body you want anyways and give up.
A similar thing can happen with sobriety. Someone who accidentally grabbed an alcoholic beer instead of a non-alcoholic beer might worry they broke their sober streak, so a full relapse or bender is inevitable. This can spiral into a self-fulfilling prophecy where a potential setback or minor deviation from a plan becomes a complete collapse into old habits.
Commentary
“I already messed up, so I might as well give up.”
“I already broke one rule, so I might as well break the rest.”
More than the following description and exploration of the term Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE), the above example might make make things very intuitive. It’s a quick path from this sentiment into believing “I’m just an addict who can’t help but fail” or “I’m just a criminal by nature who can’t fit in with others.”
There are some common strategies to combat an AVE when it comes up, with many of the more recently discussed common solutions coming out of Dialectical Behavioral Therapy.
One is to vet thoughts for all-or-nothing thinking, or that either things are all good or all bad, total success or total failure. Someone who relapses after years of sobriety still lived a sober life during that time, and those memories and experiences and impacts are all still real. Each of those days was successfully sober.
In doing so, it might be easier to see a trajectory of progress that continues from past successes, which can pull people out of catastrophizing spirals and into a solutions-focused mindset. Relapses or setbacks can provide more information to identify lifestyle changes that can be made to prevent more setbacks in the future, which can be motivating as a reason to stay optimistic.

recovery/glossary/abstinence.title: Abstinence
recovery/glossary/abstinence.content:
Summary
Abstinence refers to refraining from some kind of behavior or substance, as opposed to moderation. In the context of addiction, it means a policy of never using a substance or a process again, usually under the belief that any use will lead to unmanageable consequences.
History and Etymology
In Latin “abstinere” is formed from “ab” as “away from” and “tinere” as “to hold”. Together, it means “to hold away from.” The noun “abstinentia” came to mean “self-restraint” in a way that still could’ve applied to moderation as a type of restraint. “Abstinence” begins to appear in Middle English through Old French.
Through the 18th and 19th centuries, temperance movements in Europe and North America began promoting abstinence as the only strategy to meaningfully deal with alcohol. It wasn’t just for drinkers, but anyone and everyone, as the substance itself was seen as a problem. “Temperance” also originally meant a type of moderation or self-restraint, as in to temper one’s coldness with compassion.
Once Prohibition policies failed and the country moved away from abstinence, groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) kept using the language of “abstinence” for their own members. William Silkworth, an American physician who worked with AA founder William Wilson (Bill W.), wrote in a foreword for the AA Big Book that alcoholism was like an allergy. Just as someone with a peanut allergy wouldn’t think to themselves “eh, just this once” when they know it would lead to a potentially fatal reaction, an alcoholic similarly needed to maintain abstinence to avoid a fatal reaction.
As the medical community began seeing addiction as something treatable, they also began studying “abstinence” as a potential goal of medical interventions or recovery programs. It’s also just easy to measure, as you’re either using a zero or nonzero amount of a substance or process. Measuring something like the percent of days that abstinence is maintained or number of sustained abstinence periods is much harder, and we still struggle with this problem today.
From then onwards, “abstinence” became a widely legitimized term used in clinical, recovery, and public settings.
Commentary
Is it All-or-Nothing?
Historically, the emphasis on abstinence as a metric and an ideal outcome meant clinicians and researchers alike paid less attention to other metrics. While there were researchers like D.L. Davies in the 1960s who reported the existence of alcoholics who had returned to moderate drinking, it was still seen as a remote possibility rather than an outcome that could be reasonably achieved as a result of interventions. Still, it established that abstinence and death were not the only two outcomes for alcoholics.
In the 1970s, Linda and Mark Sobell, a married couple who collaborate often on research, ran a trial with 70 male alcoholics who were assigned to a goal of either controlled drinking or abstinence, and then either a control group or a group receiving Individualized Behavior Therapy (IBT). The results showed that, aside from the IBT group having significantly better functioning across the board, some alcoholics had maintained controlled drinking behavior by the 1 year mark.
This stirred a lot of controversy, and by the 1980s, researchers had produced new evidence and reexamined the Sobells’ original experiment. On a 10 year follow up of the 20 experimental subjects, only 1 had maintained controlled drinking and 6 had become abstinent. 8 continued drinking excessively, 4 died from causes related to their drinking, and 1 went missing after becoming severely disabled as a result of their drinking. The controversy over the experiment led to an investigation into the Sobells, which established they did not falsify their research. The scientific community remained divided as the Sobells pointed out that multiple independent investigations exonerated them.
Nevertheless, valid questions about the methodology used in these studies was raised.

recovery/glossary/absurdism.title: Absurdism
recovery/glossary/absurdism.content:
Overview
Absurdism is a tradition of existential philosophy popularized by Albert Camus that argues people should live passionately in defiance of an ultimate meaningless universe. Rather than becoming a nihilist who stops living life because they see no meaning it or creating your own meaning as a substitute, Camus argued you should accept the meaninglessness and live your life without seeking a grand purpose.
History and Etymology
Commentary
I am strongly biased towards existentialist and metaphysical concepts in just about any paradigm. If the root of an issue isn’t found within the fundamentals, the fundamentals should at least provide a steady compass to navigate the issue. In the case of substance use disorders, this means unpacking the modes of experiencing reality after consuming a substance. Our goal of treating the disorders towards abstinence, usually with some urgency, leads us to a focus on stabilizing a sober life so that the states of severe and chronic substance use are avoided altogether due to the negative consequences associated with it.
However, this tendency means we often overlook the reality experienced by those in active addiction. It’s somewhat justifiable since active addiction comes with a lot of incoherent blackouts, paranoia, delusions, hallucinations, and other experiences that are not terribly intelligible. Stil, if we wish to understand addiction existentially, we ought to try and understand substance use as a continuum of existential perspectives that span across a life which includes diverse states of mind.
An Existential Model of Addiction
In 2021, Dr. George Grech from Malta published a paper, “An Existential Model of Addiction”, which frames addiction as a coping mechanism for the existential anxieties of psychopathologies, specifically the avoidance of “existential givens” that include death, freedom, existential isolation, and meaninglessness. He then defines addiction as “being-with-drug” to reflect that one’s modes of existence and relation to others are redefined in the context of a relation to a substance or process.

recovery/glossary/abuse.title: Abuse
recovery/glossary/abuse.content:
Overview
Abuse generally refers to using a position or tool in a way that it wasn’t intended to be used, often in the context of someone having power or influence that they use to harm someone else.
Commentary
Abuse is really difficult to discuss, and not just because no one likes to think of themselves as an abuser or having been abusive at some point. “Abuse” as a term has arguably suffered from a process called “concept creep” where something is analogized or compared to the current concept of abuse in a way that expands it.
For example, we might agree that a politician who threatens to use their platform to harass an ex-partner is obviously abusing their power. We might also agree that a parent who gets drunk and hits their child is physical abuse. What about an older sibling who calls their younger sibling annoying or stupid? Some people might read that question and recall a long, conflict-driven relationship with their sibling, while others will recall fights they now laugh about. What about having vicious screaming arguments in front of a child without explicitly yelling at them? The child isn’t the target of the disturbance but might still find it traumatic and have their emotions neglected. Calling the parents “abusers” in this scenario might not feel that it was in the spirit of identifying domestic violence or exploitation from people with formal positions of power. What about a partner who uses the silent treatment after an argument? We might agree that it’s toxic or immature, but it might be harder to say the partner is being abusive in the same sense as someone who hits their partner after an argument. The former dilemma might be resolved through communication or counseling, but the latter might reasonably be elevated to criminal investigation.
It becomes difficult to discuss the topic at all because people begin with entirely different baselines for what they consider abuse, influenced both by community and interpersonal dynamics. Much like the discussion around addiction, the fear of being labeled as an “abuser” means almost no one is willing to discuss a past where they may have done something abusive. It’s also difficult for people in dynamics they don’t want to leave to label another’s actions as abusive, both because of the stigma around being a “victim” but also because they may not want to leave or demonize the person as much as resolve the pattern of behavior. Whether or not we may think it’s best for them to leave, the person in question may have reservations that prevent them from seeking help for abusive patterns.
On the other hand, the expansion of the use and concept of “abuse” is arguably a reflection of our growing perspective about forms of harm and lasting trauma. Maybe it’s not in the spirit of the original context to use “abuse” to describe an older sibling teasing a younger sibling over a mistake, but the fact someone might hold onto that feeling even after a long time indicates some unresolved feelings or thoughts about the event which are as worth exploring as anything else for the individual’s wellbeing. Maybe a boss yelling at their employee on a bad day isn’t the same type of abuse as a partner beating their spouse, but it’s still an inappropriate use of power that can cause lasting harm and feelings of hostility in the workplace.
There’s also a dimension to abuse that heavily implies a power dynamic that creates an abuser-victim dyad, which is nuanced in its own model of situations. We certainly don’t want to imply a victim is responsible for someone else’s decision to abuse them, but it’s also not always clear how the power dynamic has manifested. Each person has entirely different realities across strength, money, social status, immigration status, health conditions, and other aspects of the human experience. Someone who has disabilities and is financially dependent can still physically assault their partner, which complicates the way we measure power dynamics. It’s possible for two people in a relationship to regularly be physically violent with each other, and we might get into some very weird math if we start looking at each person’s biology to figure out their capacity for strength.
Personally, I take the perspective that a person should embrace the terms that they feel best describes their experience, but also that we should respect that in other people and be mindful about the terms we choose to use with others. We shouldn’t label  actions abusive without context,

recovery/glossary/accessibility.title: Accessibility
recovery/glossary/accessibility.content:
Overview
Accessibility refers to the ability for resources to be accessed. It might sound self-explanatory, but the nuances of accessibility can raise complex issues around design tradeoffs when managing resources. Some studies find that only 5% of websites comply with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) designed to wrap around standards derived from the American Disabilities Act. When it comes to substance use disorders, a lot of people aren’t even informed about what they can request as accommodations, either for a substance use disorder in non-treatment contexts or other disabilities in a treatment context.

recovery/glossary/accidental-poisoning.title: Accidental Poisoning
recovery/glossary/accidental-poisoning.content:
Overview
“Accidental poisoning” generally refers to the unintentional ingestion of a substance or amount of a substance that produces unwanted, and generally negative, outcomes.
This is meant to encompass more than just accidentally consuming drugs like eating a spiked brownie thinking it was a standard brownie. It also includes chemicals, foods, plants, and venoms that can be harmful after unintentional exposure. Further, even when there’s an intention to use a substance, “accidental poisoning” still applies if the amount taken was not intentionally determined; someone might have decided to only take one dose but forgotten if they did or not, leading to a second dose. As a technical term it has specific desginations within the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) and codes of the Center of Disease Control.
Often, if someone presents with an overdose and there is no evidence or reason to believe that someone wanted to harm themselves, it will be classified as an “accidental poisoning.”
History and Etymology
Before “overdose,” it was much more common in addiction literature to see the term “poisoning,” particularly from the 1960s to the 1990s. As with all things related to addiction, the sociopolitical circumstances played a huge role in determining which context each term was used in.
Pharmaceutical drugs were seen as distinct from illicit drugs in both social use and physiological mechanisms, so “dependence” or “addiction” to pharmaceutical drugs was difficult to comprehend as something that could happen in white middle-class neighborhoods. The stigma of “addiction” was tied heavily to marginalized communities after centuries of propaganda associating illicit drug use with black and brown communities, as well as working-class white communities. Pharmaceutical companies didn’t want their products associated with that class of illicit drugs or marginalized people either, and historically the industry has been quite keen on deregulation that allows them to sell products without the efficacy.
Yet, there were clearly habit-forming substances that were causing social and health issues within white upper and middle class communities, and a term had to be used to discuss them. Thus, many doctors at the time attempted to discuss substance use by describing the effects as “accidental poisonings” resulting from inadequate guidelines in medical contexts and poor regulation in the drug manufacturing marketplace. “Addiction” could be classified as a moral failing that plagued minority communities while “accidental poisonings” were attributed to systemic issues for middle-class white communities.
Links

jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2826704

recovery/glossary/accountability.title: Accountability
recovery/glossary/accountability.content:
Overview
Accountability in its everyday sense refers to the ability to render judgment based on someone’s actions. Holding the government accountable means allowing the voters to judge their actions for transparency and competence to decide if power should change hands. Holding a teenager accountable for curfew means judging their adherence to it with consequences for a lack of compliance.
Commentary
Accountability is a really difficult term to use precisely. Everyone grows up in a culture and environment with its own set of norms around agency and obligation, so we load a lot of implications into accountability that can make it very easy to talk past each other.
On a personal note, at a philosophical level, I am generally uninterested in accountability for the past, or what is sometimes called desert-based blame. “Desert” here refers to “deserving” rather than the environment. To the extent that blaming someone in the past might be a deterrent to future actions, I can see the practical use of it, but I don’t generally subscribe to ideas rooted in “deserving.” I just translate a statement like “I believe Bob deserves to suffer” to “I would experience satisfaction at seeing Bob suffer” or “Bob should be the recipient of the consequences of this situation.” I take an instrumental approach, which is to say that the past is unchangeable while the future is potential, so focus on the future.
Consider driving under the influence. If someone causes harm while driving, I can see the value in revoking their driving privileges to prevent future harm, as well as incentivizing treatment as an alternative to incarceration. However, I think someone who drives under the influence without hurting someone should generally receive the same baseline treatment as someone whose intoxicated driving led to a fatal accident. If they had a similar state of mind in similar circumstances prior to getting into their vehicle, then the problem to be corrected is ultimately the same, even if consequences of the problem’s existence differ.
Where I do take interest in accountability is as a tool for keeping agents aligned with a plan for the future. If you accept that you are accountable for something, you signal that you expect to exercise your judgment and agency over that thing. A parent is accountable for their child’s wellbeing. A child is accountable for their homework. A teacher is accountable for teaching a child the skills to do that homework. However, all of these systems of accountability are interconnected; if one link in this chain collapses, whether it’s a neglectful parent or a child with an undiagnosed learning disability or an overworked teacher, it might be rather unreasonable to hold the others to account.
Can a teacher receiving an expanded student class size that violates union regulations (something that happened multiple times in the course of my own schooling) be held accountable for a drop in test scores? Can those students be held accountable for not performing as well as the students who came before them? Can the parents be held accountable for not knowing enough to be a part-time at-home educator for their child after a 9-5 that might not even make ends meet? I would argue that none of these individuals can reasonably be held to account, even if it is possible for them to overexert themselves in the short-term to meet expectations. Instead, what is required is a systemic shift in resources: more educators need to be hired and more classes need to be built. Children sitting on the ground to study Calculus because their parents haven’t figured out how to fund the education system in their own community is, to me, the very obvious and disgraceful problem to be corrected. In that case, I hold people accountable not necessarily for their role in a system, but what they advocate for in terms of changes to the system.
If someone believes we should cut taxes that fund education and social services, whether they’re a parent or a teacher or even a student, and it goes predictably wrong, accountability should come in the form of that person’s judgment being recognized as lacking competency. If a politician wants to raise taxes to fund services but then allocates the funds ineffectively, that official should also be recognized as lacking leadership or budgeting skills required to implement their plans. If someone sits out of the discussion in a desire to remain non-political or non-controversial, that person should be held accountable for supporting the system as it currently exists and lacking the initiative or courage to improve the world they live in while leeching off the risks others take.
To put it simply, I’m mostly interested in holding people accountable for the systemic changes they support, not for their individual role in a broken system.
When it comes to substance use disorders, I am staunchly against moralizing accountability at a systemic level. One of the reasons I find some of A.A.’s ideas fairly horrifying to apply at a personal level is that it prompts the participant to take a “moral inventory” of “defects of character” while surrendering to “God as we understood Him” by “praying only for knowledge of His will for us,” and to seek an “easier, softer way” is to be an “unfortunate” who is “constitutionally incapable” of “rigorous honesty” because they “seem to have been born that way.” I’ll always add this caveat to my A.A. opinions: if it works for you, great. It’s aggressively rooted in Protestant theology and moral psychology, but that can work for people whose backgrounds and values align with that. For others, it can be deeply alienating.
Therapeutic and clinical institutions largely inherit these moral psychology structures. If someone prays to God but still suffers, a priest can argue the issue lies in a lack of faith, a secret sin, or weakness in committing to God’s will. If someone undergoes therapy but still suffers, a dogmatic practitioner can argue that the issue lies in the client’s failure to internalize the tools, a repressed dysfunctional core belief, or generally resistant or non-compliant attitudes. The practitioner and the manual are akin to a preist and scripture; all the messy and complex details are attributed to the dysfunctionality of the individual ego while the system and institutions remain unchallenged. What was once labeled sinful behavior that the individual is responsible for abstaining from is mapped onto a pathology that the individual is responsible for managing. “Healing” from trauma by “doing the work” takes on the same moralistic undertones as purifying oneself of sins through confession and atonement.
Even the relationship with law and the judicial system is imported. European monarchies practiced a form of surveillance where citizens who failed to show up for church services with verbal confessions or sign written confessions were marked as potential rebels. In modern Western nation-states, judicial systems allow forensic psychologists and psychiatrists to provide testimony that is based on unfalsifiable subjective constructs, if not outright pseudoscience. A licensed medical professional possesses the power to deprive individuals of due process and constitutional rights on the basis of a subjective clinical assessment of someone’s internal state of mind.
In so many of these aspects of our institutions, moralization serves to further the assignment of blame to individuals and away from the systems at work. Notably, if we did want to assign blame to individuals within a system, we ought to start with those who have the most influence and power over shaping it. Yet, it is precisely those individuals who escape with the least accountability while deflecting dysfunction onto those with less influence. In the same way that the moral debate of a death penalty cannot be separated from the requirement that we trust an institution to decide when it should be enacted, we similarly cannot discuss accountability for individuals without considering the institutions that administer it.
I have sat in multiple groups where someone in their 20s describes being given drugs by their parents as teenagers after repeated physical and sexual abuse, but remains entirely focused on blaming themselves for choosing to accept and use the substances. There is no impulse from therapists or facilitators to discourage that notion, instead seeing that as a sign of increased accountability and agency. I’m no expert, but I tend to think people who survived an extremely long history of trauma are very likely to have internalized the idea that they are to blame for their trauma in order to maintain the belief that the world is fair and fundamentally good, and what is framed as heightened accountability and agency can just as easily be reinforcing a pattern of self-blame and low self-worth.
Attributability, Answerability, and Accountability
Some scholars like David Shoemaker have attempted to delineate some of the nuanced interpretations packed into “accountability.” Specifically, Shoemaker argues that a comprehensive theory of moral responsibility should treat attributability, answerability, and accountability as three distinct components.
Links

www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/659003
www.mit.edu/~shaslang/mprg/ASmithAAA.pdf

recovery/glossary/acculturation-habits-a.title: Acculturation, Habits, and Interests Multicultural Scale for Adolescents (AHIMSA)

recovery/glossary/actor-network-theory.title: Actor-Network Theory (ANT)
recovery/glossary/actor-network-theory.content:
Overview
Actor-Network Theory (ANT) is a social theory that posits that social phenomena are the result of a network relationships between interacting entities rather than dividing the world into a material reality and a social reality.
For instance, a conventional biomedical perspective of addiction might frame the problem as beginning with exposure to substances, escalating to chronic use that changes brain chemistry and tolerance levels, developing into a dependence or addiction, and leading to drug-seeking behavior with its associated consequences.
A more ANT-centric perspective steps back from a linear cause-and-effect chain to instead examine the network of relationships from which a substance use disorder emerges. We might end up with a non-linear list:


a pharmaceutical company oriented towards profitability as a result of shareholder, managerial, and worker interests manufactures and markets an addictive substance after a series of clinical trials, regulatory approval processes, and patent applications


a public policy agenda supports private insurance companies as a way to fund healthcare protocols that involve processing prescriptions to the products of a pharmaceutial company


an insurance company decides which substances it will pay for and under which conditions through a combination of risk-analysis algorithms trained on healthcare data, documentation from Electronic Health Records, and contractual policies involving prior authorization


a treatment facility or clinic hires from a competitive marketplace of medical professionals who have varying educational credentials and memberships with professional organizations whose outputs are regularly cited in private and public standards


medical education institutes train physicians according to regulatory guidelines from accreditation organizations that examine the state of academia and research to derive guidelines and consolidate core materials for physician education


a physician prescribes this addictive substance to patients according to diagnostic criteria and protocols, including pain scale assessments that negotiate between a patient’s expression of pain and a physician’s interpretation of pain


a patient’s family has a history of health issues and substance use disorders, which a physician evaluates through their engagement with risk-related discourse and genetic research


a patient suffers from major trauma that leads to a clinical encounter with a physician whose interpretation of the patient’s expression of pain leads to a prescription to an addictive substance


a patient lacks culturally or religious compatible support networks around them, leading to increased isolation and the substance as their primary means to alleviate pain or suffering


a patient’s neurochemistry changes to produce cravings and dependence that lead to job performance issues and unemployment at the discretion of an employer that might or might not be understanding of substance use disorders


public intoxication laws criminalize the dependence for homeless individuals with substance use disorder, further marginalizing them while adding the traumas associated with the abuses of incarceration and increasing potential exposure to illicit addictive substances or those who can provide them


political coalitions formed by middle and upper class communities reject proposals to fund social services through systemic reforms out of concern for their tax burdens and property values


So on and so forth. In a system like this, we can’t really isolate any single thing as the cause or even cleanly carve out a discrete set of causes. In fact, we can keep unpacking each phenomenon as the product of an even more granular network, like pointing out that the political coalitions are comprised of local politicians and property owners navigating the forces of housing and labor markets through digital media as information exchange platforms.
Each actor or agent influences how other actors and agent’s have the capacity and incentives to act. When we consider this model of social phenomena, it becomes increasingly hard to see addiction or substance use disorder as solely a health issue within an individual’s mind-body duality. I would argue that this guides us away from hyperindividualized, radically materialist perspectives of lived reality and towards concepts like interconnectedness and impermanence, which are found very commonly in the “Eastern” traditions” before being crudely adapted into “Western spirituality.”

recovery/glossary/acute-stress-disorder-.title: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD)
recovery/glossary/acute-stress-disorder-.content:
Overview
Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a short-term mental health condition that generally develops in the first month after experiencing or learning about a traumatic event. Symptoms include anxiety, intrusive thoughts, avoidance, and dissociative symptoms that interfere with the activities of daily life.
Links

Cleveland Clinic

recovery/glossary/adaptive-coping.title: Adaptive Coping
recovery/glossary/adaptive-coping.content:
Overview
“Adaptive coping” refers to the pattern of choosing methods to manage suffering or problems that are better than the alternatives. Someone who feels mild anxiety in social settings might have a drink to loosen up at a networking event, which could be considered adaptive in an environment where extroverted behavior is the expectation and drinking is the norm. If that same person continues drinking after work to deal with any anxiety they have about their career and future, we might begin categorizing that as a “maladaptive behavior” instead.
History and Etymology
In 1990, Bruce K. Alexander published “The Empirical and Theoretical Bases for an Adaptive Model of Addiction” that argued addiction itself can be an adaptive mechanism to certain psychosocial circumstances. Virtually by definition, addiction is considered a pattern of substance or process use that an individual feels compelled to continue even after observing the consequences and wishing to stop. It seems logical at face value to consider it maladaptive by definition, but Alexander’s paper asks us to consider what the development of an addiction might be an adaptation to.
Recall that “adaptive” doesn’t mean healthy or normal, but just a choice that appears to be the best in a particular circumstance. Someone who experiences uncontrollable panic attacks might adapt by drinking often, which might increase baseline anxiety and irritability but decrease the occurrence of these attacks. Someone who lives in cycles of poverty without a clear way out might adapt through substance use, which provides extremely reliable pleasure and relief in a community where no other kind might be available, particularly if the individual is struggling with other health issues like Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and lacks access to adequate interventions. Someone trapped in an abusive and traumatizing environment might similarly use substances as the only method to feel in control of their own experiences.
With this framework, we can consider more options both prevention and treatment than assuming the problem lies solely in a brain that learned the “wrong” lessons.

recovery/glossary/adaptive-treatment-str.title: Adaptive Treatment Strategy
recovery/glossary/adaptive-treatment-str.content:
Overview
An adaptive treatment strategy (ATS) involves tuning treatment plans based on a patient’s history of responses to previous treatments. Chronic diseases and health conditions that require ongoing management and long-term coordination implicitly follow an ATS, but some patients may also have an explicitly specified ATS.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2739674/

recovery/glossary/adderall.title: Adderall
recovery/glossary/adderall.content:
Overview
Adderall is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant that uses mixed amphetamine salts to increase dopamine and norepinephrine levels in the brain. It’s most commonly used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy, usually through improving focus and impulse control. In the United States, adderall is classified as a Schedule II drug as it has high potential for becoming part of a substance use disorder, so it requires a prescription for controlled doses that stabilize chemistry rather than producing a high. Even if taken exactly as prescribed, over a long period of time, the body can adapt to it so that sudden cessation leads to withdrawal symptoms like fatigue and depression.

recovery/glossary/addicere.title: Addicere
recovery/glossary/addicere.content:
Overview
From classical Latin, addicere meant roughly “to be given over” and was used in the context of someone being given over to a creditor as a slave to pay off their debts. It also was used in the context of divination to reveal the will of gods as a means of describing the strong devotion it took to perfom augury rituals. In its simplest uses, it could just mean to have a strong preference towards something.
History and Etymology
John Frith (1503-1533) is the first author we’ve found to use “addict”:
“Be not partially addict to the one or the other, But judge them by the scripture”
In this case, he uses “addict” in a way we might consider interchangeable with “biased”. As the word caught on amidst an early Protestant wave that sought new terms for concepts to describe their theology, it was seen as an action rather than a force. You could “addict” yourself to something, rather than “addiction” seizing control of you. In doing so, it occupied a space between an irresistible compulsion and a freely voluntary choice.

recovery/glossary/addiction.title: Addiction
recovery/glossary/addiction.content:
History and Etymology
“One of the defining features of addiction is an impairment of self-control: addicts are people who (to all appearance) find it especially difficult to bring their behavior into line with their best judgments. Addicts often report a loss of control, and theorists have often used the language of loss of control to describe addiction.” - Neil Levy, Addiction and Self-Control: Perspectives from Philosophy, Psychology, and Neuroscience

recovery/glossary/addictive-personality.title: Addictive Personality
recovery/glossary/addictive-personality.content:
Overview
An “addictive personality” is an informal collection of traits that are considered to place someone at a high risk of developing an addiction. These might include a strong preference for novelty-seeking and risk-taking behaviors, high emotional sensitivity that can compel a desire for immediate relief, or alignment with high-stress roles in professional and personal lives.
It should be noted that there is no clinical term or diagnosis for an “addictive personality.” It emerged primarily out of pop-psychology through memoirs and armchair theorizing about the kinds of persistent psychological mechanisms that raise someone’s risk of developing an addiction. There is no single profile or personality type that has been empirically validated so that it can be described as an “addictive personality,” even if researchers find that certain traits are associated with a higher risk of addiction.

recovery/glossary/adenosine.title: Adenosine
recovery/glossary/adenosine.content:
Overview
Adenosine is one of the four components of RNA and forms adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as the main source of energy in human cells. It directly interacts with dopamine pathways and reward circuits in our brains, which can be disrupted through chronic substance use. Adenosine can function as a kind of “brake” for excessive dopamine signaling, so if it depletes in the course of a dopamine surge from a substance or process, its receptors become desensitized as well. Once dopamine flows without breaks from adenosine, the brain reduces overall dopamine receptors to protect itself, which then lowers the brain’s baseline dopamine production. This leads to dampened rewards experienced from daily life while fueling cravings for more of the addictive substance or process.
Caffeine directly blocks adenosine receptors, so the brain’s natural dopamine prduction flows more freely. The brain responds by building more adenosine receptors, which is how tolerance for caffeine builds over time and fatigue headaches set in when suddenly stopping. On the other hand, alcohol floods the brain with adenosine by blocking a protein, called the ENT1 transporter, that would remove extra adenosine. This explains how caffeine and alcohol can both be addictive to the brain and interfere with dopamine pathways while also producing the exact opposite effects in terms of alertness and sedation.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5767594/

recovery/glossary/adjustment-disorder.title: Adjustment Disorder
recovery/glossary/adjustment-disorder.content:
Overview
Adjustment disorders refer to a pattern of atypical strong reactions to changes or events that usually involve intense stress. Someone might find that they begin to feel depressed or act unusually reckless. Separation anxiety is one way that adjustment disorders can manifest, particularly in children.
Links

www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/adjustment-disorders/symptoms-causes/syc-20355224
my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21760-adjustment-disorder

recovery/glossary/adolescence.title: Adolescence
recovery/glossary/adolescence.content:
Overview
“Adolescence” refers to a transitional stage of development between childhood and adulthood, suggesting that a process of “maturing” has started. The World Health Organization formally defines the age range for adolescence as between 10 to 19 years old, but studies show that the brain continues significant development that impacts independence and judgment into the 20s.
History and Etymology
The stage of adolescence comes with a lot of new impulses that are difficult to regulate with a brain still developing the mechanisms associated with stable judgment and long-term thinking. Many cultures have acknowledged that this liminality between childhood and adulthood is a sort of crossroads for a growing human in which their impulses can meet dangerous temptations that they struggle to resist. This can include substance use and risky behavior, though the idea of what constitutes risky behavior is of course subject to cultural influences. In 19th century Western medical institutions, masturbation was treated as a psychological problem relating to a lack of self-control that should be developed in adolescence. Repeated indulgence was thought to form unhealthy habits, similar to gambling and drinking alcohol.

recovery/glossary/adverse-childhood-expe.title: Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE)
recovery/glossary/adverse-childhood-expe.content:
Overview
Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are events or situations experienced by minors that could potentially have caused trauma or other lingering effects that impact one’s health and wellbeing.
The 10 core types of ACEs currently used are physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, physical neglect, emotional neglect, intimate partner violence, household substance misuse, household mental illness, parental separation or divorce, and incarcerated household member.
History and Etymology
While the concept of childhood trauma is an old one, the exact term “Adverse Childhood Experience” was coined by a CDC-Kaiser study in 1998 that surveyed over 17,000 adults found that nearly two-thirds had at least one ACE, which dramatically changed the assumption among many medical practitioners that trauma with lasting health impacts was rare. The idea to measure ACEs started in 1985 at a Kaiser Permanente obesity clinic where Dr. Vincent Felitti observed that the majority of patients who rapidly regained the weight they dropped had experiences severe childhood abuse, suggesting that eating habits were linked to coping mechanisms that provided safety, comfort, and/or relief. Studies have since showed that an increase in ACE scores is correlated with a drastic increase in the risk of developing chronic disease as an adult.
The 10 ACE types above are directly lifted from the CDC-Kaiser study from 1998, so some modern frameworks have tried to expand ACEs to include systemic issues and community trauma, like racism, bullying, and economic hardship. The original 17,000 adults surveyed were mostly middle-class Americans with education and health insurance.
Links

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11522112/

recovery/glossary/aerosol.title: Aerosol
recovery/glossary/aerosol.content:
Overview
A mixture of either liquid or solid particles suspended in a gas.
Many substances are consumed through aerosols, such as e-cigarettes and cannabis, but also traditional medications like some metered-dose inhalers (MDIs) used for asthma. Compared to digestion or other forms of consumption, aerosolized delivery of a substance goes to the bloodstream faster through the lungs. The specifics of the compounds determine what part of the ear-nose-throat system they land in for absorption. As a result, studying the impact of aerosolized substance use requires studying the effects that aerosolization itself has on substances prior to entering the body. It’s also hypothesized that the rapid delivery of the substance into the bloodstream plays a role in reinforcing substance use patterns with stronger behavioral reinforcement.

recovery/glossary/affect.title: Affect
recovery/glossary/affect.content:
Overview
In the context of psychology, “affect” refers to the observable external expressions of someone’s internal emotional and mental state. That can mean facial expressions, body language, tone of voice, etc.
Types of affects used in the Mental Status Examination (MSE) for clinical purposes include:


Broad/Normal Affect


Restricted/Constricted Affect


Blunted Affect


Flat Affect


Labile Affect


Inappropriate Affect


Congruent Affect


Incongruent Affect


Commentary

recovery/glossary/affective-world.title: Affective World
recovery/glossary/affective-world.content:
Overview
“Affective world” (also referred to as “affective landscape”, “affective environment”, and “Umwelt”) describes the subjective emotional filter through which every piece of reality is interpreted.
For instance, “I am safe” might be a subconscious baseline in an affective world in which trauma is absent or managed well, whereas “I am under constant danger” might be the baseline for someone who has unresolved negative impacts from past trauma. In the first person’s affective world, well-intentioned criticism might only lead to fleeting irritation. In the second person’s affective world, the criticism might be seen as preceding a threat of abandonment or discipline. Another example is social anxiety. To the first person, a crowded room might be seen as energizing with many opportunities to socialize. To the second person, the room might seem like a place where threats could come from any direction, so they might scan for exit routes or more secluded spaces.

recovery/glossary/agape.title: Agape
recovery/glossary/agape.content:
Overview
Agape is a Greek word that refers to an ultimate form of love that’s unconditional and self-sacrificial. Within Christian scriptures and philosophical literature, agape is used to describe God’s unconditional love for humanity that humans should aspire to practice for each other.
History and Etymology
Ancient Greek had several different words for “love” depending on the context and relation. “Eros” refers to romantic passionate love, while “philia” refers to brotherly love or friendship.

recovery/glossary/ageism.title: Ageism
recovery/glossary/ageism.content:
Overview
Ageism refers to prejudices or biases against older adults that can lead to discrimination. Unlike most other prejudices around immutable characteristics, all healthy adults eventually experience some degree of ageism over time.
Ageism can be a barrier to accurate diagnoses in older adults, since some of the symptoms of chronic substance use can align with stereotypical expectations for older adults or symptoms of dementia, such as memory loss and frequent falls. Public health campaigns discussing the dangers of substance use or pathways to treatment are focused on younger people and prevention.
Discrimination can work the other way as well. A distinct set of organizations (Young People in Alcoholics Anonymous, or YPAA) formed to support younger people in Alcoholics Anonymous as the traditional demographics skewed towards older people, and there was often a sentiment that younger alcoholics had not experienced enough consequences, or hit “rock bottom,” to be ready for reform. While younger people may not have the extensive history of drinking, they can definitely have had the trauma and rapid-onset of substance use disorders to benefit from treatment and peer support.

recovery/glossary/agency.title: Agency
recovery/glossary/agency.content:
Overview
“Agency” refers to the capacity to act. In everyday terms, we might use agency to describe an individual’s autonomy.
To imprison someone is to deprive them of the agency to freely move and participate in society. As children grow, they feel a stronger sense of agency over the environment around them through both experience and brain development. Medical euthanasia gives people with terminal health conditions the agency to decide a more peaceful or pleasant end to their life.
Because action is central to our human understanding of change in the world, agency and its related concepts (such as free will) are central to practically every metaphysical framework that’s applicable to human experiences. We can find discussions about thoughts, intentions, actions, and agency in the works of Aristotle.
Philosophers tend to break down agency into types including:


intentional agency


unintentional agency


mental agency


shared agency


collective agency


relational agency


artificial agency


Commentary
Agency is potentially the thorniest aspect of discussing the ethics and metaphysics of addiction.
Consider that we might label an instance of someone having sex with someone who passed out drunk as sexual assault, but we would pursue criminal charges against someone who passed out drunk behind a wheel. In both cases, someone clearly has impaired agency, but we might feel very differently about how that connects to responsibility and accountability. Susan Dimock addresses this issue in 2012 by noting that we can expand our concept of agency beyond someone’s choices in the present moment. If someone goes to a bar while intending to drive themselves home after, it seems fair to hold them responsible for the consequences after that even if their agency later was impaired. If someone goes to a bar and gets blackout drunk, they didn’t preemptively consent to having sex with anyone, so we can still examine it as sexual assault that violates consent.
Addiction by its modern definition involves compulsions that are thought to impair agency by interfering with standard reward pathways and compulsions. We might not want to say someone planned to develop a substance use disorder, but neither can we say that someone has no agency in addressing the way the deal with their substance use patterns, which can include denial of more severe usage and association with consequences. In many Alcoholics Anonymous groups and related literature, addiction is described as a “disease of the will” that has to be remedied with embracing the will of a Higher Power. The Serenity Prayer is often recited at the end of the meetings precisely to define the limitations of individual human agency in the universal order.
Links

plato.stanford.edu/entries/agency/

recovery/glossary/agitation.title: Agitation
recovery/glossary/agitation.content:
Overview
“Agitation” in everyday use refers to a state of restlessness, tension, and nervousness or excitement. However, the term has clinical significance as well that can feel much stronger than the casual use of it you might be more familiar with.
A 2024 paper posits that “Agitated individuals can be dangerous to themselves and others, making agitation an emergency. Acute presentations of agitation can include restlessness, inability to stay calm, paranoia, suspiciousness, irritability, hostility, confusion, disorientation, inability to communicate, changes in vital signs, and violent behavior.”
The DSM-5-TR defines agitation as “Excessive motor activity associated with a feeling of inner tension. The activity is usually nonproductive and repetitious and consists of behaviors such as pacing, fidgeting, wringing of the hands, pulling of clothes, and an inability to sit still.”
The federal Food and Drug Administration has borrowed the International Psychogeriatric Association’s definition of agitation for dementia that includes pacing, rocking, restlessness, yelling, profanity, grabbing, shoving, throwing objects, hitting self or others, repetitive mannerisms, etc.
The International Experts’ Meeting on Agitation in 2016 acknowledges the lack of consensus around a definition for agitation, though they did provide a working description as “a state where patients cannot remain still or calm, characterized by internal features such as hyperresponsiveness, racing thoughts, and emotional tension; and external ones, mainly motor and verbal hyperactivity, and communication impairment.”
Agitation is also distinct from, but related to, aggression. In fact, aggression is sometimes defined as “behavioral expression of severe agitation with the potential to cause harm to oneself or others.”
If you’re using agitation in an everyday context, you might not mean anything as serious as clinicians and researchers do when discussing the agitation associated with a health condition. It’s good to be mindful of that distinction when reading literature.
Links

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493153/

recovery/glossary/agonist.title: Agonist
recovery/glossary/agonist.content:
Overview
An agonist is a molecule that mimics the behavior of a bodily compound as it binds to cell receptors and triggers a biological response.
A full agonist produces as much response as possible from the cell. A partial agonist produces a weaker response. An inverse agonist produces the opposite response of a regular agonist once it binds to the same receptors. A co-agonist activates the receptors in conjunction with another molecule.
Methadone, a full opioid agonist, and buprenorphine, a partial opioid agonist, are highly effective Medication-Assisted Treatments (MATs) for those with Opioid Use Disorder (OUD).
Vareniciline is a partial nicotinic agonist that can ease withdrawal symptoms while making smoking less rewarding, while standard Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) products like patches, gums, and lozenges are full nicotinic agonists.
Benzodiazepines are GABA agonists prescribed for panic disorders and acute withdrawal symptoms.
Buspirone is a partial serotonin arguments commonly used to treat Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) since it’s non-addictive and doesn’t form physical dependence.

recovery/glossary/ahimsa.title: Ahimsa
recovery/glossary/ahimsa.content:
Overview
Ahimsa comes from Sanskrit and means “non-harming” and is commonly translated as “nonviolence,” though it refers to forms of harm beyond just physical violence.
History and Etymology
The Early Vedic religious practices were developed around 1500-800 BCE, and many  included animal sacrifices, or “yajna.” This didn’t mean violence in general was permissible, but rather that the permissiveness was extremely context-specific. The ritual, the victim, the presence of experts to monitor the procedures, the mantras, and the intended purpose all changed the religious status of the sacrificial killing. It might be understood as a necessary but dangerous act that required care and expertise to carry out successfully. The Brahmanas detail discussions of sacrificial killings leading to potential injury, pollution, and spiritual contamination. Arguably, there was already an anxious ambivalence surrounding any kind of killing within Vedic communities, so ritualizing it allowed a way for killing to be contained by elaborate methods that took it out of the context of daily life. I think it’s important to keep that anxiety over killing in mind, given how we have a tendency to see humans of the past as more crude and violent than our purportedly advanced selves today.
The Upanishads of the Late Vedic period contain some of the earliest occurrences of “ahimsa” as an ethical concept as part of a relocation of sacrifical rituals into the internal world of the self. Rather than sacrificing physical objects into a literal fire, living life by virtues was seen as a sacrifice itself. Namely, these virtues are tapas (austerity), dana (generosity), arjava (sincerity), ahimsa (non-harming), and satya (truth). This is also the period where a spectrum of religious traditions emerge from ritualistic householding to ascetic renunciation.
In the Jain tradition, ahimsa is developed as a foundational systemic principle to minimize injury to all living beings, which can lead to a very extensive set of rules based on a broad concept of what “living” means. Buddhism takes a less consequentialist approach by asking about the intentions behind harmful actions. Brahmanical yogic traditions consider ahimsa not just part of a doctrine of virtue ethics but part of a disciplined practice to achieve personal transormation. Accordingly, the goal is not just have a compassionate disposition to others and oneself, but to cultivate a mode of being that is no longer organized around harm, possession, or disturbance. Many Hindu schools of the Advaita Vedanta tradition argue that harm stems from the ignorance of misidentifying oneself with a limited ego instead of part of a greater ultimate reality, as it is simply illogical to cause harm to the same ultimate existence one is a part of.
