recovery/glossary/aian-american-indians-.title: American Indians and Alaska Natives (AIAN)
recovery/glossary/aian-american-indians-.content:
Overview
“American Indians and Alaska Natives” (AIAN) is a demographic category defined by U.S. federal government standards as ” having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America (including Central America), and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment.”
History and Etymology
In 1977, the United States Office of Management and Budget (OMB) adopted the Standards for Maintaining, Collecting, and Presenting Federal Data on Race and Ethnicity for consistency in demographic data across government. This established four categories for race: American Indian or Alaskan Native, Asian or Pacific Islander, Black, and White. It also established Hispanic and Not of Hispanic Origin as the two ethnicites. If you feel that this is not necessarily the most thorough classification system for grouping people of similar backgrounds and identities together, you are not alone.
Officials and agencies were free to allow or provide more specificity, so many who fell under the American Indian or Alaskan Native category would provide specific tribal affiliations as forms would permit. As of 2026, there are 575 federally recognized tribes, but the term can be used by anyone who self-identifies with indigenous tribal heritage regardless of federal recognition.
“American Indian” has a legal legacy as a term used in federal treaties and statutes, and it remains in usage for the sake of continuity and consistency despite the frequent confusion with the term “Indian American.” The term “Alaskan Native” (changed later to “Alaska Native”) was appended because the indigenous communities of Alaska have a distinct cultural and legal history than indigenous nations of the continental United States, though the two groups have shared a unique sociopolitical status with claims to ancestral lands occupied by the U.S. government and its citizens.
Some revisions and changes have been made since, notably in 1997.
Links

civilrights.org/blog/the-decades-long-fight-for-accurate-race-and-ethnicity-data/

recovery/glossary/akathisia.title: Akathisia
recovery/glossary/akathisia.content:
Overview
Akathisia refers to a severe restlessness that produces an uncontrollable urge to move around, such as pacing, rocking, fidgeting, or constant shifting.
Within substance use disorders, it can be both a risk factor and a complication of withdrawal. Medications that block dopamine receptors like antipsychotics or alter serotonin levels like SSRIs can trigger akathisia. It’s also possible for withdrawals from opioids, alcohol, benzodiazepines, and stimulants to provoke akathisia as one’s neurochemistry undergoes rapid changes. At the same time, someone who experiences akathisia might end up self-medicating with those very substances to alleviate the physical and mental discomfort, which can quickly become a rapid spiral of using substances to avoid the symptoms caused by using the substances. It’s unfortunately possible for akathisia to be mistaken for worsening psychiatric symptoms, which can lead doctors to increase the dose of medications that trigger it.

recovery/glossary/akrasia.title: Akrasia
recovery/glossary/akrasia.content:
Overview
Akrasia is sometimes translated as a lack of self-control, but it specifically is used in a situation where one intentionally acts against their own judgment. In active addiction, for example, someone may have complete understanding of all the consequences of using a substance again and have a sincere desire not to, but a craving might be so overwhelming that they give in.
Those like Socrates via Plato argued that people acting against their own interest is the result of ignorance as they necessarily choose whatever feels like the best choice. Aristotle instead believed internal conflict in people could explain seemingly contradictory facts, like knowing something is bad for you but doing it anyways.

recovery/glossary/alcohol-tobacco-and-ot.title: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs (ATOD)
recovery/glossary/alcohol-tobacco-and-ot.content:
Overview
Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs (ATOD) was a designation that emerged in the 1980s to capture emerging trends in neuroscientific studies that showed alcohol, nicotine, and other substances shared biological mechanisms that impacted the brain’s reward system. In 1985, the American Public Health Association (APHA) officially created an Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs Section that repeated terms like “chemical dependency” and “substance abuse.” The phrase was intentionally crafted to explicitly categorize alcohol and tobacco as drugs and tackle the assumption that legal and illicit substances were inherently different.
In 1989, the United States Congress passed The Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act (DFSCA)  which requires all educational institutions receiving federal funding to create prevention programs for substance use. One vendor for these Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention Programs (DAAPPs) was D.A.R.E, or Drug Abuse Resistance Education. D.A.R.E. adopted the ATOD framework guide three categories of responses, usually through an umbrella narrative that alcohol and tobacco were “gateway drugs” to illicit substances.

recovery/glossary/alcoholism.title: Alcoholism
recovery/glossary/alcoholism.content:
Overview
Alcoholism refers to the compulsive and habitual consumption of alcohol in spite of worsening consequences, health or social.
The history of terms used to describe compulsive and habitual substance use are as varied as presentations of substance use disorders themselves. “Alcoholism” and “alcoholic” have a lot of baggage that produces a lot of stigma, though some groups, particularly Alcoholics Anonymous (A.A.), embrace the term as one that can bring unity among their fellowship. Sharing at a meeting usually begins by announcing “my name is… and I’m an alcoholic/addict.” SMART Recovery, Recovery Dharma, Refuge Recovery, and other groups either forego this tradition or discourage its usage to create distance from the stigma. “Alcohol use disorder” is more commonly used in clinical contexts. For the purposes of this site, “alcoholism” is often used for brevity and interchangeably used with “alcohol use disorder” or “substance use disorder” in hopes of diluting the stigma.
History and Etymology
Magnus Huss termed habitual drunkenness as “Alcoholismus Chronicus”, from which we get the term “alcoholism.”

recovery/glossary/alexithymia.title: Alexithymia
recovery/glossary/alexithymia.content:
Overview
Alexithymia literally translates from Greek as “a lack of words for emotions,” coined in 1973 by the Greek-American psychiatrist Peter Sifneos. A similar description of a phenomenon had been created by earlier French clinical psychoanalysts like Pierre Marty who noticed some patients presented with physical illnesses but couldn’t articulate their internal emotional reactions to it, instead speaking almost entirely in literal operational terms (“pensée opératoire”). Sifneos similarly observed that some patients struggled immensely with traditional psychotherapy that came to a standstill if emotions couldn’t be identified and processed.
Just two years later in 1975, Henry Krystal formally discussed alexithymia in his research into the internal world of people with substance use disorders, arguing that they tended to experience emotions as chaotic physical states rather than psychological feelings. Under this framework, drugs were a physical chemical shield that substituted for the cognitive mechanisms responsible for managing intense emotional experiences.
This led Edward Khantzian to propose the oft-cited Self-Medical Hypothesis in 1985, which has worked its way into general public discourse through “self-medicating.” Khantzian used Krystal’s connections from alexithymia to substance use as evidence that addiction is generally a self-regulation disorder where individuals learn that substances are predictable solutions to coping with unmanageable internal states. How often do we hear someone say “I need a drink” after a stressful day at work? That’s arguably a mild form of self-medication that addresses stress with an external substance.
In the 1980s, Graeme Taylor, Michael Bagby, and James Parker proposed the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS) as a tool to empirically measure degrees of alexithymia. Early surveys shows that it presents in about 5-10% of the general population, but up to 78% of people seeking treatment for substance use disorders. Since then, modern neuroimaging through fMRIs have shown that presenting with high alexithymia scores correlates with reduced activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which is responsible for connecting bodily states with emotional awareness.
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37712663/

recovery/glossary/alignment.title: Alignment
recovery/glossary/alignment.content:
Overview
“Alignment” as a concept has wide applicability in psychology, self-help, spirituality and religion, and recovery circles. In general, it refers to bringing different components of an overall system into coordinated functionality. Some examples include alignment of mind-body-soul, of internal values with external behaviors, and of oneself with one’s environment.
History and Etymology
One of the earliest concepts of misalignment in modern clinical psychology comes out of cognitive dissonance theory, advanced by Leon Festinger in 1957, which posits that when people’s behavior contradicts their internal beliefs, they experience psychological distress. Though it doesn’t explicitly use the concept of alignment, we can easily see how the language of misalignment can be applied to the mismatch between internal and external realities.
In 2011, Mary Leamy and a team of researchers who proposed the CHIME Framework after a meta-analysis of 97 papers from 13 countries led them to identify five core components of recovery processes:


Connectedness: a sense of belonging fueled by supportive relationships, community participation, and social inclusion


Hope and optimism: a belief that change and recovery are possible, which often involves role models and aspirations


Identity: a sense of self based around one’s positive attributes that challenge external and internalized stigma


Meaning: a pursuit of purposeful existence guided by personal values, principles, and philosophies


Empowerment: a sense of agency, autonomy, and authority over one’s life that allows decision-making according to one’s strengths and values


“Alignment” as a term is used explicitly when referring to the mapping between daily actions and the CHIME components, especially for Identity and Meaning.

recovery/glossary/allostasis.title: Allostasis
recovery/glossary/allostasis.content:
Overview
Allostasis is the active process through which the body anticipates changes and adjusts itself in an effort to maintain stability. As the body undergoes perceived changes in its environment, the brain constantly adjusts hormones, neurotransmitters, and signals throughout the nervous system. For instance, when exercising or physically working, the body raises its blood pressure to ensure it can keep up with the increased pace of activity.
When someone uses substances, the brain experiences a spike in dopamine and other neurotransmitters that are countered with chemicals like corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) to protect oneself from overstimulation. In brief intermittent uses, this means the body eventually returns to a baseline, but chronic usage can permanently lower the baseline such that substances are used to alleviate a low mood rather than achieve a high mood. Allostasis describes the process through which these internal parameters are adjusted by the body in response to exposure from the environment, and the term “allostatic load” is used to describe the long-term effects on the body from these changes.
History and Etymologu
The origin of the concept of allostasis is closely tied to community-level health observations that found stressful events correlated heavily with chronic health issues developing later in life. While we might take this for granted, it was often thought prior to Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer’s work that a reduced mortality rate when young would correlate with more chronic diseases later in life. Instead, Sterling and Eyer found that groups experiencing the most social disruption, such as unemployed Americans struggling with financial instability and African-Americans struggling with the interpersonal and systemic impacts of racism, were also the most likely to develop hypertension. Previously this was hypothesized to be a result of genetic predisposition, but Sterling and Eyer countered with a mind-brain-body model that connected external stressors to internal physiological changes and long-term health consequences. The model of homeostasis didn’t explain why blood pressure didn’t return to a normal state after fluctuations throughout the day and instead responded primarily to the presence or absence of stressors. Chronic stress could also lead to long-term changes in blood pressure, suggesting a form of adaptation and self-regulation that the idea of a steady baseline the body seeks a return to can’t explain. The cumulative damage incurred by a body under chronic stress is often called an “allostatic load.”

recovery/glossary/allostatic-load.title: Allostatic Load
recovery/glossary/allostatic-load.content:
Overview
“Allostatic load” refers to the cumulative damage the body experiences as a result of chronic stress, often measured by blood pressure, cortisol levels, cholesterol, blood sugar, and inflammation. These can manifest in everyday life as increased symptoms of anxiety or depression, higher risk of heart disease and diabetes, and persistent fatigue.
Substance use disorders come with intense allostatic loads that can lower the baseline ability to receive pleasure from daily activities as the brain repeatedly tries to counteract overstimulation by releasing chemicals that can depress moods. Instead of using substances to achieve a high or a euphoria, someone might begin using substances just to feel their earlier baseline rather than

recovery/glossary/ambivalence.title: Ambivalence
recovery/glossary/ambivalence.content:
Overview
Ambivalence refers to the state of holding mixed feelings or thoughts, though it is often incorrectly used to mean “indifferent” rather than “conflicted.” For instance, one might really love their family but also experience a lot of stress talking to them, which means that the idea of interacting with them can feel conflicting. Another common example is wanting to quit a job that feels unbearable but also finding the financial instability of unemployment unbearable.

recovery/glossary/amnesia.title: Amnesia
recovery/glossary/amnesia.content:
Overview
Amnesia is a loss of memory or information connected to physical or psychological trauma. Contrary to stereotypical media portrayals of amnesia, it is not associated with a huge change in personality, identity, or intelligence. Amnesia tends to be categorized as either retrograde amnesia, meaning memory loss before the date of a traumatic event, or anterograde amnesia, meaning an inability to form new memories for long-term use. More specific labels can be used as well: transient global amnesia for a sudden onset of temporary memory loss, dissociative amnesia associated with stress and loss of personal information, childhood amnesia over recalling memories of early life (which isn’t uncommon), and post-traumatic amnesia after some kind of damaging neurological event leads to disorientation and confusion. It is also possible for someone to experience a combination of these or for amnesia to present in a complex form that operates at different layers.
Substance use can also trigger episodes of amnesia; drinking until blacked out is a form of drug-induced anterograde amnesia where someone might be awake and conscious with access to past memories but no ability to transform short-term memory into long-term memory. Blackouts are often described as either fragmentary blackouts with bits and pieces being remembered, in which case some people refer to them as “brownouts,” or en bloc blackouts where no memories at all are recorded over some period of time. This generally happens because substances like alcohol and marijuana directly impact the receptors in the hippocampus region of the brain, which plays a dominant role in filing memories into long-term storage. In severe cases of chronic substance use, permanent amnesia can set in through conditions like Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome which has a comparable memory loss pattern to dementia.
At the same time, people who suffer from dissociative amnesia after traumatic events can turn to substance use as a form of self-medication. Dissociative amnesia is thought to be a form of psychological self-defense in which the brain blocks out traumatic memories that are too overwhelming to process, but it doesn’t prevent the confusion or distress that arises from experiencing that dissociation. Amnesia in general weakens someone’s ability to recall information from the past that would be relevant for future choices, which can impact how individuals choose to use substances despite past consequences. The brain leans increasingly on unconscious and automated habits that can involve substance use.

recovery/glossary/amor-fati.title: Amor Fati
recovery/glossary/amor-fati.content:
Overview
“Amor fati” translates from Latin to “love of fate,” reflecting an attitude of embracing everything that happens in life whether it involves pleasure or pain. It’s a phrase that invokes a lifestyle of radical acceptance of the world in order to empower oneself into action every moment.
History and Etymology
A popular misconception is that “amor fati” is ancient Stoic motto, but the major Stoic philosophers like Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus wrote their works in ancient Greek. The ideas of Stoicism certainly played an influential role in the development of the term and concept, but it’s a far more modern invention.
The phrase was actually coined by Friedrich Nietzsche, who was likely inspired by Ralph Waldo Emerson’s beliefs about transcending external limitations by aligning one’s will to something independent of them, and Baruch Spinoza’s concept of “Amor intellectualis Dei,” which translates to “love of God or Nature” as a love for everything that happens in the universe as a necessary unfolding of its existence. Nietzsche, whose philological background exposed him to ancient Stoic metaphysics, derived a thought experiment called the Eternal Recurrence in which time is an infinite loop so that every person is bound to repeat every moment of their life for eternity. The only way Nietzsche could handle the existential anxiety of this idea, as he suffered from many physical health issues throughout his life, was to move beyond traditional Stoicism that focused on “tolerare,” or the enduring of hardship, and into an active love for the role suffering plays in life. To give meaning and even love to that suffering made the idea of repeating it forever more tolerable. He also sought to find empirical evidence for his thought experiment, eventually forming an argument relying on the Law of Thermodynamics to reason that a finite number of particles over an infinite amount of time would achieve and repeat every possible combination of their arrangements.
Nietzsche didn’t use the term often though. Robert Greene, a pop psych author, popularized the term in his books like The 48 Laws of Power (1998) and The 50th Law (2009) for high-powered ambitious individuals as a type of strategy for setbacks. Rather than processing the typical emotions around a problem or a defear, one could simply embrace it as something meant to happen for a reason in order to pivot into a new strategy. Ryan Holiday, a former research assistant for Greene, blurred the lines of its origin in his works like The Obstacle Is the Way (2014) and The Daily Stoic, tying “amor fati” directly to the lineage of Stoic writers like Aurelius and Epictetus. The Daily Stoic sells merchandise like brass medallions that are marked with “Amor Fati.”

recovery/glossary/analgesia.title: Analgesia
recovery/glossary/analgesia.content:
Overview
Analgesics are compounds that relieve the experience of pain while maintaining consciousness. Anesthetics cause the loss of consciousness, so while anesthetics are routinely used in surgery, analgesics are used to address pain in a more ordinary daily context. Colloquially, analgesics are referred to as “painkillers,” and they can come in the form of opioids, NSAIDs, and acetaminophen so they have the potential to be addicted.

recovery/glossary/anhedonia.title: Anhedonia
recovery/glossary/anhedonia.content:
Overview
Anhedonia is the state of being unable to experience happiness or joy. This is in sometimes conflated with alexithymia, which is the inability to articulate the emotions someone might be experiencing. Someone with alexithymia might physically feel a fast heartbeat but not be aware if it’s fear or excitement. Someone with anhedonia doesn’t feel reward or pleasure when engaging with activities that ordinarily give people pleasure, like spending time with loved ones or eating their favorite food. It can be tied to depression or trauma, which means it can be temporary. In fact, in cases of severe depression, both can occur such that someone can neither experience happiness nor realize that they don’t experience happiness.

recovery/glossary/anorexia-nervosa.title: Anorexia Nervosa
recovery/glossary/anorexia-nervosa.content:
Overview
Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder in which someone restricts their consumption of sustenance leading to a low enough body weight that health issues can arise. This can be a result of an extreme fear of gaining weight, often fueled by body dysmorphia in which someone can persistently feel overweight or in possession of too much fat even while presenting as skinny or seeing metrics establishing that they’re underweight. Anorexia has the second-highest death rate of any mental health condition, with the first being opioid overdose, as the malnutrition and mental distress associated with it can lead to fatal heart conditions and a high occurrence of suicide. It can also lead to a cessation in menstruation.
Much like substance use disorders, those with anorexia experience changes to their brain that make the disorder much more than just lifestyle choices or destabilizing insecurity. Studies show that people with anorexia have notable reductions in various parts of the brain that, and these reductions are two to four times larger than the variation of brain proportions found in individuals with other mental health conditions. This means a combination of physiological treatments and mental health interventions are deployed to address recovery from anorexia.
The most effective treatments known for adolescent anorexia involve family-based treatment (FBT), where 60% achieve full clinical remission as defined by achieving a healthy weight and normal eating patterns. Up to 87% at least achieve partial remission. This is twice as effective as individualized Adolescent-Focused Therapy (AFT). 75-90% of those who recovered through FBT maintained a healthy weight and, as applicable, regular menstruation long-term.
For adults, enhanced cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-E) can have medium-to-large effects on reducing compulsive thoughts, restricting diet, and potential purging behaviors. Trials show that 60% of adults who undergo a 40-week protocol achieve substantial recovery; in a study evaluating virtual-first CBT-E, 50% of adults achieved at least 95% of their expected body weight. Specialist Supportive Clinical Management (SSCM) is an alternative approach that structures clinical exams, nutritional edu ation, and practical therapy focused on symptom management. The Maudsley Model of Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA) is a specialized therapeutic interventions focused on cognitive and emotional aspects of one’s mind that sustain anorexia like perfectionism. Studies show that these approaches generally have similar effectiveness in long-term recovery outcomes.

recovery/glossary/answerability.title: Answerability
recovery/glossary/answerability.content:
Overview
Answerability in philosophical discourse refers to the responsibility an agent has in providing rational justifications for their actions. For instance, an animal can’t articulate a reason for its actions, so even though we can attribute actions to it and deliver consequences as a form of accountability to learn from, so it might not make sense to assign moral responsibility to it. Similarly, a toddler can’t provide a moral justification or reason for their actions as they lack the cognitive ability to consider abstract ethical principles, even if they can understand agency and consequences. Of course, there are plenty of grey areas and subjective evaluations when we apply this to adults who have at some point had the capacity to evaluate ethical principles.

recovery/glossary/antagonist.title: Antagonist
recovery/glossary/antagonist.content:
Overview
Antagonists are substances that block or reduce the body’s biological response by binding to cell receptors to stop other chemicals from binding to it, applicable to both natural chemicals produced by the body as well as external chemicals called agonists. In some cases, antagonists can displace chemicals already in the body to prevent ongoing reactions. Beta-blockers are a form of antagonists that block adrenaline from increasing blood pressure and straining the heart. Antihistamines, as the name suggests, block histamine receptors to reduce the itching and swelling that accompany allergic reactions.
Naloxone, or narcan, is one of the most critical antagonists used to prevent overdoses by instantaneously blocking opioid receptors.

recovery/glossary/anterior-cingulate-cor.title: Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC)
recovery/glossary/anterior-cingulate-cor.content:
Overview
The anterior cingulate cortext (ACC) is a part of the brain involved in decision-making, reward anticipation, and impulse control, all of which factor into substance use disorders. After chronic substance use, the gray matter involved in detecting harmful decisions can atrophy while the regions that process negative emotions can become hyperactive. The combination leads to difficulty in associating the choice to use a substance with harm while also feeling strong urges to seek relief to strong negative emotions. The neurotransmitter glutamate is used to communicate with the striatum that facilitates habit-formation through reward processing, and chronic substance use disrupts the glutamate receptors so that the habits associated with compulsive substance use solidify. When processing a substance, the ACC is hyperactivated, and when resisting compulsions to use again, the ACC is hypoactivated. Over time, the ACC reassigns salience, or the perceived significance, from natural survival needs and long-term goals to addictive substances or processes that provide a strong reward.

recovery/glossary/antidepressants.title: Antidepressants
recovery/glossary/antidepressants.content:
Overview
Antidepressants are a class of medications that target the production of monoamine neurotransmitters like serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine which are thought to be associated with depression and anxiety.
The old biological theory of depression posits that an imbalance between these is responsible for depression, and this is still the narrative commonly found in the public consciousness thanks to pharmaceutical marketing campaigns, but the consensus in research circles is that reality is more complex. Consider that if you take aspirin to address a headache, we wouldn’t necessarily say you had an aspirin-deficiency. Yet, this was the assumption made by researchers and clinicians upon observing that providing patients with drugs that boosted their serotonin levels also improved their symptoms of depression. In 2022, a study led by Joanna Moncrieff at University College London analyzed decades of data and found no consistent evidence that low serotonin levels were the cause of depression.
Instead, modern research is interested in neuroplasticity and neurogenesis as explanations. The inflammation and floods of cortisol from chronic stress is thought to drop a protein called Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) which stimulates the repair and rebuilding of neural pathway. Antidepressants might work by increasing the activity of BDNF over the course of weeks or months; this means that they can increase neuroplasticty, but not that they automatically provide feelings of happiness without a psychosocial framework that takes advantage of the brain’s capacity to change.

recovery/glossary/antisocial.title: Antisocial
recovery/glossary/antisocial.content:
Overview
“Antisocial” in the context of psychology and psychiatry refers to a pattern of disregard for the rights and wellbeing of others. While it might be used casually to refer to introverted dispositions or self-isolating behavior, the [[diagnostic-and-statistical-manual-of-mental-disorders|Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders]] lays out specific criteria for Antisocial Personality Disorder that manifest before the age of 15 outside of episodic co-occurring disorders:


Failure to conform to social norms and lawful behaviors


Deceitfulness through lying for personal gain


Impulsivity or failure to plan ahead


Irritability & Aggressiveness including physical assaults


Reckless disregard for safety for oneself or others


Consistent irresponsibility such as a failure to maintain a work ethic or meet agreed-upon obligations


lack of remorse through indifference or rationalization


Individuals diagnosed with ASPD are almost 8 times more likely to develop substance use disorders as the general population, though this shouldn’t be taken to mean that most people with substance use disorders have antisocial personality traits. Instead, psychologists consider that someone with ASPD and substance dependence are both part of an externalizing spectrum of vulnerabilities around behavioral control. Those on the externalizing spectrum are more likely to express their negative feelings outwardly through actions rather than inwardly through depression or anxiety. Both disorders are connected to impaired or reduced activity in the prefrontal cortext that’s responsible for judgment and self-control, which then amplifies short-term rewards over long-term consequences. They’re also related through low serotonin levels that fuel irritability and impulsivity that can drive a desire for instant relief despite consequences. ASPD often features a low baseline for emotional activation that presents as boredom or feelings of emptiness.
A 2012 twin study found that the genetic risks of ASPD have two dimensions:


disinhibition factor: this measures a genetic predisposition towards impulsivity and novely-seeking behaviors that heavily overlaps with substance use disorders


agressive-disregard factor: this measures a genetic predisposition towards irritability and a lack of empathy that can result in physical outbursts


Other twin studies find that the factors involved in the causes of antisocial behaviors shift dramatically based on age. When under 15, twins experiencing juvenile delinquency show that shared environments through family dynamics, community trauma, and socioeconomic status play a big role in the behaviors that meet the ASPD criteria. In early adulthood however, the influence of shared family environments declines almost entirely while genetic factors and environmental factors such as specific trauma or peer groups are seen as more dominant drivers. In short, we might expect teens to act out impulsively and destructively in response to a traumatic environment, but whether that baseline continues into adulthood depends a lot on genetic factors and individual trauma. It has similar heritability to conditions like bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
Commentary
Frank Cotton, The Hellbound Heart
[[the-hellbound-heart|The Hellbound Heart]] by Clive Barker can be interpreted as a depiction of an extreme case of unmanaged ASPD told through the lens of Gothic transgression. I’ve elsewhere given an interpretation of the character of Frank Cotton that compares his desire to experience something transcendental beyond what normal earthly sensations can provide to compulsive substance use to experience any change at all to in intolerable present state. Frank can also be seen as a stereotypical case of ASPD, as we find out that, unlike his twin brother, even as a teenager he lacked the baseline rewards from ordinary life, which compelled him to try riskier and more hedonistic options to feel something. At the same time, there’s a strong stigma attached to ASPD that can deter individuals with it from seeking treatment to the benefit of both themselves and the society they are antisocial within. Cognitive therapies addressing ASPD often reframe an individual’s approach rather than their desires, so even though they may have the desire to do something illegal for personal gain, they can pause and reason that other legitimate avenues to personal gain can be more sustainable. It appeals to rational self-interest rather than attempting to frame a disregard for others as a cognitive distortion to be challenged. With characters like Frank, it can be easy to dismiss those with ASPD as born rotten, especially when heritability studies are interpreted to mean someone was doomed to be destructive rather than at-risk.

recovery/glossary/antitoxic.title: Antitoxic
recovery/glossary/antitoxic.content:
Overview
“Antitoxic” refers to compounds and processes that act to neutralize something identified as toxic.
History and Etymology
In the early 1900s, physicians like George Pettey and Ernest Bishop argued that chronic substance use should be studied as:
“A disease, a toxemia, of drug, auto- and intestinal origin, the management and treatment of which belong to the field of internal medicine and not to neurology. The vital and essential principle of the treatment advocated is elimination.”
Links

 The Narcotic Drug Diseases and Allied Ailments: Pathology, Pathogenesis, and Treatment

recovery/glossary/anxiety.title: Anxiety
recovery/glossary/anxiety.content:
Overview
The American Psychological Association defines anxiety as “an emotion characterized by apprehension and somatic symptoms of tension in which an individual anticipates impending danger, catastrophe, or misfortune. The body often mobilizes itself to meet the perceived threat: Muscles become tense, breathing is faster, and the heart beats more rapidly.”
When used as a casual shorthand, anxiety is often interchangeable with fear in general or Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), in which someone experiences chronic and uncontrollable anxiety across multiple areas of life that lasts longer than six months in ways that disrupt daily life. However, the two cases are very distinct; anxiety as an emotion is considered a normal response to specific stressful event like a public speaking obligation, but generalized anxiety involves chronic worry about a wide variety of things without a specific stressor. GAD also comes with distinct physical sypmtoms like restlessness, frequent or constant fatigue, muscle aches and headaches, and trouble sleeping.
Links

www.apa.org/topics/anxiety

recovery/glossary/anxious-attachment.title: Anxious Attachment
recovery/glossary/anxious-attachment.content:
Overview
Anxious attachment is a type of attachment style in developmental and relational psychology that’s characterized by deep fears of rejection or abandonment. This can result in seeking constant validation or reassurance in the desire for close intimacy, observed through overthinking, people-pleasing, low self-esteem, and “clingy” behaviors. Anxious attachment styles are often thought to develop out of inconsistent or unpredictable attitudes from caregivers in childhood. Children who observe sudden swings between warm and cold treatment from their parents or guardians can end up insecure in their attachments without constant temperature checks.

recovery/glossary/apatheia.title: Apatheia
recovery/glossary/apatheia.content:
Overview
“Apatheia” is a term that originates from ancient Greek Stoic philosophy in which one’s state of mind is undisturbed by passionate temptations. While the current term “apathy” seems derived from “apatheia”, “apathy” has a connotation centered around negative indifference while “apatheia” is closer to stability and composure.

recovery/glossary/applied-behavior-analy.title: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA)
recovery/glossary/applied-behavior-analy.content:
Overview
Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is a discipline that studies the way behaviors are learned and reinforced by one’s environment, especially as a form of therapy. It’s commonly used with developmental disorders or autism spectrum disorder (ASD) as an evidence-backed modality that involves positive reinforcement to reward desired behaviors while reducing undesirable ones.
A core model for ABA is the ABC model that tracks an Antecedent (what happens before the behavior), Behavior, and Consequence (what happens after the behavior). This lends itself easily using data to drive and evaluate the reinforcement patterns. Specific protocols include:


Discrete Trial Training (DTT)


Pivotal Response Treatment (PRT)


Early Start Denver Model (ESDM)


Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA)


In the United States, ABA practitioners must have credentials achieved through the Behavioral Analyst Certification Board (BACB). Generally, these practitioners tend to be:


Registered Behavior Technician


Board Certified Assistant Behavior Analyst (BCaBA)


Board Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA)

recovery/glossary/armchair-expert.title: Armchair Expert
recovery/glossary/armchair-expert.content:
Overview
An armchair expert is someone who has no training or experience in a particular subject but provides commentary or critique as if one does. It’s why I try to emphasize that I have no inherent qualification that makes me better than anyone else at interpreting the evidence I look like, and I characterize my work as a series of amateur and opinionated literature surveys.

recovery/glossary/assay.title: Assay
recovery/glossary/assay.content:
Overview
An assay refers to a laboratory test used to measure the presence of some target, such as a drug, protein, or cell.
Qualitative assays are generally binary, reporting either the presence or absence of a target. Quantitative assays measure the relative concentration or absolute amount of a target.
In the context of addiction, assays are used as tests to detect specific drugs or their metabolites (the compounds that a drug breaks down into once it has been processed, or metabolized). They’re a standard part of initial clinical assessments to confirm which substances might be in a patient’s system as well as the relative concentration. Illicit substances, and even legal substances from companies that don’t comply with safety regulations, often have dangerous additives that the patient may not be aware of. Fentanyl is among the riskiest of these additives. Treatment providers use the results of these assays to calculate the initial detoxification plans and the medication dosages that are most appropriate for the patient’s condition. It also allows providers to check if patients are taking their medications as prescribed. In the case of multiple substances that might cross-react in ways that complicate assay results, advanced assays may be necessary.
Assays are also valuable from a legal perspective, as child custody cases, professional licensing boards, and probation all use assays to help determine if someone has been compliant with the requirements.
Just the act of random drug testing with assays can be a reliable psychological deterrant against use.

recovery/glossary/assertive-communicatio.title: Assertive Communication
recovery/glossary/assertive-communicatio.content:
Overview
Assertive communication refers to expressing yourself clearly without passively downplaying your boundaries or aggressively imposing your needs on others.

recovery/glossary/ataraxia.title: Ataraxia
recovery/glossary/ataraxia.content:
Overview
“Ataraxia” is an ancient Greek term that translates roughly to “lack of disturbance,” so “tranquility” and “equanimity” are often used as the translations. Different Greek philosophies interpreted ataraxia differently, with Stoic philosophers like Seneca often using it interchangeably with “apathaeia” though Epicurean philosophers would challenge that.

recovery/glossary/atman.title: Atman
recovery/glossary/atman.content:
Overview
Atman is a Sanskrit word referring to a true inner core of a living being upon which temporary aspects of existence like body, mind, and ego are constructed. Within most Hindu theology and cosmology, the atman is immortal and is reborn into cycles of living, usually until the realization of one’s true nature liberates oneself into unity with Brahman, or the ultimate reality.
This is also one of the biggest points of divergence between Hinduism and Buddhism as belief systems heavily reliant on impermanence and interconnectedness. Buddhism rejects that there is a permanent soul-like aspect to our existence in the first place, instead using the concept of anatta or anatman to refer to a “not-self.”

recovery/glossary/attachment-theory.title: Attachment Theory
recovery/glossary/attachment-theory.content:
Overview
Attachment theory refers to a framework of understanding the way our development influences our attachments within relationships. While the conventional formulation of attachment theory tends to separate styles into secure, anxious, avoidant, and anxious-avoidant with a strong emphasis on childhood development, modern researchers tend to see anxiety and avoidance as continuous spectrums subject to neuroplasticity. That means healthy relationships and positive experiences can help adults achieve “earned security” in their connections with others. Modern psychologists have also moved away from centering the relationship between infants and mothers to include all family members, community caregivers, peer groups, and early romantic engagements as having influence over the dimensions to attachment.

recovery/glossary/attention-deficit-hype.title: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
recovery/glossary/attention-deficit-hype.content:
Overview
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is widely defined as a neurodevelopment disorder that impacts executive function and makes it difficult to sustain attention, regulate emotions, and manage impulsivity. In most cases, ADHD is genetic with a heritability rate of 80%, thought it has sometimes been observed to occur in adults who experience traumatic brain injuries (TBIs). Diagnosing ADHD can be difficult since many other disorders can be responsible for symptoms that include impulsivity and difficulty maintaining focus.
As of the DSM-V, ADHD comes in three primary presentations:


Predominantly Inattentive: overlooks details, makes careless mistakes, has difficulty focusing on a single task, losing focus when spoken to without competing distractions, fails to complete tasks or follow instructions as written, struggles with organization and deadlines, expresses reluctance to start tasks that might require long periods of focus, losing track of essential items for life or work, easily distracted by external stimuli or internal thoughts, forgets to complete daily activities for living


Hyperactivity-Impulsivity: fidgeting and squirming while sitting in place, trouble sitting still during occasions where remaining seated is expected, pervasive restlessness, appearing uncomfortable when not in motion, talking excessively, interrupting people to finish sentences or answer a question, struggling to wait in a queue, impulsively uses other people’s things without asking


Combined: criteria for Inattentive and Hyperactive-Impulsive are both met with neither having a clear predominance


ADHD and substance use disorders both are characterized in part by a shortage of neurotransmitters along reward pathways. Specifically, brains with ADHD struggle to produce and transport dopamine and norepinephrine, which address our ability to focus, retain motivation, and experience the sensation of a reward for completing a task. The prefrontal cortex then struggles with impulse control, future planning, and emotional regulation. Consequently, those with ADHD are at a higher risk of developing substance use disorders both because of an increased impulsivity to experiment with substances and to bridge the natural deficiency in dopamine. It’s common to find that those with both disorders had been using substances to self-medicate, whether it’s stimulants to provide an artificial boost to clear brain fog or depressants to mute the brain’s hyperactivity and anxiety. Some studies show that as many as 25% of people in substance use disorder treatment also have ADHD.
Commentary
Anecdotally, it’s extremely common for people to only find out in treatment that they had been dealing with ADHD, among other disorders, their whole lives. The failure to screen for these disorders in childhood and provide children with adequate treatment is obviously one of the most glaring flaws in our approach to addressing mental health. We save a lot of time, money, resources, heartache, and suffering when we address health concerns at the earliest possible moment instead of leaving someone to self-medicate in far costlier and more dangerous ways.

recovery/glossary/attention.title: Attention
recovery/glossary/attention.content:
Overview
“Attention” is one of those terms that suffers from being used so often that it has numerous definitions put forward by different institutions.
From Lindsay, 2020:
“Attention is the important ability to flexibly control limited computational resources. It has been studies in conjunction with many other topics in neuroscience and psychology including awareness, vigilance, saliency, executive control, and learning.”
From Krauzlis et. al, 2023:
“We define attention as ‘the set of evolved brain processes that leads to adaptive and effective behavioral selection.’ Our emphasis is on understanding the biological and neural echanisms that make the behavioral properties of attention possible.”
Links


 Attention in Psychology, Neuroscience, and Machine Learning (Lindsay, 2020)


 What is attention? (Krauzlis et. al, 2023)

recovery/glossary/attributability.title: Attributability
recovery/glossary/attributability.content:
Overview
With addiction, the debate around attributability centers on whether chronic substance use as a disease impairs judgment enough for addictive behaviors to no longer be attributable to someone’s core character, comparable to a brain injury or dementia. Most with a substance use disorder genuinely want to quit and live a sober life, but they struggle with cravings and withdrawals intensely enough that they also struggle to align their behaviors and intentions. A few may not have any desire to quit or have any regard for the consequences of using, even if it affects others or could lead to their own death.
Those with an addiction are also generally able to articulate their reasoning for using which satisfies the answerability pillar of moral responsibility. However, we can also see that cravings and withdrawals can operate as strong forms of pressure, similar to how someone who feels like they’re starving or dying of thirst might commit acts of violence in order to get food and water. They can answer questions about their justification for the actions, and they might be able to do so without being hypocritical; “I only wanted to use it one last time before quitting” might be a flawed idea, but it can seem quite logical under the pressure of cravings that feel intolerable.

recovery/glossary/avoidance.title: Avoidance
recovery/glossary/avoidance.content:
Overview
Avoidance in a psychological context is a coping mechanism where someone either acts or fails to act in a way that evades an unwanted experience. In the short-term, this serves as a coping mechanism that provides immediate relief in response to a distressing encounter, but in the long-term, this can end up reinforcing avoidance as a reaction instead of addressing the roots of triggers.

recovery/glossary/avoidant-attachment.title: Avoidant Attachment
recovery/glossary/avoidant-attachment.content:
Overview
Avoidant attachment refers to a style of attachment that’s characterized by hyper-independence when encountering stress or the prospect of emotional intimacy. Historically, under conventional attachment theory frameworks, the avoidant attachment style is thought to emerge from a pattern of neglect or rejection from caregivers in response to a child’s needs, leading the child to believe they must handle their difficulties themselves in order to maintain a relationship.

recovery/glossary/axiom.title: Axiom
recovery/glossary/axiom.content:
Overview
An axiom is a proposition that serves as a starting premise for a line of reasoning or argumentation.
Commentary
Kurt Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem is thrown around a lot in lay debate contexts, which I myself am guilty of, and I don’t have strong foundations in the philosophy of math to comment too heavily on it, but the high-level consequences of it are very relevant to the limitations of logical reasoning.
In short, Godel proved that a formal system cannot prove its own consistency, so any set of axioms we propose as a logical system cannot end up proving its own validity. At some point, we are forced to rely on some concept akin to intuition or faith in order to arrive at our axioms from which we can then construct a system that we vet for consistency and completeness. I found this revelation to be impactful on a personal level.
Rebecca Goldstein, a philosopher who wrote the biography Incompleteness: The Proof and Paradox of Kurt Godel, noted that Godel himself hated a mechanistic view of the world that distilled everything into rational algorithmic processes. Human intuition was often approached as either random noise or an evolutionary development, stemming from a combination of genetic predispositions and environmental conditioning to approximate rationality. My own background skews heavily towards the computations of intelligence; to me, this intuition is fundamentally what separates a machine from a sentient organism. A computer can only detect the logical blind spots that its programmed axioms permit it to explore, whereas a human can use intuition to detect a failing in logic even before they can articulate the logical proof or rationale for exploring it.
Alan Watts, a philosopher who occupies a space in popular counter-cultural movements that sought to reconcile New Age spiritual mysticism with Western scientific revelations, has frequently invoked and consequently popularized Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem in public discourse. Watts criticizes the “Western” impulse to “define and conquer” the world by placing new concepts within the bounds of a familiar hyperrationalist system that neutralizes intuition, mysticism, and subjective expression as immeasurable byproducts of a messy organic brain. I’ve made many of the same criticisms myself. It leads to reductionism that deflates the nuances of new ideas.
For instance, Western cultures are highly predicated on the moral-psychology of Abrahamic religions that affirm strong dualistic binaries, such as Heaven against Hell, sacred against profane, good against evil, etc. When we examine Eastern belief systems like those of Hindu sects through this lens, the notion of devas and asuras collapses into “angels” and “demons,” which is radically different. Within Hindu cosmology, devas and asuras are born of the same father and different mothers, with the former representing a transcendental presence of harmony through unity and the latter representing a materialist presence of chaos through division. The moral-psychology of sorting the world into good and bad is itself an ideology associated with the asuras. Yet, both are required to continue the motion of the cycles that sustain the universe as it exists.
In axiomatic terms, Abrahamic moral-psychology posits the existence of a definite good and definite evil locked in a moral war. Hindu moral-psychology posits order and chaos as inherent parts of the universe and the self, such that destruction of the agents of chaos is a destruction of the self, so self-discipline and evolution are necessary to navigate these conflicting forces. The goal is not thus to kill off one’s ego the way one would want to kill off the compulsion to “sin,” but to understand the ego’s purpose in driving one’s actions while ensuring it adheres to a higher purpose than its own satisfaction. This sounds abstract, but it directly influences how we see concepts like punishment, justice, retribution, change, repression, and other threads that compose our daily moral fabrics.

recovery/glossary/barbiturate.title: Barbiturate
recovery/glossary/barbiturate.content:
Overview
Barbitutares are a class of nervous system depressants that have a sedative-hypnotic effect inducing relaxation and drowsiness. They were commonly used in the past to address anxiety disorders and insomnia but have since been replaced with safer alternatives like benzodiazepines. Barbiturates are considered to have a high risk of addiction, severe withdrawal if stopped suddenly, and overdose. Phenobarbital is the example that’s usually most familiar to people as a medication to address seizures. Pentobarbital is sometimes used in veterinary medicine.

recovery/glossary/bath-salts.title: Bath Salts
recovery/glossary/bath-salts.content:
Overview
“Bath salts” actually have nothing to do with baths. They refer to a class of stimulants called synthetic cathinones derived from the khat shrub that grows in East Africa and southern Arabia. Manfacturers that were intending to evade drug enforcement laws disingenuously marketed their products as “bath salts” so that they could argue they were never intended for consumption. Some cathinones have been approved as medication, such as bupropion which you might recognize as Wellbutrin, which can treat Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and nicotine cravings. Ongoing research is attempting to see if bupropion can address stimulant use disorder too.

recovery/glossary/bed-sores.title: Bed Sores
recovery/glossary/bed-sores.content:
Overview
Bed sores are injuries to the skin and underlying tissue that result from being stationary in a single position for a long period of time. The constant weight applied to a single area can constrict blood flow, and certain postures can lead to skin and bones being slid in opposite directions. In extreme cases, it can lead to deep sores and wounds that expose muscle, tendons, and/or bone. This can be seen in some people with substance use disorders as heavy intoxication or compulsive processes like gaming lead to fixed positions for hours or even days. Other conditions like severe depressive withdrawal can also lead to someone lying in bed for similar lengths of time. Malnutrition and substances that constrict blood vessels can increase the risk of developing sores as well.

recovery/glossary/bedside-manner.title: Bedside Manner
recovery/glossary/bedside-manner.content:
Overview
“Bedside manner” refers to empathetic communication skills that clinicians exercise to build trust with patients. Historically, the stigma around substance use disorders has led to an assumption that punitive measures must be taken to correct someone’s behavior. Recent studies show that labeling substance use as “substance abuse” is still associated with less empathy and more punitive attitudes in a clinical setting. Despite what the latest research has shown, a prevalent prejudice is that pain and suffering are just par for substance use and even a component of successful recovery. This can be completely counterproductive as people with substance use disorders and co-occurring conditions face enormous stigma that discourages seeking treatment or efforts to recover. Patients fearing stigma can underreport symptoms or avoid seeking care out of fear of judgment or punitive medical practices.

recovery/glossary/behavioral-economics.title: Behavioral Economics
recovery/glossary/behavioral-economics.content:
Overview
“Behavioral economics” is a field that incorporates psychology into economic theories and models instead of assuming humans are purely rational actors. It accepts as a constraint the fact that humans have limited time, information, and resources to make decisions, so they often settle for what seems “good enough” rather than finding the optimal choice. Even when we try to optimize, we might arrive at a “good enough” assumption of the optimal path. We also have a litany of biases at work, such as loss aversion that treats negative experiences as more impactful than positive ones or cognitive shortcuts like stereotypes.
Addiction has posed a big challenge for traditional economics since it cannot possibly seem rational to acknowledge that a substance or process could ruin your life and present no long-term gains but choose it anyways. Behavioral economics attempts to model addiction through additional concepts, such as delay discounting that argues people weigh immediate rewards heavily over future ones. The immediate physical relief that a substance or process provides is heavily favored over the abstract delayed benefits of sustained sobriety. Another useful concept is bounded self-control which describes the limits people have to resist temptations as stress, fatigue, and external pressures can wear down their decision to abstain.
At the same time, some really impactful treatment designs have come out of the emphasis on behavioral interventions. Behavioral Activation (BA) is one of the most effective ways to help people not just struggling with substance use disorders but depression as well, and it begins by guiding patients into making small but achievable steps towards establishing a positive reinforcement cycle from pleasurable and sober choices. Contingency Management (CM) is one of my favorite concepts for addressing addiction as it simply provides an immediate tangible reward for clean drug tests and participation in treatment, which appeals to the same bias for short-term rewards that substances provide.
Both BA and CM show either comparable or higher effectiveness to cognitive therapies that locate the sources of a patient’s distress within their worldview rather than the incentives in their actual world. In fact, some studies show that trying to combine Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with CM actually leads to worse outcomes, splitting the patient’s focus between cognitive self-assessments and the behavioral rewards that might change cognition. It helps to see CM as a competing economy or choice framework to a patient’s previous framework that made substance or process use seem compelling, which is especially helpful for people whose material problems cannot be reduced to cognitive distortions. “I won’t have enough money to afford food” is addressed immediately when a CM reward provides a grocery voucher while CBT negotiates it as “catastrophizing” or “future-tripping” that can be addressed with coping skills until things somehow work out.

recovery/glossary/behavioral-neurology.title: Behavioral Neurology
recovery/glossary/behavioral-neurology.content:
Overview
Behavioral neurology is a field concerned with the impacts of physical brain changes on memory, thinking patterns, emotional processing, and external behavior. Dementias like Alzheimer’s disease are among the most common conditions addressed by behavioral neurologists, though they deal with all kinds of incidents ranging from strokes to traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) to diseases responsible for sudden personality changes.
The behavioral neurological perspective on addiction concieves it as a chronic brain disorder resulting from structural changes in neural circuits as a result of prolonged substance or process use. Compulsive behaviors emerge as a result of changes in the pathways that govern reward, memory, and self-control. When using a substance, the ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens are flooded with dopamine.

recovery/glossary/behaviorism.title: Behaviorism
recovery/glossary/behaviorism.content:
Overview
“Behaviorism” within psychological circles generally refers to an approach to understanding humans through an examination of their behavioral outcomes.
For empiricists who embrace behaviorist perspectives, assessing a state of mind is impossible except for the end results that can be empirically observed. If someone says they hate ice cream but eats it every day, there is nothing we can conclude about their beliefs that differs from someone who says they love ice cream and eats it everyday. B.F. Skinner is perhaps the most famous foundational behaviorist, who described his philosophy as “radical behaviorism.” Staunch behaviorists might be entirely uninterested in neuroscienctific and psychological models, or see them as theoretical exercises comparable to fictional worldbuilding where a system of logic is clearly at work but only applicable to the real-wold insofar as it is observed. Others might acknowledge them as useful for explaining the mechanisms through which behavior occurs, but not a useful way to explore the independent sources of behavior.
Cognitive scientists and neuroscientists usually reject radical behaviorism, arguing that treating humans like black boxes won’t provide a complete enough explanation to model our attitudes and actions. Humans generally seek explanations preceding behavioral change that work with our mental model of reality.
Commentary
I’m a big fan of behavioral interventions like Contingency Management (CM) and Behavioral Activation (BA), and I’ve expressed criticism of cognitive therapies, but I wouldn’t classify my thoughts as anything resembling radical behaviorism. I really enjoy exploring psychological and neurological models, not just for the sake of intellectual completeness but also because I find it intuitively uncomfortable to treat our internal worlds as black boxes.

recovery/glossary/bender.title: Bender
recovery/glossary/bender.content:
Overview
“Bender” is colloquially used to refer to an extended period of substance use in which someone is almost perpetually under the influence. For chronic substance users, benders can last from days to weeks to months.

recovery/glossary/benzedrine.title: Benzedrine
recovery/glossary/benzedrine.content:
Overview
Benzedrine was the brand name for the first commercially successful synthetic stimulant in the world.
History
In 1927, Gordon Alles injected himself with a synthetic amphetamine in the course of investigating an alternative to ephedrine to address asthma. He published clinical results in 1929 and was granted a U.S. patent for oral amphetamine salts by 1932. The same year, the pharmaceutical company Smith, Kline, & French (SKF) patented a volatile base form of the same chemical before launching an over-the-counter (OTC) version called a Benzedrine Inhaler. In 1935, SKF purchased Alles’s patent and monopolized the manufacturing and distribution of Benzedrine. They released Benzedrine Sulfate as tablets to address depression, narcolepsy, fatigue, and weight loss. The Allies in WWII experimented with Benzedrine rations as a tool to boost the endurance of their soldiers.
In 1951, the United States Congress passed the Durham-Humphrey Amendment which made Benzedrine tablets prescription-only, although the inhalers were still available OTC. Recreational users would open the inhalers to swallow the internal strips, which contained the equivalent of the dosage of dozens of tablets. Jack Kerouac (in)famously relied on Benzedrine and coffee for a three-week nonstop writing marathon to complete his novel On the Road, a stream-of-consciousness inspired by his road trips printed onto a 120-foot long scroll. The Beat Generation cultural movement adopted Benzedrine and amphetamines generally to invoke these altered states of mind.
Unfortunately, amphetamines were quite destructive to the body, and after observing a spike in cardiovascular events related to usage of the Benzedrine inhaler, the FDA banned it in 1965. After Congress passed the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970, the Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs classified all amphetamines as Schedule II controlled substances, which took it out of recreational usage and firmly into the territory of regulated prescription substances. Benzedrine is no longer manufactured today as the brand name drug, but the generic active ingredient amphetamine sulfate are still used in medications to address ADHD, narcolepsy, and obesity. Adderall is probably the most commonly known modern variant of it.
Benzedrine should not be confused with Benzedrex, which are nasal decongestant inhalers that are far less likely to be used dangerously for recreational purposes.

recovery/glossary/betel-nut.title: Betel Nut
recovery/glossary/betel-nut.content:
Overview
Betel nuts are seeds of a palm tree species called Areca catechu that are chewed as a recreational stimulant. It’s the fourth most commonly used substance associated with addiction in the world after alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine. That might be surprising to many in cultures driven by Western trends, but it’s used with relative regularity in South Asian nations and the Pacific islands, particularly for special occasions and local traditions. The market for it is localized and decentralized unlike tobacco, which has massive multinational conglomerates lobbying against regulations.
The World Health Organization (WHO) categorizes betel nuts, through the alkaloid called arecoline, as a Group 1 carcinogen right next to alcohol and tobacco. It’s a leading cause of oral and esophageal cancers among other health issues like tooth decay and painful stiffness in the jaw. The United States outright bans the importation of betel nuts.

recovery/glossary/bigotry-of-low-expecta.title: Bigotry of Low Expectations
recovery/glossary/bigotry-of-low-expecta.content:
Overview
The “bigotry of low expectations” is an oft-repeated phrase that argues that having different expectations for minority groups who have been historically discriminated against is itself a form of discrimination that assumes they are bound to perform worse than their peers. It’s heavily politically charged, with many arguing that it’s used in bad faith against diversity initiatives that factor the skills developed under socioeconomic hardship into someone’s evaluation.

recovery/glossary/binge-drinking.title: Binge Drinking
recovery/glossary/binge-drinking.content:
Overview
Binge drinking is used casually to refer to a period of heavy drinking, but the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines it specifically as drinking enough alcohol to raise blood alcohol concentration (BAC) to 0.08% or higher. That’s also the standard legal limit for driving in the United States. For the average person, this means consuming 4-5 standard drinks in the span of roughly two hours. Anecdotally, a lot of people I’ve met who actively drink overestimate the amount needed before it’s considered binge drinking, or only use the term “binge drinking” in the context of “problem drinking” rather than the “weekend warrior” routine.

recovery/glossary/biohacking.title: Biohacking
recovery/glossary/biohacking.content:
Overview
“Biohacking” is a marketing term that refers to commercialized health trends which repackage health and wellness paradigms with the aesthetics of sophisticated technical optimization.
One of the problems with health and wellness fields is that the ultimate arbiter for the success of any particular practice is the human whose mind-body is being evaluated. If someone is absolutely convinced that a cold water plunge makes them feel better, it becomes true through the strength of the belief alone. After all, they might become quite distressed if they aren’t able to keep up that routine. The mind-body system is also incredibly complex with a lot of reasonable disagreement over the interpretation of different measurements, so it’s possible to find some type of evidence for almost any claim provided you’re willing to look far enough and back enough. It’s very easy to promote correlations between different biometrics as a causal connection, and there’s ample incentive for media institutions to lean into sensationalism over scientific literacy.

recovery/glossary/biopsychosocial-models.title: Biopsychosocial Models (BPSM)
recovery/glossary/biopsychosocial-models.content:
Overview
Biopsychosocial models emerged as health models that consider the connection of biological, psychological, and social dimensions to someone’s lived experiences. It was first advocated for within modern medicine by George Engel in 1977, and it has steadily grown in interest and adoption since. In comparison to the biomedical model that preceded it which prefers mechanistic physiology as the mode of analysis for health, the biopsychosocial model is a more holistic iteration that emphasizes the connection between different angles to life. It’s especially beneficial when managing chronic health issues or conditions that are difficult to precisely define like substances use disorders that can impact multiple areas of life without standard discrete solutions.

recovery/glossary/black-and-white-thinki.title: Black-and-White Thinking
recovery/glossary/black-and-white-thinki.content:
Overview
In clinical settings, black-and-white thinking refers to a type of cognitive distortion where someone thinks in extremes or polar opposites. For example, they might define success on an exam by achieving 100% and anything less to be a failure, or they might go between wanting to break up with a significant other to putting them on a pedestal.
In the context of substance use disorders, black-and-white thinking can manifest as an Abstinence Violation Effect (AVE) which can lead someone who deviates from their standards of abstinence to spiral much harder. “I messed up, so fuck it, I give up” is a very common thought preceding one of these relapses, whereas sometimes people can recognize that they don’t have to let a night of drinking become a whole bender.

recovery/glossary/black-market.title: Black Market
recovery/glossary/black-market.content:
Overview
Black markets are exchanges for products and services that have been outlawed by a state entity.
Historically, government efforts to ban substances like alcohol or addictive processes like gambling tend to shift economic activity into black markets. Localized crime rings or organized crime syndicates often recognize that laws do not remove people’s incentives to pursue illicit activities or contrabrand, so they build alternative economies that take advantage of the limitations of a system to surveil itself. Even the most totalitarian regimes in countries like North Korea fail to successfully crackdown on contraband, although, the price of illicit goods and services can go up to skirt regulations just as they do when complying with regulations.
The United States had a famously disastrous Prohibition of alcohol that led to a constitutional amendment banning alcohol. In practice, bootleg operations filled the gap with poorer quality products that led to an increase in public health issues. Wealthy individuals were still able to procure alcohol for lavish parties while working-class drinkers visited black market sellers. It was enormously profitable for organized crime syndicates that considerably marked up both.

recovery/glossary/blackout.title: Blackout
recovery/glossary/blackout.content:
Overview
A blackout is a period of time in which someone might appear to be functional but is failing to transfer any short-term experiences into their long-term memories, so they have no recollection of what happened during the blackout.

recovery/glossary/block-grant.title: Block Grant
recovery/glossary/block-grant.content:
Overview
“Block grants” in the United States refers to a form of federal funding for programs that delivers money to state governments rather than directly to individual citizens. In theory, this means each state can use the funds to design a program for their unique needs instead of hoping a federal program can manage to fit everyone’s needs. In practice, this can lead to an extremely uneven distribution of services as each block grant then has to go through each state’s own political bureaucracies before reaching the taxpayer at the end.

recovery/glossary/blood-alcohol-concentr.title: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC)
recovery/glossary/blood-alcohol-concentr.content:
Overview
Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) measures the amount of alcohol someone has consumed by testing the weight-to-volume ratio within their body’s bloodstream. 0.08 grams per 100 milliliters, or 0.08%, is generally the legal limit for driving in the United States, which is reached on average after 4 standard drinks defined as 14 grams of pure alcohol, though of course this varies enormously by each individual’s unique body composition. Body mass can make a huge difference, as well as biological sex since women generally have lower levels of enzymes to process alcohol than men of similar body mass.

recovery/glossary/bodhi.title: Bodhi
recovery/glossary/bodhi.content:
Overview
“Bodhi” is a Sanskrit term that roughly means “enlightenment.” Buddhist traditions generally conceive of bodhi as a state free of suffering and endless cycles of rebirth through achieving an enlightened understanding of an impermanent reality and one’s self, or not-self, within it. The Buddha is said to have attained bodhi when meditating and contemplating reality under a fig tree. It is also used as a first name as an auspicious appeal to the wisdom gained from enlightenment.

recovery/glossary/bodhicitta.title: Bodhicitta
recovery/glossary/bodhicitta.content:
Overview
Bodhicitta is a Sanskrit word composed of bodhi, meaning “enlightenment,” and citta, roughly referring to “heart-mind” or “consciousness,” so combined, it means “the heart-mind of enlightenment.” While attaining bodhi as an awakening to the reality of non-duality is the goal of many Buddhist traditions, bodhicitta is the mindset to cultivate in the process which breeds compassion for the suffering of all sentient beings.

recovery/glossary/bodhisattva.title: Bodhisattva
recovery/glossary/bodhisattva.content:
Overview
A Bodhisattva is a Buddhist practitioner who has taken a commitment to delay their own liberation through enlightenment into Nirvana until every other living being has also been able to achieve this liberation. This generally involves taking a vow to demonstrate that one has cultivated bodhicitta, or the heart-mind of an enlightened being.
Mahayana and Zen Buddhism put forward four vows for Bodhisattvas to take:


Beings are numberless. I vow to save them.


Delusions are inexhaustible. I vow to end them.


Dharma gates are boundless. I vow to enter them.


The Buddha’s way in unsurpassable. I vow to attain it.

recovery/glossary/boredom.title: Boredom
recovery/glossary/boredom.content:
Overview
Despite boredom being a universal experience that extends even beyond humans to other species, researchers and clinicians have historically neglected to create a consensus around its definition. In 2012, John Eastwood was part of a team that proposed a framework in a journal called Perspectives on Psychological Science:
“…boredom is best described in terms of attention. A bored person doesn’t just have nothing to do. He or she wants to be stimulated, but is unable, for whatever reason, to connect with his or her environment - a state Eastwood describes as an ‘unengaged mind.‘”
The American Psychological Association references this paper in its online coverage of boredom as a concept.
Links
www.apa.org/monitor/2013/07-08/dull-moment

recovery/glossary/borrachos.title: Borrachos
recovery/glossary/borrachos.content:
Overview
“Borrachos” translates to “drunkards” in Spanish, referring either to a group of people who are actively drunk a group of people who are generally heavy drinkers.
History and Etymology
In 1629, Diego Velazquez completed a Baroque painting for King Philip V that was officially called The Triumph of Bacchus as a depiction of the god of wine Bacchus, the Roman interpretation of the Greek Dionysus, placing a crown on working-class peasants as a symbol of wine providing relief to the grief and misery of daily life. However, to much of the Spanish public, what stood out most were the peasants who seemed to be inviting the viewer to have a drink with them. The painting was referred to widely as Los Borrachos instead as a representation of celebratory drinking rituals that was strongly embedded and institutionalized in many Latin American communities.
