recovery/glossary/confession.title: Confession
recovery/glossary/confession.content:
Overview
The concept of a confession is much deeper than just sharing a secret with someone, which is how we commonly speak of it.
Etymology and History
The New Testament was originally written in Ancient Greek, where the term “homologeo” was used in the place of “confession”. “Homo” means “same” and “logos” means “word”, so from “same words” we actually arrive at the idea of agreeing by saying the same things.
When the Romans were translating this to Latin, they use the word “confiteri”, with “con”/“com” meaning “together” and “fateri” meaning “to acknowledge.” So, the verb “confiteri” meant roughly “to acknowledge together”, and the noun “confessio” meant something like “total acknowledgement.” St. Augustine wrote his “Confessions” in the 4th century right as arguments about translations were happening. He uses it to mean both acknowledging the sins of his past and declaring his love and faith in God.
In Old French, the word “confession” adopted a more specific meaning under the Catholic Church as part of a sacrament to disclose one’s sins to a priest. It’s at this point that we can see how the concept of confession has implications for the way institutions assert control. The schism between Catholicism and Protestantism led the Catholic Church to alter the nature of confessions as a method of tightening control by preserving stricter, more distinct identity of what Catholicism required against Protestantism. The confessional booth was invented by Charles Borromeo to incorporate anonymity and isolation into the act.
By the 16th century, “confession” replaced terms in Old English like “andetnes” (acknowledgment) and was adopted by legal systems to mean a formal admission of legal guilt. European monarchies had begun surveilling their citizens’ participation in church confessions, sometimes requiring written “Confessions of Faith” to be signed. To avoid attending a church confession or signing a written confession would raise suspicions that you could be politically rebellious or traitorous. Criminal statutes inherited this value on confessions, so Eurocentric judicial systems placed a lot of value on being able to get a criminal to issue a confession as the gold standard for evidence or proof. This confession of guilt was literal; the criminals were expected to explain the psychology that drove their actions, not just the mechanisms through which they broke a law.
Those like Michel Foucault argue that in the 19th century, Western institutions secularized confession while preserving its structure as a tool to extract repressed desires and pathologize them. Confessing a “sin” to a priest in a confessional booth was replaced with confessing “perversions” and “sickness” to a professional in a clinical setting. The priest saves your soul from sins, the professional saves your mind-body from symptoms.
As much credit as Freud gets for emphasizing the importance of subconscious processes in psychology, Foucault argues the opposite: psychoanalysis introduced a scientific dimension to a culture obsessed with self-surveillance to inspect oneself for deviations that lead to damnation. Rather than being sexually repressed because we couldn’t confess our desires, we become even more repressed by the incitement to confess these desires in spaces where institutions can monitor and regulate it while also engaging in a public discourse that shapes cultural norms. It’s arguably even more controlling than the confessional, where you at least have the agency in identifying sins as discrete actions connected to higher principles. Within the premises of psychoanalysis is the notion that your subconscious or unconscious mind has the truth that your conscious thoughts are hiding, and you must seek a credentialed analyst to construct truth out of their interpretations or inferences about your mind.
The most recent evolution of confession emerged in the post-WWII mass media space that feuled the growth of the attention economy. Daytime television as a business model is effectively the turning of confessions into content for consumption. In fact, generating attention from confessions actually meant someone’s social capital increases from performing a successful confession. Consider Oprah. The studio assumes the role of a sacred space that was once occupied by a church or temple. Oprah is the recognizable spiritual leader who guides an audience seated in rows resembling pews. Guests coming to confess state the trauma they experienced (or caused), display their true inner feelings as a result of reflection, and then are absolved when Oprah and the crowd cheer for their growth. It’s not even a joke to say that Oprah occupies the same space in many people’s lives as a high priestess would.
Fast forward to 2026, and we see AI-boosted algorithmic analysis and delivery of confession as content to be measured for engagement costs and return-on-investment.
Interpretations
Confessional Technologies
“Confessional technologies” is a term coined by Michel Foucault.
Commentary
Bojack and Ben Affleck
I’m sympathetic to Ben Affleck as a celebrity whose struggles with alcoholism made him a poster boy he didn’t ask to be. My analysis of The Way Back is built on the premise of the movie being a form of confession for him in a format he’s most familiar and expressive with as an actor. It’s not a very remarkable movie if taken at face value, but seeing it as Affleck working through his history with drinking and recovery, as well as the impacts it had on his career and relationships, elevates it quite a bit.
Bojack Horseman is not a show I’m actually very interested in unpacking. While I’m very partial to media criticism and Southern California, I don’t think the show says too much about mental health or addiction that isn’t readily available at face value. There are some slices of it that are helpful to pull out in the context of other discussions, and this is one of those instances. In the first season, Bojack is looking to inject fresh life into his career by publishing a book, though his lack of work ethic and chronic substance use leads to him relying on a ghost writer, Diane. Contrary to his expectations of a glowing PR piece, she writes a deeply flawed portrayal of him through his trauma and bad decisions. Contrary to making him look bad, it’s met with great acclaim by the public who feel a sense of vindication themselves from seeing him as more relatable through his flaws.
The contrast between Ben Affleck, whose project inspires catharsis, and Bojack, whose project still leaves him dissatisfied as to the question of whether he can be a good person, is noteworthy. Confession can still have the catharsis that promotes real healing for an individual, but it can just as easily be a form of trying to raise social capital from a history of developing a portfolio with toxic assets.
Wouldn’t I be a hypocrite if I said managing this site wasn’t doing the same for me?

recovery/glossary/confidentiality.title: Confidentiality
recovery/glossary/confidentiality.content:
Overview
Commentary
Honestly, I don’t really believe that any policy about confidentiality is really confidential.
Alcoholics Anonymous is explicit that communication in groups is not legally privileged in any way and relies on the trust of the fellowship, many of which resemble high school cliques in terms of gossip and drama.
A survey of 500 psychologists conducted by Kenneth Pope showed that 62% of admitted to breaching patient confidentiality at least once accidentally, with 50% believing that confidentiality is the easiest ethical rule to accidentally violate. 8% of therapists admitted that they talked about their clients by name to outsiders. The American Psychological Association reports that 15% of the complaints tracked by the Ethics Committee concerned confidentiality issues. The Association of Marital and Family Therapy Regulatory Boards (AMFTRB) publishes state licensing board data that reveals confidentiality violates and failure to maintain records as the most common reasons therapists face official repercussions for their conduct.

recovery/glossary/contingency-management.title: Contingency Management
recovery/glossary/contingency-management.content:
I fucking love Contingency Management (CM). It is one of the fastest ways to throw a wrench into the works of hyperindividualistic broken-brain models that discourage psychosocial analyses that would lead to systemic critiques and calls for reform.
Overview
Over three decades of research into contingency management interventions has shown that it routinely outperforms Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and 12-step facilitation models. It is the gold standard for stimulant use disorders, which have no FDA-approved medications. Adding CM to Medication for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD) protocols substantially improves cigarette use, medication adherence, illicit opioid use, polysubstance use, and therapy attendance. Even after the external rewards stop, those who completed a contingency management program were significantly more likely to maintain long-term abstinence.
Types
By Reinforcement
Voucher-Based Reinforcement
Stephen Higgins pioneeered this model by awarding points or vouchers for passing drug tests, with each voucher having monetary value that can be used to buy groceries or other goods.
Prize-Based CM (Fishbowl Method)
Nancy Petry designed a stochastic method of contingency mangement that could lower costs: instead of a guaranteed voucher for a set amount, participants who pass a drug test can draw a slip from a bowl that contains anything from encouraging words to a substantial prize (up to $100).
Financial Incentives
These methods cut to the chase and directly exchange money for clean drug tests without constraints on how it’s used.
Clinical Privileges
Found largely in Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) where medications like buprenorphine and methadone exist, these systems give patients more liberty for consistent behavior like doses to take-home as a sign of trust and convenience.
Therapeutic Workplace
Developed by Kenneth Silverman at John Hopkins University, therapeutic workplace programs are evidence-based interventions that provide training and employment as an incentive to maintain sobriety.
Yes, people will literally stay sober if you promise to guide them into a job. Just like people will commit fewer crimes if they have stable employment and housing. Just like people will report a higher quality of life when they don’t have chronic stress building from financial instability.
This is one of the only interventions I’ve found that have incredibly strong empirical support for long-term sobriety and quality of life improvements that addresses the psychosocial causes of substance use, which is alarming since we claim to now work through a biopsychosocial model of health yet completely overlook this in favor of expanding manualized therapies that are less effective.
I’ll put it this way: I have been in psychoeducation classes that consisted entirely of YouTube videos featuring TedTalks and sound bowl ASMR, with facilitators saying, quote, “I get paid either way” if clients say don’t see it as valuable or if one client derails an entire session. We’re not talking minimum wage jobs either; they have proudly quoted $35/hr with free daily meals. This is the same formula as a substitute teacher turning on Bill Nye the Science Guy and turning a blind eye to everyone being on their smartphones. This class might then be followed by one about projection, so that if you did have any feedback about the process, you can learn about how the real problem is you being judgmental to deflect from your own insecurities. Or it might be a class about taking responsibility, though not if it leads you to feeling responsible enough for your recovery that you would try to adjust the treatment you’re receiving. If you really keep pushing as I once did, you’ll get told that you should leave it to professionals since your own judgment got you to where you are, which completely tosses out our biopsychosocial premises in favor of a Puritan moral-psychology that elevates obedience and confession to authority over humanist ideas of treating people as the center their own lived realities.
That exact same hourly wage could have been allocated to helping some of these clients with their career goals. Many have expressed a desire to become peer counselors who can use their own trauma and recovery as experience to guide others, which seems to me far preferable to paying babysitters who will literally use an ASMR stream to get paid while napping.
By Target Behavior
Abstinence-Based
Most contingency management programs aim to test sustained abstinence with urine testing or breathalyzer screenings.
Attendance/Adherence-Based
Some models experiment with rewarding patients for participating in treatment, such as showing up for therapy sessions and taking medications as prescribed, regardless of their drug use.
Goal-Directed CM
Because every individual has their own goals from not just recovery but life in general, these models set up rewards or incentives for completing long-term goals tailored to someone’s specific circumstances, like building a resume or submitting applications for housing.
By Format
Digital CM
Modern devices make it much easier to deliver contingency management programs without requiring visits to a clinic. Remote testing devices and digital cards mean that we can both instantly validate someone’s drug or treatment status and instantly reward them upon completion.
Variable Ratio Schedules
Variable scheduling changes some aspect of reward delivery with respect to time. For instance, if someone has maintained a streak of hitting their goals, the value of the reward might increase as well. If the streak is broken, the reward schedule might reset to square one.

recovery/glossary/dopamine.title: Dopamine
recovery/glossary/dopamine.content:
“Dopamine is an enormously important molecule in addiction, central to th experience of learning and reward prediction, but its functioning is far more complicated than it is commonly portrayed. In a way, the popular stories about dopamine still rely on a circa-1980s level of understanding… For one thing, dopamine is not a ‘pleasure’ molecule: it has more to do with the feelings of desire and ‘wanting,’ not enjoyment and ‘liking’”
Roy Wise, the neuroscientist made famous for identifying dopamine as the pleasure molecule in the wake of the American 1980s crack epidemics, actually retracted the notion that dopamine was a pleasure molecule after more experiments in the 1990s.

recovery/glossary/entheos.title: Entheos
recovery/glossary/entheos.content: In Ancient Greek, entheos is formed out of en (within) and theos (god), forming the phrase “the god within.” It was used to describe people who appeared so passionate or talented that they seemed possessed by some kind of divinity. The word “enthusiasm” comes out of “entheos” and originally referred to operating with something that seems like a divine inner spark.

recovery/glossary/falsifiable.title: Falsifiable
recovery/glossary/falsifiable.content:
Overview
Falsifiable refers to the ability for a proposition to be tested and shown to be false.
For instance, page 58 of the Alcoholics Anonymous Big Book states “Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path,” which is also part of the conventional preamble before meetings. This is unfalsifiable: if someone has remained sober while working the program, it’s proof of the success, but if someone continues drinking, it means they didn’t work the program thoroughly enough. Under this unfalsifiable statement, the program’s effectiveness cannot be challenged through empirical evidence.
History and Etymology
Commentary
A big problem in recovery is that repetition of unfalsifiable cliches or paradigms that lead to continual self-blame rather than practical reforms. Some of these include:


“Your best thinking got you here.” Well, duh, you can’t use anyone else’s thinking except your own. You can take suggestions, but it’s your own thinking that will decide to take them or not. This phrase is generally used as a response to challenges


“It’s not a drinking problem, it’s a thinking problem.”


It can be both, or both can be part of a bigger overarching problem. If we use the widely accepted biopsychosocial model of individual health, there are structural changes caused to the brain from chronic substance use that you cannot reverse simply by following different thought patterns. That’s why behavioral interventions like Behavioral Activation (BA) and Contingency Management (CM) are so effective compared to Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) which focuses on challenging cognitive distortions and irrational thinking.

“It’s not a religious program, it’s spiritual.”

This is one of those statements that might make sense if you come from a background with a hierarchical religious organization, as many Christian families do. It makes less sense if you come from a background with a decentralized syncretic belief system, as many Hindu and Buddhist families do. Devout Hindus do not necessarily have the same mandates to attend organized practices or rituals, and where it does happen, it’s often for the sake of community integration rather than personal belief systems. Also, even within the American legal system, courts have ruled consistently that AA at least includes “general religious content” such that it cannot be mandated as part of a legal punishment without violating the Establishment Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

“You have a case of terminal uniqueness.”

If you claim there’s something unique about your situation that isn’t being factored into a discussion, you can get hit with this dismissal. Arguably, this is in the interest of uniformity and solidarity, but in the same way that every shape can fit into a square peg once you cut enough of it off. It begins with a conclusion and dismisses details that challenge its fundamentals, rather than considering all the details and drawing a conclusion that’s consistent with those details.
Also, while the U.S. Census Bureau estimates that 60% of the population is white, AA’s internal tracking shows that it consistently hovers around 88% white. 86% identify as Christian, with 84% saying they had a pre-existing belief in God beforehand, and the vast majority explicitly use God or Jesus Christ as their Higher Power. The average age of an AA member is 50, with 74% of the organization being over the age of 40. 62% of the members identify as men. 26% have a Bachelor’s degree or higher compared to 35% of the general public. To be blunt, or rather, rigorously honest, this is not a diverse organization. Its culture is rooted in the mid-20th century social networks of white middle or upper class Christian professional men who became skeptical of corporate bureaucracy, medical institutions, and the government. They worked on Wall Street, had surgical practices, led high-powered sales careers, etc. These were people who had immense privilege and opportunity but squandered it in the course of their drinking, not people who had struggled their whole lives against systemic barriers that have nothing to do with their individual conduct.
I’ll simplify my point: the vast majority of people who use this phrase about “terminal uniqueness” cannot describe at a basic level Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Shintoism, or any of the belief systems practiced by billions of people across the ocean. I don’t think you can claim people are all fundamentally the same when you don’t actually understand people who didn’t grow up in the same culture and community as you.

“Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic. This disease is doing push-ups in the parking lot.”

Substance use disorders are generally considered chronic health conditions that are progressive if left untreated. However, a significant number of people who once met the criteria for a substance use disorder eventually don’t, whether it’s the result of abstinence or low-risk moderation. If someone in that category relapses after 30 years, this adage is used to argue that the disease of addiction was always building in the background, and the only way to ward it off is constant hypervigilance that weaves the rituals of AA into daily life. A lot of Americans may not realize how rooted in Protestant theology that is. Early American Puritanism framed the Devil as a constant threat lying in wait behind every daily temptation. To combat this threat, people needed to be engaged in constant spiritual warfare against the “cunning, baffling, powerful” enemy.
“Everything happens for a reason.”
This one is easy to see as unfalsifiable. Either you can find a reason that fits into your worldview, or you can assume one exists but you haven’t found it yet. There’s no way to prove that something happened for no reason.
As humans, we really want to believe this, because the notion of a random universe that is indifferent to our experiences can be scary. It’s much more comforting to imagine there’s a plan or a reason we just aren’t aware of, and some entity with more knowledge and power than us, who cares about us, is administering it. I’m not attempting to discourage religious belief with this, as I do think there are religious philosophers who have a more consistent and coherent worldview than me and I couldn’t claim to refute theirs.  I’m just focusing on the way this is thrown around in isolation as a cliche that essentially dismisses the very genuine and valid feelings someone has who believes in a random or indifferent universe.
Lest you think I’m singling out A.A. or Abrahamic religious systems, here are some from contemporary traditions in psychology and psychiatiry:

“You’re being defensive and resisting the process.”

This can come up in the context of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), where therapists often deliver worksheets or curriculums from manualized intervention protocols intended to develop coping skills. If these don’t align with the patient’s experience, there is no way to falsify the effectiveness of the tool. If the patient agrees with the therapist’s assessment, the intervention works. If the patient is reporting that the coping skills either don’t work or aren’t making sense, the therapist can interpret this as resistance or defensiveness, which is just proof that there’s a deeper truth the patient is avoiding but the therapist must elucidate.

“If you claim to have tried Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and don’t think it works, tell me about the cognitive distortions and core beliefs you’ve challenged before with the tools.”

I’m unsure how someone is supposed to report their own cognitive distortions, because if you recognize something is a distortion, you don’t really have the distortion anymore. If you’ve challenged your core beliefs, you’ve likely reevaluated them into new or modified versions of the core belief. And if neither of those were really your problem to begin with, you simply have nothing to report, which is then seen as proof you didn’t really do CBT correctly. The premise behind this line of argument is that the professional therapist is guaranteed to find distortions or dysfunctional core beliefs if they look hard enough, so a lack of distortions is only proof of a lack of CBT.
It becomes very difficult for anyone to express that CBT isn’t addressing their problems or aligns well with them, especially since general psychoeducation classes are often just rehashed CBT modules with a group-discussion component. If you complete every worksheet and assignment provided by a CBT practice, but still remain depressed or chronically stressed, the only lever CBT provides is that you haven’t adequately challenged enough distortions to uncover the true core beliefs at the root of your suffering. In this way, we essentially have recreated the Christian confessional model of counseling. If you’re suffering, it is because of some sin or flawed core belief that has not been confessed, and the role of the authoritative expert is in eliciting this confession and sorting it into a narrative to change the individual’s conduct. To challenge the ideological underpinnings of CBT in this situation is akin to questioning the existence of God in a confessional booth.
Even if you succeeded in presenting the argument and gained a concession, what have you actually accomplished except upsetting someone with significant control over labeling you as non-compliant? In moments when I’ve completely rationally explained my situation, my reaction, my past distortions and beliefs and how I’ve changed, I’ve literally been asked by a therapist: “so what’s the problem? Why are things going wrong?” Buddy, that’s what I’m fucking paying you to figure out.
Thankfully, I did encounter another therapist who, at the very first session, broke down the difference between insight and capacity, noticed I didn’t struggle with insight into myself but executive dysfunction from co-occurring disorders, and quickly facilitated further evaluation.

“You need to accept that sometimes in life we are going to be overwhelmed and distressed, but we shouldn’t catastrophize about them or try fortune-telling.”

This one is profoundly condescending. A therapist has an extremely limited ability to assess a patient’s life outside of the short hour-long sessions in which they try to communicate their perspective from their lived experiences. Dismissing a patient’s reasonable concerns about a potential catastrophe as low distress-tolerance and rational capacity to assess future risk is incredibly damaging.
In my own case, I’ve had a therapist condescendingly retort that I don’t understand the job market because “you’re 25” when I was referring to a type of job I’ve done for over a decade - longer than they said they had been a therapist. They also thought that I was in too much of a rush to apply for jobs that I knew could take weeks to arrange, reflecting a fundamental out-of-touch perspective that they reiterated often with derogatory remarks about “young people these days” lacking in work ethic. There was no way for me to falsify any of their positions. If I argued that my concerns about sustainable employment in the face of managing new health conditions and a volatile job market were justified, the therapist would read that as resistance to having my cognitive distortions challenged. As I said above, there is no lever that says “your disturbance in response to the circumstances of your life are completely rational and systemic reform is necessary to change those circumstances.”
I credit that experience with helping me feel vindicated in critiquing therapeutic modalities and institutions. The heavy emphasis on individual therapists to determine someone else’s rationality or cognitive distortions invites subjectivity that can be deeply harmful.

recovery/glossary/fascism.title: Fascism
recovery/glossary/fascism.content: In the aftermath of WWII, researchers became interested in potentially identifying markers of a “fascist personality” and even designed some psychometric assessments.

recovery/glossary/geneva.title: Geneva
recovery/glossary/geneva.content: A metonymy (I think) referring to Swiss liquor.

recovery/glossary/gin-craze.title: Gin Craze
recovery/glossary/gin-craze.content: The Gin Craze described several decades of a trend of “rotgut gin” being consumed in increasingly large quantities by the English populace. From Carl Erik Fisher’s book The Urge: Our History of Addiction (2022), gin consumption doubled from 1700 to 1720 and then again by 1729. 1743 had six times the levels of 1700.

recovery/glossary/intertemporal-bargaini.title: Intertemporal Bargaining
recovery/glossary/intertemporal-bargaini.content:
Intertemporal bargaining is a behavioral economics concept that refers to a person making a strategic decision that alters the benefits or consequences of their future self. Eating a whole row of Double Stuf Oreos might seem very appealing in the short-term, and the impulse to act on that might cause you to decide that the sugar intake is a problem you’re willing to pass onto your future self.

recovery/glossary/madya.title: Madya
recovery/glossary/madya.content:
At the time that the Vedas were written, alcohol wasn’t known as a distinct concept. Madya originally referred to something providing exhilaration or intoxication.
In the Charaka Samhita, a foundational Sanskrit text for the Hindu medical system of Ayurveda, alcohol is described as either amrita, implying a medicinal substance, or visha, implying a poisonous one, depending on how it’s used. Consumed correctly in appropriate quantities alongside meals, it might alleviate mental anxieties and make it easier to exert strength. Drinking inappropriately, without constraints or when dehydrated, and it can be toxic.

recovery/glossary/passive-aggressive.title: Passive-Aggressive
recovery/glossary/passive-aggressive.content:
Overview
“Passive-aggressive” refers to a communication style in which someone doesn’t explicitly articulate how they feel while still acting or saying things that suggest they have negative opinions or feelings. Critically, the term did not originate from academic or research circles, but instead emerged in the context of compliance to orders in the United States military.
History and Etymology
WWII
During WWII, military psychiatrists were tasked with evaluating soldiers who resisted orders without openly refusing them. They might have expressed dissatisfaction through visible emotions (called “pouting”), stubbornness before complying with a rule, and a lack of instrinsic motivation to improve efficiency. In some cases, this resistance came in the form of outright noncompliance or sabotage akin to civil disobedience. In 1945, the War Department Technical Bulletin, Medical 203 under William C. Menninger, proposed the term “passive-aggressive” to refer to the hostility or resistance engendered in soldiers who want to resist orders. The model of passive-aggressive behaviors contained two parts: the observed behavior and the inferred (sometimes subconscious) motivations. It appeared under a category called “Immaturity Reactions” and was pathologized as a psychiatric disorder resulting from excessive routine stress. Menninger thought passive-aggressiveness was the most common psychiatric disorder in the military.
After WWII ended, several psychiatric centers under the Veterans Administration (VA) approved the adoption of “passive-aggressive personality” as a clinical term. The War Department Bulletin proposal was reprinted in the Journal of Clinical Psychology in 1946 to introduce it to everyday psychiatry. Shortly after, in 1948, the American Psychiatric Association’s Committee on Statistics set out to esablished an authoritative taxonomic classification of known disorders and diseases. George Raines, who led neuropsychiatry at the Navy Department Bureau of Medicine, argued that the classification system should take in a wide variety of evidence and sources, but it seems the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the DSM-I, was still largely influenced by Medical 203 and related literature from the War Department. Even the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) adopted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1948 drew heavily from the War Department.
DSM-I
The DSM-I description of “passive-aggressive personality” split its reactions into three interchangeable subtypes based on the underlying response to frustration or stress:


passive-dependent: stress leads to helplessness and dependency


passive-aggressive: stress leads to resistance and obstruction


aggressive: stress leads to overt irritation and destructive tendencies


The model underlying the “passive-aggressive personality” still assumes both an immature dependency or frustrated hostility. The notion of treated disorders as “reactions” came out of the work of Adolf Meyer at Johns Hopkins University and Sigmund Freud, using the contemporary notion within psychoanalysis that psychiatric symptoms were the result of emotional disturbances related to childhood development. This framework claimed that stress can lead to the ego being disorganized and anxiety to overwhelm the individual, with the repressed impulses leading to the behaviors described as “passive-aggressive.”
DSM-II
The DSM-II was established in 1968, led by Ernest Gruenberg. By this point, the 8th edition of the WHO’s ICD was also being released, so there was an ambition to align the new DSM with the ICD for consistency’s sake. The “reactions” within the “passive-aggressive personality” were consolidated as a single personality disorder characterized by indirect resistance and hostility. It still drew from psychoanalytic theories, but less explicitly so, partly because the late 1960s had major breakthroughs in psychopharmacology that reinforced the brain’s biological involvement in psychiatric disorders. While psychodynamic perspectives were still strong, there was a growing understanding that the DSM-I’s categorization wasn’t as stable as previously assumed. The ability to treat disorders pharmacologically opened the door to using treatment information to shape diagnoses and criteria.
DSM-III
The DSM-III was completed in 1980 after psychiatrists had been exploring the use of operational or diagnostic criteria.
Samuel Guze relates the story of meeting William Menninger’s brother Karl at an APA meeting delivering a talk. Karl

recovery/glossary/tabula-rasa.title: Tabula Rasa
recovery/glossary/tabula-rasa.content:
Summary
Tabula Rasa translates to blank slate, and it suggests the mind is blank slate on birth that is shaped entirely by the stimuli given from the outside world, and thus the individual self is the product of external conditioning.
Commentary
We as humans tend to take consistently common elements of our lives for granted. Do you deliberate about the sun failing to come up tomorrow? Do you ever worry gravity would suddenly switch off? I would hope not.
We do the same with the ideas and rituals shared within our community. Culture shock can be as disorienting as it is because it challenges the markers of stability in our alignment with the environment.
Tabula Rasa is one such idea. It seems that much of Western Enlightenment philosophy was based on the notion that at the time God creates souls to be placed into bodies, we are blank slates. Even as the societies incorporating these philosophies secularized, the notion of a mind that’s a blank slate remained embedded in public consciousness and philosophical culture. One of these consequences is a “mindset is everything” mentality in which our model of reality can be shaped through a reconfiguration of the mind’s thought processes. As Locke wrote, “Madness seems to be nothing but a disorder in the imagination.” So, in theory, if we can simply “fix” the imagination, we can fix mental ailments.
Those like Thomas Trotter took this as a cue to build relationships with patients that encouraged them to develop new habits in the place of compulsive substance use.
In modern debate culture, tabula rasa is a competitive rule or practice in which a judge will set aside all beliefs and information they gained from the outside world so that the debate determines the parameters of reality. Only the claims and arguments brought up by the debaters in that round will be relevant, even if the judge is aware of information that contradicts those claims. Some argue that it allows debates to be fair as it minimizes bias outside of the control of the debaters, while others argue it removes discussions about real issues from real-world applications.

recovery/glossary/victim-mentality.title: Victim Mentality
recovery/glossary/victim-mentality.content:
Commentary
This is perhaps one of the worst phrases I’ve encountered in mental health circles.
First of all, “victim mentality” is not an academic or clinical term. It is not something that appears in the DSM-V or the ICD-11. It is a term forged through pop-psych and political rhetoric to dismiss the aftermath of trauma, particulary for those on the receiving end of oppressive policies. It is ambiguous enough that it blurs the line between someone who was actually a victim of a traumatic event and the perception people have that they are victims of an event. In fact, in many studies, this distinction is of little interest to the researchers who frame “victimhood” as a narrative that functions as a type of social credibility or personal rationalization.
“Self-defined victimhood is a psychological state whereby, regardless of the etiology of the feeling or the “truth” of the matter, one who perceives herself to be a victim is a victim (see Bayley 1991; Garkawe 2004). The perception of being wronged is victimhood (Zitek et al. 2010). We are not concerned with the “truth” of one’s victimhood.2 As such, concepts like intent to harm or genuine unfairness do not bear on self-defined victimhood. One must merely think of oneself in such terms, or behave in such a way, to “be” a victim (Jacoby 2015). The consequences of self-defined victimhood should manifest regardless of genuine victimization.”
From one study, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7778419/
I wasn’t exaggerating when I said actual trauma and victimization is not of interest to many of these researchers. They’re interested in the psychology of someone who has already declared themself a victim or has a predisposition towards doing so. In other words, “victim mentality” and “victimization” are terms used to assess the same qualities within a narcissist defending themselves as a someone articulating symptoms of PTSD.
This disregard for the truth value of victimhood claims is at best lazy, since the unfalsifiable nature of these propositions allow them to be repeated like any other cliche. “Everything happens for a reason” can be used in response to anything because it’s not falsifiable; you can easily claim that the reason exists but is just currently unknown. Similarly, “you have a victim mentality” can be used equally to describe a genuine victim of trauma and a narcissist who perceives themselves slighted. And you absolutely should not treat these as the same.
Research shows that trauma survivors are overwhelmingly likely to blame themselves than others for their own experiences. The entire fawn response within fight-flight-freeze-fawn is predicated on the idea that, by assuming responsibility for others and blaming oneself, one can reduce the chances of getting external punishment. A child being abused might think “adults are good because they take care of me, so when they hurt me, it’s because I’m doing something wrong, so I need to do more to be good.” This is a predictable process our brains use to both maintain a stable sense of the world where good things happen after good actions and search for new options to use in the future.
To someone like this, suggesting they have a “victim mentality” without assessing the truth value of the claim is activating that exact script that calls on them to blame themselves.
In the worst applications of this concept of “victim mentality,” institutional actors can avoid taking accountability for their complicity in a system by instead blaming individuals for expressing the way an action or policy impacts them. Without getting into specifics, I have heard people express misconduct or errors on behalf of facility staff members in groups or meetings, and the response is generally to ask what role the offended party played in that situation since that’s all they can control. Ironically, this is done in the name of bursting the bubble of learned helplessness, even as it engenders a sense that one is helpless to change their circumstances and is limited to changing mindsets.
There was an attempt by some researchers to create the construct of a “Tendency for Interpersonal Victimhood (TIV)”, which measures four traits:

a need for recognition
moral elitism
lack of empathy
rumination

Do any of these traits have anything to do with actually being a victim? It seems like an antisocial or narcissistic personality test that’s being labeled as “victimhood”, which conveniently sweeps up abusers and victims into the same group with no acknowledge of the context between them. Rumination could easily be a facet of another disorder like depression or OCD, and is in fact pretty common in trauma victims who replay incidents as a PTSD response. “Need for recognition” is also one that can really depend on what “recognition” means; is someone who fawns attempting to gain recognition so that the offending party recognizes the fawning and deescalates the situation?
Also, the studies they refer to involve playing “The Dictator Game” on a computer, and they were told that they were playing against another person who had selfishly kept the money in the game for themselves. Individuals who scored higher on TIV assessments also engaged in higher levels of revenge-seeking that took money away from their opponent even if they didn’t get a reward themselves. They were also more likely to recall their hurt with more intensity and for longer duration.
I mean it’s genuinely astonishing someone would publish an article like this talking about the concept, and then also mention at the very end: “The relationship between seeing oneself as a victim and a history of actual trauma was unclear in this research.”
Yeah, no shit. It’s a computer game that’s explicitly framed in adversarial terms where the opponent seems to be playing selfishly without remorse. It doesn’t even slightly resemble a real-life situation with real-life stakes. It’s a short-term assessment of how someone feels after a game. I don’t doubt that there is some predictive value to this whole setup, especially if it picks out narcissistic or antisocial personality disorder, but it in no way provides an empirical basis for a construct like a “victim mentality.” TIV reflects a tendency within perceptual processing, whereas mentality implies entire thought processes.
If we look at the origins of the term, it becomes clear how “victim” has been tortured into meaning “claim of powerlessness” rather than “affected by trauma.”
“Victimology” was a term coined in 1947 by Benjamin Mendelsohn to describe the study of crime victims within the broader umbrella of criminology.
Early on, this meant a focus on “victim precipitation,” or the extent to which a victim is responsible for their victimization. In the context of a nation-state that imposes a system of laws on its populace, breaking the law is first an offense against state authority to maintain law and order, with the actual victim being a secondary consideration in the course of justice. Determining the victim’s role in the crime was thus driven by the goal of having a full accounting of people’s actions leading up to a law being broken.
The idea of “victim facilitation” qualified this by limiting the scope to unintentional actions that increased the risk of becoming the target of a crime. A woman whose drink is spiked with drugs at a bar is not blameworthy, but a victimologist might argue that leaving her drink unattended unintentionally raised the risk of being drugged and assaulted. On the flip side, “victim provocation” explicitly considers what the victim had done that might have incited another person to violence.
Notably, Mendelsohn was a lawyer who studied rape victims, and his victim typology that arose closely connected ignorance and voluntary participation in events preceding a crime with guilt. The category “victim with minor guilt” referred to victims who were either ignorant or unintentionally increased the risk of harm.
In 1948, Hans von Hentig published The Criminal and His Victim: Studies in the Sociobiology of Crime which sought to identify the characteristics of victims that made it more likely they would end up in a criminal-victim dynamic. He identified 13 types of characteristics that he reasoned were inherently associated with being victimized:

young
female
old
immigrant
depressed
mentally defective/deranged
acquisitive
dull normal
minority
wanton
lonesome
tormentor
blocked, exempted, and fighting

Von Hentig posited that whether someone with these qualities ends up becoming a victim depends on the actions they take given those characteristics. For young women, it might be taking risks that attract the attention of criminals. For immigrants and minorities, it may be a failure to assimilate to a “civilized” culture while retaining their “primitive” ways. For the depressed and lonesome, they may fail to recognize danger or somehow seek it because of their mental state. Tormentors maintain a constant aggressive disposition that incites others into harboring ill will towards them that can escalate into violence.
Marvin Wolfgang in 1957 was the first person to look at empirical data in regards to victimization, identifying 26% of all homicides in Philadelphia as “victim precipitated.” His student Menachem Amir would claim 1 in 5 rapes in Philadelphia were “victim precipitated” through either wearing revealing clothing, using risky language, or having a reputation for promiscuity or deviance.
In 1968, some time after the victim typology trend started among victimologists, Stephen Schafer wrote The Victim and His Criminal: A Study in Functional Responsibility. He proposed seven categories,
Whether or not you were a victim of something has no bearing on what your choices are after, and so it has no bearing on your ability to choose a course for your life that’s best suited for you. Acknowledging that you were a victim of something only means you’re acknowledging that you were affected by it in a way you don’t like. You have a right to feel that way. You just don’t have a guarantee that anyone will treat you like a victim who deserves compensation or sympathy.
There’s also plenty of evidence to the contradictory of such a mindset existing. Neuroscientists have argued that what gets characterized as a “victim mentality” is often the autonomic nervous system reacting in predictable ways to trauma or executive dysfunction that goes deeper than mindset or cognitive distortions.
I would argue there is a pseudoscientific self-help-driven mindset at work here instead that takes a borderline religious view of mind-over-matter in a way Descartes would never have approved of.

recovery/literature/books/fiction/crime/.title: Crime
The Man with the Golden Arm
recovery/literature/books/fiction/crime/.content:
Overview
The Man with the Golden Arm is one of the first post-WWII era novels to document the difficulties soldiers experienced when readjusting to civilian life. Nelson Algren, the author, himself served in WWII as a medical corpsan, and he intended to write novels about experiences he had on the battlefield. After coming back to Chicago and observing how his fellow soldiers had trouble integrating into a corporate careers, he grew upset at the narratives he saw promoted by government and media figures that depicted soldiers adjusting just fine to daily life. Rather than homes in the suburbs, many lived in poverty and fell into a cycle of substance use, whether it was drinking or heroin. Algren decided to explore the rough low-income neighborhoods himself to document, with as much accuracy as possible, the lives of those veterans caught in a cycle of drinking.
Commentary
The book has a sharp vaudeville wit to its banter that speaks to Algren’s dedication to capturing the authentic conversational styles and mannerisms of the 40s Chicago neighborhoods he explored. There’s a lot of playfulness under the dark humor and cynicism. I haven’t yet finished it, but I intend to update this once I do.
Notable Quotes


“That night, while the little twenty-watt bulbs burned on in a single unwinking fury down the whitewashed tier, Frankie Machine was touched by an old wound fever and dreamed, for the second time in his life, of the man with the thirty-five-pound monkey on his back.”


“Man, I wasn’t hooked, I was crucified. The monkey got so big he was carryin’ me. ‘Cause the way it starts is like this, students: you let the habit feed you first’n one mornin’ you wake up ‘n you’re feedin’ the habit.”


“A monkey on the back” is an English idiom that refers to a hard and stubborn problem or burden. Algren popularized the euphemism in the context of drugs as a habit that was hard to kick.

“The great, secret and special American guilt of owning nothing, nothing at all, in the one land where ownership and virtue are one. Guilt that lay crouched behind every billboard which gave each man his commandments; for each man here has failed the billboards all down the line. No Ford in this one’s future nor ever any place all his own.”

Algren was deeply skeptical of America’s orientation towards consumerist materialism as a value and marker of goodness. The postwar boom oversaw a shift in production towards household commodities, associating peace and victory with wealth and consumption under a Puritan moral-psychology. State, media, and corporate institutions were all running high on this prosperity narrative while the reality of many soldiers who served was abject poverty and a revolving door with criminal justice systems. Algren specifically calls out billboards as a transmission vector for this narrative, with an advertisement depicting success and victory that induced guilt if you didn’t have what was being sold. Were you not working hard enough to be prosperous enough to buy the American Dream?
Billboards grew in this era as more Americans adopted cars as a center of their lifestyle amidst the growth of the Interstate Highway System. Owning a Ford represents the progressive nature of this consumerist process; you drive down the road in a car that shows you all the other things you have yet to buy to achieve the Dream when you get to where you’re going. After that, you drive some more to find more things to buy at the next place you’re going. Eventually you buy a new Ford to replace the old one, and you keep going until you don’t.

recovery/literature/books/fiction/detect.title: Detective
The Moonstone - A Romance by Wilkie Collins (1868)
recovery/literature/books/fiction/detect.content:
Overview
The Moonstone: A Romance is one of the earliest modern detective novels and strikes a little close to home. The namesake jewel in the novel is associated explicitly with Chandra, the god representing the Moon in Hinduism, which is also what my name translates to. It also helped popularize the trope of jewels being taken from a colonized and oppressed peoples before being taken again through an elaborate conspiracy.
While writing the book, Wilkie Collins was struggling with both gout and the recent death of his mother. He found relief in laudanum, a drink that mixed alcohol and opium. After the publication of the novel, he claimed to have taken so much laudanum at some point that he didn’t recall writing many passages, though characters in the novel suffer from memory distortion as a result of their own drug usage.
Notable Quotes

“The progress of the disease has gradually forced me from the use of opium to the abuse of it.”

Domestic
The Glass; or, The Trials of Helen More
recovery/literature/books/fiction/didact.content:
Overview
Some scholars argue that “Maria Lamas” is likely a pseudonym used by a female author in order to publish a work that would otherwise be seen as too transgressive or gruesome for a woman to write. The titular female protagonist, Helen More, is a woman born into a wealthy family and constrained by both patriarchal institutions and the influence of alcohol on herself and the men in her life. Rather than a stereotypical damsel in distress though, Helen attempts to regain control in her own life by using her status and beauty to encourage the men around her to drink to excess, which serves as a transgression of her role and is punished with a ruination of the entire family.
It was common for temperance novels to operate under a patriarchal framework even in its advocacy for improving the status of women. By leaning into preconceptions of women being the moral backbone that holds the family together, the argument was not so much that women have a separate-but-equal sphere of influence in domestic life, but that women have a role to play in supporting a patriarchy that allowed a family unit to prosper. By the end of the story, More is saved from a spiral into the abusive institution of an Alms House by a former suitor who has maintained a functional family unit without the presence of chronic drinking.
Notable Quotes
“I throve physically in spite of the neglect, but my moral culture, or rather lack of culture, implanted in my breast the seeds of a hundred foibles, which were to blossom and bear pernicious fruits in the after time.”

recovery/literature/books/fiction/didact.title: Franklin Evans
recovery/literature/books/fiction/didact.content:
Overview
There are various anecdotes floating around about Walt Whitman writing this temperance novel while heavily drinking himself, which does explain why critics have called it “an incoherent and often aesthetically dissatisfying text.” The historian David Reynolds biographical accounts of Whitman include a claim that he wrote the novel in three days while drinking heavily. However, there seems to be some dispute about the veracity of this report. Whitman himself generally saw temperance virtues and movements favorably based on his written works as a journalist. It’s possible that the rumors or jokes persist as an explanation for the work being regarded as far worse than other writings from Whitman; perhaps Whitman himself found the explanation convenient. Some scholars interpret the work as a historical artifact rather than a literary work that represented Whitman’s own racism and bigotry despite a reputation among readers suggesting otherwise.

Infinite Jest (1996) by David Foster Wallace
Walden Two
recovery/literature/books/fiction/philos.content:
Walden Two: Electric Boogaloo
There’s a very justifiable stereotype about academics that they live in elitist ivory towers, turning the rest of the world into variables to be studied and eventually controlled.
However, some of the most influential academics are often motivated by manifesting a worldview rather than just building a successful career. Francis Bacon was motivated to study the laws of the natural world as the laws of God, meant to be unpacked to be appreciated. Einstein presented defenses of socialist projects with critiques of the evidence generated by economics researchers. In his novels, Stephen Hawking would describe the Theory of Everything with an almost spiritual commitment to finding answers from the universe.
BF Skinner wrote Walden Two in the context to describe a world in which operant conditioning was accepted as a basic building block for the design of social systems. He argues through a fictional utopia that, with the right combination of incentives, a community could be fundamentally cooperative, peaceful, and leisurely. The society would be decentralized
To be continued.

recovery/literature/books/fiction/the-lo.title: The Lost Weekend
recovery/literature/books/fiction/the-lo.content:
There isn’t any cure, besides just stopping. And how many of them can do that? They don’t want to, you see. When they feel bad like this fellow here, they think they want to stop, but they don’t, really. They can’t bring themselves to admit they’re alcoholics, or that liquor’s got them licked. They believe they can take it or leave it alone – so they take it. If they do stop, out of fear or whatever, they go at once into such a state of euphoria and well-being that they become over-confident. They’re rid of drink, and feel sure enough of themselves to be able to start again, promising they’ll take one, or at the most two, and – well, then it becomes the same old story over again.
The Lost Weekend is a 1944 novel by Charles R. Jackson that’s been described as “obviously semi-autobiographical.” Jackson himself struggled with addiction after tuberculosis left him with a single lung and he struggled to find work during the Great Depression. He was closeted about his bisexuality until the end of his life, when he had become estranged from his family and began living with a male partner in 1965. Throughout his life, he struggled with mental health and especially depression. His death was ruled a suicide by barbiturates.
Still, to his credit, Jackson did maintain sobriety for extended periods of time. He joined Alcoholics Anonymous in 1953, eventually going on to speak to large audiences about his experience with alcoholism.
In 1945, the book was adapted into an Oscar winning film.

A History of Agnostics in AA by Roger Paul Couvrette
recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/hi.content:
Introduction
“The whole book is all about two things. First is the identification of the problems faced by we agnostics, atheists and freethinkers in AA. And these can be broken down into one simple fact: we don’t attribute our sobriety to a supernatural Higher Power. Nor need we in AA. Read Tradition Three. And as Bill W put it, ‘All people must necessarily rally to the call of their own particular convictions and we of AA are no exception. All people should have the right to voice their convictions.‘”
“And second, the book is about how these problems could and should be dealt with as our secular movements gains momentum within AA. There is no longer a ‘fake it until you make it’ approach to being a non-believer in AA. That’s over. That’s history. Let us all acknowledge that ‘To thine own self be true’ is a healthy and essential approach to long term sobriety.”
I’ll be honest, I never quite understood how it was possible to fully do AA as an atheist or someone who believed in an impersonal God or force behind reality. I really admire those who do though, especially if they’ve endured in groups that didn’t adopt revised secular versions of the literature. Here’s one used by We Agnostics Kansas City:
We are Alcoholics Anonymous, members of a world-wide fellowship of men and women united by a common purpose to stay sober and help others to recover from alcoholism. For us alcohol was cunning, baffling and powerful. It took us to that great jumping off place where we met terror, bewilderment, frustration and despair. Without help it was too much for us!
But we found help in Alcoholics Anonymous and the collective experience of those who preceded us in recovery. Here, we learned that honesty, open mindedness and willingness were indispensable if we were to reclaim our lives. Although our personal stories and experiences vary, this is a general description of the path we took.
We admitted we were powerless over alcohol – that our lives had become unmanageable. This humbling admission was a relief, the fight was over. We came to believe we could be helped through the fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous, and we made a decision to turn away from obstinate denial, to let go of our old ways, and to follow suggestions.
And so on. Many say that this is far easier to digest than the original How It Works. Here’s a secular 12-steps:
We admitted we were powerless over our addictions – that our lives had become unmanageable.
Came to accept that we needed strengths beyond our awareness and resources to cope with our problems.
Made a decision to use the program to overcome our addiction.
So there are definitely ways to tweak the core idea of a fellowship from AA to suit those with agnostic, atheist, or non-theistic belief systems.
What took me aback then was seeing that the motivation for this book includes “the not uncommon and relatively recent ‘rejection’ of agnostic groups and metings by Intergroups in Canada and the United States.” The author’s home group was kicked off an official list of AA meetings over a dispute about God in the Steps that was escalated to a human rights council. More on that later.
I’ve been adamant that AA is inherently religious. Multiple lawsuits that reached US Circuit Courts have reached the same conclusion. A quick look into the historical development of AA’s spiritual principles reveal explicitly Christian roots through the Oxford Group; in fact the original formula for the group considered regularly reading from the Bible to be more critical than attending meetings.
However, I wasn’t actually aware of the disputes involving dedicated agnostic, atheist, non-theist, or secular groups. My analysis was based primarily on examining the literature and its historical development, not the behavior of present-day AA members and organizations. I know lots of accepting and inclusive religious members of AA, and I in no way want to denigrate them or the support they’ve provided because of a few bad apples. This book dives right into the modern disputes instead, which I thought made for an interesting contrast to my approach. I come at this as a relative newcomer, but Roger C. here has decades of experience on me. As such, I’ll let him relay his experiences and chime in if I’ve experienced it too.
Chapter 1
“the God that is talked about at meetings is often a Christian God, an anthropomorphic (created in man’s image - “Father”, “He” or “Him”) and interventionist (who can solve a problem with alcohol “if He were sought”) supernatural being”
This is definitely the impression I got right away, but I also am willing to give this part the most benefit of the doubt as a relic of the era it was written in. Relatively speaking. I think this alone rises to the level of general religious content, but I could see someone using this framing to still convey secular recovery paths.
Most of us believe that what works in AA to keep us sober are two things: first, tapping an ‘inner resource’ (see Appendix II of the Big Book) that makes us strive to be sober, and better, human beings. And, second, the fellowship. Going to an AA meeting and talking with others who understand the problem of alcoholism is a wonderful form of group therapy.”
My initial approach to a Higher Power was framing my idealized potential as something powerful and beyond me, yet attainable with effort and the support of the right community. From Appendix II of the Big Book: “With few exceptions our members find that they have tapped an unsuspected inner resource which they presently identify with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves.” This seems to be a common intuition among not just among atheists and agnostics but anyone, including devout Christians, who has some hesitance about the way the program asks them to think about God or a Higher Power.
The God talk might even be tolerable except for one thing and that is our second problem: we agnostics in AA are often not allowed to be honest at “traditional” AA meetings and even suggest that we personally don’t believe in God… Many agnostics and atheists are treated with disrespect in AA, if not outright contempt.
I will say that it is not uncommon at all to hear someone express that you cannot get sober without God or that seeking a secular recovery path is the result of fearing surrender more than fearing the consequences of addiction. It’s not most people, but it almost certainly will happen at some point if you attend diffrent meetings regularly. I had an AA old-timer warn me about this really early on in my journey before I experienced it myself, and I admit I had casually dismissed the warning as a generational thing that we would be over in 2026. I have learned since then that many things we had hoped to leave behind in past generations are still thriving in 2026.
“the third problem, that many of us experience in AA are meetings that end with the Lord’s Prayer. To say that AA is ‘spiritual not religious’ and then recite the Lord’s Prayer, well, that just doesn’t wash. The Lord’s Prayer is found in the New Testament in the Gospel of Matthew (6:5-13) with a shorter version in the Gospel of Luke (11:1-4). It was said to have been taught by Jesus to his disciples and is considered the essential summary of the gospels, of the religion of Christianity.”
This is true, and courts have pointed to this exact feature as unambiguously religious. Even if we replace the Lord’s Prayer with the Serenity Prayer as many meetings do, it’s still a prayer written unambiguously in the context of Christian faith. These prayers are also often done while holding hands in circles, and you are definitely looked at weirdly if you decline. I don’t even want to hold hands with people I like.
For me, as for many other agnostics in AA, it’s the fellowship that makes the difference.
I agree. Addiction is an incredibly isolating disease, and isolation is perhaps the aspect of addiction that spirals quickest into itself. To have access to a group that can share stories and tries to uphold a culture of listening without judging is amazing. You don’t have to relate to most of what people say to at least realize you’re not alone. It’s just a shame that that isn’t enough to be completely welcome at AA when explicitly the only requirement for membership is a desire to quit drinking. As the book points out, William Wilson (Bill W) himself realized that he was pushing the religious angles too hard and scaring away people looking for fellowship.
Chapter 2
The next chapters go back and forth between the controversy with the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) Intergroup and some of the founding history of AA. Right away, we see one of the reasons that motivated the initial impulse to favor autonomy and oppose formal organization within AA’s culture and traditions. Just like any other document that declares principles or rules as a canon whose founders have passed, different interpretations inevitably lead to disagreements about the same exact actions. If we added a few centuries to AA’s existence, we might see AA lawyers emerge.
In this case, the author addresses the argument that he violated Traditions One and Ten by reaching out to the Toronto Star to discuss his home group being booted from the Intergroup registry and being asked to not use the AA name.
From Tradition One:
“Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole. A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die. Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward.”
The author’s response:
“Our common welfare should without a doubt come first, and it includes the welfare of agnostics, atheists and freethinkers. It is appalling - the word ‘sinful’ jumps to mind - that the Intergroup didn’t understand this basic AA principle. But clearly it didn’t.”
“Sinful” feels a bit like the kind of jab I catch myself making and try to avoid. I can’t blame Couvrette for it given the situation he’s describing, but I try to avoid bringing up hypocrisy if it’s not directly related to the matter at hand. Warranted or not, anything that can be interpreted as mean-spirited can turn off a reader unacquainted with the controversy.
If I’m honest, I’ve grappled with this tradition when it comes to my own attendance and participation at meetings. For instance, if someone says that it’s not possible to get sober without God, but I were to raise an objection similar to Couvrette’s, I would unquestionably be disrupting some aspect of the group conscience that provides for the common welfare. In public society, I can justify this by reasoning that a majority has no right to be comfortable if it’s at the expense of others, and that we are only as strong as our weakest link so we should prioritize helping the most vulnerable.
In AA meetings, I understand that each is a privately formed group attempting to maintain a culture best suited to its members. I don’t think it’s an issue if AA meetings want to be religious, provided they do honestly disclose that they include general religious content even if it’s non-denominational. I treat it the same as a friend inviting me to their church choir’s recital. I don’t need the church to match my beliefs or my beliefs to match the church’s in order to appreciate the choir. For that, I can just walk across the street to a Hindu temple that has its own set of functions for festivals.
It changes the calculation quite a bit though if agnostic and non-theistic AA groups are actively excluded from registries that could keep members who would be wary of a program asking for surrender to a Higher Power who is referred to as God for convenience.
I’ve previously bemoaned the fact that the official AA nonprofit organization makes no mention of other recovery paths for existing while those other paths, like SMART and Recovery Dharma, are very open about acknowledging AA. I tried to charitably rationalize it as a form of taking no opinion on outside issues. AA’s official stance is that they cooperate but don’t affiliate with other organizations, so perhaps acknowledging other recovery paths would come too close to their idea of affiliation. After all, they would need some heuristics to determine which groups to cooperate with, and that would unquestionably be a very controversial subject.
But surely the line makes no sense to draw at “non-theistic AA meetings.” In doing so, I have to question whether cooperation as a decision is more a matter of ideological conformity than organizational principle. After all, from Tradition One:
“No A.A. can compel another to do anything; nobody can be punished or expelled. Our Twelve Steps to recovery are suggestions…
So if an AA group wants to modify the Twelve Steps or the traditional preamble, especially with the explicit goal of making it more welcoming to a newer generation that might have grown up in a more pluralistic religious culture than 1930s America, that shouldn’t be a problem. The Steps are suggestions. Any two meeting of alcoholics can be called an AA meeting; that’s one of the most attractive premises to AA as a fellowship. The promise of that flexibility is why SMART Recovery and Recovery Dharma can say that they have members who keep their AA commitments. It may not be nearly as easy to see that if the Twelve Steps were mandatory as written instead of suggestions and members who think otherwise would be expelled from AA.
As for Tradition 10:
“And finally, we of Alcoholics Anonymous believe that the principle of anonymity has an immense spiritual significance. It reminds us to place principles before personalities; that we are actually to practice a genuine humility. This to the end that our great blessings may never spoil us; that we shall forever live in thankful contemplation of Him who preside over us all.”
It’s true that contacting “press, radio, films, and television” to discuss an internal issue breaks through the “protective mantle which covers our whole Society and under which we may grow and work in unity.”
But critically, anonymity as a principle was for the benefit of the members, who face social stigma and scrutiny for having any kind of dependency or problem in a society that perceives mental health issues as individual weakness. The goal was to keep members humbled from pursuing fame or notoriety, especially in a way that would attract attention to others in the group who had shared very intimate personal details with the fellowship.
The tradition itself acknowledges that bringing AA to the public consciousness or bringing members to AA necessarily required letting go of pure anonymity:
“As a rule, the average newcomer wanted his family to know immediately what he was trying to do. He also wanted to tell others who had tried to help him- his doctor, his minister, and close friends… When opportunities to be helpful came along, he found he could tak easily about A.A. to almost anyone…Though not in the strict letter of anonymity, such communications were well within its spirit.”
Couvrette’s justification is arguably also in the spirit of preserving the character of AA. We’re kind of in the same territory as discussing whether breaking a rule to save the rulebook is justified. He states:
“There are standards that AA has to meet, and not just standards within our fellowship. The Ontario Human Rights Code, adopted in 1962, prohibits discrimination based upon an individual’s belief, or lack thereof, and goes on to say that this principle ‘extends to situations where the person who is the target of such behaviour has no religious beliefs whatsoever, including atheists and agnostics’.”
AA itself says that they are a microcosm of the society it exists in and that no AA member is above the law. Recall that AA has even said that any communication in meetings is not privileged in any way, so if anonymity must compromise to abide by the law, certainly the suggested Twelve Steps can be compromised. Continuing his justification:
“When my home group was booted out of the AA Intergroup, my conscience screamed at me to act. To act immediately… Any delay in a response was going to be a problem that would further hurt those already victimized. And so I acted. And I have no doubt that it was the right thing to do.”
I think it’s plainly obvious that there was harm being caused by this debate about excluding agnostic and non-theistic groups for using a different version of the suggested Twelve Steps. The question is about whether the harm was justified or necessary. I can buy that Couvrette was acting in the spirit of AA’s principles by attempting to use outside discourse to correct exile resulting from an inside issue. After all, AA is not separate from society, but a microcosm of it. If we accept that public accountability of our institutions is one of the most effective checks on their overreach or misapplication of power, that whistleblowers provide an invaluable service in taking personal risk to bring an issue to light, then we should be able to accept the spirit of Couvrette’s actions.
“The action taken by the GTA Intergroup was extreme. But let us be clear: there has always been tension between agnostics and the Christian members of Alcoholics Anonymous. What happened at the Intergroup meeting in that church basement in Toronto merely exposed a long festering wound within AA.”
Chapter 3
“Bill and Bob were both members of a Christian revivalist movement, the Oxford Group. ‘The early meetings were quite religious, in both New York and Akron. There was always a Bible on hand, and the concept of God was all biblical… I started fighting nearly all the things Bill and the others stood for, especially religion, the ‘God bit.’ But I did want to stay sober, and I did love the understanding Fellowship… The consensus seems to have been that they hoped I would either leave town or get drunk.”
The excerpt above cites Sober for Thirty Years by Jim Burwell, who joined AA in 1938 as a “self-proclaimed atheist, completely against all religion”. It is exactly this sentiment that I wish to avoid bringing upon myself by being argumentative at meetings, especially not in our very polarized social climate. To be fair though, Burwell’s objections led to some important changes in the AA literature and philosophy to this day. The first is “God as we understood Him” and the second is adding “suggested” to the Twelve Steps. William Wilson (Bill W) said Burwell ultimatey “had widened our gateway so that all who suffer might pass through, regardless of their belief or lack of belief.” Still, I think it’s noteworthy that even though there was a commendably vocal atheist in the room, the program’s starting point is still with a Biblical foundation that was slightly tweaked to accommodate others.
“Jim Burwell went on to start AA groups in Philadelphia, Baltimore, and San Diego. Among the first ten members of the fellowship on the East Coast, he is often considered the third founder of AA. Jim is the first agnostic AA member to die sober. His sobriety date was June 15, 1938, and he died on September 8, 1974.”

recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/hi.content:
I mentioned elsewhere that literature about management and leadership is difficult to appraise because the nature of leadership is such that they have influence over the shape and spread of their own narratives. In that spirit, this book is best seen as a primary source reflecting how AA’s leading figures wished to present themselves and the organization in 1957. I’ll be treating it as such anyways while cross-referencing this work with other significant histories that have been published since. Specifically:


Not-God: A History of Alcoholics Anonymous (1979) by Ernest Kurtz


Slaying the Dragon - The History of Addiction Treatment and Recovery in America (1998) by William L. White


My Name is Bill (2004) by Susan Cheever


Writing the Big Book: The Creation of AA (2019) by William H. Schaberg


From Schaberg’s book:
“Bill Wilson, the man who contributed more ‘factual’ information than anyone else to the traditional story of A.A., was by far the worst offender when it came to accuracy regarding their early history. This may sound harsh to Wilson’s many worshipful admirers in the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous, but it is an undeniable fact… Wilson’s divergence from the truth was so common and so pervasive that it can only be compared to a dark cloud looming over any attempt to write an accurate history of A.A.’s early years, obscuring and even falsifying what happened at several key points in the story.”
