Writing the Big Book - The Creation of AA (2019) by William H. Schaberg
recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/hi.content:
Chapter 1
“While these real-time documents provide the most unassailable evidence for what happened in Alcoholics Anonymous between late 1934 and early 1939, that history is further embellished by the later writings and statements of four early participants in the story: Bill Wilson (A.A.’s founder), Ebby Thatcher (the man who first exposed Bill to the ideas that led to the creation of A.A.), Jim Burwell (an early atheistic member of A.A.), and Ruth Hock (A.A.’s first secretary). The word ‘embellished’ is used here deliberately to emphasize the fact that each of these four major eyewitnesses has proven to be unreliable, to one degree or another, once their testimony is critically compared with the available archived materials.”
Schaberg’s tone feels a little coy here. “Embellished” is not a term used to convey the normal inaccuracy that goes with a flawed human memory, but instead the exaggeration and elaboration that comes with a generally intentional distortion of the truth.
He elaborates though that it’s “not meant to impugn everything that was said at some distance from the actual events, but knowing how defective and creative memory can be demands that we check and, if possible, correct those errors by comparing them with the more reliable, more believable evidence provided by contemporary documentation.”
It sounds like a focus on fact-checking, but we also get some narrativizing to preface that right away:
“Bill Wilson, the man who contributed more ‘factual’ information than anyone else to the traditional story of A.A., was by far the worst offender when it came to accuracy regarding their early history. This may sound harsh to Wilson’s many worshipful admirers in the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous, but it is an undeniable fact… Wilson’s divergence from the truth was so common and so pervasive that it can only be compared to a dark cloud looming over any attempt to write an accurate history of A.A.’s early years, obscuring and even falsifying what happened at several key points in the story.”
“Wilson became increasingly aware of the need to curb his natural tendencies toward grandiosity… Bill regularly sidestepped these ego traps by modifying the facts, changing the story in ways that deflected attention away from himself.”
Embellished, indeed. Bill isn’t around to defend himself anymore, and while I know many AA members certainly are, I’ll still keep that in mind. I’m a little wary of works that begin by rhetorically priming the reader for a position before laying out something concrete to interpret. Schaberg explicitly points to Pass It On for corroboration, citing that Wilson was “never reluctant to stretch a fact for the sake of emphasis” and “was never likely to pass up the opportunity to deliver a parable where he thought it could do some good.” These do feel a little euphemistic to me.
“Finally, many aspects of the true stories just did not make for comfortable retelling once Alcoholics Anonymous became a successful national institution. This was the case, for instance, concerning A.A.’s early partnership with the Oxford Group”
While I don’t agree with everything about A.A. and have expressed that openly, I will repeatedly give it credit for providing a genuinely accessible fellowship network of people pursuing recovery and a fulfilling sober life.
The Oxford Group has no such distinction. Frank Buchman, its founder, thought a utopia on Earth would be possible through Christian dictatorships and wanted to convert Hitler. Wilson has credited the Oxford Group for being the primary source of the spiritual principles behind the Steps. I had assumed that this only meant that there was some overlap in membership before Wilson tried to create a space exclusively for alcoholics. “Partnership” implies something deeper than that, which piques my interest.

The Making of Buddhist Modernism (2009) by David L. McMahan
recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/hi.content:
Abstract
“Buddhism modernism is not just Buddhism that happens to exist in the modern world but a distinct form of Buddhism constituted by cross-fertilization with western ideas and practices.”
“The book creates a lineage of Buddhist modernism that includes liberal borrowing from scientific vocabulary in reformulations of Buddhist concepts of causality, interdependence, and meditation. It also draws upon Romantic and Transcendentalist conceptions of cosmology, creativity, spontaneity, and the interior depths of the human being. Additionally, Buddhist modernism reconfigures Buddhism as a kind of psychology or interior science, drawing both upon analytic psychology and current trends in neurobiology.”
“In its novel approaches to meditation and mindfulness, as well as political activism, it draws heavily from western individualism, distinctively modern modes of world-affirmation, liberal political sensibilities, and modernist literary sources. The book also examines this uniquely modern Buddhism as it moves into postmodern iterations and enters the currents of global communication, media, and commerce.”
Introduction
The abstract for this book can sound technical and dense. I appreciate that the author relays an anecdote that conveys their thesis:
“I asked my students in an introductory class on Asian religions - our first day dealing with Buddhism - to relate some of their ideas and images of the tradition. After the various impressions from popular films and magazine articles, someone faithfully conveyed that semester’s version of what has become a standard view: that Buddhism is a religion in which you don’t really have to believe anything in particular or follow any strict rules; you simply exercise compassion and maintain a peaceful state of mind through meditation. Buddhism values creativity and intuition and is basically compatible with a modern, scientific worldview. It is democratic, encourages freedom of thought, and is more of a ‘spirituality’ than a religion.”
“What many Americans and Europeans often understand by the term ‘Buddhism,’ however, is actually a modern hybrid tradition with roots in the European Enlightenment no less than the Buddha’s enlightenment, in Romanticism and transcendentalism as much as the Pali canon, and in the clash of Asian cultures and colonial powers as much as in mindfulness and meditation. Most non-Asian Americans tend to see Buddhism as a religion whose most importamt elements are meditation, rigorous philosophical analysis, and an ethic of compassion combined with a highly empirical psychological science that encourages reliance on individual experience. It discourages blindly following authority and dogma, has little place for superstition, magic, image worship, and gods, and is largely compatible with the findings of modern science and liberal democratic values. While this picture draws on elements of traditional forms of Buddhism that have existed in Asia for centuries, it is in many respects quite distinct from what Buddhism has meant to Asian Buddhists throughout its long and varied history…”
I’m not a Buddhist, but I am technically Asian American. I would largely agree with everything listed here. The student’s description of Buddhism is almost verbatim what I’ve heard many times over as a description of it by non-Buddhists in America. I’ve distilled Buddhism down in those ways too, especially if I have to quickly explain the concepts to someone who is just looking for a functional idea of what it is. I admit though, if I had known earlier that AA also calls itself “spiritual” rather than religious, I probably would’ve started referring to Buddhism as a religion more assertively.
Don’t mistake my derision for his though. I’m jaded from being bombarded with New Age literature within contemporary spiritual and recovery-oriented circles. I don’t doubt McMahan has a far more balanced set of experiences on the adoption of Buddhism and South Asian beliefs in America than me. I appreciate the perspective he gives in the place of my own hesitation to acknowledge the fusion of beliefs:
“It is, rather, an actual new form of Buddhism that is the result of a process of modernization, westernization, reinterpretation, image-making, revitalization, and reform that has been taking place not only in the West but also in Asian countries for over a century.”
This is a completely fair point, and I concede that I can reconcile my hesitation with it. If we accept that belief systems are constantly being shaped by the circumstances of life, then it stands to reason that religions are always in a state of change. Impermanent, if you will. Where I specifically feel friction is when the modernization of these concepts isn’t part of the narrative presented to us, leading to the impression that we’re receiving universal truths from long-lost ancient sources. McMahan calls out a pitfall I nearly stepped into moments before writing this sentence:
“It is tempting to think of the various modernizing forms of Buddhism as ‘Western Buddhism,’ given the influence of western science, philosophy, and psychology on modern variations of the dharma, as well as the visibility of American and European authors on the subject… The modernization of Buddhism, however, has in no way been an exclusively western project or simply a representation of the eastern Other; many figures essential to this process have been Asian reformers educated in both western and Buddhist thought. Nor can the motivations of major Asian figures in this process, such asn Anagarika Dharmapala, Daisetz T. Suzuki, and of late, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, be reduced to the simple accommodation of Buddhism to western forms of modernity… Buddhist modernism- has been, therefore, a cocreation of Asians, Europeans, and American.”
I nearly used that exact term, in part because I was just reviewing Unsubscribed by Josh Korda where he describes a rationale for his own translation of the Pali Canon, but in ways that appear to inject more of a “Western” existentialist idea of an incomplete self yearning for wholeness. That makes it suitable for a lot of Western therapeutic concepts that discuss a narrative about the self, but misses the emphasis on interrogating the mental constructs that produce cravings for worldly attachments in the first place.
To be continued.

recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/mo.content:
“Much, too, was gathered from two smokers whom I subsequently had under treatment, and a number of the American smokers, male and female, in this city, and some from California and Nevada, who have kindly come to my house to smoke, thus affording me unusual facilities for studying the effects of the drug, when thus used, on different individuals and upon the various systems, organs, and apparatuses of each.”
“Two of my male nurses very kindly obliged me by smoking the drug a number of times, thus affording me special facilities for study, as they were constantly under my observation, and I was able to note more closely and accurately both the immediate and remote effects upon the novice. Finally, I smoked myself a number of times, both in large and small amounts, and often to decided excess, so that I might be the better able to fully understand subjective symptoms. Otherwise I should have been obligated to depend upon the word of the habitual smoker, which is not always reliable.”
Science used to be wild. You could just smoke opium with your homies in a lab or bring the lab to your home, write down a hundred or two pages of your trips and come downs, and influence federal drug policy for decades. Now that’s research. My guy took the Green Goblin approach and I respect it.
On a serious note, self-experimentation was a much more acceptable method in the past when the infrastructure to set up randomized controlled trials (RCTs) wasn’t available like today. Today, we might consider someone self-experimenting “for the sake of science, bro” to be in need of some form of institutionalization. On the other hand, we still do have an industry based around the idea of performing genetic modifications at home through mass-produced kits, so how far have we really come?
To Kane’s credit, he does make some observations that hold up today.
“The very fact that opium-smoking was a practice forbidden by law seemed to lead many who would not otherwise have indulged to seek out the low dens and patronize them, while the regular smokers found additional pleasure in continuing that about which there was a spice of danger. It seemed to add zest to their enjoyment.”
To make something taboo is to coerce people into repressing any expression of desire for that thing, and that in turn makes it an exotic thrill or relief to indulge it as an escape from repressive conditioning or social norms. At least, that’s what an armchair psychoanalyst might suggest. In modern times, we’ve seen a strange trend of anti-drug education in K-12 schooling actually being associated with an increase in use long-term. One explanation is that students who would have had no interest in trying an illicit substance were now informed about it, and the hysteria around it inadvertently implied it was a common practice to skirt institutional authorities to partake in the subcultures that practiced drug use as a ritual. Kane himself notes that,
“The practice spread rapidly and quietly among this class of gamblers and prostitutes until the latter part of 1875, at which time the authorities became cognizant of the fact, and finding, upon investigation, that many women and young girls, as also young men of respectable family, were being induced to visit the dens… No one can question the fascination of a vice, the strength of a habit that will lead people into such degradation for the gratification of the abnormal appetite.”
While the San Francisco Opium-Smoking Ordinance of 1875 was driven in part fears that Chinese men were corrupting young women by luring them into opium dens and either seducing or trafficking them, depending on which demonization upset the public more, Kane’s work points out that sexual immorality was associated with opium itself. Thus, even white young men using opium became an issue as far as the “protection” of women’s purity from such “abnormal appetites.” From an interview in the July 25, 1881 edition of the San Francisco Chronicle that Kane includes in his book:
“It will rapidly increase. The habit in past years, so far as whites were concerned, was confined to hoodlums and prostitutes mostly. Few decent men or women would care to come into Chinatown and smoke in the filthy dens here. Now that there are scores of places where the habit can be contracted in clean rooms and in respectable portions of the city, the practice will gradually extend up the social grade. Schoolboys and clerks who would never have gone into a Chinese den are already finding out the respectable places and learning to like the habit…”
Prior to modern addiction and drug use terminology, it was common to hear compulsive substance use referred to as “the habit” or “the vice.” We’re lucky enough actually to see a comparison between drinking and opium-smoking made here too:
“You know that there are some men who stand very high in the community who sometimes lose their balance and go on howling drunks. It’s nine chances to ten that if they are men moving in good society, they will wind up in the lowest dives on the Barbary Coast, where they drink the vilest whiskey they can get until they can be safely packed in a carriage and taken in charge by their friends. It’s part of the disease to want to get way down in the mud, and it’s the same with some opium smokers… The anti-opium-smoking ordinance drove the white smokers out of Chinatown, but the vice came along and scattered the smokers, planting them, in fact, in every portion of the city.”
Notably, the officer in this interview does refer to both the habit of drinking and opium-smoking as a “disease” well before a disease model had consensus from scientific institutions or the establishment of a group like Alcoholics Anonymous.

recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/ph.title: Philosophy
What Would You Do Alone in a Cage with Nothing but Cocaine? (2026) by Hanna Pickard
recovery/literature/books/non-fiction/ph.content:
“Do the cocaine” is the obvious answer, but the book has a lot more to say than that.
Introduction
Commentary
It took me a while to appreciate the critical perspective philosophers of science provide about our research institutions. We take our instruments and traditions of knowledge for granted out of a very common human impulse to respect the legacy of the humans who came before us, so that those who inherit the legacy also inherit the legitimacy. Pickard summarizes the situation succinctly:
“In 1997, Alan L. Leshner, then directory of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), published his seminal article ‘Addiction is a Brain Disease, and It Matters,’ cementing a broken brain model of addiction as scientific orthodoxy. Since then, the brain disease model has grabbed the spotlight, claiming by far the lion’s share of funding and credibility, and putting neuroscience and animal models at the center of addiction research. Dissent is heresy. Junior scientists would be foolish to question the paradigm, while senior scientists have built their labs and legacies within it.”
This is a hurdle that, once recognized in research, pops the illusion of objectivity that holds academia beyond the reproach of institutional criticism, especially when the dominant paradigms for those modes of analysis are developed in those same academic institutions.
It’s especially easy to see this with AI research in 2026. Corporate labs completely outpace academic labs in funding and infrastructure, so academic talent is often forced to accept partnerships to do certain cutting-edge research projects at all. That’s assuming they don’t outright quit academic to work full-time for corporate labs or use their lab as a pipeline to startups they have a hand in. This means a lot of breakthroughs happen behind closed doors without independent auditing or peer-review. Even researchers have to consider the attention economy when hype and marketing are directly related to the interests of corporations, and therefore the probability of receiving research funding and opportunities for career advancement. Ethics researchers who study algorithmic bias or safety vulnerabilities are ignored if not harassed or blacklisted.
Addiction and recovery research struggles under a different set of pressures, but they impact the field nonetheless. The stigma and expense of any treatment or program make it difficult to get funding from sources outside of federal agencies, which are slow to pivot in response to new research and subject to sociopolitical headwinds. Policies like harm reduction that have strong empirical support are characterized by non-experts as proposals from morality or empathy rather than scientific rigor. Groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) have been enormously successful in spreading their approach to recovery, but they developed prior to modern science and relied heavily on PR campaigns that treated mental health issues and addiction as “diseases like any other.” So to protest against the brain disease model isn’t just brushing up against established scientists with careers, but also against the conventional wisdom that the public has been made aware of through the education efforts of philanthropic and mutual aid societies. I couldn’t agree more with Pickard’s framing, but I think she sells her own point short by marking the 1997 Leshner paper as a singular event that cemented the brain disease model as orthodoxy in science. Or, as Pickard says, the “broken brain” model. There was a long history of AA collaborating with doctors and researchers behind it too.
I’ve said a lot without actually describing the broken brain model as Pickard frames it:
“The core idea of the model is as gripping as it is familiar. After prolonged drug use, ‘a metaphorical switch in the brain’ is flicked and the brain is ‘hijacked’ by drugs… the brain disease model treats addiction as occurring when the kind of freedom of will that we normally take for granted is lost: The ordinary, voluntary behavior of a rat or a person - pressing a lever, downing a drink, swallowing a pill, injecting, inhaling, or snorting a substance - becomes compulsive, transformed into a passive, involuntary symptom of a brain disease.”
“Hijacking” is one of the most common ways that the relationship between drugs and the brain’s dopmaine system are explained within recovery spaces, and I’m including psychoeducation classes in this. As a quick test, I spat “do drugs hijack the dopamine system” into Google, and received the following answer:
“Yes, addictive drugs completely hijack the brain’s natural dopamine reward system. They flood pathways with massive chemical surges—up to 10 times higher than natural rewards like food or social connection—rewiring how the brain processes motivation, pleasure, and control. You can review detailed scientific breakdowns of this process via the National Institute on Drug Abuse.”
Upon following the link to the NIDA page here nida.nih.gov/publications/drugs-brains-behavior-science-addiction/drugs-brain (published July 2020) and we see:
“Simple activities in everyday life can produce small bursts of neurotransmitters in the brain bringing pleasurable feelings. Drugs can hijack that process.”
“It was once thought that surges of the neurotransmitter dopamine produced by drugs directly caused the euphoria, but scientists now think dopamine has more to do with getting us to repeat pleasurable activities (reinforcement) than with producing pleasure directly.”
Clark Fisher, author of The Urge, has mentioned that it’s not necessarily a coincidence that “hijack” was produced as a term following the crime hysteria of the late 1990s, following carjacking being coined and popularized by national media like Nightline. The notion of a hostile invader suddenly seizing control of the path someone takes was already embedded in the public imagination. The notion of hijacking was intuitive and utilized as an attempt to combat stigma, though it had a lot of unintended consequences as well, such as increasing the risk of some patients developing a sense of learned helplessness from feeling they have no agency. It has remained controversial, though the ease of delivering the explanation has remained a factor in its popularity.
Also, Pickard makes an excellent shout-out to contingency management as “the most effective treatment for cocaine and some polydrug addictions… not pharmacological but behavioral… It is based on operant conditioning principles… elaborated by B.F. Skinner in the 1930s and 1940s” - well before the brain disease model and hijacking metaphor were commonly accepted. I truly love to highlight contingency management whenever it comes up. It’s the easiest counterargument to the idea that addiction can be understood and managed solely through the lens of an individual being internally disordered. In fact, from the studies we’ve done on animals since 1985, Pickard notes that 90% of rats would forego cocaine for sweetened water, and nearly 100% of rats would choose one minute of playtime with another rat over cocaine:
“So much for the idea that rats are compelled by their cocaine-broken brains to keep pressing the lever for more, when all it takes to lure them away is a drink of saccharin water, a minute of playtime, or the whiff of a buddy… Why then did they take so much cocaine in Bozarth and Wise’s 1985 experiment, when they were alone in a cage with nothing but cocaine? Presumably, because they were alone in a cage with nothing but cocaine. The currenly dominant scientific paradigm is broken. It is time for heresy.”
I reveal my own bias when I say this, but I can’t hide my love of writing that delivers the catharsis of cutting through a Gordion Knot that’s been sitting in my stomach. One of the best things about standing on the shoulders of giants is that there’s so much to see from the heights they’ve reached and depths they’ve traversed. But to step down and find a new vantage point, perhaps slaying the giant in the process, becomes more difficult too. The bigger they are, the harder they fall, and the harder it is to fell them. Pickard’s sword comes in the form of a paradigm which,
“can be distilled into two core and connected characteristics: humanism and heterogeneity.”
Humanism
Admittedly, the very first time I heard of the term humanism, I chalked it up as a feel-good garnish on top of a “real” substantive theory that was driven empiricism and rationality. I have since repented for my STEM bro ways.
Humanism historically has referred to a distinct approach within the umbrellas of psychology and philosophy that rejected Freudian psychoanalysis that treated unconscious drives as deterministic while also rejecting Watson’s behaviorsm that reduced human complexity to conditioning. Instead, humanism posits that each person exists within the center of their own subjective interpretation of reality shaped by their unique capacity for processing experiences. To the extent that fundamental biological drives for humans can exist in this framework, it is to reproduce the experience of itself with growth, differentiation, and fulfillment. A lack of congruence, or alignment, between an ideal self and a real self is seen as the source of pathological suffering. Cognitive distortions or denial supported by rationalizations are defense mechanisms against the tension of incongruence. Rather than external institutions or social expectations determining the success of an individual’s function, humanists tend to trust an individual in their own interpretation of reality to evaluate the feedback provided by their own subconscious processes. In fact, external imposition of the conditions of worth is considered one of the main reasons individuals are deterred from actualizing themselves according to their own feedback.
Pickard explains incongruence without using the term, sparing readers from jargon in a way I refuse to do myself:
“people with addiction tend to speak of when and why they first started using; where they use; who they use with; what makes them want to use; what drugs do for them; what drugs mean to them; how they crave them, love them, need them, hate them; how they feel when they use; how they feel when they don’t use; how they feel about the fact that they use; and even, for some people, how their use is part of their identity - their sense of who they are. Often, although not always, they also express uncertaintly about the brain disease model, which sits uneasily with their own experience of addiction.”
To some extent, duh. People rarely experience their life as random spiritual possession that actually hijacks the direction of their life. Isn’t that how we get the most boring horror movies too? Alien (1979) is the top rated horror movie on IMDB, and it’s not because the details concerning the biological process of the Xenomorph reproduction cycle was of intense interest to anyone except maybe hard sci-fi fans. There are countless nature documentaries about parasitic insects that scratch that itch far better. Alien shows us an apex biological predator indifferent to human suffering paralleled closely with a manmade corporation’s indifference, explicitly inspired by the cosmic apathy found in Lovecraftian horror. The android programmed to fulfill the corporation’s mission admires the alien as a “perfect organism” compared to the “expendable” working-class crew who are simply trying to earn paychecks for survival.
It’s similarly of little interest to us to consider addiction just a mechanistic process in which a substance has altered our biology. The term “hijack” is loaded with narrative implications that shape a subjective construction of one’s experience with a substance. It suggests an independent force or agent at work that overrides one’s autonomy and identity, not unlike a malevolent spirit or parasitic alien that hijacks one’s body. Before the instruments of modern medicine that allowed us to explain the world through material mechanisms and physical laws, lots of cultures built their systems of knowledge on the premise of spiritual laws. For instance, many in Ancient Greece thought that drinking invited the consciousness of the god Dionysus to inhabit one’s body, but this is arguably a deeply humanist perspective rather than a mechanical explanation. Dionysus as a concept served as a way to discuss an altered state of consciousness in which repressed desires and thoughts can emerge to drive action. The dissolution of ego, felt internally and perceived externally, in the process of Dionysus taking over introduces a liminality through which social and personal transgressions are negotiated. The word “enthusiasm” has its roots in exactly this type of possession referred to as enthousiasmos.
Not to wax nostalgic about an era I was never born in, but it feels often that in replacing supernatural explanations with mechanistic materialist ones vetted by rationality and empiricism, we pathologized common expressions of our experiences so that they could be mapped onto standardizable measures. Dionysus no longer possesses us when we drink; the GABA receptors responsible for inhibitory neurotransmitters are obstructed while our prefrontal cortex downregulates. Both Jung and Nietzsche used the myth of Dionysus to critique the hyper-rational and hyper-material paradigms that defined the trajectory of “Western” civilization. From a humanist perspective, Jung calls out the repression of the self that results from the conditioning of worth imposed by external social mechanisms. Nietzsche argued that the passions of life had been stifled and sterilized through the worship of reason and logic, thereby leading to a nihilism that reason cannot address.
