recovery/literature/presentations/ted-ta.title: Ted Talks
The Simple Secret of Being Happy
recovery/literature/presentations/ted-ta.content:
Foreword
Anyone who says they have a “simple secret” to anything immediately flags my snake oil detector. I think there are as many “get-happy-quick” schemes as “get-rich-quick” schemes.
Introduction
“When I was 10 years old, things started shifting between my parents and not for the better. One day, they called a family meeting… they told us that we’d be moving from our little log cabin in northern British Columbia, Canada to the southern part of the province. And that they would be divorcing… my father, Peter, had always been this happy-go-lucky guy. The divorce was extremely hard on him, and he was becoming more and more withdrawn. He was less engaged with my sisters and I, he had less energy, and I barely recognized him anymore. I remember thinking to myself, ‘is this my new dad?‘”
This sounds like depression, but I’m no doctor and good doctors don’t diagnose people over secondhand anecdotes from the Internet. Still, the Mayo Clinic has a page about signs you can observe among friends if you suspect depression, which includes “sadness, tearfulness, emptiness, or hopelessness… loss of interest of pleasure in most or all normal activities… tiredness and lack of energy… slowed thinking, speaking or body movements…” Divorce can certainly be a trigger for depression, and men demonstrate a higher risk for the first-onset of major depression after divorce than women. So, I assume this is going to be a story about the choices someone can make to combat depression in the face of tragedy that brings about the true definition of well-being according to Graham, which is resilience. Right?
“One day I woke up at his hosue… and I could hear music playing downstairs, which was very unusual… and there was my dad, Peter, dancing and making pancakes… I said ‘Wow Dad, you seem really happy today…‘”
“You know, Tia, I have had three of the worst years of my entire life, and I woke up this morning and I thought to myself, ‘I’m not going to have another bad year’.”
“I saw my dad choose happiness.”
Oh. Scrap the depression to delight story. That’s on me for being presumptuous.
People suffering from depression can end up in a vicious cycle where they lose interest and pleasure in activities they used to do, so they become less active, so there are fewer activity-reward pairings for the brain to experience, which lowers their mood further. Behavioral Activation (BA) has been one of the most evidence-backed treatments for addressing depressive symptoms. It breaks the cycle by assuming action precedes motivation and that the brain needs to regain momentum towards positive reinforcement through tiny manageable steps that grow over time.
For instance, if cleaning the house feels impossible, try putting dishes from the sink into the dishwasher, and allow yourself to celebrate that as a success. If going to the gym feels impossible, try a short walk. If your personal hygiene feels like it’s slipped out of control, just aim to put your toothbrush in your mouth or wash your face. Commit to it ahead of time like an appointment or deadline so that you’re prepared to do it regardless of your mood.
“One day at a time” and “just for today” are cliches in recovery circles that build on this concept: don’t think about never having a drink again, just focus on not having a drink for today. Reward yourself for that, and it gets easier each day to imagine staying sober.
In other words, recovering from anything, depression or addiction, tends to be a gradual progress. One does not wake up and simply choose to be happy. One can choose to try a small step towards giving your brain a little reward, which is going to be hard even as it gets a little easier each day. With a good support system, consistency towards rebuilding the systems that produce pleasure is possible. Having a good therapist can make all the difference in clarifying your values and monitoring your activities.
Remember that depression has a high rate of comorbiditiwa, and a therapist can flag something to look into with a psychiatrist. For instance, 60% of people with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) also meet the criteria for an anxiety disorder, 14% for substance use disorder, and 72% with a chronic physical condition like diabetes, high cholesterol, hypertension, COPD, back pain, etc. Anecdotally, this isn’t surprising at all. I’ve known at least one person for each of those conditions mentioned who has also struggled with depression. They can even be the reason someone is restricted from the usual activities that bring them pleasure, which can start the negative reinforcement cycle.
I say all this now because depression is never actually mentioned in this video, so there won’t be a discussion about the author challenging their thesis with a condition that impacts 1 in 10 US adults and 1 in 5 young adults 18-25. I imagine those are the people most likely to click on a YouTube video about achieving happiness. In fact, I find it a little concerning that Graham begins with a very realistic premise for someone suffering from depression - years of low moods and energy following the fracture of a family dynamic - but pivots into happiness simply being a choice.
“So what did he do exactly? He started doing things that he enjoyed doing. So he played upbeat music all the time. He went back to school and changed careers. He exercised outside, spent time with his horses, and he spent a lot of time with his friends.”
So, he didn’t choose to be happy. He chose a series of rather major risky life changes that resulted in happiness rather than despair because they fortunately worked out. There’s a very big difference between making a playlist of good vibes for yourself and changing careers as an older worker when you have several young children dependent on you. The first could be a reasonable starting step for BA, but the second is a major step not everyone can or should take. Only 52% of adults over the age of 25 complete a degree in 6 years, of which three-quarters achieve the initial career goals they set out for. Obviously doable, but still a risk not everyone can make. Remember that these statistics don’t include people who want to make a career change but can’t afford the risk.
“at age 18 and 19, I was really struggling, and I was not happy… I knew there had to be more to life, and I knew that I had to choose happiness for myself. This decision took me from living in Calgary, Alberta to Hilton Head Island, South Carolina, where I worked with children one summer…it exposed me to the travel and hospitality industries. This experience led me to a 15-year career in the hospitality industry that I was passionate about and successful in…
I don’t understand this example. I understand that Graham made a major career change just like her dad which paid off. I understand that this career was international and lucrative. I’m missing the part that connects her decision to be happy to the professional success she attained later. Notice that her language attributes agency to the decision to choose happiness for herself rather than explaining the rationale of how the move lines up with her values: “The decision took me… it exposed me…”
“Remember, I’m from a little log cabin in northern Canada.”
This is technically true, but not honest. Set aside the fact that her dad owns horses and could return to school for a career change, or that her mom returned to school prior to the divorce after being let go from her old job. According to Graham’s podcast:
“my mom and dad were living in Northern British Columbia Canada, and they were running a ski area together called Powder King Ski Resort… my grandfather, my dad’s dad was a very large investor in this company… he made an executive decision that they were going to hire a professional marketing company… my mom was no longer needed at the ski area… She is instantly thrust into survival mode and she is not okay. She decides to take us down to the southern part of British Columbia where we have a little lake house and where we’d spend some time in the summer to get away from everything.”
It’s a little disingenuous to say you’re just from a little log cabin in rural British Columbia when your family actually runs a ski resort profitable enough to afford a summer lake house. In fact, the resort has a Wikipedia page and was listed for over $8 million in 2022: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder_King_Mountain_Resort
“In 1983, Peter Graham Jr., president and majority shareholder in the family-owned that had operated Azu Village for the previous four years, and Peter’s then-wife Claudia, presented a $7.7 million expansion plan… A real estate development at the base of the mountain would comprise 47 single-family lots and 106 multi-family units.”
So not just running a ski resort, but planning multi-million dollar expansions to develop the real estate to hold hundreds of people. This isn’t exactly a mom-and-pop shop. It’s totally possible that the real details reveal something like a land rich, cash poor family or an heir who threw away a fortune, but “little log cabin” is implying some rags-to-riches story based on the decision to be happy.
“A happy life is not about feeling happy all the time. This is a huge misconception.”
Is it? Are people going around expecting to be happy all the time?
“Here is the simple secret of being happier: spend time doing things you really enjoy doing. Society tells us what happiness is, what happiness looks like, but what really matters is how you feel. So many people struggle with happiness… Whether it’s kids, work, finances, politics, non-stop technology, social media, family, or the never-ending 24/7 negative news cycle.”
Surveys show that at least 40% of American households do not earn enough to cover basic necessities like housing, utilities, and child care. 62% of employed professionals report feeling financially unstable or struggling to pay their bills. 83% of individuals report significant financial stress from inflation on top of the high cost of living. Some studies suggest that over 75% of doctor’s office visits are directly linked to chronic stress and related ailments like chronic inflammation. 51% of adults report regular exhaustion without explanation, 48% report lying awake at night because of racing thoughts or excessive worry, 44% suffer from tension headaches or migraines, 34% experience stomach distress related to anxiety.
36% of young adults aged 18 to 25 meet the criteria for at least one mental illness, with an unstable job market and debt as their top stressors. 66% of teens report feeling overwhelmed by the issues of climate change, economic volatility, and political polarization. 27% of adults under 30 report a lifetime depression diagnosis which has doubled since 2017. These numbers get worse in some subgroups: high school girls are twice as likely as boys to present with severe depression, over 40% of LGBTQ+ youth report feeling seriously suicidal, and over 60% of young adults of color experience at least moderate anxiety and/or depression.
My guess is that far more people are barely treading water while worrying about existential challenges to the future of human society than expecting happiness all the time in an untroubled life.
If we were being charitable, we might think this is rhetoric aligned with the critiques of positive psychology and a “happiness industry” that promotes unrealistic standards of happiness.
For context, studies show that:


people with negative beliefs about emotions in general tend to present with more symptoms of anxiety and depression


people tend to predict that events, positive or negative, will impact them more severely and for a longer duration than they actually do


people who strongly value being happy tend to feel less happy when in a positive mood compared to others, which can be interpreted as the result of monitoring your own happiness excessively


I would agree with the idea of treating episodes of negative experiences as normal instead of always a problem to be solved until happiness is achieved. Good listening can just mean letting someone vent while asking questions from another perspective, rather than trying to categorize and change their emotional state. The latter can come across as invalidating their reaction and proposing they should have another.
Ironically though, that’s what saying “a happy life isn’t always going to be happy” does. Imagine the depressed young adult stumbling upon this video who worries about an unstable job market and polarization in communities, only to see that massive life changes were necessary for this immensely privileged speaker to be happy even some of the time.
This is exactly why I feel it’s necessary to call out the systemic context behind the “mindset is everything”, “happiness is a choice”, “the real prison is in your mind” types of mantras. Graham had a summer lake house to process “survival mode” while most Americans are chronically stressed about paying rent or mortgages. Of course someone like Graham has to make better choices to be happy: that’s the only way their life can get better since they have all the material advantages required to not have the chronic problems most unhappy people do.
“A happy life has meaning and purpose, and a happy life has different experiences that make you psychologically rich. You think happiness comes from meeting other people and society’s expectations, but really, it comes from creating your own.”
Note that neither Graham, her dad, nor her mom were struggling with meeting social expectations before. That’s not mentioned in the TED talk, though admittedly I haven’t gone through her entire podcast to see if she elaborates elsewhere. Either way, within this video, she only mentions her father’s divorce and her own vague unhappiness that led to partying and dropping out of college. There is no elaboration on how this connects with social expectations as a driver of unhappiness. It’s just shoehorned in as a truism.
Also, it’s not a very true truism. People do tend to report greater well-being when they pursue goals that are personally meaningful rather than imposed externally, which is rather obvious: you feel better doing things you want to do than things others make you do. However, people don’t find their values or idea of meaning independently of other people and broader society. That’s yet another example of hyperindividualism that attempts to assert that there is a self or an ego that can exist in a vacuum with complete control of itself.
A 2023 study of almost 38,000 adults found that the top predictors of well-being were loneliness, satisfaction with social activities, self-rated health, financial security and success, and personality (mainly neuroticism). This is a pretty consistent finding across time. A 2004 study by Martin Seligman found that the strongest correlates of well-being are social relationships, employment, health, freedom, and trust. A 2026 study of over 148,000 adults across natinos found that an internal locus of control (belief that one has control over their life) and state of health were the most important predictors. After that, household income, marital status, in-group trust, acceptance of homosexuality, and age.
Hardly any of that is related to creating your own expectations while shunning other people and society’s expectations. The two are in an inseparable loop with each other. You can’t have meaningful relationships, social engagements, or community participation without aligning yourself with the environment around you. That also means having the courage and responsibility to accept your agency over the environment and act on it.
But there’s no simple secret to addressing loneliness or financial insecurity. That requires social reform, which is hard and controversial, unlike TED talks which explicitly seek simple ideas to spread in 10-minute presentations. We’ll see what kind of literature she does end up referencing instead pretty shortly.
“I personally struggle to feed my family three times a day, seven days a week, every single week. I am not a good cook, and I don’t like cooking. Obviously, I would never make it on Top Chef. Bottom Chef called and said ‘don’t even bother.‘”
First of all, meal prepping isn’t hard. It’s a habit to learn like anything else. You can freeze some meals for months and they’ll still taste great when you reheat them. There are countless guides to do this online. My college had workshops to teach students about budget meal prepping. This is a solved problem.
Second of all, notice how “struggle” here went from “kids, work, finances, politics, non-stop technology, social media, family, or the never-ending 24/7 negative news cycle” to finding it inconvenient to assign yourself the task of making fresh meals from scratch three times a day for a family? We went from external threats to your peace and security to what I assume is an attempt to come across as relatable to unhappy middle-class moms, which is kind of her whole brand.
“Gallup’s research showed that 79% of people, globally, are disengaged while they’re working. That’s almost 80% of people. Many people are doing work that they don’t like or that’s not meaningful to them. Also, according to Gallup’s global research, 41% of people have a lot of stress and worry on a regular basis. The World Health Organization said one in four are not getting enough execise, and the term ‘work-life balance’ has over 2.8 billion search results on Google. And your brain, my brain, all of our brains have a negativity bias, which is really unfortunate. We have to work extra hard to be positive and optimistic.”
Notice that being disengaged with work is considered a proxy for unhappiness or lack of purpose. Why? You’ve never had a job you did just for a paycheck so you could enjoy the rest of your life or at least try to achieve basic security?
For those who don’t know, TED Talks have a reputation for being the kind of content that managers show employees when they want to avoid making any systemic changes in the workplace if boosting morale and positivity can fix it. Spoilers: it can’t. As Demings said, a bad system beats a good person every time. If you want people to be engaged in the workplace, give them engaging incentives. That’s as obvious a principle as “do things you enjoy in order to enjoy life more” or “do esteemable things if you want self-esteem.”
Also, our negativity bias isn’t necessarily “unfortunate.” It likely developed because paying more attention to threats and losses than rewards can be a good strategy for survival. You can run out of food and starve to death, but you can’t somehow eat more food now to avoid eating later, so loss can have more significance than gain. We might say that a bird in hand is worth two in the bush. Optimism is not in and of itself something desirable, it’s just a proxy that can tell us something about your general mental state.
“I’m going to share with you four things that many people really enjoy doing. I’m going to connect them to the science of happiness. And I want you to think about these for yourself.”
Happiness Choice Number One
“Happiness choice number one- Spend a lot of quality time with your friends and your family…The Harvard Grant Study of Adult Development, an over-80-year study, proved that our relationships and how happy we are in our relationships directly affect our health and our happiness.”
Setting aside the technical issues with the word “proved”, we see that Graham does in fact use the same literature I referenced above, with seemingly no awareness of how it contradicts the idea of creating expectations from within yourself instead of meeting those of other people and society.
You cannot have a happy marriage if you disregard your spouse’s expectations of you. You cannot be a good parent if you disregard your children’s expectations of you. You cannot keep a job if you disregard your employer’s expectations of you. You cannot sell to customers if you disregard the customers’ expectations of you. Simply put, you can either have relationships or you can be be a lone wolf, but you can’t be both. You can absolutely negotiate expectations within a relationship to align yours with another’s, but the fact they exist is an inescapable fact of life.
A 2022 study examined the 2003-2020 American Time Use Survey and found that nationally, social isolation increased while social engagement and companionship decreased. The COVID quarantines only accelerated consistent trends we observed. The study specifically highlights that “Hours worked per week emerged as a structural constraint to social connectedness.” So people who have to work more to make ends meet are less likely to spend time with their friends; remember that 40% of Americans don’t make enough to afford basic needs. That hardly seems like a choice someone can change.
Here’s a quick thought experiment: imagine that no one in the world had to work for a living at all, and basic needs are completely provided through a magic wand. How many people do you think would choose to keep doing exactly what they’re doing now, and how many people would quit to spend time with loved ones and/or traveling the world to meet new people?
Happiness Choice Number Two
“Happiness choice number two is getting a good night’s sleep. This means sleeping seven to nine hours a night, every single night. Research shows that sleep increases our happiness, improves our brain functioning, and improves our overall quality of life. So even though those streaming shows are so good or even though you could stay up just one more hour, just answer a few more emails, go to bed and leave your phone in the kitchen.”
Remember above that we talked about a vicious cycle, and how half of Americans lose sleep because of racing thoughts and excessive worry about the future? There are two main ways to interpret the combination of these facts. Either the use of technology before bed causes racing thoughts and worry which then prompts more technology use as a distraction, or people stressed about their lives can’t sleep use screens while lying in bed awake.
One 2025 meta-analysis looked at 21 studies with almost 550,000 participants. Each hour of daily screen time was associated with 3-5 minutes less sleep and 13.2 minutes of delay in bedtime. In 2024, a review of 25 studies across 4652 participants found that “daily screen time has a small” correlation with delayed sleep time, and “short-term daily fluctuations in screen time appear to have minimal impact on sleep duration, efficiency, or quality. Screen time may delay bedtime but is not inherently detrimental to other aspects of sleep health in youth.”
Another 2025 meta-analysis that looked at about 4,200 adults across 42 randomized controlled trials found that sleep hygiene education (SHE) produces only weak to modest impacts on insomnia relative to other approaches. Partial Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), exercise, and accupressure all outperform sleep hygiene as factors in alleviating insomnia.
So overall, evidence shows that if you want completely optimal sleep, then improving sleep hygiene and cutting down on screen time can help. However, the top predictors of physician-diagnosed insomnia, according to a 2023 analysis that examined 684 variables, seem to be depression symptoms, age, a physician recommendation to exercise, weight, and waist circumference. In fact, depression symptoms contribute four times as much as age and ten times as much as body weight.
Another study aimed at subjective sleep quality instead of diagnosed insomnia found that the 38 objective variables analyzed for over 1400 adults could only explain 11-17% of the variance. In other words, factors other than sleep efficiency (percent of time spent in bed asleep), total sleep time, and number of sleep stage transitions are primarily responsible for subjective sleep quality.
It seems that symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress, age, body composition, physical health, and dysfunctional beliefs about sleep are consistently the biggest predictors we find. Screen time does appear to have a modest effect on sleep quality, duration, and efficiency but sleep hygiene overall isn’t that impactful. Depression, on the other hand, has an incredibly massive impact.
The evidence suggests, at least to me, that people are struggling with sleep for reasons unrelated to their screen time and turn to technology for something to do in bed. Once you notice how often communicators leap from loose associations to strong prescriptions, it’s hard to unsee.
Happiness Choice Number 3
“Happiness choice number three - Moving at least four times a week. Exercise increases our happiness, increases our brain functioning, and decreases stress and anxiety. Do not exercise to look good; exercise to be happier. And I know you’re busy. You don’t need to do an hour workout class. Even if you move 15, 20 minutes, you will get the benefit.”
Exercise is definitely associated with increased happiness and decreased stress and anxiety, particularly in individuals who have more of both. The encouragement to move even 15 or 20 minutes is largely in line with the tiny steps I mentioned above as part of Behavioral Activation. This is probably the most defensible recommendation in the talk.
It should be noted though that the relationship between depression and exercise is bidirectional. Depression is associated with becoming physically inactive over time, and people with higher physical activity are less likely to develop depression. 40% of respondents to the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) cite a lack of time as their primary issue, and as many as 25% cite health problems or disabilities as an obstacle. Remember that over half of American adults report exhaustion without a clear explanation.
Also, I haven’t been pointing out how interconnected these issues are. Someone worried about making ends meet is more likely to pick up more hours, which means anxiety and a higher workload will both be contributing to less sleep. They might also have to cut out social engagement activities that doubled as physical activity. That can lead to more health complications like an increase in the symptoms of anxiety and depression or aggravation of another underlying health condition like hypertension. It’s easy to see someone spiral into that vicious cycle we mentioned before.
The gap between the highest-income adults and lowest-income adults in terms of meeting aerobic activity recommendations is about 20%, strongly suggesting that more financial security enables healthier lifestyle choices. Is that really surprising to anyone? Keep in mind these statistics include the fact that lower-income groups have more physical activity at work while higher-income groups incorporate more recreational exercise. Someone who works over 40 hours a week in a warehouse is probably not going to have the energy to hit the gym after or in the middle of the workday. For contrast, I’ve had a lot of meetings with at least one coder walking on a treadmill placed under their standing desk or squeezing in a home gym routine around lunch.
Happiness Choice Number 4
“Research shows that meaningful work makes us happier and way more motivated while we’re working and makes us happier in our personal life. And if you don’t have the opportunity right now to change jobs or change careers, just spend more time helping people, and your work will be more meaningful.”
From a Pew Research Center survey, 55% of American workers considering job changes were concerned about losing income, and 45% were concerned about losing benefits like healthcare. 50% of adults involved in some type of education or training report a lack of time due to work and family obligations as a barrier to their advancement. 20-30% of adults considering further education and training also have caregiving responsibilities. Women on average spent roughly twice as much time on caregiving for children than men, while men on average spend more hours working to support a household financially. As I said before, this type of career change is certainly doable, but definitely not equitably distributed.
As for helping people, there have been studies on something called “task significance” which tracks the belief that one’s work has an impact on others, but studies show it accounts for 14% of the variation in job satisfaction. In other words, it can definitely help yourself feel better to help others feel better, but you are heavily constrained in this by the parameters of your workplace. Also, if you have ever worked anything even closely resembling customer service, you’re probably laughing a little bit at the idea that you would be happier if only you tried to be more helpful.
Note that the solution being proposed is asking you to do more work with a positive attitude to feel better. It’s almost like positivity propaganda, and it’s not hard to see why managers might share this with their employees.
Conclusion
“There are many other happiness choices, such as spending time in nature, meditating, volunteering, journaling when you’re going through pain. It’s about you.”
There’s a rhetorical sleight of hand here where self-care that’s central to your health is being conflated with a “happiness choice.” These are entirely different things. There’s a really big distinction between reducing negative moods, increasing positive moods, increasing life satisfaction, and increasing a sense of meaning or purpose.
Also, the literature shows that all of these have small to moderate impacts on well-being on average. There seems to be an assumption that happiness is a linear combination of the “happiness choices” listed above. If you add up all the small changes, a big change must necessarily happen that puts you into the “happy life” category, right?
No. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised to see that there has been substantial criticism from scholars lately about this exact framing. Nicholas J.L. Brown & Julia M. Rohrer provide an incredibly comprehensive breakdown of the assumptions behind the “happiness pie” model that proposed 40% of our happiness can be attributed to individual actions in our control. I couldn’t possibly add anything in the way of commentary to the substance of the work, so I’ll shamelessly cite them directly:
“Consequently, there is little reason to believe that 40% is a reliable estimate of the variance in chronic happiness attributable to intentional activity—for example, if Lyubomirsky et al. had chosen a different (but, in our view, at least equally plausible) set of estimates, they might just as easily have concluded that as little as (100% − 80% − 15% = 5%) of variance in chronic happiness can be attributed to volitional activities. Of course, because of the conceptual issues that we have discussed, we do not believe that such an estimate would necessarily be more reasonable or more interpretable.”
They also include a sharper critique of the point about privilege I made before:
“Likewise, researchers should carefully reconsider the usage of terms such as “volitional activities”. What might be a matter of choice for some people can be a question of circumstances for others.”
“For example, middle-class Western parents with a comfortable household income can exercise a wide range of choice over the diet that they and their children consume; they can choose to drive their car to the farmer’s market instead of taking the bus to the discount grocery store, and afford to place organic blueberries rather than canned, syrup-laden fruit cocktail in their shopping cart. They can also enjoy a wide range of recreational activities, such as vacations to awe-inspiring or culturally important destinations, enabling them to enjoy the benefits of feeling that they are part of a meaningful world (Gilovich and Kumar 2015).”
“Indeed, Lyubomirsky et al. (2005) themselves described the types of volitional activities that they were considering in decidedly middle-class terms: “rather than running on a track, a fitness-seeking wilderness lover might instead choose to run on a trail through the woods… rather than learning classical pieces, a jazz-loving piano student might instead choose to work on jazz standards” (p. 122).”
Just like I said above, Graham’s examples also seem to be marketed at the middle-class moms (though these days we might say upper-middle class) whose idea of “struggle” might mean making three fresh meals everyday rather than affording subsistence-level meal prepping. Graham, like many get-happy-quick gurus, is just marketing “happiness circumstances” as “happiness choices” for the particular demographic whose circumstances allow them to make those choices.
“A subsistence farmer working from dawn to dusk in a developing nation, a worker who spends 14 h per day assembling electronic devices in a south-east Asian factory, or a single Western parent living in less fortunate circumstances than the family just mentioned, may not be in a position to make such choices. As with many phenomena studied by primarily Western psychologists (cf. Henrich et al. 2010), the list of volitional activities that are available to improve one’s well-being may be less than universal, not just for cultural reasons but also precisely because of one’s life circumstances.”
Anecdotally, if you ever want to make it really awkward in a room where someone is promoting a viewpoint from positive psychology, just bring up racism or sexism or another -ism. Ask what kind of self-care or volitional activities you need to offset the circumstances of systemic bigotry to your wellbeing. I have never once seen this point handled gracefully or tactfully, because the premise of this worldview is that you have freedom through consumer choice and the civil rights afforded by a liberal democracy. In practice, your freedom is limited by your access to capital, whether financial or political.
As someone from an Indian and Hindu background, my grandparents were alive to witness the liberation of Goa from Portuguese rule, a struggle that lasted from the 1490s to the 1960s. A huge misconception about Indian independence is that Gandhi and friends held peaceful hunger strikes with his best friend Martin Luther King Jr. that made the British and Americans feel silly enough to stop being racist and give rights. In practice, European powers stayed long after the 1947 deal for independence was struck. For 14 years, nonviolent and diplomatic attempts to negotiate the freedom of Goa from a Portguese dictatorship continued. It became an international affair that involved the UN, US, UK, Brazil, Mexico, and other parties with a stake in either India or Portugal.
In November of 1961, Portguese troops shot at a passenger boat and killed one while injuring the chief engineer. This was far from the only death that had happened since 1947 among unarmed nonviolent Indians in proximity to Goa, but it became an inflection point where enough was enough. By December, Prime Minister Nehru declared that the era of peaceful negotiation and adaptation to the occupying forces was over: “Continuance of Goa under Portguese rule is an impossibility.”
Prime Minister Salazar of the Portuguese had ordered “there will be no surrender rendered because I feel that our soldiers and sailors can be either victorious or dead.” Governor General Manuel Vassalo e Silva told the press “If necessary, we wil die here.” The Portguese President had ordered a scorched earth policy, so that Goa was to be destroyed before being conceded to India. This is the kind of detail that’s important to remember when discussing the conditions of developing nations and formerly colonialized territories.
The United States, both outside and inside the forum of the United Nations, was critical of India’s use of force for independence, which is rather ironic considering how the US obtained independence. Go listen to Hamilton if you’ve forgotten. On the other hand, the USSR had vetoed a UN Security Council resolution that would have condemned India’s liberation of Goa. Brezhnev criticized the response of Western institutions as coming “from those who are accustomed to strangle the peoples striving for independence… and from those who enrich themselves from colonialist plunder.”
Operation Vijay took 36 hours to force the Portuguese to surrender. 14 years of diplomatic resolution and adaptation was nowhere near as effective as just acting decisively and collectively against an obvious injustice.
My ancestors did not improve their lives by incorporating more exercise or turning off the TV sooner before bedtime when they didn’t even have the consistent electricity to have a fridge. They organized collectively to challenge institutions and force changes that they were told they would never be able to make. That created political and financial capital by recognizing community rather than the individual ego as the fundamental unit of human society. Individuals repeatedly made sacrifices to benefit the collective with the understanding that they were investing in the future prosperity of those who would one day call them ancestors. That gives meaning, purpose, and a place in the world. You cannot know what you can or cannot change until you try your absolute best to change it, and your absolute best only comes out when you’re working with people who empower each other.
All this to say, I have a very different frame of reference for what counts as “struggle” or “survival mode” than no longer having a job in a lucrative family business or wanting to cook three fresh meals every day. Perhaps the radically individualist positive psychology of “happiness choices” works for those who have reaped the benefits of colonialism to give themselves that choice. It doesn’t seem to work as well for those on the receiving end of it.

recovery/literature/studies/1990-1999/im.title: Images of the Twelve-Step Model, and Sex and Love Addiction in an Alcohol Intervention Group for Black Women
recovery/literature/studies/1990-1999/im.content:
Abstract
“The Alcoholics Anonymous twelve-step model was developed to help a specific population of white, middle-class, heterosexual men with a specific problem: alcoholism. As the program is applied to a wider variety of issues, with diverse populations, the model’s generalizability has been called into question. Its applicability to outgroups is, at best, uncertain. At worst, the addiction model and its notion of powerlessnesss could have serious negative consequences.”
I would argue this entire site is the product of radical skepticism towards the generalizability institutions engage in as they scale, which involves manualizing and operationalizing protocols according to metrics that are easily gamed. I don’t object to AA, I object to AA being treated as a neutral non-religious baseline when the basic steps ask you to find a God of your understanding, and plenty of alternatives exist that are never mentioned.

recovery/literature/studies/2010-2019/pu.title: Public Health and Public Order Outcomes Associated with Supervised Drug Consumption Facilities - a Systemic Review
recovery/literature/studies/2010-2019/pu.content:
Abstract
“Consistent evidence demonstrates that SCFs mitigate overdose-related harms and unsafe drug use behaviours, as well as facilitate uptake of addiction treatment and other health services among people who use drugs (PWUD). Further, SCFs have been associated with improvements in public order without increasing drug-related crime. SCFs have also been shown to be cost-effective. This systematic review suggests that SCFs are effectively meeting their primary public health and order objectives and therefore supports their role within a continuum of services for PWUD.”

recovery/literature/studies/2010-2019/su.title: Supervised Injection Services - What Has Been Demonstrated? A Systematic Literature Review (2014)
recovery/literature/studies/2010-2019/su.content:
Links

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25456324/

“Results: Seventy-five relevant articles were found. All studies converged to find that SISs were efficacious in attracting the most marginalized PWID, promoting safer injection conditions, enhancing access to primary health care, and reducing the overdose frequency. SISs were not found to increase drug injecting, drug trafficking or crime in the surrounding environments. SISs were found to be associated with reduced levels of public drug injections and dropped syringes. Of the articles, 85% originated from Vancouver or Sydney.”
“Conclusion: SISs have largely fulfilled their initial objectives without enhancing drug use or drug trafficking. Almost all of the studies found in this review were performed in Canada or Australia, whereas the majority of SISs are located in Europe. The implementation of new SISs in places with high rates of injection drug use and associated harms appears to be supported by evidence.”

recovery/literature/studies/easy-as-happ.content:
Abstract
“We conclude that there is little empirical evidence for the variance decomposition suggested by the “happiness pie,” and that even if it were valid, it is not necessarily informative with respect to the question of whether individuals can truly exert substantial influence over their own chronic happiness level.”
2 Does the “Happiness Pie” Add Up?
“Lyubomirsky et al. recovery/marketplace/technology/apps/ope.title: Sobriety
recovery/marketplace/technology/apps/ope.content:
Summary
From the README file uploaded to the GitHub repository:
“I mostly designed this out of spite for I Am Sober, which monetizes addiction recovery. This started as something I just wrote in the time I had between classes for a friend who was struggling with addiction and couldn’t get an I Am Sober subscription to track all the things he was struggling with, and I really just decided to publish it because I didn’t see a reason not to”
“I’m only half joking when I say I hate I Am Sober. It has several trackers and requires far more permissions than is reasonable for the features it provides, and the fact that a subscription is required to track more than two individual addictions is just horrific to me. Displaying the time since a given date, and allowing that date to be reset to the current time, are such simple features to implement that I genuinely cannot fathom how they can in good conscience monetize them, especially when their target audience is people struggling with addiction.”
“I just find the whole concept somewhat upsetting. For that reason, Sobriety will never have any trackers or anything of the sort, and will always be completely free. I want to help people, not profit off of their struggles.”
The project appears to have been started by Katherine Isabella Del Toro, going by the handle seaglade on GitHub, while a student at the Rochester Institute of Technology. The most recent update appears to have been in 2024.
Notes
I love this README.
That’s more or less the rationale I had before launching this site. It started out of spite for The Four Agreements, and in the process I ended up putting together notes that could pass for articles. I couldn’t think of a reason not to share it with others who have a deep-seated disgust for the way the New Age self-help and happiness industries monetize addiction recovery while discouraging collective action and systemic reforms. Also, I am not joking in the slightest when I say I think the world be on balance better off if every copy of The Four Agreements was burned.
So, I’m biased, but I like the cut of this dev’s jib. Fight the power, my friends.

Adam Curtis’ basic thesis behind the documentary is that the world became too complex for the institutions of power to actually manage, so they instead turned to managing the simpler narratives that set the parameters for reality, namely the feelings and mindsets at the atomized individual level. Hypernormalisation refers to the way everyone can clearly see reality is broken, but changing the world seems either overwhelming or outright impossible in comparison to changing personal feelings about it. He draws a constellation with this pattern through social media as a tool to control information flows, pharmaceuticals to remedy social conditions that precipitate mental illnesses, a wellness industry worth multi-trilliong-dollars, recycling and carbon footprint campaigns, and liberal counterculture that grew cynical about changing systems when retreating into self-expressive activities was easier.

recovery/media/games/bloodborne.title: Bloodborne
recovery/media/games/bloodborne.content:
Introduction
“In Yharnam, they produce more blood than alcohol, as the former is more intoxicating.”
Bloodborne is not shy about embracing addiction themes as part of its eldritch Lovecraftian vibes. The “Old Blood” is explicitly said to be more intoxicating than alcohol, and the citizens of Yharnam pursue blood despite the insanity and gruesome decay it brings. The Old Blood as a substance and the Hunt as the chase for it form a good allegory on their own, but, to me, the really compelling aspect is in how heavily the game explores the notion of transcendence given how central that concept is to what we seek from the world outside our finite human selves.
Lovecraft
Like many prolific writers who suffered from a particularly severe case of bigotry, Lovecraft attempted to reconcile his deeply held contradictions through his work but becomes more interesting as an artifact of study himself.
Lovecraft was deeply passionate about science though he held no formal qualifications himself. Both his parents had experienced violent episodes that led to institutionalization in a psychiatric hospital, and he himself experienced a litany of both physical and mental health ailments while living through extreme poverty. These were debilitating enough that he never completed high school or attended college, but he still wrote to publish work about scientific topics in local newspapers. At one point he published his own independent periodical that reviewed astronomy while maintaining a home chemistry lab and telescope setup. His works sometimes go into great authentic detail when describing these labs, no doubt a reflection of his enthusiasm for actual laboratory work and analysis.
Unfortunately, a passion for science does not translate to anything resembling an approach free of predetermined biases and prejudices. Consider the following excerpt:
“…could not by any stretch of the imagination be call’d human. They were monstrous and nebulous adumbrations of the pithecanthropoid and amoebal; vaguely moulded from some stinking viscous slime of earth’s corruption, and slithering and oozing in and on the filthy streets or in and out of doorways in a fashion suggestive of nothing but infesting worms or deep-sea unnamabilities.”
He’s not describing any creature out of his stories here. This is how he chose to describe Syrian and Italian immigrants he observed in New York. As for Chinatown,
“You can’t imagine the horror of being engulfed in a maelstrom of repulsive Orientals whose aberrant physiognomies & rat-like temperaments grate more & more on the sensibilities of an aesthetically impressionable person.”
And he did head-to-head comparisons too:
“There is here a grave and mighty problem beside which the negro problem is a jest—for in this case we have to deal not with childlike half-gorillas, but with yellow, soulless enemies whose repulsive carcasses house dangerous mental machines warped culturelessly in the single direction of material gain at any cost.”
Lovecraft’s revulsion here is pure in its irrationality. He simply does not like non-Anglo-Saxon people as an axiom of his worldview, so much so that even when he did like a non-Anglo-Saxon person, he would bend his reasoning in very unscientific ways. He was actually married to a Ukrainian-Jewish businesswoman and immigrant, Sonia Greene, for a brief two years, which he rationalized as an exception that proves the rule.
He would say Greene had shown assimilation to a superior Western culture was possible for lesser races that could sever a connection to their inferior heritage, even though Lovecraft was the one struggling financially, physically, mentally, and professionally. Greene was seven years older than him (he was 33 and had never been with a woman before) and almost took a maternal caretaking position to support him, which Lovecraft might have appreciated given how early he lost both his parents. After an economic downturn ruined Sonia’s fashion business, Lovecraft looked for work on the streets of New York, but he would regularly launch into racist tirades upon seeing immigrants on the street. He was not exactly a team player. Greene could no longer look past this prejudice and bitterness, and she left him.
So, despite Lovecraft’s love for science, absolute atheism, and strict materialism, he struggled immensely with intense emotions rooted in irrational aversions, and he tortured almost every instance of diversity into confirmation for his biases.
The “cosmic horror” he writes about is derived from the Others he was horrified about in his own life, directly provoking his imagination of what an otherworldy (literally, Other-worldly) entity behind the forces of change might look like. The protagonist of his story is often an educated and radical skeptic who leans on scientific processes and rationality to feel an order to the universe. The secondary antagonists are often a conspiratorial cult or secluded society who represent the agents of primitive degeneration walking on Earth. He was not subtle about using minorities, immigrants, and indigenous nations as inspiration for these agents.
It’s also noteworthy that Lovecraft strongly despised the Theosophist Society as one such pseudoscientific occult subculture, yet loved their mythology for world-building and borrowed heavily from their concepts. He wrote in letters that he too was building a mythological pantheon, but without the pretense of trying to start a religion. The opposite, in fact. He wanted to illustrate that the universe was indifferent to humans, that the “primitive” peoples worshipped the indifferent materialist forces while scientific skepticism reveals the harsh truth. Recall above that Lovecraft characterized Asians, and in particular Chinese ethnic groups, as ruthlessly efficient towards material pursuits as a result of lacking soul and culture. Totally unrelated to rationalizations about his own financial instability and reliance on a Jewish immigrant as a sugar mommy. After all, to him, he was just a temporarily embarrassed aristocrat who appreciated art and culture as human achievements, while the classless immigrants and minorities were ruining the community by pooling together capital earned from low-wage jobs to start businesses especially in underserved markets and communities. That script might sound a little painfully familiar.
Retrospectively, it’s a little amusing to see two different types of racist pseudosciences interact with each other. Lovecraft attempted to make self-aware and critical references to the Theosophists as a pseudoscientific occult group. Meanwhile, the Theosophists, particularly after his death, believed that Lovecraft was genuinely a medium receiving some kind of spiritual insight that his personal resistance and lack of training prevented him from interpreting correctly.
Transcendence
The core framework of transcending is nothing new. We can go back to Hesiod and the Dionysian Mysteries to see examples of this in Ancient Greece. Some of the oldest branches of Hinduism build on the premise that turning inwards and looking past the ego leads to a recognition of oneness with the world. The American transcendentalist movement with Thoreau and Emerson is often considered the first philosophical movement to have grown from American soil, and it’s no coincidence that it emerged out of dissatisfaction with “Western” industrialization and exoticism of the “Oriental” cultures. You can find a lot of interconnectedness and impermanence repeated in modern DBT techniques and Buddhist-inspired spiritual programs. Jungian psychoanalysts examine the archetypes surrounding transcendental experiences and operators. I certainly reference the concepts a lot in my ranting.
My notes about Talk to Me draws heavily on what Jung’s successors have said about substance use in youth subcultures that are driven by a desire for transcendental experiences to develop both their own identity and connections to a community. We know there must be more within this infinite universe than our finite sense show us, or at least our imagination can process the concept of infinity as something we lack. Yet, we are bound only to what our bodies allow in their limited form. To escape it and transcend or connect with something outside of ourselves, perhaps even greater than ourselves. Then, we want to share that transcendental experience in the hopes of deepening or heightening it through our connections with others.
Lovecraft’s work deals with a corruption of this concept of transcendence. As his protagonists seek to grow their insight into the truths of the world, their own sanity and ability to handle the universe are questioned. The creatures worshipped as gods in his stories come closer to an alien species that have incomprehensible rules and experiences of consciousness. Yet,he still ends up articulating a WASP (White, Anglo-Saxon, Protestant) moral psychology featuring original sin, predestination, indifference to prayer, nature as a corrupt foil to pure civilization, and suspicion of curiosity as temptation for forbidden knowledge. These are just expressed in terms of cosmic horror and incomprehensible entities that engage with us in our profane world rather than a philosophy of sacred divinity that set a universe in motion.
In stories like The Shadow over Innsmouth or The Rats in the Walls, original sin manifests through ancestral connections. In the former, a captain meets a mysterious tribe that maintains relations with an amphibious alien race and brings these aliens back for intermarriages under the promise of abundant wealth and immortality. Lovecraft is not just critical of a decline due to exchanges with exotic cultures, but also capitalism as a driving force behind the exchanges as a result of prioritizing profit over everything else, including cultural and racial purity maintained through strict segregation.
The second story is where many of Lovecraft’s contradictions come to a clash. The protagonist in this case is a stereotypical refined scholar and gentleman whose family curse reveals an original sin that tainted their descendants. He wrote the story just a couple years after his mother died in the same pyschiatric asylum his father also died in. I mentioned this contradiction earlier in the context of his marriage: despite claiming to be from a superior pinnacle of “Aryan” evolution, Lovecraft was experiencing the downfall of an old-money family in a rapidly changing community with new people and practices he didn’t recognize. We can see how this leaks into the protagonist’s journey as he explores an ancestral home revealing a history of imprisoning humans for perverse rituals that included cannabalism. A common notion in Lovecraft’s day was to project the qualities of individual organisms onto social organizations like family, ethnicites, and countries. In the same way an organism is born, matures, and dies, family bloodlines might have at one point peaked before degenerating into insanity and ill health as time went on. Perhaps Lovecraft thought it was good to be in something from the ground floor, but he came too late for that, at the end, when the best is over. His father’s commitment to a psychiatric institution was the result of neurosyphilis, which was highly stigmatized and assumed to cause degeneration in offspring. Lovecraft no doubt saw his own health issues as a type of original sin haunting his bloodline. Many scholars have argued that this also allowed him to deflect from taking accountability for himself if he was biologically predetermined to be more degenerate.
It’s also in this notion of original sin and ancestral decay that we see how Lovecraft, despite his atheism and materialism, craved something akin to transcendence, at least psychologically. He was an avid traveler even as he lacked funds, with a special appreciation for old colonial architecture. From the perspective of cosmic proportions nurtured by his passion for astronomy, he could see his own life’s tragedies and supposed degeneration as ultimately insignificant. In his imagination, this meant the freedom to explore the pantheon of eldritch entities and symbols he created for his stories. Engaging with cosmic insignificance and the awe of a mechanistic universe across literature and astronomy allowed him to experience something akin to the transcendence of the ego without a core religious or spiritual framework.
I’m reminded of a phrase from Hellraiser here: “the doors to the pleasures of Heaven or Hell, I didn’t care which.” Frank Cotton, the movie and source novel’s antagonist, finds that totally submitting to extreme hedonism has left him with nothing on Earth to pursue for fulfillment anymore. At some point he’s so desperate for a new experience to chase that he ends up unlocking an eternal torture from otherworldly beings who obliterate the distinction between pain and pleasure that parametrize the limits of human experience. Clive Barker, the creator, explicitly connects this mindset to addiction and consumerism. The Cenobites who answer Frank’s call mention that they are “demons to some, angels to others.” Recall how Lovecraft said that his eldritch creatures appeared as gods to the “primitive” humans, while others could see them as extra-terrestrial beings with frightening indifference to human affairs at best, and malicious sadism for personal amusement at worst.
Trickle-Down Economics
Bloodborne consistently weaves threads of ambivalence and ambiguity into the story beats surrounding transcendence, but notably inverts Lovecraft’s perspective as an elitist repulsed by those suffering in the lowest classes of society. The institutions of Yharnam are to blame in this story for the hubris of chasing transcendence through an appeal to eldritch entities. The residents who follow these institutions, be it from fear or faith, are led into a tragic nightmare in an arguably literal sense. The Victorian aesthetics of Yharnam invites comparisons to the historical intersections of healing, science, and religion through apothecaries, colleges, and churches.
From Software, the studio that made the game, uses environmental storytelling with extremely minimal narration, so rather than going through the game’s events, we might look at the lore chronologically.
The Great Ones are the eldritch entities of Bloodborne’s universe who mostly lived in a network of caverns underground. Millions of years before the city of Yharnam was built, an ancient civilization called the Pthumerians built a sophisticated civilization carved into these caverns. They resembled humans, but are a distinct species in the fashion of Theosophic Root Races. When the Pthumerians discovered the Great Ones slumbering in these caves, they started collecting what we later call the “Old Blood” from the bodies and secretions of these entities. Consuming it unlocked supernatural powers and conscious awareness of higher dimensions that could not have been ordinarily perceived through the finite limits of a mortal organic body.
The Old Blood became a critical part of the structure of Pthumerian civilization. A hierarchical caste system formed around the distribution of Old Blood, with the final ruler being Queen Yharnam after who the city we play in is named. Other layers of the caste involved ritual keepers who dedicated themselves to the collection, processing, and allocation of the Old Blood. There were also guardians for the Great Ones as they slept, which the player encounters should they go exploring in these underground ruins.
The Great Ones are not a monolith, however. They have complex motives and agendas that are far deeper than the typical Lovecraftian indifference to humans. And that’s actually more horrifying than apathy might be. It’s said that “Every Great One loses its child, and yearns for a surrogate.” In other words, the Great Ones are conscious and sympathetic to the humans who venerate them. Since the Great Ones are incapable of reproducing, they form relationships with humans to bear cosmic children. Oedon, a formless Great One who is known only through sound and presence of blood, chooses Queen Yharnam to bear his, named Mergo. This stands out starkly with Lovecraft’s framing of mating with alien races as a secret degeneration of the race under the surface of civilization; it is the aspiration of this advanced civilization to merge with otherworldly aliens. The Pthumerians celebrated the fusion of a royal bloodline with a cosmic one as a form of ascension. Unfortunately for the Pthumerians, mass consumption of the Old Blood did not actually lead to mass ascension but mass mutation. Rather than Lovecraft’s emphasis on original sin that haunts bloodlines, individual destinies were shaped by their contemporary relation to the Old Blood.
The guardians and enforcers who consumed massive amounts of blood gained immortality but still decayed, so the players fights them as emaciated skeletal figures. In particularly brutal instance, Pthumerians surgically altered giant guardians to replace their limbs with weapons, including cannons bolted into their spines. Others that sought pyromancy powers appear charred and ashen, as if slowly burned alive. Some seem to have succumbed to bloodlust, which leads to a beastly transformation that resembles something between a satyr and minotaur, and other Pthumerian creatures attack them in the dungeons. The ruling castes seem to have grown obese and doughy, working in tight groups to continue their blood-drunk euphoria.
Flora and fauna were impacted by exposure to the Old Blood too. Rats that ate rotting Pthumerian corpses grew giant and sprouted multiple eyes. Plants that sprouted from soil tainted with the Old Blood grew into sentient centipede-like creatures capable of channeling cosmic energy. Their giant watchdogs also transformed with flesh crystallizing into armor and blood boiling to the point of fire.
Blood also wasn’t the only thing driving madness and transformations. Another avenue to asenscion is found in Insight, representing the “eyes” spiritually and mentally within someone, though sometimes also displayed through the growth or implantation of physical eyes.
An enemy called “Labyrinth Sages” are Pthumerians whose pursuit of Insight rather than the Old Blood produces a different kind of madness. One might almost liken them to different addictive substances. They were part of an elite caste of religious scholars whose purpose was to discover and preserve the intellectual traditions of the Old Blood and Great Ones. Through excessive Insight, the Sages attempted to internalize information too overwhelming for a finite limited brain to process, and so they seem to have lost their senses except to continue attacking any threats. Some Sages wield the bodies of other Pthumerians as weapons, possibly as holy relics as in the case of a saint’s corpse, although some of them are still alive. These Sages appear to be constantly twitching, hyperaggressive, and
Surrogacy
The servants of Queen Yharnam become enemies called “Shadows of Yharnam”, and the Blood Rapture Rune that they drop has a description that reads:
“‘Blood Rapture’ is the raw euphoria of the warmth of blood. Restores HP with visceral attacks, one of the darker hunter techniques. This rune resonates with servants of the Queen, carrier of the Child of Blood, who yearn for their Queen’s blood with little hope of requitement. For them, they find solace in ‘Blood Rapture,’ that serves as a surrogate for their desires.”
The word “surrogate” appears again here, which is no coincidence. A recurring theme in the game is how often people are seeking a substitute for something they cannot have or do themselves.
The Great Ones seek human surrogates since they are doomed to lose any child after conception. The leaders of both the Pthumerians and Yharmanites seek the Old Blood for an evolution they cannot induce within themselves. There’s a symbiotic surrogacy in their dynamic as Great Ones grant surrogate pregnancies in exchange for the transformation seen as ascension. The Moon Presence, having lost a child before, treats Gehrman as a surrogate child which gives the main hub the appearance of a serene nursery with dolls, flowers, and books. The Great One named Kos loses her child as well, so she chooses a human scholar Rom to transform into a mindless premature Great One. Oedon is formless yet is still able to choose Queen Yharnam as a surrogate.
The servants of Queen Yharnam, as well as the later servants of another Queen Annalise, derive their purpose and connection through service to their ruler’s apparently divine and royal bloodline; in its absence, they seek euphoric sensations of blood to fill that lost purpose. The hunter Gehrman was once in love with his pupil Lady Maria, whose guilt for her actions as a hunter lead to her committing suicide, so he crafts a doll in her likeness that becomes animated by a Great One (referred to as The Moon Presence) as his caretaker.
Master Willem and his then-student Laurence, the leader of Byrgenwerth College and later-First Vicar of the Healing Church respectively, used to have a surrogate father-son dynamic. Willem believed insight through eyes was needed to perceive the true nature of reality, while Laurence believed ingesting the Old Blood was the way to understand it. Their split is characterized by Willem as a betrayal, as if Laurence was in line to succeed Willem and the philosophy of insight.
We know there must be more within this infinite universe than our finite sense show us, or at least our imagination can process the concept of infinity as something we lack. Yet, we are bound only to what our bodies allow in their limited form. To escape it and transcend or connect with something outside of ourselves, perhaps even greater than ourselves. Then, we want to share that transcendental experience in the hopes of furthering it through our connections with others.

You either don’t know this game or wish you didn’t know this game. It’s not so dissimilar to addiction in that way, which is no coincidence. Bennett Foddy, the designer of the game, is one of the few people who can claim to have both studied the philosophy behind gaming and addiction as well as developed them with those principles in mind:
“You’re shooting for benign, minor addiction that the person will break free of eventually… I want them to play intently for a while and then get over it.”

recovery/media/movies/dramas-and-dramedi.title: Smash-Up, the Story of a Woman (1947)
Sports
The Way Back
recovery/media/movies/dramas-and-dramedi.content:
Commentary
Disclaimer
Disclaimer: I’m not a sports guy. I can occasionally watch basketball (Go Kings), I can play Madden (Go Lions), I can binge hockey fight compilations (Go Canada), and I can get hyped about competitive Melee (Fox, Final Destination). But I just can’t get into sports the way most people can, and that means sports movies tend to bore me as well. The genre has all the formulaic trappings of the horror genre without the option of rooting for the protagonists to die if you don’t really like them.
So when I went into The Way Back, I didn’t expect to like it and wanted to preface any commentary with a disclaimer that it’s just not my kind of movie. I come into the genre as someone who barely engages with it.
It surpassed expectations: I kind of liked it, because it’s only loosely about sports. It’s much more about Ben Affleck working through his own journey with alcoholism on screen with a sports plot wrapped around it, and the sincerity shows in his performance in a way that resonated with me. He described his experience as “therapeutic” and “cathartic” with the hope of providing that for others as well. It also raised questions for me about how a public figure whose life is examined under a microscope works traditional recovery steps that others do with the safety of anonymity, and perhaps what we can learn from that in the Internet age where everyone is given their 15 minutes of fame.
Spiritus Contra Spiritum
“You see, “alcohol” in Latin is “spiritus” and you use the same word for the highest religious experience as well as for the most depraving poison. The helpful formula убакс мультикам therefore is: spiritus contra spiritum.” — Carl Jung
Recovery is not just about staying clean physically but also about having a clean conscience and mind, which often requires healing from underlying sources of distress through holistic lifestyle changes. For many, this includes growth across the mind, body, and soul — the last of which is commonly associated with spirituality. As Carl Jung wrote in a letter to Bill Wilson, the founder of Alcoholics Anonymous, about a client of his:
“His craving for alcohol was the equivalent, on a low level, of the spiritual thirst of our being for wholeness, expressed in medieval language: the union with God.”
“The only right and legitimate way to such an experience is that it happens to you in reality and it can only happen to you when you walk on a path which leads you to higher understanding. You might be led to that goal by an act of grace or through a personal and honest contact with friends, or through a higher education of the mind beyond the confines of mere rationalism.”
“I am strongly convinced that the evil principle prevailing in this world leads the unrecognized spiritual need into perdition, if it is not counteracted either by real religious insight or by the protective wall of human community. An ordinary man, not protected by an action from above and isolated in society, cannot resist the power of evil””
As a result, most recovery programs either explicitly embrace religion and spirituality or leave room for it. Even evidence-based scientific and secular approaches like SMART Recovery, which integrates principles from Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Rational-Emotive Behavioral Therapy (REBT), find utility in spiritual practices like meditation:
“I think of meditation as REBT in action: REBT is based on the understanding that our thoughts and beliefs determine how we react to situations – that we create our own happiness (and suffering). Buddhist teachings are derived from essentially the same precept – the slogan “pain is inevitable, suffering is optional” pretty much sums it up.”
“It helps me practice acceptance (of self, others, and life); builds my capacity for not getting upset over the upsets; untangles the feelings from the thinking and beliefs about the feelings; and is a big part of how I let go of unhelpful beliefs – importantly, by first bringing those beliefs (and/or patterns of thinking and reacting) into conscious awareness. Much easier to dispute irrational beliefs if you know what they are!” — Charlotte Miller, SMART Recovery Facilitator
Anthropologist Mary Douglas wrote in Purity and Danger (1966) about the ideas of “dirt” throughout history within the context of cleanliness and sacred rituals. As the adage goes, “hurt people hurt people”: a simple way of describing the notion that suffering spreads through society in the way that a pollutant or illness might.
““There are two distinct ways of cancelling a pollution: one is the ritual which makes no enquiry into the cause of the pollution, and does not seek to place responsibility; the other is the confessional rite… Reflecting on this instance, we can suppose that confession, since it always makes precise the nature of the offence and enables blame to be allocated, is a good basis for demanding compensation.””
In trying to stay “clean,” addicts confront not just the physical impurities in their bodies by drug abuse, in which someone’s state of mind is altered to favor destructive ends, but also the underlying psychic wounds within themselves and society that resurface as triggers. Otherwise, many addicts find themselves in a state of chronic relapsing that progressively gets worse over time. Organized spirituality has its roots in organized religion, so it’s worth taking a moment to explore the foundational teachings that inform cultural norms and appeal to diverse individuals.
Christianity
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us.”
— 1 John 1:9
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
— Psalm 51:10
In Christianity, the framework of sin mediates the understanding of suffering, with sin considered a crime against God that results from innate character defects within humans as limited beings. Thus, even when others are hurt as a result of one’s sin, the primary crime is against God. Through sacramental rituals such as baptism and confession, one can repent to seek forgiveness from God before putting their renewed self into action. In doing so, God also forgets the sin, giving a “clean slate” when judging an individual’s soul for the afterlife and hopefully a clean conscience while on Earth. As for forgiveness from those who suffered as a result of sin:
“If you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift… first be reconciled to your brother.”
— Matthew 5:23–24
“If you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.”
— Matthew 6:15
Confessing one’s sins to another and seeking forgiveness as part of reconciliation is highly valued, even preceding the command to seek forgiveness from God. In turn, the victim of one’s sins is commanded to provide that forgiveness, or else they will not be forgiven for their own sins. This reciprocity provides a foundation for social conduct that encourages amends and restitution as evidence of repentance but is distinct from the ultimate forgiveness that comes from God. It also lends itself as a moral justification for certain legal systems based on compensation and restorative justice, a philosophy on justice that dates back to Aristotle.
Consider adultery. In a culture that sees monogamous relationships as a type of contract between two individuals and their offspring as the rightful inheritors of one’s estate, an affair is seen as a violation that harms one’s partner if not the entire family unit. If someone cheated, we tend to think that this person should confess their affair so that their partner can renegotiate the terms of the relationship, whether it’s placing new rules or moving on.
“You ask, ‘Why?’ It is because the LORD is the witness between you and the wife of your youth. You have been unfaithful to her, though she is your partner, the wife of your marriage covenant.”
— Malachi 2:14
No-fault divorce is a relatively recent norm — California was the first US state to implement it in 1969. Australia established it in 1975, and Canada established it in 1986. Fault-based alimony in divorces came from the idea that a husband, traditionally expected to be the breadwinner and more likely to commit sexual misconduct, should provide for a wife since she would be expected to raise any children resulting from the marriage. If the wife was at-fault instead, that might void the alimony.
So we can see that the framework for confessing a sin has played a role morally, socially, and legally — sometimes all at once. Figuring out who is at fault and undergoing some kind of consequence as penance is seen as necessary before restitution, reformation, or absolution is achieved.
Judaism
“For transgressions between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones; however, for transgressions between a person and another, Yom Kippur does not atone until he appeases the other person.”
— Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah
Similar to Christianity, Judaism frames sin as an offense against God, but also clarifies that God does not have the moral right to grant forgiveness for the suffering caused to other people. Before God grants forgiveness, one must fulfill their obligation to seek forgiveness from others. There’s a greater emphasis on seeking forgiveness from fellow humans than in Christianity, where God has the ultimate right to forgive all sins if they’re confessed and repentance is sought.
To atone in the eyes of God, practicing Jews observe Ten Days of Repentance starting with Rosh Hashanah and ending with Yom Kippur. To receive forgiveness, one must repent with sincere regret, a commitment to improve, and then a confession to God. As part of proving this resolve not to commit the sin again, one is instructed to seek forgiveness from those they have harmed three times. If this is not given, as Judaism does not command forgiveness with the same emphasis as Christianity, then one has at least shown God their resolution to improve and can seek forgiveness from God for their sins against Him. The motivation to forgive one’s fellow humans is in hoping that one too will be forgiven for their sins if they open themselves up to the process of amends. One can repent and atone repeatedly in their lives, but the Ten Days of Repentance provide a collective ritual in which people can humble themselves together in seeking forgiveness.
Buddhism
In many Buddhist traditions, suffering and wrongdoing are considered the result of ignorance with natural consequences in the form of negative karma, and forgiveness is a practical virtue of the victim rather than a code of conduct for actions that produce suffering. If someone commits adultery, they may suffer natural consequences in the way of reputational harm, internal shame, communicable disease, pregnancy, or other disruption to their life. For the victim, a common piece of wisdom is given: no one has ever died from a snake’s bite, but the venom their body holds onto. Similarly, forgiveness itself is a purifying action for the one who is bitten, not necessarily something that cleanses the snake of its nature to cause suffering.
“By oneself is evil done; by oneself is one defiled. By oneself is evil left undone; by oneself is one purified. Purity and impurity depend on oneself; no one can purify another.”
— Dhammapada 165
Buddhist ethics emphasize individual action and discipline in the maintenance of oneself even as it promotes the harmony of an interconnected world. This defies the stereotypical collectivism vs. individualism dichotomy that is often imposed in discussions about Eastern vs. Western cultural spheres. In fact, the Serenity Prayer is a good entry point into this perspective, where the principle of focusing only on the things we can control is defined as the purification of oneself, although there is value in expressing generosity and compassion towards others. The natural state of a being without attachment that produces suffering is assumed to be compassion.
Though the belief in deities and divinity is not in contradiction with Buddhist ethics, divine forgiveness or validation does not play a role in one’s own karma. Rituals may be an aspect of cultivating discipline, but the simple act of a ritual doesn’t purify oneself. Because of this, confession does not have inherent value in purifying oneself of wrongdoing either.
