recovery/media/movies/horror/10-cloverfi.title: 10 Cloverfield Lane
recovery/media/movies/horror/10-cloverfi.content:
There’s one scene specifically in this movie that I like as just a very succinct story about self-sabotage that stands alone.
Emmett explains how he lived his whole life in a 40 mile radius, and how he sabotages his own literal ticket out because of his insecurities about failing. Specifically, he makes sure to get so drunk that he would fail to wake up in time to move. There’s something about that self-sabotage that’s like self-destructing to break some version of oneself that seems destabilizing or misaligned. In that sense, something liberating, as if the self is so intolerable that destruction is preferable to living with it further. Repeat that process for long enough, and you arrive at the reasoning behind a lot of alcoholism.

recovery/media/movies/horror/hellraiser.title: Hellraiser
recovery/media/movies/horror/hellraiser.content:
“The doors to the pleasure of Heaven or Hell. I didn’t care which… I thought I’d gone to the limits. I hadn’t. The Cenobites gave me an experience beyond limits… pain and pleasure, indivisible.”
The original Hellraiser movie is comfortably a contender for one of my favorite movies of all time. The sequels have been not as good, to say the least, including one movie clearly made to extend the IP rights.
In the 2022 sequel, the protagonist is overtly struggling with addiction as part of the plot, but I still feel the original was far better at tapping into the raw themes underlying addiction.
One of the most confusing aspects of addiction to people who have never abused substances or struggled with compulsions is how someone can keep using despite the pain outweighing the pleasure. It’s actually confusing for most addicts who attempt recovery too, which often leads to the conclusion that one must simply be incapable of valuing anything over the addictive stimulus. The quotes above from Frank Cotton, the real antagonist driving the events of the film, reveal some of this thinking in a visual narrative that’s helpful to dissect.
Clive Barker
“I think one of the things that fantastic writing does is that it joins up the places of power. It actually says to the reader: ‘This thing that you remember from your childhood, this moment of epiphany you know from your childhood, is actually connected up with this piece of physics, and this piece of physics is actually connected with the theory of magic, and the theory of magic is actually connected to your ideas about sex and your ideas about sex are actually connected to your ideas about love, which, in turn, are connected to your ideas about death which are, in turn, connected with higher physics’… We live in such strictly decompartmentalised times, when it’s all about specialisation.”
The Hellbound Heart
The movie is a loose adaptation of The Hellbound Heart which had the great fortune of involving the author, Clive Barker, in its production. I’m going to avoid referencing too much of the book here, but I find it hard not to analyze the book and movie at the same time, seeing both as the result of the same perspective on escapism and hedonism.
the written description of the experience of using the Configuration within the opening of the novella is very close to a bad trip. Frank’s backstory, which is mostly dropped in the movie, features waves of depression, suicidality, and nihilism that persisted since his adolescence. Larry, or Rory in the book, turns out to be a very vanilla man who finds the routine of ordinary life to be engaging and overreacts to mild disturbances.
Frank
Frank is shown to be a hedonistic thrill-seeker who has no regard for norms or rules. He travels the world in search of taboo pleasures beyond what everyday life could provide, obviously including drugs and sex. He has an affair with his brother Larry’s wife, Julia, which introduces the elements of Frank’s debauchery into the family. Kirsty, Larry’s daughter, is our primary protagonist as a stereotypical coming-of-age woman seeking to carve out an independent life for herself.
In the book version, Frank’s hedonism burns through the capacity for normal life, and he becomes jealous of Larry’s ability to be fulfilled in his routine ordinary life with a family. In the movie version, we see Frank put on Larry’s skin after a murder as a disguise, but the context from the book adds another dimension to Frank becoming Larry and having an affair with Larry’s wife. He wants to be his brother, and he horrifically attempts to literally enact the substitution.
I’m going to avoid referencing too much of the book here, but the written description of the experience of using the Configuration within the opening of the novella is very close to a bad trip. Frank’s backstory, which is mostly dropped in the movie, features waves of depression, suicidality, and nihilism that persisted since his adolescence. Larry, or Rory in the book, turns out to be a very vanilla man who finds the routine of ordinary life to be engaging and overreacts to mild disturbances.
From this perspective, the addiction analogy seems natural. When Frank says he doesn’t care whether he found heaven or hell, he’s reached the point that many addicts do where nothing on Earth seems to satisfy the desire for instant intense gratification.
The Lament Configuration that he finds on his travels to Morocco has the same promise of exotic transcendentalism that give substances their allure. Talk To Me plays with a similar concept by treating its hand as something ancient and traveled. The Lament Configuration is a puzzle box which someone must activate intentionally before knowing what the outcome can be, mimicking the ritual preparation that goes into using substances alongside the risk of something horrible happening after. The way Frank brings the box back to the old home Larry, Julia, and their daughter Kirsty move into isn’t very different than the way drugs can cross borders to end up in the hands of everyday people.
Kirsty is the protagonist of the film, a teenager on the threshold of exploring adulthood. She’s beginning to explore sexuality with her boyfriend at the same time that she encounters Frank and the Lament Configuration, which we can read as experimenting with drugs she stumbled upon. No peer pressure, no crazy partying, just the all-too-common story of kids  finding an adult’s stash and applying their basic human curiosity. Even though she was absentmindedly playing with the Configuration, she still activates it to summon the Cenobites. Rather than dragging her away though, she has the presence of mind to cut a deal that would lead the Cenobites to Frank, their escapee.
The Cenobites are a great concept that stands out in an era were villains like Freddy Krueger and Jason Vorhees became breakout icons of the horror genre. Fun fact, Clive Barker was inspired by his visits to underground BDSM clubs for the movie’s costuming choices, so if your instinct upon seeing them was to scream “BDSM DEMONS”, you’re definitely not alone. Well, as the iconic Cenobite Pinhead says: “Demons to some, angels to others.”
We can conclude then that Frank was born into a mental or neurological state that predisposed him to seeking more risks and pleasure to fill that void, rather than experiencing a traumatic upbringing or inflicting some curse on himself. He’s almost tragically relatable in trying to counter numbness with drastic measures. By the time he gets to the Configuration: “this new addiction quickly cured him of dope and drink. Perhaps there were other ways to bend the world to suit the shape of his dreams.” So the book is explicit about the box being a reference to addiction. There are some really good passages I’d love to keep referencing, but I’ll save it for the page about the book.
Anyways, the deal Kirsty proposes the Cenobites can be read as deciding that

recovery/media/movies/horror/talk-to-me.title: Talk to Me
recovery/media/movies/horror/talk-to-me.content:
Overview
Commentary
Spiritual possession is a way for us to try and model behaviors that seem too far out of the ordinary for us to understand. If someone presents with symptoms of schizophrenia and hears voices, without a neurobiological explanation, we might conclude that they’re attuned to a different space of consciousness than the rest of us where other beings exist. Dreams can be interpreted as visions, messages, or warnings. Seizures or dissociative identity disorders might be considered the result of another consciousness intruding into the body. “Antisocial” behaviors might be seen as the result of malicious influence, such as the Devil tempting people into sin when they follow a compulsion or sirens luring sailors when long isolation causes them to hear things. PTSD flashbacks could be seen as lingering spirits stuck in the past with “unfinished business” that take over someone’s body. After all, to the person who presents these behaviors, their experiences are as real and impactful as anything else in their life.
Scientific discoveries don’t necessarily make mental health easier to understand either. Arguably, since the Enlightenment era, we’ve become more convinced of the mind-over-matter paradigm; if we can just identify the material cause of a problem, we just need to make the rational decision to choose a material solution. This paradigm encourages the perspective that you’re defined primarily by your cognition which governs your body’s behavior, so the responsibility for your behavior lies with your willpower to change your mind to change your behavior. Being impacted by your environment comes to be seen as a kind of vulnerability or even flaw that you have to find the internal resources to overcome.
The metaphor of spiritual possession persists as a way to discuss our minds, our consciousnesses, and our behaviors when we lack rational explanations. We stay in toxic and abusive relationships even when we know we should establish boundaries. We’re scared to fly even though it’s far more statistically safe than driving. We resist seeing the doctor because we’re more scared of being judged than suffering from a treatable illness. We buy things we don’t particularly want or need just because they’re on sale. We know we’ll regret saying something mean that we can’t take back, but we do it anyways. We know social media platforms lead to doomscrolling but keep them on our phones. We’ll refuse to believe surveys in favor of a close friend’s anecdote. We’ll do something self-destructive just to spite someone we don’t like. We’ll do something stupid and dangerous to get the attention of someone we do like. Studies show we tend to eat more when people around us eat more too, even though their stomachs have nothing to do with ours. We’ll give contradictory advice to people who won’t listen anyways. We think infinite growth is possible even though we live in a finite world.
By externalizing these behaviors as a spirit, we can discuss them without the same expectations we reserve for individuals. We might expect someone with depression to take rational steps to improve their mood or someone with substance abuse disorders to reliably summon the willpower to abstain, but by reframing the issue as an entity that attacks the rational consciousness that we assume defines us, we can better communicate the non-rational influences we battle with.
The Babadook is one of the best examples of this. A single mother struggles to keep her life together after losing her husband and receives very little empathetic support in her life. Her job still expects her to show up, she can’t relate to her friend group’s daily lives anymore, doctors prescribe medications that don’t address her underlying suffering, child protective services grow concerned not about her but whether she’s an adequate guardian, her son is overactive with behavioral issues, etc. In the middle of all this, she begins to be plagued by a spirit that seems to want to drive her insane until she violently attacks her son. The director described her motivation as wanting to depict “the fear of going mad” through the darkness within us in the middle of something as romanticized as parenthood.

recovery/media/shows/dramas-and-dramedie.title: Severance
recovery/media/shows/dramas-and-dramedie.content:
I almost forgot that Mark is actually a functioning alcoholic in this show.
One of the things that caught me off-guard was how Mark at work didn’t seem to struggle with compulsive urges at all. It’s not particularly unusual for functional alcoholics to make it through the workday without a drink or withdrawal symptoms. Mark at work definitely carries the physical effects of drinking from the night before, but his attitude and behaviors at work are still entirely distinct from his depressed self at home, which is the self that has the source of his self-medicating. This actually lends itself to a really good demonstration of the psychosocial aspects of substance use disorders.
The chip in his brain has not altered the neural pathways into “curing” his drinking habits. It only changes his memories concerning his identity to be reestablished in a new environment. We’re forced to examine Mark as a character whose transformation between different states of mental health can’t be attributed to something like a chemical imbalance or “hijacked” reward pathways. The chip erases the trauma of losing a loved one, gives him a new stable environment with clear objectives and incentives, and sustains social reinforcement through cooperative peers and feedback from authorities.

Alcoholics Anonymous Agnostica
recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.content:
Summary
AA Agnostica was founded in 2011 by Roger Couvrette, an atheist AA member from the Greater Toronto Area.
The inspiration came from a controversy where We Agnostics and Beyond Belief, two secular AA groups, were removed from the GTA Intergroup’s meeting directory after the groups began using an alternative version of the Twelve Steps and Traditions. While documenting these events and the history of secularism in AA, Couvrette realized there was far more than he expected for an initial investigation. So came about the website. Generally, “agnostic” as a term is used to signal that you at least accept that no belief in God is required to work the Twelve Steps, without asserting a claim about God in general.
In 2015, Couvrette published Do Tell! Stories by Atheists and Agnostics in AA which documented stories from 15 men and women each about their gratitude for AA Agnostica. In 2017, Couvrette published A History of Agnostics in AA that compiled the research collected over the years.
Note: In April 2026, AA Agnostica announced they would no longer post new articles to their site after 14 years and 777 articles, though it remains up and accessible. The site had seemed to cease publishing new content in an early announcement in 2022 with 742 articles, but they seem to have restarted at some point before stopping again.
I would be doing a disservice if I did not credit this website for being an invaluable inspiration for what an independent knowledge base about recovery can look like.

Should we embrace addiction?
recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.content:
Overview
You might have guessed that the title is a bit sensationalist; “Should we embrace addicts?” sounds less controversial, doesn’t it? That’s what Elizabeth F.S. Roberts actually suggests here though, and it’s a reasonable challenge to the hyperindividualism that’s become standard in America. As she says:
“In the United States, a predominantly Protestant nation, which preaches individuality, we suspect dependency of any kind. While my neighbors in Mexico City embraced dependency as key to survival, in the United States, we are profoundly uncomfortable feeling dependent on anything or anyone. This discomfort is ever-present in how we define addiction…”
I don’t disagree with this chunk at all. In fact, the longer I’ve been exposed to recovery circles, the more this becomes obvious. There’s a consistent pattern in American recovery approaches attempting to fuse concepts from cultural traditions that emphasize interconnectedness and impermanence without any changes to the atomized society we exist in. This isn’t to say that the compulsive habits are perceived as a good thing in other cultures, but dependence on something external is far less likely to be treated as a pathology warranting punitive measures than a cause for sympathy and charity.

recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.title: Happy Pie
recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.content:
“Note that the 40 percent allocation to intentional activity is a value obtained by the method of subtraction. If we assume that 50 percent of all variation in happiness is genetic, that 10 percent is circumstantial, that intentional action is the only remaining source of variation, and that the estimates are free of error, then the remaining 40 percent must be attributable to intentional action. If these assumptions are met, the method of subtraction has logical force. But are they met?”
“Suppose you learned that 50% of the variation in body height was due to genes and 10% was due to circumstance (e.g., diet). Would you conclude that 40% is due to intentional action?”

recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.title: Psychology Today
What Really Makes You a Happy Person?
recovery/media/websites/blogs-and-publis.content:
Introduction
“According to a popular idea about the science of happiness, 10% of the variance in happiness in a given population is due to life circumstances (age, nationality, sex, race/ethnicity, and income); 50% is due to genetics; and 40% remains under our direct control. These numbers have been repeated in countless journal articles and books, and discussed as fact in college courses around the world.”
“Be skeptical.”
“These perfectly round numbers raise more questions than answers, and as of today, I still don’t trust them.”
Skeptical is probably the word I’d pick if you only gave me one to describe myself. It might have at one point been nihilistic or cynical or jaded, but I’ve since come to appreciate that substantive solutions to problems are real. They’re just hidden under a pile of marketing for get-X-quick schemes: get-rich-quick, get-happy-quick, get-laid-quick. These exploit the common human desire for shortcuts in a consumerist society driven by the mantras “time is money” and “greed is good.” But, it is possible to find some pretty solid answers if you remain radically skeptical. Trust no one, not me, and not yourself.

recovery/news/data-breaches.title: Data Breaches
recovery/news/data-breaches.content:
Overview
I love data, but I am highly skeptical of centralized databases of any kind. I don’t like it when groups of people make lists of other people they want to monitor. I don’t like it when private corporations do it, I don’t like it when rogue militias do it, I don’t like it when state agencies do it. Yet, it’s in the nature of institutions and systems that they only exist insofar as they can draw boundaries between themselves and the outside world to be defined, modeled, and controlled. Data and surveillance are key ingredients for institutions seeking to construct a predictive model that enhances their ability to monitor their influence and control.
On a personal level, I am constantly torn between the desire to collect data to detect patterns and the desire to preserve privacy and anonymity for maximal freedoms. I don’t include any tracking mechanisms on this site to collect your data aside from what Cloudflare tells me as the hosting service for these pages. I can see unique visitors, total page requests, geographic distribution, and some other adjacent surface metrics, but nothing that gives me a clue about who you actually are or what you do once you leave my site. Some people think that’s excessive paranoia, and they might be right, but on the other hand, most of us aren’t aware of most security issues that exist in the technology we use. I record the ones I’m aware of here.
Also, many of these breaches involve class action lawsuits, so get that bread, friends.

recovery/news/harm-reduction-hysteria.title: Harm-Reduction Hysteria
recovery/news/harm-reduction-hysteria.content:
Overview
Stories
The Atlantic
The Cities That Said Yes to Drugs (07/30/2026)
Article Link
“Seattle, like a striking number of other liberal American cities, has embraced a radical form of “harm reduction,” which is more a philosophy about treating addiction than a scientific approach to it.”
No. This is false.
Harm reduction is absolutely an evidence-backed scientific paradigm towards, as the name says, reducing the harms caused by substance use. There is nothing about harm reduction that prevents us from offering programs and treatments geared towards abstinence. It is not an alternative philosophy to abstinence-based policies. It is not the product of some bleeding-heart ruinous empathy from a nanny state, or whatever the terms are now for anything other than the most punitive policy option.
The fact is that not everyone is going to choose abstinence-based treatment, so we should reduce the harms of that choice. People who use clean needles provided by a center instead of dirty needles that have been in a dozen other veins are less likely to develop health issues that require emergency interventions, which are far more expensive and scarce as resources than mass-manufactured supplies.
We have decades of research that show harm reduction interventions prevent overdoses, lower rates of infectious diseases like HIV, and become bridges towards long-term recovery by supporting incremental but lasting change. Some evidence indicates that those who use harm reduction services are five times more likely to enter treatment than those who don’t.
Powell also cites the New York Department of Health’s page to define harm reduction as a “social movement” to “building leadership” among drug users. The more complete sentence he butchers actually reads:
“It is a belief in and respect for the rights of people who use drugs and strategies that include building leadership among people who use drugs and supporting communities in reducing the negative consequences associated with drug use and the harms associated with the context of drug use such as racism, homelessness, violence, and poverty.”
You know who else believes in building leadership among people who use drugs and supporting communities in reducing the negative consequences?
Alcoholics Anonymous.
As well as every other recovery group out there: Crystal Meth Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous, Recovery Dharma, Refuge Recovery, SMART Recovery, Lifering Secular Recovery, etc. All of these groups very explicitly state their philosophy revolves around peer support rather than professional or institutional mechanisms. Harm reduction interventions lean into the fact that it often takes someone who has experience with substance use to reach others still struggling with it. It works with these networks rather than cracking down and disrupting them.
Powell makes it sound like they’re giving leadership courses to drug dealers to better organize crack houses, like a cartoonish version of Stinger Bell.
“in some rare cases they’ve created dedicated spaces for addicts to shoot up. Meanwhile, police departments struggling with staffing shortages and budget cuts have stopped devoting resources to sweeping users and dealers off the streets or out of parks and playgrounds.”
It’s almost as if creating dedicated spaces for people to use substances under medical supervision reduces the need for law enforcement to sweep them out of other public spaces…
I’ll comment on the rest of this article, but I feel confident in condemning it as poorly researched at worst and bad faith at best, and sensationalist either way.
Also, I for one do not want to live in a society where a government’s agents, rather than trained healthcare professionals, can label someone as having a health condition requiring institutionalization. I would rather pay fewer taxes while affording more freedoms for myself and a higher quality of life for those in active addiction, than pay more taxes to expand a surveillance state into nabbing anyone off the streets and into a box.

recovery/organizations/activists-advocac.title: Mexico
Pro-Vapeo Mexico
recovery/organizations/activists-advocac.content:
Overview
Pro-Vapeo Mexico is a civil advocacy group that represents vaporizer/e-cigarette companies and consumers that argue for harm reduction over total bans.
Context
Mexico has some of the strictest anti-tobacco laws in the world. Cigarettes can be legally bought and possessed, but smoking is banned in all public places including outdoor patios and individual private rooms in hotels.
In 2008, the General Tobacco Law banned the production and distribution of any product that resembled a tobacco product, including vapes, though the Mexican Supreme Court ruled in 2015 that it was unconsitutional to ban vapes while traditional cigarettes were still legal. President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador (AMLO) issued multiple decrees from 2020-2022 attempting to ban the importation and commercialization of any electronic nicotine prducts, though the Supreme Court pushed back again in 2021. Eventually, in 2024 under President Claudia Sheinbaum, the Mexican Congress approved a constitutional amendment that included a vaping ban, placing vapes into the same legal category as fentanyl. In 2026, Sheinbaum proposed criminal penalties to enforce the ban since vaping companies were still selling their products.
Organizations like Pro-Vapeo Mexico argues that this repeats the same mistakes that the United States made with its own Prohibition amendment on alcohol. Businesses that were willing to comply with regulations were replaced with organized crime that use violence and distribute products that can’t be monitored for safety.

Phoenix House Foundation
recovery/organizations/activists-advocac.content:
From 1967 to 2019, the Phoenix House Foundation was a nonprofit that offered alcohol rehabilitation throughout the United States. It adopted several methods from Synanon, a very controversial group that became something of a cult. The documentary Born in Synanon goes into detailed interviews with its members, including children born and raised according to the program’s leaders. The Phoenix House itself was not affiliated with the cult aspects of Synanon; Dr. Mitchell Rosenthal had observed early Synanon group practices and brought them with him when founding Phoenix House.
In 2005, the United States Department of Justice labeled it a “model program.”
In 2019, the Foundation dissolved into stand-alone regional organizations.

Addiction Technology Transfer Center (ATTC) Network
recovery/organizations/government/united.content:
The Addiction Technology Transfer Center (ATTC) Network emerged as a federally-funded network of 11 regional centers coordinating with a National Office in order to help community-based treatment programs adopt the latest treatments.
That originally came in the form of funding more professionals, facilitating training courses, building partnerships with education and research institutions, and developing cross-discipline curriculums. Like many organizations and projects in this era, it sought to work across disciplines that interacted with addiction, like nursing, criminal justice, social work, and psychology.
Over time, the network also began focusing on supporting change in systems and organizations rather than just educating clinicians on the latest tools and protocols. A recurring theme in information-sharing projects is that simply presenting information doesn’t actually lead to long-term changes in practice. Producing change in organizations is a field unto itself called Implementation Science that grew in popularity through the 90s.
Wait, Mank, isn’t your website just presenting information? That was already presented?
Shut up. This is different. Shut up. Moving on.
On average, it takes an average of 17 years to integrate a new medical intervention into standard healthcare practice. That lines up with what a professor once gave me as a rule of thumb: assume that American protocols are 5-10 years behind the international standards and assume the international standards are 5-10 years behind the research consensus for state-of-the-art approaches. Some of the evidence-based interventions included motivational interviewing, contingency management, and buprenorphine treatment. CM is among my favorite proposals to address addiction as both social policy and individual assistance.
The ATTC Network remains one of the longest running public efforts to translate evidence from research into clinical practice.

recovery/organizations/higher-education/.content:
Based on an analysis from 2011-2015, New Mexico had the highest rate of alcohol-related deaths in the United States. CASAA’s ambition is to be the focal point of substance abuse studies and treatments for the state of New Mexico.
Findings
A survey of Pre-Post COVID-19 drinking habits found that drinking increased in 60.1% of respondents and remained the same for 27.0%. The top three reasons given where stress, boredom, and increased availability. Of those who consumed any alcohol over the past 30 days, 34.1% reported binge drinking at least once (~20% of all respondents) and 7% reported extreme binge drinking habits. Alcohol damages the body immune system, which means drinkers are more likely to get sick, which can then lead to more stress and boredom if required to isolate.

recovery/organizations/mutual-aid-and-pe.title: Alcoholics Victorious
recovery/organizations/mutual-aid-and-pe.content:
Alcoholics Victorious (AV) is one of the “Christian AA” groups that considers AA to be secular and prefers a more overtly Christian approach to recovery. As their website states, “there is a ‘spiritual’ element in addiction that must be addressed through the true GOD.” Non-Christians or non-believers can attend, provided they “feel compelled to search out the true ‘higher power’ Jesus Christ, attempting to identify Him, to come to know Him, and then to trust Him for healing power.”
AV is an official program of Christians in Recovery, which is a ministry of TechMission, which is a nonprofit organization that operates City Vision College. AV chapters are required to annually renew their charters with the official organization, including forms and fees. Meetings can involve Bible teachings but are not intended to be Bible study groups.
History
Alcoholics Victorious was founded in 1948.
The “True Higher Power”
“Those who have not yet placed their faith in Christ have an opportunity to come to know the true “Higher Power” spoken of in AA, finding an atmosphere of accepting Christian love in which to form a personal relationship with the Lord.”
It’s interesting that the premise of the group isn’t necessarily a meeting space for those who have chosen Jesus as their Higher Power for the Twelve Steps, but those who believe that the Higher Power of AA is Jesus. The term “true higher power” appears multiple times on the site.
“Founded in 1948, Alcoholics Victorious support groups offer a safe environment for people recovering from the effects of alcoholism or drug addiction. We recognize Jesus Christ as our “Higher Power” and gather together to share our experience, faith, strength and hope. AV meetings use the 12 Steps, the Bible and the Alcoholics Victorious Creed.
June 2019 News: Royal CBD is offering 30% off to all Alcoholics Victorious chapter members on their 250mg and 500mg CBD oils using code AV30.”
No, that’s not a mistake. That text about the CBD oil is there because that’s literally on the front page of Alcoholics Victorious. Since it’s from June 2019, I’m willing to bet that it’s probably not an active offer and it’s safe to share without enticing anyone.
My guess as to what happened has to do with this article from July 2019: www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/cbd-cannabis-christian-book-distributors-weed-marijuana-a9013666.html
Apparently, there was a company called the Christian Book Distributors that went by the acronym CBD and held the domain www.cbd.com
““I was driving my mum down the road recently,” he told the New York Times. “She saw a sign that said ‘CBD sold here.’ I was like, ‘No, mum. That’s not us.’””
Major advertising networks like Google Ads banned cannabis-related ads, which means companies like Royal CBD are far more dependent on search engine optimization (SEO) to appear higher in Google search results. One approach to SEO is to place links to your website on niche high-authority websites. Alcoholics Victorious is a niche community, so the official home page has high authority on the topic. The website owners may have thought that the CBD making them an offer to be paid for a backlink was somehow related to the Christian Book Distributors, especially if the latter or an agency they hired was sneaky about the pitch. It’s plausible that someone not familiar with marijuana might interpret “CBD oils” as some kind of accessory wellness product sold alongside spiritual wellness literature.
Either that, or this is a really, really flexible group.
There’s other things about the website that are strange too. If you’re compulsive about numbers, you may have realized that if AV was founded in 1948, then to be serving needs for 66 years brings us to 2014.
Unfortunately I couldn’t find much material about Alcoholics Victorious out there. It seems to have always remained a niche but enduring group for Christians whose spirituality might come entirely from Biblical teachings.

recovery/organizations/mutual-aid-and-pe.title: All Addicts Anonymous
Anorexic and Bulimics Anonymous
recovery/organizations/mutual-aid-and-pe.content:
Anorexic and Bulimics Anonymous (ABA) adapts the Twelve Step approach of AA for eating disorders.
Some studies find that 1 in 4 individuals diagnosed with an eating disorder will also develop a substance use disorder. Among adult women specifically with eating disorders, up to 50% report a history of substance abuse. Up to 35% of individuals with a substance use disorder also present with a co-occurring eating disorder. For context, that’s about 11 times higher the baseline of the general population.
It’s not so hard to see the connection between substances and appetite in general. Marijuana induces food cravings which can induce binge eating.  Depending on the person, alcohol can increase or decrease appetite. Chronic heavy drinking can have long-term impacts on appetite and nutritional absorption. Nicotine and caffeine are widely used as appetite suppressants, hence the “European breakfast” consisting of coffee and cigarettes. There’s evidence of business in the early industrial eras providing their workers with those to avoid raising wages to cover a real breakfast. It should be noted though that studies about the effectiveness of their appetite suppression are mixed, and each person’s body will react differently of course. And by no means should you actually pick this up as a habit to lose weight, it’s not safe.
It should go without saying, but I’ll say it anyways: nothing on this site constitutes medical advice or should be seen as a substitute for consulting a medical professional. I’m just some dude looking at studies from actual experts. I do feel confident though in saying that you should not skip meals in favor of drugs.
From my understanding, at the level of peer support groups and recovery programs, treating the compulsive thoughts associated with eating disorders similarly to the cravings associated with addiction is a solid approach. Those with co-occurring disorders can apply recovery philosophies and tools throughout their lives, such as dealing with overlapping triggers at once.
On the other hand, unlike substances or many process addictions, no one can achieve complete abstinence from eating, so modified programs frame the issue as abstinence from the behaviors associated with their eating disorders.
Plus, while many recovering from substances do face nutritional imbalances, many in recovery tend to feel better simply through supplements and a restored appetite. That isn’t to say there isn’t a whole field and industry around remedying the ways substances interfere with nutritional absorption or deficits. However, for those with eating disorders, it’s far more likely that they will need medical professionals to assess physical complications that can stem from eating disorders. Starvation and purging cause different metabolic changes than chronic substance abuse, though both are real and serious. An alcoholic who hasn’t eaten a real meal in weeks might struggle to regain hold down food and return to their baseline appetite, but severely malnourished patients who attempt to return to baseline appetite can trigger fatal events. There are tragic stories you may have heard about Holocaust survivors who died from eating and drinking too quickly after being freed.
When the body begins to receive nourishment, it releases a surge of insulin that can drive essential minerals out of the bloodstream and into cells, triggering heart failures, respiratory arrest, and seizures. Sudden fluid shifts that produce electrolyte imbalances can trigger cardiac arrythmias in heart muscles that were weakened as they were broken down for energy. Stomach muscles that are responsible for pushing food through the intestines also atrophy, so eating can cause intense nausea and pain. I could keep going on, but I hope the point comes across: eating disorders require unique medical interventions from experts who know exactly how to calibrate meals and fluid ingestion, sometimes intravenously.
I’ve also been generalizing “eating disorders” as one group when they have extremely different characteristics. Anorexia nervosa can involve compulsions like addiction, but binge eating mimics substance use much closer since the body receives signals from the food as an external source.
Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)
ARFID is an eating disorder that was introduced into the DSM-5 in 2013 where someone limits their food intake for reasons unrelated to body image or weight. Rather than anorexia or bulimia, it results from sensory sensitivity, past trauma, and a low drive to eat. To meet the criteria, there must be weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, dependence on tube feeding or nutritional supplements, and interference with regular social activities.
Eating Disorders in Men
There are countless women who have spoken about eating disorders and how it has affected their lives, and how systemic sexism in every layer of society plays a role in reinforcing harmful body standards. This section is not in any way intended to detract or denigrate their perspectives or the real data researchers have collected behind these standards. I only started with this section before Eating Disorders in Women because I’m a little more equipped to speak on standards of men.
While women are more likely to develop eating disorders than men, and that speaks to social gendered standards we all internalize, men still represent roughly 1 in 3 cases of eating disorders.
There are some notable differences in presentations, such as men being more likely to use excessive and compulsive exercise to compensate for calories while women are more likely to induce vomiting and abuse laxatives. Exercise can be a process addiction itself too, and one that many substance addicts can switch into in early recovery as a seemingly healthier substitute, but all things can be used in excess as an unhealthy crutch.
Also, men are less likely to be screened or seek help for eating disorders due to the assumption that it only impacts women, so when they do receive treatment, they tend to have more severe complications. Men who identify as LGBTQ+ are significantly more likely to experience issues with body image and eating disorders.
From 2000 to 2018, the prevalence of eating disorders across the world doubled and seems to continue rising, with men experiencing a faster growth rate than women. The post-pandemic tracking shows that the ratio of male-to-female cases has gone from 1:10 to 1:5 acccording to post-COVID pandemic data. The increase seems concentrated among 10 to 14 year old girls, but also 20 to 24 year old adults regardless of gender identification. Under the ARFID diagnostic category, we see a roughly equal gender split among the 6% of 10 year olds who meet the criteria.

Eating Disorders as Addictions
I’ll admit, I have little exposure to anything about eating disorders aside from what has been confided in me privately by people I’ve met. This section will thus rely heavily on what I found in the literature.
The general concept of disordered eating patterns is as old as the concept of habitual drunkenness, which is to say that you can find descriptions matching the disorders as far back as ancient Greece. Psychiatry as we know it emerged in the last couple centuries.
In 1868, Sir William Withey Gull, a doctor for Queen Victoria of England, observed a pattern of weight loss, cessation of regular periods, and dangerously low heart rates in young women that didn’t seem to result from any physical illness. In 1973, he used “anorexia nervosa” to mean a “nervous lack of appetite” and pointed towards a mental origin. The treatments he recommended involved removing patients from their old environments and implementing strict feeding schedules regardless of the patient’s appetite.

The Hazelden alumni is expansive.
Spin-offs from Hazelden’s early single-modality program include Chit-Chat Farms (Caron), established in 1959 in Wernersville, Pennsylvania, Cumberland Heights, established in Nashville, Tennessee in 1969, Lynnville Treatment Center, established in Jordan, Minnesota in 1969, and Carrollton Treatment Center, established in Cedar Rapids, Iowa in 1973.
Direct spin-offs from Hazelden’s multimodality program include Northwestern Hospital in Minneapolis (1970), Edgewood Treatment Center in St. Louis, Missouri (1971), St. John’s Hospital in St. Paul, Minnesota (1971), Nebraska Methodist Hospital in Omaha (1971), St. Joseph Community Hospital in Vancouver, Washington (1973), St. Vincent Hospital in Sioux City, Iowa (1974), Clifton Springs Hospital and Clinic in Clifton Springs, New York (1976), Mississippi Baptist Hospital in Jackson, Mississippi (1976), and Mercy Hospital at Council Bluffs, Iowa (1977). All of these were established by former Hazelden staff.
Finally, there was the Parkside chain of alcoholism treatment hospitals spawned by Nelson Bradley’s program at Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge, Illinois. By 1989, Parkside delivered addiction treatment at nearly 100 sites. The Parkside chain collapsed in the mid-1990s.
Hazelden also became the country’s biggest publisher of addiction treatment materials in the 1970s, publishing countless video and audio tapes of their lectures.

recovery/organizations/research-and-educ.content:
Founded in 1980, the Anxiety and Depression Association of America is a nonprofit organization in Silver Spring, Maryland. They function as an educational and research organization that advocates for addressing anxiety, depression, and other related disorders. They also maintain online peer communities for anxiety and depression through a partnership with HealthUnlocked, a social media network centered on health operated by PPD Inc, which is a subsidiary of Thermo Fisher Scientific: healthunlocked.com/anxiety-depression-support
As of the writing of this sentence, there are 106,455 members and 97,968 posts, with more added every few hours.
Note that posts are still indexed by search engines, so consider how much you value anonymity before participating. Medical information isn’t just more personally sensitive than your Instagram pics, it can also function as an identifier like a fingerprint if you describe the same set of symptoms in the same way. They also collect some data for research and collaboration with private partners, including pharmaceutical organizations.
I haven’t found any controversies online about HealthUnlocked or the ADAA peer communities specifically, but it would be prudent to apply the same precautions you would if you were trying to be anonymous on any other platform.
Remember that unverifiable anecdotes shouldn’t be taken as certain facts, all online communities can become echo chambers that either confirm your biases or judge without knowing the details of your life, every single database can be hacked or leaked, and no online site’s service should be interpreted as medical advice that substitutes for the opinions of healthcare professionals.

American Psychological Association (APA)
recovery/organizations/research-and-educ.content:
Overview
With over 190,000 members, the American Psychological Association (APA) is the largest psychology association in the world.
Students who grew up in the American education system are likely to have been taught about the MLA style guide for formatting writing. The APA style guide is an alternative that many students see but haven’t been introduced to unless they spend time specifically exploring social science literature.
Commentary
As a result of being the largest psychology association in the world, the APA has sociopolitical significance that regularly leads to controversy and public scrutiny.
The Resignation of Christopher J. Ferguson
In 2021, Christopher J. Ferguson wrote an open letter to the American Psychological Association that he “cannot in good ethical conscience continue” membership as he feels “the APA has lots its way as either a science organization or an organization representing good clinical practice.”
Keep in mind that the APA President in 1946, Henry E. Garrett, was a rabid racist and eugenicist. He gave testimony in favor of school segregation in a case that was combined into Brown v. Board (1954), claiming that desegregation would bring “total demoralization and then disorganization in that order.” The Univerity of Virginia brought him on as a visiting professor in the Department of Education in 1955. In 1961, he published “The Equalitarian Dogma” where he argued “Blacks” were biologically intellectually inferior to “Whites.” In 1968, he wrote “Despite glamorized accounts to the contrary, the history of Black Africa over the past 5,000 years is largely a blank” and “The crime record of the Negro in the United States is little short of scandalous.” He would go on to accuse Jews and Jewish organizations of spreading the dogma, and in 1972 became Director of the Pioneer Fund, an organization inspired by the leading Nazi eugenicists behind the Nuremberg Laws. The American Psychological Association openly acknowledges the eugenicsts existed within their ranks existed into the 1980s. The 1997 winner of the Gold Medal Award for Life Achievement in Psychological Science, Raymond Cattell, supported eugenics and publicly acknowledged neo-Nazis and white supremacists so much so that the backlash to the announcement led to his withdrawal.
So surely, Ferguson must be objecting to the slow pace at which the APA prunes its ranks of pseudoscientific and harmful ideas right? No. The opposite actually.
Ferguson’s first complaints are about the APA distorting evidence on violent video games, spanking, and “guidelines for Men and Boys” that are “disparaging more traditional men.” He does not elaborate on what any of this means; one might reasonably speculate that this is just prefacing the discussion about race with a layer of other objections to imply that he’s spotted a constellation of issues.
On discussions of racism, his argument is that “adopting a dystopian and data-deficient view of the present is likely to do more harm than good.” Don’t let the expert credentials and clinical tone fool you, this is simply rehashing the standard “victim mentality” rhetoric used to dismiss the prevalence of racism by relocating the issue to internalized hysteria. The decline of explicit or implicit racism on average in no way suggests that existing discussion of racism is somehow fearmongering over a fantasized dystopia. Just because the average person on the street is less likely to think racial slurs when they see someone of a different race or would vote for Barack Obama over McCain and Romney doesn’t mean that racism has disappeared in other aspects of society.
Studies have repeatedly shown no statistically detectable decline in anti-Black hiring discrimination since 1989, with a 2017 meta-analysis by Lincoln Quillian showing that White applicants received 36% more callbacks than equally qualified Black applicants. A 2024 study by Josh Leung-Gagne reveals that the deadliest local police departments kill almost 7 times more frequently than the least deadly departments. Police violence is the 6th leading cause of death for men ages 25 to 29, with Black Americans almost three times as likely to be killed than White Americans. These trends can also be found in Native American and Latino communities. Further, a 2021 study published in The Lancet estimates that over half the deaths from police violence were either unreported or misclassified in the National Vital Statistics System used by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
Ferguson’s only discussion of this “complex and nuanced issue” is to accuse the APA of having a distorted perspective through the availability heuristic and social pressures that lead to an excessive focus on the murders of George Floyd and Ahmaud Arbery. Ironically, it’s Ferguson who has fixated on these cases while an absolute avalanche of evidence about the persistent effects of racism have been produced by his colleagues.
He also lazily brings up the claim that “evidence suggests class issues, rather than race, may predict negative outcomes” as if the preponderance of evidence doesn’t indicate both play a role. A 2024 study of the 100 largest US municipalities found that violent crime was mostly associated with income inequality and educational attainment rather than race, but a 2025 analysis of fatal shootings across >32,000 ZIP codes found that race remained an independent predictor after controlling for other factors.
Further, certain forms of racism have actually gotten worse over time. Anti-Asian hate crimes multiplied by a factor of nearly 5 from 2019 to 2021 following COVID-19, so Ferguson’s jab at the term “pandemic of racism” as a cliche is almost willfully ignorant of the long history of associating illness with “outsiders” and “foreigners”, or the Other. An NBER study found that even as public violence overall was declining, there was an observable increase in racially motivated violence against Asian Americans. Roughly one-third of Asian Americans reported experiencing some form of bias in the wake of the pandemic. FBI data shows that hate crimes in general increased 32% from 2019 to 2020, with anti-Black hate crimes increasing 49% and anti-Asian hate crimes increasing 77%. A recent 2026 paper by Manuel J Galvan et al. that models the distribution of racism finds that discriminatory effects are widespread rather than concentrated in just a few bad areas. Even though the total number of hate groups in the United States have been declining, the Southern Poverty Law Center identified that white-nationalist groups increased by 55% from 2017 to 2019.
And then, Ferguson drives his car right off the roads into the lake of culture wars, as he claims the APA “appears to sway with the political currents to what may be its optimal inward-focused gain at any given time. This appears to be as true regarding its historical involvement with the mistreatment of detainees as documented in the Hoffman Report as it is regarding its capitulation to ‘wokism’ in the present.”
The Hoffman Report was a 2015 analysis that found that leaders of the American Psychological Association had cooperated with the Department of Defense to develop ethical guidelines that allowed psychologists to participate in post-9/11 interrogations involving torture, euphemistically referred to as “enhanced interrogation techniques.” It is a Facebook-tier argument to suggest that the forces of “wokism” have the same influence on scientific institutions as the United States military. Remember that there is a long history of pseudoscientific eugenics tied to sociopolitical movements that Ferguson could have pointed to if he wanted to show the APA’s pattern of straying from science, but he chooses instead the comparison to the DoD that alludes to coercive and corrupt intentions.
It also seems Ferguson had no colleagues proofread this letter, as it is impossible to overlook that he says on one hand that “we also give extreme power to outrage and moral grandstanding as well as inaccurate sources of information such as anecdotes and ‘lived experiences’” while saying just one paragraph away that his opinion is “informed in part by my own time on the Council of Representatives, but also watching the APA’s public facing communications.” Outrage over ancedotes for me, but not for thee.
And of course, we can’t end one of these vague general complaints that everyone is talking too much about racism without a preemptive ad hominem defense that implies some maverick or underdog status: “I understand that my words will be unwelcome to the APA and perhaps many others aligned with this current movement on the sociopolitical left (and note, I identify as a liberal myself).”
Why shouldn’t they be unwelcome, when they rely on dystopian and data-deficient views of the present that is likely to do more harm than good? We would only be adhering to the standards Ferguson himself wishes the APA to adopt to keep out confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance driven by lived experiences.

The American Psychological Association No Longer Represents Good Science or Clinical Practice: An Open Letter on My Resignation from the APA

Josh Korda
recovery/people/activists-advocacy-and-a.content:
Note: The foreword of this book is written by Noah Levine, who has since been involved in sexual misconduct allegations through his leadership role at Against the Stream (ATS) and teaching role with Spirit Rock Meditation Center. ATS later dissolved and Spirit Rock revoked his license to teach. No criminal charges appear to have been filed concerning any of the allegations, and Levine denies any wrongdoing. This page will focus on the contents of the book itself.
Foreword
“The Buddha’s teachings are perfect in all ways and will lead any who thoroughly applies them to a profound transformation.”
Yes, it’s the first sentence but I already have to object. I’ve been critical of AA literature for making strong, sweeping statements about how the program can’t fail you, only you can fail the program. This is the same problem again, and it’s common marketing among a lot of self-help products that don’t ever come under scientific scrutiny. Let’s look at some quotes actually attributed to the Buddha.
From AN 3.65:
“Do not go by oral tradition, by lineage of teaching, by hearsay, by a collection of scriptures, by logical reasoning, by inferential reasoning, by reflection on reasons, by acceptance of a view after pondering it, by the seeming competence of a speaker, or because you think, ‘The ascetic is our teacher.‘”
“When you know for yourselves: ‘These things are unwholesome… these things, when undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering’—then you should abandon them.”
“When you know for yourselves: ‘These things are wholesome… these things, when undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness’—then you should enter and remain in them.”
From MN 22, Alagaddupama Sutta:
“I have taught the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping”
From DN 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta:
“Be islands unto yourselves, be your own refuge, with no other refuge; let the Dhamma be your island, the Dhamma your refuge, with no other refuge.”
Obviously, the Buddha is depicted as having critical awakenings to share, but it’s hard to imagine that someone encouraging a radical skepticism towards himself would also approve of such a blanket endorsement.
“As modern American Buddhists we are in the rare and fortunate position to not only receive the Buddha’s Dharma, but to also receive the dharma of psychology. With his teachings and this wonderful book, Josh joins the emerging trend of integrating the best practices of Western theorists with the highest wisdom of the Buddha.”
This is tripping a lot of red flags I got reading The Four Agreements about unifying theories from different cultures in some kind of perennialist fusion, but I’m going to try set that bias aside and be upfront when I recognize it in myself.
Preface
As I make some final touches to this book in the early days of November 2016, I cannot help but note the storm clouds looming in the background of this endeavor… the United States, never to be dramatically outperformed, always seeking the spotlight of history, elects a bigoted sexual predator as president.
Oh, you poor sorry bastard. Just wait until 2026. I yearn for 2016. Simpler times.
On a serious note, I appreciate someone being upfront about their social and political stances. I’m of the opinion that everything is political, and if you don’t feel that it is, it’s because the status quo political situation is fine by you. Not making a choice is a choice.
Addiction is incredibly political. Study after study shows that the biggest factors in determining an individual’s capacity for sustained abstinence involves their access to recovery capital. The movement of capital will always be a political question. The concept of a worthy life enabled by the society we live in will always be political.
All of us suffer, and by trying to achieve peace of mind and security by trudging down capitalism’s Yellow Brick Road of workaholism, careerism, consumerism, fame seeking, and social-media-reputatioan fixation, we waste what little time we have, and wind up absolutely nowhere, not even treated to a glittering, extravagant spectacle such as Oz. Trying to acquire or achieve security and serenity keeps the economy buzzing, chews up our resources, and turns us into competitors, mistrusting each other, viewing each other as obstacles, fighting over slices of an ever-dwindling cake.
One doesn’t need to be a psychologist to discern that constant busyness is a symptom of avoidance, for when we run out of fuel and idle to a full stop, what do we experience? The voidness of meaning that is simply surviving in this world.
There’s not much I can say about capitalism that hasn’t been said a million times before and a million times better. I’d like to focus on the workaholism angle though, because it is unquestionably true that our society elevates certain addictions while stigmatizing others.
I’m reminded of a controversy back in 2017 when Andrew Ng, Stanford Professor and Coursera founder, opened job postings for software engineers to work 70-90 hours a week. I grew up in the Bay around tech people, so there were plenty of stories about tech CEOs, including some you still see making headlines, throwing temper tantrums because their employees weren’t on the 9am to 9pm grind.
I recall a presentation about study abroad during my time at UC Irvine where a slide was dedicated to the culture shock experienced by American students bragging about sleep deprivation as evidence of their hard work. We were told that students in other countries tend to see that as concerning, indicative of either poor work ethic or poor health.
Workaholism is perhaps the most acceptable addiction there is. We elevate it as a form of self-sacrifice and maximization of inner potential. Someone’s works often becomes their legacy. “Greed is good” is unironically a mantra we use to rationalize profit-seeking as meaning-making.
It follows logically that if we elevate one addictive behavior, and addictive behaviors are commonly interchangeable, then we’re elevating addiction itself as a virtue. Addiction to profit, addiction to consumption, addiction to power, addiction to dissociation, addiction to problem-solving, addiction to conflict, addiction to chaos, addiction to stress, addiction to winning, addiction to risk-taking, so on and so forth. A substance or few is just an addition to the pile.
After all, who works more single-mindedly towards a goal than someone in active addiction chasing the next fix? Eventually we elevate cheating as proof of commitment to prioritizing a goal over rules, ethics, integrity, sustainability, and relationships.
“I would sacrifice my child, negotiate with terrorists, and skirt the Geneva Convention if it raised the share price” is simply honoring one’s fiduciary duty to the shareholders.
“having more only leaves us wanting more… the underlying premise is that the answer is out there, not available to me already”
This definitely captures the core of Buddhism. From the Dhammapada, verse 187:
“Sensual pleasures give little enjoyment and much suffering- knowing this, the wise person finds no delight even in heavenly pleasures.”
From MN 75 Magandiya Sutta:
“Now suppose that there was a leper covered with sores & infections, devoured by worms, picking the scabs off the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing embers. The more he cauterized his body over the pit of glowing embers, the more disgusting, foul-smelling, & putrid the openings of his wounds would become, and yet he would feel a modicum of enjoyment & satisfaction because of the itchiness of his wounds. In the same way, beings not free from passion for sensual pleasures — devoured by sensual craving, burning with sensual fever — indulge in sensual pleasures. The more they indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their sensual craving increases and the more they burn with sensual fever, and yet they feel a modicum of enjoyment & satisfaction dependent on the five strings of sensuality.”
From core Buddhist principles, one posits that there is no amount of material or worldly pleasures that will finally satiate one’s appetite for them. This doesn’t mean that we can just ignore these needs either, but we can’t expect to find a lasting solution to suffering from satisfying our fleeting desires. That’s the same as scratching a wound for the short-term relief, when it will quickly become itchy again as a deeper wound.
To tie it back to our modern America, the entire premise of advertising as an industry is that people can be convinced that part of their insatiable needs will be addressed through the consumption of some product that has relevant value. Go watch Mad Men, which is explicitly about the way an addict uses his own lack of fulfillment as inspiration for advertisements that resonate with consumers in a world celebrating Ayn Rand’s brand of selfish individualism.
One distinction though is that traditionally, Buddhism was not focused on the internal narratives we hold in the same way that modern “Western” psychology tends to emphasize them. After all, if we accept the impermanence of all things, then how could there be a permanently true self? The self and its cravings are both subject to dependent origination, thus an independently true self in a vacuum doesn’t really make sense.
So, it’s less that the answer to suffering is internally available by simply modifying our internal narrative of the self that’s been socially conditioned, and more that the answer to suffering lies in recognizing the constructs of the mind that produce craving through attachment. That tends to go in the opposite direction of many humanistic Western therapeutic interventions though, which can try to find some authentically true self that has experienced alienation but can achieve self-actualization through a transformation into wholeness.
This distinction will become relevant many times throughout the book. For instance, Korda states:
“All of the versions of Buddhist suttas in this book are my own…I find there’s an unfortunate tendency among some to render the early Buddhist transcripts in stitled phrases and word choices, which obfuscates ideas that can actually be quite accessible.”
More of those red flags from the The Four Agreements are coming back to me. I am generally wary of attempts to simplify the core teachings of a belief system for standalone self-help products. It’s one thing for someone beginning a serious study of a discipline who might need to get their foot in the door somehow, but it’s another to start repackaging a version while claiming you’ve preserved the integrity of the original canon. To Korda’s credit, he explicitly does say that you can “consult the now-standard translations of Thanisaro Bhikkhu, Bhikkhu Nanamoli, or Bhikkhu Bodhi” for deeper study. Even so, within the example he gives, we can observe a problem.
From the original Korda cites:
“Suppose there is no hereafter nor fruit of deeds done well or ill. Yet in this world I keep myself safe and happy, free from hatred and malice…”
From Korda’s translation:
“Look, even if there is no such thing as rebirth—if our experience ends with our death—and no way to feel the results of our actions, it’s still worth- while to act harmlessly, as we’ll feel better about ourselves while we’re still alive.”
First, I don’t think the cited excerpt is so challenging that one “would be hard-pressed to understand the Buddha’s important, though straightforward message.” There aren’t any technical terms being used there at all. I assume the word “hereafter” can be frightening?
As for what’s lost or gained in translation, Korda’s interpretation includes an element of self-evaluation. He writes that we should avoid doing harm because we would experience less suffering with a self-image that doesn’t involve doing harm. That goes back to the idea of actualizing an improved self rather than freeing one’s mind from the attachments involved in harm, like spite and obsession. The excerpt comes out of the Kalama Sutta where the Buddha is describing something akin to Pascal’s Wager, except that if there is no afterlife, you can still reduce suffering and have peace in this life. That’s not the same as feeling better about yourself.
Introduction
“I’ve been through riots, arsons, and blackouts, stood witness to the birth screams of punk and the slow death-by-greed of once-vibrant neighborhoods, run from the batons wielded by thugs operating under the guise of law and order, and mourned legions of beautiful artists, writers, and musicians lost to a disease that the most powerful man on earth couldn’t be bothered to speak about.”
I really thought he was talking about COVID until I remembered this book just referenced November 2016, so he’s actually referring to Ronald Reagan’s record of ignoring AIDS as a public health crisis. Make of that what you will.
Korda then describes experiencing 9/11 in New York and losing a firefighter friend he met in AA when the second tower collapsed. In the subsequent existential crisis, he notes:
“I had to face the fact that I, just like everyone else, was falling through time toward my inevitable death with absolutely nothing to cling to…” And what the fuck was I doing with my life… The truth is the lure of a solid paycheck, dangled before the financially struggling, is powerful. The truth is I sold out.
“And what did the twelve-step programs have to offer? They work for a lot of people, but all I got were patronizing pats on the head offered by smug true believers who, armed with quotes from the AA Big Book, dutifully insisted that my clinical depression was repayment for my atheism and lack of effort.”
I might be more skeptical about the negativity in this account if it weren’t for having seen the open disapproval of non-theistic beliefs myself. I’ve met really swell people who believe in AA but have never pushed their beliefs on me, so I don’t think it’s fair to assume that this is all AA has to offer, but that’s how it goes when we have a decentralized autonomous meetings. There will be immense variation between groups, and the East Coast has lots of traditions that the West Coast doesn’t.
