recovery/people/activists-advocacy-and-a.title: Oxford Group
Secular Recovery
Barbara Ehrenreich
recovery/people/activists-advocacy-and-a.content:
Favorite Quotes
“Breast cancer, I can now report, did not make me prettier or stronger, more feminine or spiritual. What it gave me, if you want to call this a ‘gift,’ was a very personal, agonizing encounter with an ideological force in American culture that I had not been aware of before- one that encourages us to deny reality, submit cheerfully to misfortune, and blame only ourselves for our fate.”
I can now report, the institutions of recovery and mental health function the same way.
“The question is why one should be so inwardly preoccupied at all. Why not reach out to others in love and solidarity or peer into the natural world for some glimmer of understanding? Why retreat into anxious introspection when, as Emerson might have said, there is a vast world outside to explore? Why spend so much time working on oneself when there is so much real work to be done?”
I’m a huge fan of Barbara Ehrenreich. Although she doesn’t explicitly spell this out, her work is a robust argument for a perspective about the self that resonates more with me, perhaps through an indirect connection with “Eastern” thought.
Ralph Waldo Emerson and other American transcendentalists, oft-described as the nation’s first homegrown philosophical movement, drew heavily on romantic appropriation of “Oriental” cultures. It was, and arguably remains, a common fashion in the West to project onto the East the qualities it considers foreign to itself. The materialist industrialist West moves forward through rationality and individualism; the spiritual nature-centric East preserves the past through tradition and collectivism. His reworkings of Eastern concepts inspired those like Helena Blavatsky and the Theosophical Society, who was among the first to popularize the concept of a superior Aryan race meant to hegemonize the world, and you can figure out what that inspired in the first half of the 1900s on your own.
Despite his hierarchical views about Western supremacy, Emerson did manage to capture a genuine notion of the self that still feels foreign to America through a succinct metaphor: the transparent eyeball. Seeing everything while occupying nothing. Free oneself to explore freely.
Emerson certainly encouraged people to lean on their own potential rather than seeking the instruction or refuge of institutions that would inevitably corrupt the individual with systemic prerogatives. But the outcome of such an endeavor would be to then experience the universe through this newly freed self, not obsess over the self as if it were the sole determinant of reality. The intention was to facilitate liberative action through disconnecting the self from the machines of society, not disconnecting the self from reality to preserve a bubble of self-care routines or happiness rituals. As he said:
“Action is with the scholar subordinate, but it is essential. Without it he is not yet man. Without it thought can never ripen into truth.”
Henry David Thoreau, a friend of Emerson, did exactly that. He moved to a cabin he built and minimized his demands of the world to his basic needs. He acted, and he built a new life away from society where he achieved an intellectual and spiritual freedom he could not find within the rat-race facilitated by institutions. Thoreau believed that you have a moral obligation to actively break unjust laws as “friction to stop the machine.”
In no way can Emerson or Thoreau be said to have withdrawn from the external world into themselves to cultivate positive thinking. Instead, they took radical responsibility for their engagement with the world to free themselves from the control of institutional standards. Changing the individual was supposed to lead to changes in the environment around individual. That’s aligned very well with the takeaway I have from the Gita. Everyone has a role to play in the universe, and you have to discover what that is for yourself, or you might die realizing you never lived.
It is with this consideration that Barbara Ehrenreich critiques the modern happiness industry by invoking Emerson’s name. By turning the ideas behind liberation from social standards into commodified self-help and spiritual guides that becomes the new social standards, the movement defeats itself while turning a pretty penny for any guru who finds their niche of miserable people to shepherd through shallow material befitting an AI chatbot.
Ehrenreich has far surpassed both Emerson and Thoreau in both action and thought, at least to me.
“Like a perpetually flashing neon sign in the background, like an inescapable jingle, the injunction to be positive is so ubiquitous that it’s impossible to identify a single source. Oprah routinely trumpets the triumph of attitude over circumstance… you’ll find a smorgasboard of workshops on how to succeed in life by overcoming pessimism, accessing your inner powers, and harnessing the power of thought.”
“A whole coaching industry has grown up since the mid-1990s, heavily marketed on the Internet, to help people improve their attitudes and hence, supposedly, their lives. For a fee on a par with what a therapist might receive, an unlicensed career or life coach help you defeat the ‘negative self-talk’ - that is, pessimistic thoughts - that impedes your progress… It has its ideologues, spokespeople, preachers, and salespersons - authors of self-help books, motivational speakers, coaches, and trainers… It was New Age meets middle-American business culture.”
Those familiar with my attitude towards The Four Agreements have likely heard me point out that the book was popularized by Ellen and Oprah. It is an insane book that says things like no one can abuse you more than you abuse yourself, so it’s really your fault for agreeing to lower your self-worth into accepting abuse. It is a masterpiece in blurring the lines between empowerment and blame.
That aside, the last sentence in that excerpt is almost exactly what I’ve said before. The contemporary American spiritual wellness movement seems to be some intersection of New Age appropriation of colonized cultures and outdated pseudopsychology embedded in the collective consciousness of institutional managers. If I had to distill our challenges with institutions into a single problem statement, it would be that institutions change their environment faster than they can change themselves. The arrogance of individuality in assuming that a system can be circumvented or ignored, whether by an anarchist outsider or a sufficiently Great Man as a leader, with the proper cultivation of inner traits is fatal. It is, literally, a superhero fantasy.
I suppose that’s the point, isn’t it? In a world where no one is coming to save you, be your own superhero. All it takes is buying a book or doing a course or hiring a coach, all of which give some variation of the advice “don’t do the thing associated with negative moods, and do the thing associated with positive moods, like spending less time watching the news and more time in nature.” In other words, despite living in a liberal democracy that was explicitly predicated on having an enlightened citizenry that would compete through debates in a marketplace of ideas, we are never to look at actually using those mechanisms to produce systemic changes. As Ehrenreich says,
“This retreat from the real drama and tragedy of human events is suggestive of a deep helplessness at the core of positive thinking. Why not follow the news? Because, as my informant at the NSA meeting told me, ‘You can’t do anything about it…’ The possibilities of contributing to relief funds, joining an antiwar movement, or lobbying for more humane government policies are not even considered. But at the very least there seems to be an acknowledgement here that no amount of attitude adjustment can make good news out of headlines beginning with ‘Civilian casualties mount…’ or ‘Famine spreads…‘”
One thing I appreciate about AA is that it wears its philosophy on its sleeve. It commits to the notion that the individual is powerless to facilitate a surrender to a Higher Power which, for all intents and purposes, is based on the Protestant concept of God. The thesis behind suffering is that the individual’s self-will has run riot and produced an unmanageable life, so only by seeking something outside of oneself for an alternative will can one find an anchor point of sanity. This is actually a far more coherent perspective than the positive thinking that becomes magical thinking, because at least God or a Higher Power is a mechanism through which meditation and prayer can lead to observable changes in the world. You can call AA a cult if you want, and I do call it religious rather than spiritual, but it’s the easiest cult in the world to leave if you don’t like it.
The happiness industry around positive thinking has no such coherence, and in fact invites you to be the God of your own life. The Four Agreements, a text referenced in psychoeducation classes in treatment centers that insurance companies pay for, says this explicitly. You’re God, I’m God, all things are God, and you have complete control of the reality that is your life once you awaken to the dream you’re in. It’s a book that makes a claim, and I’m not exaggerating in any way here, that if you tell someone their face looks like one belonging to someone with cancer, they will develop cancer within a year. It is a book that takes every critique made of the happiness industry’s absurd reliance on the power of willpower and responds with “Yes.” The entire first chapter of this book is a scathing rebuttal of such flippant claims made by New Age profit-seekers as we see Ehrenreich’s firsthand experience with breast cancer and the attitude cures. Much less a negative attitude, she suspects that years of hormone treatments at the recommendations of previous professionals increased her risk of developing cancer.
A rather heartbreaking account in the book comes from a woman writing to Deepak Chopra, who positively reviewed The Four Agreements since they used the same New Age publisher:
“Even though I follow the treatments, have come a long way in unburdening myself of toxic feelings, have forgiven everyone, changed my lifestyle to include meditation, prayer, proper diet, exercise, and supplements, the cancer keeps coming back. Am I missing a lesson here that it keeps reoccurring? I am positive that I am going to beat it, yet it does get harder with each diagnosis to keep a positive attitude.”
Chopra replies,
“As far as I can tell, you are doing all the right things to recover. You just have to continue doing them until the cancer is gone for good. I know it is discouraging to make great progress only to have it come back again, but sometimes cancer is simply very pernicious and requires the utmost diligence and persistence to eventually overcome it.”
I have a hard time not immediately thinking of televangelists and YouTube gurus who solicit money in exchange for reassurance from desperate and lost people. That money could go towards actual treatments, improving their quality of life, or simply savings for their family to use. Any of those sound better than the false hope of magical thinking disguised as a trajectory of positive thinking. And because you can’t measure a positive attitude or negative vibes, the whole theory of positive thinking is unfalsifiable:
“without question there is a problem when positive thinking ‘fails’ and the cancer spreads or eludes treatment. Then the patient can only blame herself: she is not being positive enough; possible it was her negative attitude that brought on the disease in the first place. At this point, the exhortation to think positively is ‘an additional burden to an already devastated patient,’ as an oncology nurse Cynthia Rittenburg has written.”
If you replace “cancer” with “addiction”, “depression”, or “cravings,” you get a very close approximation of the core of the American recovery philosophy. Suffering is not a condition produced relationally between an individual misaligned with an environment, but instead a dysfunction of the individual that is somewhere between personal ignorance, irrationality, and immorality. To have ended up in a position to suffer, one must have one of these vices. To escape suffering, one must remedy these vices and see their illness as some type of opportunity for an awakening. In doing so, those in suffering suffer again from these standards, whether imposed or internalized.
It’s not Just Injustice
“Clearly, the failure to think positively can weigh on a cancer patient like a second disease. I, at least, was saved from this additional burden by my persistent anger.”
Fun fact, studies show that witnessing unfair behavior actively raises our stress levels with measurable heart rate spikes, even when they don’t happen to us. Sharing it with other people, or gossipping if you want to be righteous about it, actually lowers our stress. We are built to observe something like injustice, be angry about it, and try to change it.
For America, it’s been two and a half centuries since it won independence. It’s been about eight decades since it became a world superpower and over a century since it’s been the largest economic in the world. American history talks of “The Civil Rights Movement” as a singular wave across the 1950s and 1960s that restored civil rights. The optimists thought 2008 proved America was mostly over racism by electing a black President, and 2015 showed through the legalization of gay marriage that only the most marginal groups were left out of the umbrella of egalitarianism. A reality check is sorely needed.
South Sudan was recognized as an independent state in 2011. From 1955 to 2026, only 27 years have not involved a major civil war.
Timor-Leste became an independent sovereign nation in 2002, though it wasn’t until 2012 that the United Nations ended its peacekeeping mission to facilitate democratic elections amidst refugee crises affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
Croatia, Bosnia, and Slovenia fought wars to maintain independence amidst widespread ethnic conflicts from 1991-1995 in what we call the Yugoslav Wars. Notably, Melania Trump and Luka Doncic are from Slovenia.
South Africa had its first fully democratic elections open to all races in 1994, leading to the election of Nelson Mandela and marking a pivot from apartheid policies.
Eritrea won independence in 1991 after a 30-year war with Ethiopia. Namibia, 1990 after a guerilla conflict with South Africa’s apartheid regime.
Bangladesh seceded from Pakistan in 1971, which became an international conflict involving India.
Zimbabwe underwent The Rhodesian Civil War from 1964 to 1979 as a conflict that ended white minority rule and implemented universal sufferage, with independent sovereignty established in 1980.
I’ll draw on my own heritage here.
India celebrates 1947 as the year of independence because that’s when the British decided to leave. That’s not when the French and Portuguese decided to leave though. In 1954, local Indian socialist and nationalist groups launched a violent uprising against the French encalve on the Malabar Coast. The French administrators were physically driven out ahead of an official treaty to surrender the territory. The Portuguese in Goa, which had occupied India for 451 years, was expelled within 36 hours of a 1961 military operation, after years of attempts to negotiate diplomatically and unarmed protests that were met with fatal violence. My grandparents were alive to see that. Portugal did not acknowledge the sovereignty of India until 1974, which was after my parents were born.
So, you can hopefully understand how viscerally upsetting this happiness industry is to me when it carves up our traditions into commodities for Western institutions on the receiving end of historic exploitation without reparations. The aesthetics are all too easy to adopt: vague notions of aligining yourself with the vibrations of the universe through breathing exercises, planting positive intentions for karmic appraisal, detachment from the environment coupled to increasing attachment to the ego, rearranging furniture to balance your chakras, go on a walk through nature while thanking the sun and the trees, lighting incense while making herbal teas for a lunch break, so on and so forth.
It is within the living memory of my family that things do not get better until you roll up your sleeves to lock arms in a covenant of collective action. I cannot imagine a single piece of advice from this industry I’ve heard that could be useful to anyone who has answered the human call to be angry about injustice. After all, Reinhold Niehbur, author of the Serenity Prayer, was a pro-union socialist who believed that ruling classes must be forced to concede power as they would never do so of their own volition.

recovery/people/artists/writers/1660-166.title: Daniel Defoe
recovery/people/artists/writers/1660-166.content: The author of Robinson Crusoe once defended gin and other distilled spirits out of a nationalist desire to keep wealth in the country and promote British liquor over foreign dinks. It’s also worth mentioning that his published defenses were funded by distillery companies, effectively making him paid propaganda to sell liquor while blaming the character of individuals for the sins and crimes committed while intoxicated. He condemned low-quality gin but eventually reversed course once he saw the effects that mass drinking was having in communities.

recovery/people/artists/writers/1780-178.title: Thomas De Quincey
recovery/people/artists/writers/1780-178.content:
Overview
By 1817, De Quincey was consuming more than 20,000 milligrams of morphine a day.
De Quincey’s book [[confessions-of-an-opium-eater|Confessions of an Opium Eater (1821)]] achieved a legendary status in Western societies as one of the most popular texts describing the influence of opium. In George Pettey’s The Narcotic Drug Diseases and Allied Ailments: Pathology, Pathogenesis, and Treatment (1913), the author critically acknowledges his influence as a turning point in opium consumption habits:
“Suffice it to say that the effects of the cruder forms of narcotic drugs were known to the ancients, and these were used from time to time for their pain-relieving and hypnotic effects; but, it is not believed that the habitual use of any of these agents existed to any considerable extent until after the discovery of morphine, the principal alkaloid of opium. The writings of DeQuincy during the early part of the last century doubtless did more to publish and to popularize the use of opium than any other, or possibly than all other influences had done up to that time. His exaggerated descriptions of the pleasurable effects of opium led many to experiment upon themselves with it, and often these experiments resulted in complete enslavement.”

“The Portuguese, who navigate over a greater part of the world only procure a knowledge of how best to dispose of that merchandise of what they bring here and what they shall take back. They are not desirous of knowing anything about the things in the countries they visit. If they know a product they do not learn from what tree it comes, and if they see it they do not compare it with one of our Indian trees, nor ask about its fruit or what it is like.”
From the whimsical era of European medical practitioners encountering new ingredients and materials for the first time as they began traveling the world to conquer other peoples. De Orta specifically noted that many in India would use opium to calm mental troubles, not just physical ones as the Europeans had.

recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1740-.title: Benjamin Rush
recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1740-.content:
No Rush to Judgment
Benjamin Rush is one of those influential people who happened to be around a bunch of famous and influential people, so he fades into the background easily but also pops up a lot once you start noticing him.
He attended Princeton University and the University of Edinburgh. He later taught at the University of Pennsylvania as a professor of chemistry and published one of the first American textbooks on chemistry. He signed the Declaration of Independence and was at Pennsylvania’s Constitutional Convention, briefly serving as a surgeon-general for the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. Thomas Paine, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, and a littany of physicians and chemists ran in the same influential circles as Rush. We have access to a lot of his correspondence that we can look at when examining medicine in the colonial and post-independence era. He taught both future-President William Henry Harrison and Meriwether Lewis of the (in)famous Lewis & Clarke expedition at the instructions of President Jefferson.
Rush was active in social justice in a way that shows decency was always possible, regardless of the time period and social norms. He strongly opposed slavery as “so foreign to the human mind, that the moral faculties, as well as those of the understanding are debased, and rendered torpid by it.” He thought there was no reasonable interpretation of scientific evidence that would suggest there was any natural inferiority by race, though he also thought being black was a hereditary yet curable skin disease after meeting someone with vitiligo, which warranted policies against interracial mixing. On criminal justice, he opposed public punishments, solitary confinement, slavery or forced labor, and the death penalty. Although he had prejudices against women learning advanced sciences, he proposed education plans for the women of wealthier families and helped found one of the first higher education institutions for women in America. He set up a medicinal dispensary for the poorest workers and advised various public health projects that led to a reduction in disease outbreaks. While he did subscribe to the notion that indigenous nations were “primitive” rather than “civilized,” he took a genuine interest in health disparities between indigenous nations and colonial settlers.

recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1770-.content: In 1819, Carl von Bruhl-Cramer coined the term “Trunksucht” which can be translated as “drink obsession.” The concept of addiction as a disease was not a scientific consensus at the time, so under a moral model, the term “lasterhaft” existed to describe someone prone to indulging sinful vices.

recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1830-.title: Cesare Lombroso
recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1830-.content:
Cesare Lombroso is both considered a founder of modern criminology and one of the most prolific eugenicists we’ve seen. Rather than seeing crimes and sin as part of human nature, he believed some people were born with a criminal aptitude, which he theorized was indicative of some reversion of humanity to primitive primates. He thought these natural-born criminals could be identified through physical features, and even the types of crimes they would commit could be determined. He also coined the term “criminaloid” to refer to those who conceal a “criminal personality” underneath a projection of respectability.
Lombroso’s theories ran into empirical problems even his day, but he stubbornly held fast to them. For instance, he believed men were superior to women, but this didn’t square with women being involved in crime far less than men. He actually managed a mental institution himself and became the first professor to specialize in mental health at the University of Pavia. Italian universities did not remove his school of thought from the curriculums until after WWII, because predictably, fascist movements thrived on the aesthetics of scientific legitimacy he provided.
This had nuanced implications for legal systems and policies. Lombroso and his school of biological determinists actually argued that criminality should be understood in the context of biological predisposition to crime, and he advocated for socialist ideas that expressed sympathy for the lower classes suffering from the stigma of poverty. In a way, by arguing that certain people were biologically limited from full participation in society, he was advocating for more lenience than the classical schools of his predecessors. The classical schools of thought that believed
As far as addiction goes, he thought left-handedness led to disabilities like alcoholism.
As as aside, I was watching The Gambler just before writing this, and I’m reminded of the monologue Mark Wahlberg’s character gives about the rage we experience at the unequal distribution of human talent. Someone with every privilege possible can end up completely mediocre in everything they try, while someone born with every disadvantage can be outright prodigious in a way that can be observed at the age of two. That kind of stochasticity is upsetting to people, even those who benefit from the luck of the draw. It’s a different kind of unfairness to realize that you can give your child every advantage possible as a result of your work ethic and judgment, but you can’t do anything about whether your child is predisposed to a talent you could guide or nurture. It’s also similarly uncomfortable to realize that you have access to a talent or perspective no one else does for no discernible reason. You’re different and you don’t know why, and you’re probably going to experience the world differently. That can be lonely and ostracizing in its own way. Even really bad pseudoscience can become a strongly internalized rationalization to fill the gaps.

recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1850-.title: George Pettey
recovery/people/clinicians/doctors/1850-.content:
Overview
A physician likely born around 1850-1860, Pettey was controversial in his time for criticizing substances like heroin and opium in all its forms as addictive, regardless of the method of ingestion. He also proposed a now-discarded theory of addiction that relied on toxins and internal medicine over psychology or neurology.
Pettey’s motivations were personal and social. From his 1913 book, The Narcotic Drug Diseases and Allied Ailments: Pathology, Pathogenesis, and Treatment, he writes:
“The author had, recently, under his care a Harvard graduate who, with a class of four others, became addicted to morphone during the last year of their medical course, they having the assurance of one of the faculty that the use of morphine hypodermically would not produce addiction. Four of this quintet died prematurely, two committing suicide, while the fifth after thirty-seven years of enslavement was finally released by treatment. These fallacious teachings did much to increase the number of habitual users of opium, but aside from these influences the discovery of morphine and the perfection of the hypodermic syringe have been the greatest factors in extending the use of narcotics.”
Pettey’s decision to skip over the general history of substance use to relate a tragedy he personally observed comes remarkably close to the way books are still written about addiction, treatment, and recovery. Both medical practitioners and lay writers covering the topic of addiction begin by explaining the grief and hope that motivate their work:
“It has only been during the last quarter of a century, however, that narcotic addiction has grown to such proportions as to attract much attention. The evil is now recognized as alarmingly extensive and rapdily spreading. It is hardly profitable, therefore, at this time to consider farther the origin and growth of the addiction. This has been sufficiently done by others.”

recovery/people/clinicians/therapists/si.title: Sigmund Freud
recovery/people/clinicians/therapists/si.content:
“I need a lot of cocaine…”
Sigmund Freud is a character. It’s hard to find someone else who occupies the space in our culture that he does. Highly influential, incredibly wrong, amusingly absurd.
Freud loved coke. He tried treating his friend’s morphine addiction with it, who unsurprisingly said taking coke allowed him to take less morphine. His first major scientific publication was “Uber Coca”, which translates to “On Cocaine”, which begs us to ask whether he was on cocaine when he wrote On cocaine. The answer seems to be yes.
Freud recommended that cocaine be considered for treating digestive disorders, asthma, loss of sexual potency, melancholy, hysteria, and morphine addiction. This was met with strong condemnation from the German medical community. Also, his friend was now addicted to both coke and morphone.
To quote Freud, “I need a lot of cocaine… The torment, most of the time, is superhuman”

recovery/people/daniel-anderson.title: Daniel Anderson
recovery/people/daniel-anderson.content:
Daniel Anderson joined the army from 1942 to 1945 as a radarman in the Pacific, after which he used the GI Bill to pursue higher education. He had a poor academic record (he and his friends literally made a game out of trying to get low scores in the past since they hated school), but the College of St. Thomas accepted him despite the missing courses anyways. He enrolled in 1946 and began working at the Hastings State Hospital in 1947, which inspired him to pursue psychology. Dr. Nelson Bradley was the superintendent of Hastings when Anderson met him, and the two hit it off so that Anderson followed Bradely to Willmar State Mental Hospital in 1950.
Anderson pursued a master’s degree in clinical psychology from Loyola University, a private Jesuit college, because he disliked the idea of secular psychology divorced from religious beliefs. Jean Joseph Rossi, who joined Willmar, recommended that Anderson complete a dissertation at the University of Ottawa which replaced Sigmund Freud with St. Thomas Aquinas. He abandoned his master’s thesis, An Exploratory Investigation of Anxiety in Alcoholics, but finished a doctoral dissertation in 1966: Personality Correlates of Complex Instrumental Avoidance Learning.
In the early 1960s, the Alcoholic Addiction Project had published papers about the outcomes of the Willmar model for recovery, and it wasn’t great. Only a third of patients were described as “improved” in 1957, and only 7% were described as maintaining “continuous abstinence” in 1963. By this point, Anderson had left to accept a leadership position at the Hazelden Institute, where the Hill Family Foundation sponsored an applied research program. He would serve both as Vice-President and CEO. Unfortunately, this is also where Anderson began playing fast and loose with science.
In 1976, David J. Armor, J. Michael Polich, and Harriet B. Stambull were commissioned by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) to study thousands of alcoholics across dozens of federally-funded centers:
“Client characteristics that may be of prognostic significance in alcoholism, such as social background, ethnicity, marital status, employment, and previous drinking, are examined in detail. Using a definition of remission that includes both abstention and drinking behavior within a range specified as normal, the study finds that 70 percent of those treated are in remission at 6 and at 18 months following entry. These remission rates are quite similar regardless of the type of treatment given.”
The findings would prove to be controversial, as the authors were well-aware:
“The authors are aware that some of the findings of the present study-particularly the finding that some alcoholics appear to return to and maintain patterns of normal drinking-may be controversial in some quarters. To remove any possible misunderstanding, the authors wish to emphasize that this study makes no recommendation about treatment goals for alcoholics, and in particular does not recommend or suggest that any alcoholic should resume drinking.”
Let me echo that too: no part of anything I say should be construed as permission, justification, rationalization, recommendation, or suggestion about anyone drinking.
Nevertheless, this finding posed some challenges for what had become conventions within the culture of addiction treatment. If the data shows that some alcoholics do return to drinking in a pattern that’s typical of those never diagnosed as alcoholics, that suggests some problems about the “powerless over alcohol” or “pickles can’t go back to cucumbers” lines. Abstinence-only programs could no longer say that their way was the only possible way to address addiction or chemical dependence meaningfully. That’s a problem for organizations that have spent a lot of time marketing themselves that way.
The backlash from Anderson, Hazelden, and sympathetic allies on the National Council of Alcoholism (NCA) was strong and swift. They scheduled a press conference on the same day the report was released to claim the information about remission rates would cause alcoholics to resume drinking and relapse. In terms of methodology, they argued the 18-month tracking window of the NIAAA-backed Rand study was too short for a chronic disease that lasted a lifetime. The Rand authors countered that an 18-months window was standard across federal programs. They argued it was also possible that alcoholics who internalized the “powerlessness” narratives would turn a slip at a social event into a fatal spiral over the idea of being doomed after a sip. The heightened stress and anxiety from that alone could be a driver in a relapse, or make a relapse worse.
Hazelden had its own press and publication infrastructure, which meant that information they distributed about programs and outcomes didn’t have to go through a peer-review process from the scientific community. Until 1978, Sister Mary Leo Kammeier had been in charge of the program and was consistently publishing in peer-reviewed journals. After her death, it seems everything started going through Hazelden’s own press without scientific scrutiny. In 1982, a consultant named Clark Laundergan for Hazelden published Easy Does It: Alcoholism Treatment Outcomes, Hazelden and the Minnesota Model. He claimed that 54% of patients from their program stayed abstinent while 18% reported improvement. 72% of patients benefitting from addiction treatment is certainly substantial.
In response to the counter-arguments from Anderson and Hazelden, the Rand authors did what researchers do when they encounter criticism: more experiments. They designed a 4-year follow-up study of the same cohort they had assessed before, and they found that 46% were still in active remission. 28% stayed completely abstinent but 18% no longer met the criteria for problem drinking. 1 in 5 patients admitted to programs for alcoholism resumed non-problem drinking.
Andersen’s takeaway from the study was that those who attempted non-problem drinking increased their chances of relapsing by 16% compared to those who maintained total abstinence among a subgroup that presented with high physical dependence, which he used to argue that controlled drinking was statistically so unlikely that it should be discounted. The authors pointed out that Andersen conveniently ignored those who presented with low physical dependence who attempted total abstinence actually had a higher relapse rate than those just aiming to no longer be problem drinkers.
Meanwhile, Christopher C.H. Cook analyzed the Hazelden data in 1988 and discovered that Laundergan threw out the data for over 2000 patients who had been readmitted or given extended care. He really analyzed just 1200 of the patients who seemed like clean cases that completed the program as intended. When considering all 3638 patients, 37.8% were abstinent, 9.2% showed improvement, and a shocking 53.1% reported no improvement.
This is not a minor issue in interpreting data or statistical methodology. A program that claimed to benefit a supermajority of its patients was actually a failure for most of them. Not only that, the proponents of this program sought to convince the public and policymakers to stop funding research into treatment models that conflicted with theirs. The fear they spread led to media and political backlash, including wealthy donors and philanthropists threatening to pull funding for anything other than abstinence-only guidelines.

recovery/people/developers/jonathan-blow.title: Jonathan Blow
recovery/people/developers/jonathan-blow.content:
Overview
Jonathan Blow has been one of the more vocal developers tackling the value of video gaming as an expressive medium. He likens the loops built by games like World of Warcraft to a type of drug that exploits short-term loops that are little more than a series of tasks towards an end “victory” state. To make a game have artistic value instead of just fast food-esque entertainment value, it has to challenge the player into choices and problems that are fundamentally novel.
Background
Blow is a serious developer, not just a game designer. He’s highly opinionated and dedicated towards software development, driving his own language called Jai and criticizing the over-engineering and over-complexity of modern engineering through a long career of talks, think pieces, and courses.
He’s a pioneer in building a brand around indie games through a public persona. The community of single developers was much smaller than it is now in an era where Steam dumpster diving with friends can be a lot more fun (and makes for better content) than a single playthrough of AAA games. Developers like Blow proved that indie games could not just be made by single people but also distributed through online platforms rather than physical retailers like Walmart. Braid and The Witness.
That all being said, Blow has had a bit of a reputation online for being pretentious and attention-seeking, encapsulated best by the satirical meme: Jonathan Blow Crying in a Dark Room about Soulja Boy misunderstanding Braid www.youtube.com/watch He has a lot of opinions some would consider curmudgeonly, though he’s still regarded as a skilled engineer.
That’s about the kindest this section gets, because Blow became very politically controversial after 2018, to say the least. There’s an all-too-common pattern among skilled engineers who assume that their system design skills within the umbrella of technical domains is cleanly transferable to all systems. Politics and society are especially easy for non-experts to comment on and build a following around, so an echo chamber can quickly lead to unhinged spirals from otherwise talented people. Here are some highlights:
December 2017: “Interest is not the same as ability. I believe it is likely that the sexes have different interests on average, and that biological factors play a large part in this. This is NOT REMOTELY a controversial opinion except on Weird Far Left Twitter 2017.”
October 2021: “There’s a weird disconnect in this vaccine mandate debate: many are still pretending that Covid-19 is of natural origin, which gives such mandates a different feel than they otherwise have. If a state entity does an oopsie in a lab, then forces its citizens to undergo an experimental treatment because of the oopsie, while suppressing news of side effects, and also denying that the oopsie is anyone’s fault… that’s just abusive?”
In response to SpaceX criticism from April 2024: “Reading this, I knew you had pronouns in bio before looking.”
From November 2024: “This is true, the gaming press is super left-wing, but on the other hand they have almost no impact now. I would say that the social pressure keeping ‘indies’ in line mostly comes from them being socially fearful in the normal way. (It doesn’t help that all males currently under the age of 40 were raised to be supercucks).”
In reference to President Trump from February 2025: “Are you kidding? He is the best President we have had in my entire life, by far. It’s a miracle. I just hope it doesn’t abruptly go bad.”

recovery/people/politicians-and-policyma.title: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
recovery/people/politicians-and-policyma.content:
Most known for the Moynihan Report, a 1965 report that studied poverty in African-American communities and concluded that, rather than structural or systemic momentum from an explicit racial hierarchy, the primary reasons for continued cycles of poverty could be attributed to problems with “ghetto culture.”
William J. Ryan responded to the report with a major rebuttal in his 1971 book Blaming the Victim, where is where the term “victim blaming” was coined in reference to a fallacy that confused cause-and-effect, assuming that culture affected the cycles of poverty instead of poverty affecting the culture of a community. This included observations like single-mother households and births out of wedlock.
Specifically, Ryan responded that the report “seduces the reader into believing that it is not racism and discrimination but the weaknesses and defects of the Negro himself that account for the present status of inequality between Negro and white.”

recovery/people/researchers/policy/charl.title: Charles Fain Lehman
recovery/people/researchers/policy/charl.content:
Links

manhattan.institute/person/charles-fain-lehman

Articles
Harm Reduction
Summary

www.cbsnews.com/news/nyc-drug-addiction-onpoint-harm-reduction/

“‘There is a lot of evidence that interventions of this type generally do not have an appreciable effect on overdose deaths,’ Lehman told CBS News. ‘There’s a fixed pool of resources available for helping people who are dealing with substance use disorder. If you’re spending the dollars on an intervention that doesn’t work, like supervised consumption sites … you’re not spending dollars on [addiction medication] and evidence-based treatment.‘
Commentary
Lehman is wrong. We do have evidence that supervised consumption facilities (SCFs), also referred to as overdose prevention centers (OPCs) or overdose prevention sites (OPSs), have appreciable effects on overdose deaths.
From Kennedy et. al (2017):
“Consistent evidence demonstrates that SCFs mitigate overdose-related harms and unsafe drug use behaviours, as well as facilitate uptake of addiction treatment and other health services among people who use drugs (PWUD). Further, SCFs have been associated with improvements in public order without increasing drug-related crime. SCFs have also been shown to be cost-effective. This systematic review suggests that SCFs are effectively meeting their primary public health and order objectives and therefore supports their role within a continuum of services for PWUD.”
From Levengood et. al (2021):
“Supervised injection facilities in the included studies (n=number of studies per outcome category) were mostly associated with significant reductions in opioid overdose morbidity and mortality (n=5), significant improvements in injection behaviors and harm reduction (n=7), significant improvements in access to addiction treatment programs (n=7), and no increase or reductions in crime and public nuisance (n=7).”
From Potier et. al (2014):
“Seventy-five relevant articles were found. All studies converged to find that SISs were efficacious in attracting the most marginalized PWID, promoting safer injection conditions, enhancing access to primary health care, and reducing the overdose frequency. SISs were not found to increase drug injecting, drug trafficking or crime in the surrounding environments. SISs were found to be associated with reduced levels of public drug injections and dropped syringes. Of the articles, 85% originated from Vancouver or Sydney. Conclusion: SISs have largely fulfilled their initial objectives without enhancing drug use or drug trafficking.”
What is true is that we don’t have enough studies that test whether these sites lower population-level overdose mortality rates, as the evidence we do have is limited and inconsistent. But the goal of these sites is not just to save lives, which we know it does on-site even if the users experience a fatal overdose at a later point in life. It also serves as an access point to the very medical services Lehman is suggesting we spend money on, and it draws users away from public locations towards a designated place with supervision. Studies show it succeeds at these, which is not something we can say for prohibition, mass incarceration, or the War on Drugs. As time goes on, we might find that they can reduce overdose death rates for the population as well. We do know that there is no observable increase in crime or trafficking as a result of these sites, so the fears about drug dealers using these sites as a base to find more customers is unfounded.

recovery/people/researchers/psychiatrist.title: James McKeen Cattell
recovery/people/researchers/psychiatrist.content:
Overview
James McKeen Cattell holds the honorable distinction of being the first psychology professor in the United States. He earned his PhD in Germany under Willhem Wundt, who was the first to distinguish psychology from biology and philosophy while calling himself a psychologist.
Metrics and Eugenics
Together, Wundt and Cattell explored the study of intelligence through psychometrics, though their general worldviews were often radically different. Wundt strictly opposed the biological determinism behind eugenics and the biological reductionism behind treating complex mental processes as simple physical processes to examine in a vacuum without reference to one’s identity within broader society. Cattell had somewhat of an obsession with ranking people against each other in the fashion of American management philosophy, which was undergoing the revolution of Scientific Management driven by those like Frederick Winslow Taylor and American Pragmatism championed by psychologists William James and John Dewey - both of whom were Presidents of the American Psychological Assocation as well. While Wundt and other psychologists saw their work as aimed towards discovering truths scientifically, pragmatists argued that the value of ideas were tied to their immediately measurable applications, usually in industrialized corporate environments.
Industrial-Organizational (I-O) Psychology as a field emerged out of the work of Cattell and his contemporaries, who thought the pragmatic application of psychology and psychometrics was to identify the inherent characteristics of a worker that would determine their worth in an environment. Rather than focusing on changing the workplace or seeing workers as people who could grow with time and resources, the focus became on weeding out those who scored lower on psychometric assessments as the individual culprits behind unoptimal productivity. Labor unions and traditionalist psychologists alike condemned this practice as reducing humans to interchangeable components that punished individuality and independence through conformity disguised as scientific standards. Many pragmatists, including Cattel, responded that the purpose of education in democracy was not actually to improve people’s conditions but to match individuals to the role best suited for their natural limitations.
A Hippie Side
Ever the experimentalist, Cattell continued a brave and amusing tradition of researching drugs through self-administration, though he didn’t publish a manuscript about it like many predecessors did. He experimented with cannabis, opium (legally obtainable as hashish at the time), caffeine, morphine, chocolate, etc., and he often went over the limits he prescribed for himself in the course of experimentation.
In 1917, Cattell was fired from Columbia University for opposing the draft into World War I. He sued the university and used his settlement winnings to create the Psychological Corporation. For the rest of his career, he pursued his interests in publications with applied psychology.
Eugenics
Cattell was unfortunately not immune from the anxieties of social changes that led many otherwise brilliant researchers to pursue pseudoscientific paradigms that justified their success as inherent to their being.

recovery/policy/bans/prohibition.title: Prohibition
recovery/policy/bans/prohibition.content:
Prohibition was a disaster. You can find lots of analysis from people far smarter and more experienced than me attesting to that. What’s most interesting to me though is how Prohibition was effectively a culture war.
The science of addiction, recovery, and treatment has always been very underdeveloped compared to other aspects of health. We can see that it’s in the nature of something as complex as addiction that it takes longer to discover patterns, assemble theories, and test solutions than other issues tied to a physiological function. That being said, Benjamin Rush, who signed the Declaration of Independence and held close relationships with a few US Presidents, wrote a very substantial argument in defense of treating alcoholism (“habitual drunkenness”) as a disease back in the 18th century. He argued that immoral behavior tied to drinking should be seen as a symptom of a disease that has afflicted one’s will and sanity. He added that Christians have an obligation to try and help all sinners, including someone lost to a substance.
So it’s interesting that the temperance movements which later praised Rush also abandoned the disease model for something between a moral model and a temperance model, blaming either the drinker or the drink at various points rather than assuming a public health perspective with a generous touch of communal spirituality. A ton of interests were at play that didn’t make the cut for Boardwalk Empire. There were saloons looking out for their bottom line, women’s groups fighting against domestic violence and family neglect, churches of different denominations that ventured into politics, politicians who were going to drink no matter what but needed to ride an issue into office, organized crime taking over the manufacture and distribution of alcohol, urban workers seeking a cleaner and safer environment as cities began to hold most of the American population, rural workers and labor unions seeking to disadvantage immigrants (especially Catholics) with a strong saloon culture, African-American coalitions seeking to prove their legitimacy as free Americans by holding up higher moral standards and allying with white church networks, and many others.
Before Prohibition and in the run-up to the Civil War, temperance movements were gaining steam but lost the moment when the sociopolitical framework for the institutions of slavery were challenged. The (im)morality of slavery and racism took priority over temperance, especially when it was leaned on heavily to cope with the brutal traumas they experienced. It wasn’t until the post-Civil War and post-WWI concerns about excessive drinking among soldiers and the struggles veterans had in reintegrating into daily life (which is actually the basis for America’s legal concept of disability) that temperance movements carried out a culture war.
One of the consequences of temperance movements having such a huge influence on the culture was a decline in institutions that researched alcoholism. After all, if the policies worked, millions of people who depend on that science would be completely liberated from that concern. Fewer hospitals, more factories and churches for the good sober Christian get-back-to-work mindset they would now have instead of cravings for drinking. Obviously, no such miracles happened, but the scientific, medical, and philanthropic communities had braced themselves for a massive decline in drinking that didn’t ever materialize.
Wartime Prohibition Act

recovery/policy/bans/war-on-drugs.title: The War on Drugs
recovery/policy/bans/war-on-drugs.content:
It’s hard to see a policy area that has undergone more ambitiously spectacular failures than drugs and substance abuse. In 2026, we still don’t have a consensus on how to define either addiction or recovery. Benjamin Rush, oft called the founder of American psychiatry, has argued that “habitual drunkenness,” which we might now brand as alcoholism or substance abuse, should be treated as “an odious disease” of one’s will and sanity. We could have had centuries of experimenting with policies, culture, markets, and scientific treatments if we had listened.
Instead, the temperance movements who cited him as an inspiration took a far more moralistic approach which labeled either the drinker or the drink as agents of sin. Sometimes both, and it always failed. Prohibition was a complete disaster, asylums designed for clinicians and researchers to work with addicts in a controlled environment were turned by legislators into prisons for the most vulnerable of our communities, dabbling with eugenics was a horrifying little episode that brought out the worst of elitism in science, the wealthy and powerful were obviously going to use top-shelf drugs no matter what policy was passed, and declaring a war on addicts and their dealers just led to a new crop of addicts and dealers.
Let’s take a look at this war and see how we lost.

In 1633, Sultan Murad IV of the Ottoman Empire banned tobacco, coffee, and alcohol, punishable by death. He blamed them for fueling unrest, and he personally would patrol the streets and execute suspected violators on the spot.
Murad and Sultan are now known as Turkish-tobacco cigarette brands. The drugs won that war. In fact, once he tortured twenty of his own officers to death for using tobacco, and some of those soldiers smuggled pipes in their sleeves to have a few last hits during it.

recovery/policy/prevention/education/dar.title: Drug Abuse Resistance Education (DARE) and Keepin' It REAL
recovery/policy/prevention/education/dar.content:
So, DARE doesn’t really work. Sorry. It turns out telling kids not to do something doesn’t actually make them not do it.
Some studies have found that DARE and its updated model Keepin’ it REAL are actually associated with an increase in drug use. This was more pronounced in suburban youth too, suggesting that the program actually provided a normalized introduction to drugs as a cultural element to kids who never knew much about them.
Plus, once kids realize that a lot of their older friends were smoking weed and drinking beers without going crazy, just like their moms and dads and all those fancy adults on TV, they begin doubting the messenger. Teachers and police officers lose lots of credibility in their eyes once they see that the purpose of education is control, not empowerment towards informed choices. “If they were lying about how dangerous weed is, maybe they’re lying about how dangerous meth is” a teen might think.
Remember that humans have a lot of reflexes against authoritarianism, like choosing to do something taboo or forbidden when they feel their agency is being constricted. By telling them what not to do, we’re just telling them exactly what to do in order to carve out their independence. This isn’t just a teenage impulse either. It’s a central motif in Orwell’s 1984, that book everyone cites but no one reads. The more drugs were framed as part of an exotic underworld subculture, the more it seemed like a rebellious escape from the highly institutionalized world they’re stuck in. The zero-tolerance concept amplified this distinction; if even trying drugs once meant you were no longer a “clean” student, then you might as well keep going because you’ve already failed.
Who would’ve guessed that kids need actual role models to emulate who provide consistent positive reinforcement instead of lectures and anti-drug chants?
(Yes, I’m still upset that the song they made us memorize in elementary school is stuck in my head. It’s also ironic that one of the kids they chose to read an assignment for an audience of parents ended up heavily addicted to weed beginning in high school. The program was a bit of a joke when I went through it in the late 2000s.)
Nothing Daring about DARE
You might be wondering how a program like this gets implemented with such dismal evidence behind it. The answer is disappointingly simple.
The Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act of 1986 (DFSCA) mandated that all educational institutions receiving federal funding must implement a Drug and Alcohol Abuse Prevention Program (DAAPP). Because most policymakers have no scientific background, they neglected to include a stipulation that the programs should have scientific evidence that they could reduce substance abuse. That came later in 1998 through guidelines issues by the Department of Education. In the meantime, school districts found DARE to be an easy way to check that box. Parents loved it for being a visible community initiative they could easily understand and which echoes the same advice they give before they kids go out: “just say no to drinks and drugs… until you’re 21 and then you can join us at the bar.”
Anecdotally, based on the people in recovery I’ve met, there’s a decent chance that a child is using substances because their parent or siblings introduced them. I assume that the suburban parents would be a little less enthusiastic about a program that was teaching their kids to look out for irresponsible adults alongside peer pressure.
After the 1998 guidelines, school boards began dropping DARE, which prompted DARE as an organization to respond with an update called Keepin’ it REAL.
In order to align with the scientific evidence at the time about successful interventions, Keepin’ it REAL made the shift from “Just Say No” to “The choice is yours.” It dropped the scare tactics in favor of teaching communication tactics to turn down drugs, translating the problem from a moral battle to expressing a personal preference. It drew on scientific literature from the fields of communication competence theory, narrative prevention theory, and social norms theory. In theory, this sounds like it validates autonomy. REAL stands for:

R: Refuse casually (“No thanks”)
E: Explain to diffuse tension (“I have a project to finish at home”)
A: Avoid unwanted environments
L: Leave if a situation feels uncomfortable

As for normalizing drugs, the new curriculum presents data to students that the vast majority of kids their age are not using substances, which turned down the hysteria that led kids to think everyone is doing it.
Again - in theory this should have been the case. In practice, a 2010 assessment of 29 schools found that “Students receiving either version of the kiR intervention in only the 5th grade report greater increases in substance use than did control students.” So, we’re still giving interesting knowledge about drugs to kids who previously had no knowledge or interest in drugs.
Why Education is Doomed to Fail
It didn’t surprise me at all that these programs are largely ineffective and occasionally detrimental to students. They stem from a fundamental misunderstanding of why people choose to use drugs and what drugs themselves actually do.
A 2024 study by Gene Hyeman, Ehri Ryu, and Hiram Brownell out of Boston College found that decreasing intergenerational income mobility (i.e. are children likely to earn less than their parents) was the single strongest predictor of drug overdose deaths. Regional lack of economic opportunity was a stronger predictor than local opioid prescription rates in predicted spikes of overdose clusters. At the individual level, a parental history of substance abuse (a mix of genetic predisposition and environmental factors) is the biggest risk factor for early onset addiction.
Meanwhile, one of the most effective behavioral interventions into addictions is Contingency Management, where someone is rewarded with immediate gratification from another source like prizes to directly compete with the immediate gratification of the addictive behavior. As a patient chooses the former over time, the brain strengthens the pathways related to executive functioning required to get the reward. A 2025 study (Coughlin et. al) of about 3000 veterans found that CM interventions led to a 41% decrease in the likelihood of death from all causes at the one-year mark.
In simple terms: when life sucks and the future seems bleak, people use drugs to feel better. If adults use drugs, the kids around them learn to cope the same way. If life begins to improve consistently, people are less likely to use drugs and more likely to take care of themselves in general.
You didn’t need a study to tell you any of that.
You put things in your body to feel different.
If you feel bad, you’ll keep trying to put things in your body until you feel good.
If you find something that’s good when nothing else is, you’ll want to use it more.
If you get a different reward that makes you feel good, you might prefer that one.
So, if you want to get people to not use drugs, reward them with alternatives. People follow incentives, not codes and rules.
It’s why reason Housing First is such an effective material intervention compared to incarceration or institutionalization. Let people be in safe and stable environments where they’re consistently rewarded for improved executive functioning. Leaving people in unsafe and unstable environments where they’re consistently denied opportunities to improve will not lead to improvement. Someone with housing can consistently access CM and other healthcare services, safely save up for their own rewards like improved clothing and social dinners, and avoid feeling like a social outcast in their daily lives which limits community engagement.
If we insist on viewing it in terms of capital, then investing in people’s health and housing is one of the best possible returns for a society. Recovery capital is an established framework for looking at the resources people have access to. Two of the biggest predictors of sustained abstinence for people in recovery is the increase in recovery capital while in treatment and the accessible recovery capital of their overall community. Increasing an individual’s coping and communication skills through education classes does comparatively little to changing the resources and community they can access. People quickly adapt to the environment they’re in. It’s one of the coolest things about humans as a species.
And for the politicians, I imagine a photo-op building housing would look better than clearing the encampments resulting from failed housing policies. Curing the disease sounds better than hiding the symptoms.
To Quote George Carlin
My personal recovery philosophy is a direct rip from George Carlin.
“Some of the people who had so much edgy promise, they died young. I mean, Lenny Bruce, Sam Kennison, Andy Kaufman in his way, Freddy Prince, John Belushi, Bill Hicks… it’s not always behavior, sometimes it’s just genetic, but I think there’s a degree of luck and intellect involved in giving up things that hurt you. The drug and alcohol thing it seems to me comes down to this: drugs and these things are wonderful. They’re wonderful when you try them first. They’re not around for all these millennia for no reason. First time, mostly plesaure, very little pain, maybe a hangover. And as you increase and keep using whatever it is, the pleasure part decreases and the pain part - the price you pay - increases until the balance is completely the other way and it’s almost all pain and there’s hardly any pleasure. At that point, you would hope the intellect says ‘Oh, oh this doesn’t work anymore. I’m going to die’ and I’ll do something.
“But you need people around you who can help you and you need something to live for. You have to have something to look forward to to bring you of it, you know. There are lot of people who don’t have a lot to live for and they’re sort of stuck.”*
That’s really what it comes down to in my opinion. Do you have people who care enough to help you see that you still have things to look forward to? It seems like we can go far on gift cards, a bed next to running water, and a regular thumbs-up from a social worker.

recovery/policy/public-health/housing-fi.title: Housing First Should Come First
recovery/policy/public-health/housing-fi.content:
What is Housing First?
Housing First is one of the most direct and effective ways to solve homelessness: give people housing. Permanent and not conditional on solving other health issues or commitment to an institution first. As the National Alliance to End Homelessness states,
Housing First is an approach that prioritizes providing permanent housing to people experiencing homelessness, thus ending their homelessness and serving as a platform from which they can pursue personal goals and improve their quality of life. This approach is guided by the belief that people need basic necessities like food and a place to live before attending to anything less critical, such as getting a job, budgeting properly, or attending to substance use issues. Additionally, Housing First is based on the belief that client choice is valuable in housing selection and supportive service participation; exercising that choice is likely to make a client more successful in remaining housed and improving their life. Housing First programs remove barriers faced by households trying to attain permanent housing, and do not require prerequisites to access housing support beyond what is required in a tenant’s lease.
Housing First Fact Sheet
The Overwhelming Evidence in Favor of Housing First as a Solution to Homelessness (with a quirky visual aid)
If you want to treat physical and mental health issues that lead to homelessness, you probably should give those patients a place to undergo long-term medical treatment that can involve medications that take weeks to notice a difference with, trauma therapies that take multiple phases across months to process a single traumatic incident during which a mental health crisis is still possible, and developing new healthy routines around diet and exercise that work alongside any other conditions.
If you want people to avoid using emergency services as a result of physical and sexual violence, preventable diseases and manageable disorders, exposure to the elements and pandemics, environmental pollution, and other nasty things, it would probably help to take someone out of the place where those things have a higher chance of occurring.
If you want to experiment with new approaches to addiction treatment beyond the Minnesota Model that was adopted in defiance of a strong scientific basis but has persisted in dominance thanks to regulatory capture from the private healthcare and insurance industries, create an alternative space to do that for a tiny miniscule fraction of the cost of a hospitalization.
To be blunt, it’s an extremely common-sense solution that you have to jump through many hoops and bend yourself into many pretzels to avoid. Meta-studies that explore these programs find strong quantitative evidence that it helps individuals stay housed and avoid using emergency resources that are far costlier than preventative measures. Every other intervention we propose is way more likely to succeed if we’re working with housed individuals. Obviously. Duh.
Recovery Requires Capital
The science of recovery and addiction treatment has moved away from focusing on total abstinence and CBT individualist therapies as a “gold standard,” and instead towards a holistic view of the way recovery capital influences quality of life for both an individual and their community.
Recovery Capital refers to the internal and external resources that an individual can access to begin and sustain recovery from addiction or mental health conditions. These resources span personal strengths, social networks, and community or cultural supports. Originally introduced by researchers Cloud and Granfield in 1999, Recovery Capital highlights that recovery success depends not only on individual willpower and abstinence but also on the broader social and environmental context. Unlike traditional abstinence-focused measures, recovery capital through the Recovery Capital Index evaluates the holistic components of wellbeing, enabling a person-centered approach to recovery.
If we accept that addiction is a complex biopsychosocial disorder with roots in personal trauma and genetic predisposition that cause physiological changes in the brain’s reward mechanisms after sustained exposure to a particular material environment, it makes sense to move beyond discussions about knowledge gaps and into capital gaps. All the diet, exercise, and spiritual changes in the world will not change the fact that people with diabetes need insulin, people who struggle to walk need wheelchairs, people who are deaf need hearing aids or sign language, people who are blind need Braille, and people who are suffering from multiple complex mental health disorders need a safe place with professionals, a bed, and running water to work through the instability of their lives.
Recovery Capital is generally split into three types, though this is more for convenience than an implication that these are independent categories:


Personal: Physical/Mental/Emotional Wellbeing, Balanced Nutrition, Employment Status, Job Satisfaction, Workplace Support, Formal Education, Growth Opportunities, Financial Stability and Stressors, Stable and Safe Housing, Transportation Accessibility, Clothing Availability


Social: Emotional and Practical Family Assistance, Relationship Support from a Significant Other, Friendships, Comfort and Aid Networks, Professional and Personal Mobility, Wellness Activities, Support Groups, Access to Healthcare, Community Safety


Cultural: Alignment and Respect for Beliefs, Clarity and Strength of Principles, Integration of Spiritual Practices, Meaning & Purpose, Culturally Appropriate Support Groups, Feelings of Community Belonging


Although called “recovery” capital, the many dimensions to one’s health that are discovered in the process of recovery are applicable to practically anyone. We can see how complex of an issue addiction is when there’s so much overlap and intersection from the types of capital above. This isn’t a new idea either; this was identified as a model in 1999. Its lack of adoption has a lot to do with the shape of our institutions rather than scientific justifications.
In the 1980s, American medical institutions that practiced psychology and psychiatry began seeking operationalizable methods that could fit into manuals and be readily tested with experiments. If you had a method that was 80% effective but took 3 years to do, you’re not going to get far compared to a treatment that’s 25% effective but can be tested in 3 weeks. A lot of comparative studies in therapy will do something like compare a standardized CBT regimen with worksheets to psychoanalytic therapy delivered by graduate students who had a couple days of rushed training from researchers who are biased by a prior body of work favoring CBT. Jonathan Shelder has a great set of criticisms that are really specific about the methodologies of these papers in promoting CBT as a “gold standard” modality. I had my own peek into the research world when I was in college, and I don’t have trouble believing much from the things he’s pointed out. The WEIRD problem feels especially salient.
One finding from recovery capital studies is that an individual’s recovery capital is not as strong in predicting sustained abstinence as social recovery capital. The difference between someone with a highly supportive relationship and without one tends to be larger than the difference between two individuals’ personality traits. Changes in social networks actually tend to precede changes observed in personal functioning. Someone can present in treatment with high motivation, confidence, and awareness, but they will still struggle to maintain abstinence if they lack consistent transportation, safe housing, sober friend groups, and employment opportunities. Someone with modest confidence in their ability to maintain abstinence can do better than someone with high confidence if they have access to a more supportive network.
Recovery capital is also a better predictor of overall quality of life than sustained abstinence, meaning someone with high recovery capital might relapse but not suffer from the same lowered quality of life as someone who relapsed with less recovery capital. Some people can spiral faster than others on this basis. By the same token though, recovery capital is capital; it tends to work like an investment where even a few months of stable living can dramatically improve someone’s ability to generate recovery capital.
How someone’s recovery capital changes during treatment is a better predictor for how they’ll do than the baseline recovery capital they start with. Someone who enters treatment and experiences a negative social environent might experience a net decrease in recovery capital that has more influence on sustained abstinence than the therapeutic and medication interventions. Because of diminishing marginal returns on any particular form of capital within recovery capital, those who have really low capital, who might feel the most desperate and hopeless, can actually make much more progress than those with high recovery capital at baseline. Some argue that treatment is effective because it helps increase recovery capital rather than directly addressing the compulsion to use or maintenance of abstinence.
What this means is that addressing addiction cannot come down to just teaching individuals ways to self-regulate their symptoms or keep up willpower through daily affirmations. The evidence is pretty clear that we need to expand access to social, environmental, and material resources if we want to make more effective, including cost-effective, interventions. Housing First is an extremely obvious way to start that process.
A Personal Note
Anecdotally, some of the most promising and inspiring recovering addicts I’ve ever met relapsed after returning to an unstable environment that they trusted to be stable so they could keep healing while reintegrating into some sense of normalcy.
I’ve seen people try to reconcile with violent partners for the sake of a roof. I’ve seen young people under 20 without safe families struggle over issues with insurance that led to being kicked out of sober living homes and into shelters, where they’ve been assaulted multiple times. I’ve seen elderly people struggle to get hired at minimum-wage jobs that strongly prefer desperate young people. I’ve seen people get diagnosed with other mental health disorders for the first time in treatment that they were obviously self-medicating through because of a prior lack of access, and they obviously haven’t had time to figure out how to stabilize from it during their brief time in addiction treatment. It takes weeks to even figure out how one adjustment to a medication can influence you, and it can take years to find a medication that works.
I’ve seen people of all ages get confused by their rights as people with disabilities. They have no clue what county, state, federal, and private programs exist dedicated for people in their situation with severe disabilities that impede a return to normal substantial employment and social relationships. These programs often require case managers or other professional staff to make a referral, but it’s been tragically common among my friends for their staff to have no idea what the county they’re working in even provides or how to put together the documentation for an application for benefits. That’s actually one of the reasons I chose to launch this site.
Someone needs to just make a pamphlet that says “Welcome to Addiction! Here are the rights you should know about, the public and private programs that you might be eligible for, the recovery meetings you can go to, the different ideas about how addiction and recovery work around the world and across time, the authorities in the field that do active research into new treatments, the common myths from pop culture that feed the stigma, the advocacy organizations you can join to fight for systemic reform, the stories that you might find inspirational, and some reminders that having a horrible disease does not make you a horrible person.”
Someone more qualified than me should do it, but until then, I’ll take a stab at it. I would like to prevent more of my friends from dying a preventable death.

recovery/policy/reintegration/contingenc.title: Contingency Management
recovery/policy/reintegration/contingenc.content:
This and Housing First are my favorite policy approaches to addressing addiction and recovery. It’s pure common sense that’s been repeatedly validated by empirical investigations in both conventional studies and pilot policies. It’s very difficult to imagine how you could oppose these unless you’re an armchair pseudoscientist, suicidally elitist, or a hack with an ulterior motive. Both directly increase recovery capital in ways that recipients repeatedly reinvest into themselves and their community as productive members of society.
Long-term outcomes of CM show that patients are 22% more likely to maintain sustained abstinence compared to psychosocial treatments like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and 12-step programs. The standard factors associated with poor outcomes in psychotherapy, like a history of trauma or major depressive disorder, do not impact CM’s effectiveness. In fact the most severe and complex medical histories respond best to the simplicity and predictability of it.
Committed Mismanagement
It’s bizarre to me that a basic operant conditioning framework outlined by BF Skinner i
We’ve spent decades on disastrous policies rooted in the War on Drugs to satisfy our lust for punishment against those we felt were lesser than us.
We’ve spent billions on militarizing our communities to guard against the consequences of our children realizing that the generations above them didn’t care to leave a world they can see a future in.
Despite proposals from American doctors to treat addiction as a disease since before the ratification of the U.S. Constitution, including a signatory to the Declaration of Independence, we have been unable to move past the moralization of illness and healthcare.
Our most prominent peer recovery groups emerged out of deeply religious revivalist movements that connected drug use to the influence of the Devil and weakness of the individual’s will to resist sins.
We’ve poured billions into preventation education programs to “Just Say No” or “Avoid and Leave”, only to have them backfire on our kids and sometimes increase the use of drugs and violence in conflict resolution.
There is no economic reason for this; these approaches have been expensive and regressive failures. Some of our politicians take a deeply perverse pride in taking away the little capital retained by the poorest and most vulnerable members of their constituencies.
All this time, gift cards and basic housing accommodations would have done far more for far cheaper.
Notable Mentions
Hannah Pickard, What Would You Do Alone in a Cage with Nothing But Cocaine? (2026)
“Perhaps even more surprisingly given the dominance of the brain disease model, the most effective treatment for cocaine and some polydrug addictions is not pharmacological but behavioral. Contingency management treatment reliably delivers small rewards, such as prizes, money, and vouchers for meals or movies—or, in the behavioral psychologist Kenneth Silverman’s inspired innovation of a therapeutic workplace, skills training and employment—on condition of drug abstinence. It is based on operant conditioning principles, a form of reinforcement learning originating in the psychologist Edward Thorndike’s discovery of the law of effect at the end of the nineteenth century, and elaborated by B. F. Skinner in the 1930s and 1940s.”
