recovery/policy/united-states/california.title: San Francisco Opium Den Ordinance of 1875
recovery/policy/united-states/california.content:
Summary
The San Francisco Opium Den Ordinance of 1875 was the first law in America that banned a non-alcoholic drug by making it a misdemeanor to visit places where people smoked opium.
It was driven largely over xenophobic fears about growing Chinese communities in the city, as well as concerns that it played a role in attracting white residents to Chinatown establishments away from white-owned ones. In doing so, law enforcement had the legal cover to selectively disrupt Chinese communities under suspicions of being an opium den while white neighborhoods continued using liquid opium as medicine.
Context
The 1870s were an economically rough time for California. The Long Depression of 1873 lasted until 1879 as the longest period of economic contraction recognized by the National Bureau of Economic Research.
Paradoxically, historians mark the beginning of the Second Industrial Revolution around the same time. Factories were adopting new technologies in steel, chemical manufacturing, and electrical grids. This meant goods could be cheaply mass manufactured which drove down their prices globally and cut down the profit margins businesses were expecting. Massive speculation in railroad companies after the Civil War proved to outpace actual returns. The collapse of banking house Jay Cooke & Company triggered panic that led to the temporary closure of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). An estimated 18,000 businesses and 89 railroads went bankrupt in the US in the initial years, with a peak unemployment of 14% by 1878. Layoffs and wage cuts were met with violent backlash like the Great Railroad Strike of 1877.
However, finance and economics are hard concepts. Instead of blaming the rampant financial speculation or lack of policies to help workers transition during periods of massive change in the labor market, they blamed immigrants for dragging down wages and using underhanded tactics to undermine white businesses. White saloons and gambling houses viewed Chinatown opium dens as competitors for working-class white men seeking recreational substances. Factory owners and labor leaders alike claimed that opium addiction, though not alcoholism, was affecting the productivity of white workers. The Workingmen’s Party of California demanded a boycott of Chinese-made goods and Chinese-owned businesses.
Some of the claims bordered on hysteria and conspiratorial paranoia. Labor organizations practically alleged a nefarious plan to trap white workers in drug dependency in order for Chinese communities to get ahead. Yellow journalism companies ran stories that claimed Chinese men used opium to lure, seduce, and traffick young white women into “white slavery.” They would fabricate narratives painting Chinatown as a seedy underbelly and pay locals to pose in ways that fit the story they were trying to write. For politicians, anti-Chinese hysteria became a platform that could unite upper-class business owners fearing labor unrest and working-class European immigrants who feared job competition.
Thus, America’s first anti-drug law was born out of a desire to dismantle a minority community that was growing into an economic hub. White residents could still buy laudanum, or liquid opium, sold at pharmacies and high-end hotels in white neighborhoods. Opium itself wasn’t being restricted; only the methods and locations used by Chinese communities, namely smoking opium and dens. Local law enforcement had the pretext to raid businesses through Chinatown, which disrupted commerce, devalued real estate, and drove customers to other shops.
For a while, Chinatown businesses and operators relocated from San Francisco to Oakland or further inland to the Central Valley. And the same hysteria eventually relocated with them as rural laborers echoed the complaints about opium dens being established near their farms and railroad camps. In 1881, a statewide expansion of the San Francisco ordinance gave local law enforcement in every jurisdiction the ability to disrupt and segregate Chinese communities.
If all this sounds eerily familiar, whether you’re thinking about the War on Drugs or the fentanyl crisis being blamed on China in recent years despite the finding that most manufacturing happens in illicit labs in Mexico, you’re not alone.
Outcomes
A San Francisco Chronicle interview clipping preserved by a Dr. Harry Hubbell Kane in his 1882 book Opium-Smoking in American and China gives us some insight into how law enforcement at the time experienced the crackdown. When asked if driving the white opium smokers out of Chinatown would decrease the general prevalence of the habit, Officer James Mahoney replies,
“Not much. It will rapidly increase. The habit in past years, so far as whites were concerned, was confined to hoodlums and prostitutes mostly. Few decent men or women would care to come into Chinatown and smoke in the filthy dens here. Now that there are scores of places where the habit can be contracted in clean rooms and in respectable portions of the city, the practice will gradually extend up the social grade. Schoolboys and clerks who would never have gone into a Chinese den are already finding out the respectable places and learning to like the habit…  The anti-opium-smoking ordinance drove the white smokers out of Chinatown, but the vice came along and scattered the smokers, planting them, in fact, in every portion of the city.”
By forcing dens closed, opium was simply smoked in more discrete private locations like one’s own room. It’s difficult to classify a bedroom as an opium den, and small-scale paraphernalia can easily be hidden or disposed of in case of a raid. Mahoney claims even search dogs are ineffective, which he guesses could be a result of an opium-smoker being too repulsive for a dog to seek.
A Note About Selective Enforcement
When I see someone fanning the flames of division between local communities through bigotry and prejudice, I instinctively look for the money trail. I am personally of the belief that we as humans default to diversity, trade, and forgiveness until someone thinks they build a monopoly by dividing and conquering. The history of drug regulations makes it really easy to see how arbitrary the line is between “choice available to an informed consenting consumer” and “contagious threat to the entire community that must be eliminated.” It’s depressingly simple to map that line onto the preexisting ones around race, ethnicity, culture, religion, etc.

recovery/policy/united-states/california.title: 1887 California Scientific Temperance Instruction Law
recovery/policy/united-states/california.content:
Summary
The 1887 California Scientific Temperance Instruction Law mandated every public school in California to introduce a mandatory daily lesson on “scientific temperance” that explained the harms of narcotics and alcohol.
Context
The American Civil War officially ended in 1866. The moral issues surrounding slavery and racial discrimination had taken the steam out of temperance advocacy as a moral and cultural movement. Between tax revenues and coping methods for the stresses of war, restrictions on drinking fell off the radar of political coalitions. For women who had been hoping to address issues like domestic violence and habitually drunk husbands who failed to provide for the family, this was a major setback.
From the 1870s to 1880s, the Women’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) set about building chapters throughout the country to keep the movement going. They were too small to have noticeable influence on the San Francisco Opium-Smoking Ordinance of 1875 or the Section 307 statewide law in 1881, but they were able to observe that these efforts failed to meaningfully stop drug efforts. After all, they were driven primarily by anti-Chinese and anti-immigration hysteria that grew amidst the Long Depression of 1873 when Chinese workers were scapegoated for wage cuts and luring the youth into drug dependencies to fund Chinatown businesses. Scientific evidence about opium as a public health issue was scarcely presented or discussed. The success of the policy was measured in terms of the disruption to Chinese communities and families.
Mary H. Hunt headed the WCTU’s Department of Scientific Temperance Instruction, and she operated a very tactical organization that distributed field manuals to chapters to lobby local elected officials. They coordinated single-issue pressure campaigns that asked politicians bluntly if they would mandate temperance instruction. Petitions, letters, pamphlets, and other forms of media were widely distributed by activists. Because women couldn’t vote, the WCTU framed their activism as a maternal duty to preserve social and moral purity in a society that gave men the privilege of navigating the corrupt spaces of business, politics, and war. It argued that the very gender roles that segregated women into private domestic spaces also engendered authority over that space. They argued women were better equipped to raise children with moral standards, so they mobilized husbands, brothers, and men of the church to only vote for politicians who supported temperance instruction.
There’s a very compelling argument that temperance was America’s first proper culture war - at least if we take a definition of “culture war” that isn’t rooted in explicit racial and ethnic tensions or labor relations. Emphasis on solely there, as racism and xenophobia were unquestionably still a driving factor for major swathes of the population.
Before aiming for state legislation, WCTU chapters began lobbying local school board meetings and individual principals to adopt temperance texts.

recovery/policy/united-states/california.title: Section 307 of the California Penal Code (1881)
recovery/policy/united-states/california.content:
Summary
The statute’s official title is “An Act to add a new section to the Penal Code, to be known as section three hundred and seven, relating to opium smoking.” I will refer to it as Section 307 of the California Penal Code (1881), or Section 307 for short on this page.
Broadly, it expanded an 1875 local ordinance in San Francisco that outlawed opium smoking and opium dens with the intention of giving law enforcement the ability to disrupt Chinese communities that were seen as a threat by both white business owners and white labor groups. Liquid opium was still available over-the-counter at pharmacies in white neighborhoods. The real competition was over white working-class men and youth who seemed to prefer smoking opium in dens, and as a result frequenting Chinatown establishments generally, over the alcoholic drinks sold in white saloons run by European immigrants.
Context
The San Francisco Opium-Smoking Ordinance of 1875 caused a flight of opium dens and operators out of Chinatown to Oakland across the bay and inland towards the rural Central Valley.
The Workingmen’s Party of California (WPC) was an anti-Chinese labor coalition that had called for a boycott of all Chinese businesses and Chinese-made goods. The WPC echoed a growing public sentiment that Chinese communities were responsible for a rough labor economy that was actually the result of a contraction from excess speculation in railroad companies and a Second Industrial Revolution that was driving down the cost of goods internationally. Instead, labor organizations claimed Chinese workers were driving down wages and trapping white workers into drug dependencies, even “white slavery,” where young white women were supposedly lured by Chinese men into opium dens to be trafficked.
Much of the anti-Chinese sentiment resulted in violence. In July 1877, San Francisco white workers broke into more than twenty Chinese-owned laundries and set fire to company docks across a riot that lasted two days. The local police had been overpowered, and an impromptu army of 4000 volunteers was formed under William T. Coleman to restore order.
During the California Constitutional Convention of 1878-1879 to update the 1849 Constitution that oversaw the initial Gold Rush, the WPC won massive support through two main planks: anti-Chinese and anti-monopoly sentiment. The anti-immigrant xenophobia became such a strong part of the political culture that it became a defining schism between Western and Eastern faction of labor organizations, including the Workingmen’s Party of the United States (WPUS) that followed traditional Marxist theory into universal working-class solditary. Unfortunately for the WPC, this nativist populism was short-lived.
Their most prominent leader, Denis Kearney, was routinely ignored by Eastern labor and socialist groups who saw his emphasis on nativist racial divisions to be a non-starter. This meant a national coalition for the WPC was impossible, and the most radical voices openly called for clauses that would violate the U.S. Constitution and federal treaties. They reportedly claimed to want a federal crisis over “the Chinese question”, as they put it, in a revolutionary style.
Frank Roney led another faction of the WPC which was more traditionally Marxist and comprised of experienced trade unionists, like the WPUS, but still held anti-Chinese sentiment. The notable distinction is that Roney’s faction blamed capitalist monopolies for importing cheap Chinese laborers to exploit. The members believed that focusing on racial exclusion and targeting individual workers would only divide the labor factions in the face of corporate monopolies.
The issue was resolved through brute force. Kearney accused Roney’s faction of trafficking in overly intellectual European theory for the problems of American working-class labor, of being corporate spies undermining the labor movement, of being in league with Chinese interests, etc. His faction voted to expel Roney and other socialist organizers from the convention and systematically shut down local clubs that supported Roney. The Eastern WPUS had made official statements condemning Kearney as an “unprincipled demagogue” hijacking labor solidarity movements. Nevertheless, in the short-term, the WPC won 51 seats and had the power to write anti-Chinese exclusion legislation.
In 1881, Assemblyman Thomas Frewen, a WPC delegate from San Francisco, introduced Assembly Bill No. 181 (A.B. 181), which would be Section 307. The strength of the nativist populist movements gave it virtually unanimous support from the legislature and policymakers. There was hardly any pretense that opium itself was a public health issue that just happened to involve trade relations with China or Chinese-owned businesses. Governor George C. Perkins signed it into law, giving every sheriff the power to raid opium dens and arrest smokers.

recovery/policy/vatican/1590-1599/pope-u.title: Pope Urban VII
recovery/policy/vatican/1590-1599/pope-u.content: In 1590, Pope Urban VII issued perhaps the first ban on smoking, threatening anyone with excommunication for using tobacco in or near a church. It covered smoking, chewing, or sniffing snuff. He died of malaria and holds the record for the shortest papacy in history: 12 days.

recovery/policy/vatican/1620-1629/pope-u.title: Pope Urban VIII
recovery/policy/vatican/1620-1629/pope-u.content: Unlike his predecessor who held the papacy for 12 days, Pope Urban VIII reigned for 21 years. He prohibited the use of tobacco in holy places under the threat of excommunication in a 1624 decree. Supposedly, the excessive sneezing and grime from chewing tobacco felt disruptive and disrespectful.

recovery/treatment/models/choice-theory.title: Choice Theory
recovery/treatment/models/choice-theory.content:
It’s a shame that our culture can’t separate choice and agency from blame and accountability. These terms have become laden with implications that make it really difficult to discuss something on its own terms. For instance, much of the disagreement over describing addiction as a disease comes from debate over the therapeutic value of conveying to clients that they have choice in the form of treatment and management over a disorder they didn’t choose to have. The social stigma and poor education around addiction is intense enough that it’s worth discussing the merits of choosing terms to improve communication rather than technical accuracy. This certainly isn’t a new idea: from The Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous, Dr. Silkworth framed alcoholism as both a physical allergy and a mental obsession. Researchers and clinicians have generally moved on from that description to arguing about the disease model, but that’s only partially reflected among those with substance abuse disorders. To this day, many people conceptualize their relationship with substances as an allergy that they can only manage by either abstinence or, if ingested, immediate treatment for a life-threatening crisis.

recovery/treatment/models/degeneration-t.title: Degeneration Theory
recovery/treatment/models/degeneration-t.content:
Any coverage of the history of addiction, or anything in mental health, that doesn’t touch on the hubris of eugenics is failing to be honest about the ways scientific institutions can aggregate enough hubris to try and play God.
The degeneration theories put out by those like B.A. Morel functioned as a perverse parallel to the developments preceding Darwin’s natural selection and subsequent arguments about evolution. Defining degeneration as anything that deviates from a “natural” or “normal” state, advocates of the theory attempted to model degeneration as mental capacity that declines from parent to child until a generation is born sterile. Morel’s categories of degeneration included hysteria, moral insanity, imbeciles, and idiots. Psychiatrists found it a convenient way to both connect moral theories of illness to physiology and label any disease they couldn’t find the cause of as a quirk of an individual’s degeneration process. To put it crudely, “we don’t know what’s wrong so they were probably born to be sick and immoral.”
Predictably, a lot of dumb and horrible projects came out of this idea of degeneration. The Nazis used it as a basis for eugenics, fascist movements in Europe used it in arguments about immigration, and many scientists have attempted to predict criminality from facial features or skull shape. That last one is still something being explored by researchers and law enforcement institutions, with a notable recent controversy coming out of the AI community’s computer vision models. To this day, I argue that elite academic institutions suffer from a historical bias of preferring investigations into nature over nurture. It’s not exactly an attractive proposition to take credit away from yourself and towards factors outside of yourself.
It wasn’t just the fashion of the time to believe this either. Sigmund Freud rejected Morel’s work and degeneration theory.
Links

recovery/treatment/models/disease-model.title: Disease Model of Addiction
recovery/treatment/models/disease-model.content:
Commentary
When I first heard of the disease model, I honestly shrugged. For an individual who finds themselves in a treatment program, being introduced to the label of a “disease” can feel relatively quaint. It doesn’t change the overwhelming burden on the individual to overcome it through some calibration of personal willpower, and it doesn’t lessen the impacts of addiction on loved ones or the community in which it occurs. Carl Erik Fisher writes something in his book that resonated with me:
“‘The brain disease model of addiction’ can mean different things. The most modest claims are reasonable, bordering on uninteresting: neuroscience can help us to understand addiction, including ways of helping with medical treatments, but it is not necessarily the only way to understand the problem.”
The disease model is as old as Benjamin Rush, a signatory of the Declaration of Independence who had trusted correspondence with Thomas Jefferson and John Adams.
Rush was a doctor who was unapologetic about Christian education being the bedrock of a democratic republic, but he also relied on his faith to argue against slavery, banning all women from education, and the inhumane treatment of prisoners. His faith drove his commitments to social justice, and that includes social views of those afflicted with “habitual drunkenness.” He made several observations that placed addiction into the realm of an “odious disease” or a “disease of the will” where immoral behavior was a symptom rather than a reason to condemn someone. He documented the impact of “habitual drinking” on bodily organs which meant there were undeniably impacts on physiological health, but he also included “madness” that drives one to suicide so that there was a connection between the physical and mental outcomes. Rush is often credited as one of the first American psychiatrists for exploring mental health as a systematic science tied to the body. Although some of his theories didn’t pan out (like mental illness being caused by blood vessel issues in the brain), I think that his arguments hold up today as a rebuttal to the moral model.
One of the reasons the moral model has persisted is that the disease model is really, really, really complicated. We still don’t have a universally-accepted definition for what constitutes addiction as a disease. Prohibition was based mostly in moral and temperance models of addiction, and the solutions were presumed to be legal, religious, and cultural. The eugenics movement worked in ideas about sterilizing alcoholics to prevent more from being born, and the liquor and bar industries were fighting back the regulations that cut into their profits. When those solutions failed and the institutions responsible lost the same enthusiasm to try more, researchers in the medical community kept looking at the evidence and data since alcoholics were still showing up in hospitals.
From Bellevue Hospital, Dr. Norman Joliffe formed the Research Council on Problems of Alcohol (RCPA) to finally start building secular and scientific infrastructure to study addiction as a public health crisis. Those like the Rockefeller Foundation rejected funding for the RCPA since addiction research was still politically controversial, polarizing, and suffered from very messy data as evidence. In 1939, the Carnegie Foundation agreed to fund an international literature survey that Elvin Morton Jellinek was hired for as a statistician. Jellinek’s 1942 book that catalogued decades of journals from different countries in different languages became the Classified Abstract Archive of the Alcohol Literature (CAAAL), which grew so foundational for addiction science and research that Yale University absorbed it under their Laboratory of Applied Physiology. Those like Dr. Silkworth, the same as the one from The Big Book of Alcoholics Anonymous, kept arguments for the disease model alive, but Jellinek was the researcher who consistently provided empirical evidence and statistical data for a disease model that made it impossible to ignore.
With Marty Mann, the first woman to achieve long-term sobriety through AA, and other prominent AA proponents, Jellinek and Dr. Howard Haggard at Yale launched the National Committee for Education on Alcoholism (NCEA). The goal would be to bring empirical evidence to the public that alcoholism was a disease that should be treated as a public health issue rather than a moral failing. It was hard though, especially because of AA’s anonymous design and a goal of minimizing professional and institutional influence over the program.
AA’s official magazine The Grapevine released a 36 question survey for 1600 readers to take. The response rate was less 10%, and over a third of the responses had to be discarded for being incomplete, contradictory, or impossible to decipher. Only 98 men and 15 women had fully completed and submitted the survey, but the women’s timelines were so different that combining them into a single pool of data would make it seem noisier. Jellinek was very aware of these extreme limitations and even included feedback: “Statistical thinking should not begin after a survey or an experiment has been completed but should enter into the first plans for obtaining the data.” Nevertheless, in a 1946 publication, he chronicled chronologically 43 symptoms of alcoholism as it progresses until fatality. In 1952, Jellinek conducted a survey of 2,000 male alcoholics to have actual data which would hold up to scientific scrutiny.
Dr. Max Glatt built on Jellinek’s work with his proposed signs of rehabilitation, turning a depressive progressive decline into a more hopeful U-shaped graph now called Jellinek’s Curve. Glatt ran one of the first specialized treatment units for alcoholism in the UK through the NHS. His diagram made it back across the pond to William Keaton of the State Commission on Alcoholism in Michigan, who published a Modified Jellinek Chart that replaced medical jargon in its descriptions of symptoms with clearly relatable examples like “sneaking drinks” and “morning tremors” for public distribution in clinics, jails, and hospitals.
The disease model has been around for a while and has won over academia, but the public and recovery communities alike are still negotiating the moral model with it. It’s hard to have an open discussion when the “War on Drugs” as a policy crusade used an outdated moral-temperance “Just Say No” model that’s still fresh in our memories. Regardless, science marches on. Check out some of the stuff that’s come since:

The Minnesota Model

recovery/treatment/models/minnesota-mode.title: The Minnesota Model of Recovery
recovery/treatment/models/minnesota-mode.content:
You Know It More Than You Think
From the 1990 book Broadening the Base of Treatment for Alcohol Problems:
Although treatment programs continue to vary along ideological lines, the field has seen in recent years the evolution and emergence of hybrid programs that claim to reflect the biopsychosocial model.
The major hybrid is the Minnesota Model of Chemical Dependence Intervention and Treatment (Laundergan, 1982), a treatment strategy that blends AA and professional concepts and practices. It is widely believed that today the vast majority of U.S. treatment programs, both in the public and private sectors, subscribes to the philosophy and organization of treatment services that has become known simply as the Minnesota model (Anderson, 1981; Laundergan, 1982; Hoffmann et al., 1987b).
The standardized treatment program typically delivered to persons in treatment in the course of a four week inpatient stay, either in a hospital or in a freestanding facility, consists of detoxification, education (based on the disease concept) about the harmful medical and psychosocial effects of excessive alcohol consumption, confrontation, attendance at AA meetings and use of AA materials in developing a recovery plan (“stepwork”), and disulfiram therapy.
If that treatment protocol seems familiar, whether from pop culture or from experience, it’s because it’s still the foundation of addiction treatment in 2026.
The Minnesota Model represents an intersection of religion, the private healthcare industry, and the aesthetics of science. The widespread nature of its adoption has made it almost impossible to imagine treatment for addiction outside of the model’s toolkit. That doesn’t mean the model doesn’t work, or that individual facilities haven’t iterated into something more impactful, but it does mean we got where we are for reasons that don’t involve honoring the work of addiction researchers through good science.
From 1950-1951, Dr. Nelson Bradley, Daniel Anderson, and Jean Joseph Rossi Jr. at the Willmar State Mental Hospital. Willmar was the state of Minnesota’s only hospital for “inebriates.” The professional staff had begun experimenting with a new approach that saw “the power of spiritual experience as a driving force in recovery” given the multidimensional nature of addiction. They used a combination of psychologists, social workers, doctors, clergy, and people in recovery with multiple years of sobriety to fuse the Buchmanist principles of AA with medicine and state services.
In 1954, recovered alcoholics were able to be hired under a distinct title called “Counselor on Alcoholism” that William Wilson (Bill W.), founder of AA, encouraged former alcoholics to pursue despite concerns that it was turning the 12th step into a paid-professional track. Anderson wrote:
Treatment is based on two kinds of knowing. You need the knowledge of science, but you also need the knowledge of wisdom and experience. The latter is where you get into the spiritual dimensions that recovered alcoholics bring into the mix. You have to mesh these two kinds of knowing together. The choices are a dynamic integration or a self-destructive polarization.
That seems reasonable enough. The emphasis on peer counselors who are also in recovery seemed to grow over time. By the 1960s, a counselor-patient ratio might look something like 1:40 with pods of ten patients at a time. Critically, these counselors were not attempting-
“to do group therapy in the way psychiatrists and psychologists were being trained to do groups… What was infused into the counselor role was not psychology, but the core of A.A.’s philosophy of alcoholism recovery… Willmar also involved A.A. volunteers in the treatment program and linked clients to A.A. as the primary means of continued support following discharge… Another volunteer labor force… was made up of physicians and nurses who were sentenced to Willmar in lieu of losing their credentials or going to the narcotics hospital in Lexington, Kentucky. Most of the doctors who worked on the inebriate unit at Willmar were themselves there for treatment, and alcoholic R.N.s performed a wide variety of duties on the unit… Wilmar State Hospital, Pioneer House, and Hazelden all used clergy to assist alcoholic patients in taking A.A.’s Fifth Step. Willmar brought clergy into the interdisciplinary team as full-time, fully participating members… Rev. John Keller and the Rev. Gordan Grimm…”
The format of modern treatment has certainly become less explicitly religious, but no less dependent on seeking an overlap between religion and therapy that’s reconciled through peers without training in either. Rather than clergy coming in to offer advice, it’s common that a recovering addict will lead a discussion using a book of religious principles like Just For Today or The Four Agreements. It’s actually very amusing to read Rev. Keller describe the experience of being approached:
*“We have been looking around the country for a pastor to go full-time into specialized ministry in alcoholism and we think you are the guy.” That statement made absolutely no sense. My ministry in three congregations was marked by a lack of knowledge, no involvement with alcoholics, and total silence on alcoholism. The answer was “no”.
Keller did eventually agree to joining after meeting with Bradley, though I’m still trying to figure out what convinced him. It seems like the opportunity to be on the ground floor of defining religious and spiritual guidelines for a disease that had been around for centuries was very compelling for a young preacher compared to regular Sunday services.
By 1961, barely a decade after they arrived, Bradley, Anderson, and Rossi had all left Willmar for different reasons. Bradley had a salary dispute, Anderson accepted leadership at Hazelden to replicate the model used at Willmar, and Rossi continued to research alcoholism.
The Alcoholic Addiction Project was formed to study the outcomes of Willmar’s treatment program, and they published two papers in the 1960s into the Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol. This link has the full tables: www.practicalrecovery.com/prblog/how-alcohol-treatment-became-divorced-from-alcohol-science-the-rise-of-the-minnesota-model/
To summarize, the first showed that by 1957, 34% of patients “improved” while 32% were “unimproved” and 6% were “dead”. 20% were “unknown” and 8% were “motivated.” The second analysis of outcomes from 1963 showed 5% institutionalized, 6% dead, 17% lost to follow-up, 22% were mild drinking, and 43% were serious drinking. Only 7% reported continuous abstinence. So, at best it seemed to help a third of the patients in some way with only single-digits staying sober.
You might be wondering how the Minnesota Model came to be accepted across institutions if there was substantial evidence about its limitations. The answer isn’t too far from the reasons Anderson and Hazelden were pushing a defense of their model so aggressively despite challenges from new evidence. Let’s hop over to the Johnson Institute.
Vernon E. Johnson was an Episcopal priest whose own struggles to recover from alcoholism led to seeking treatment at the Hazelden Foundation in 1962. Convinced that addiction could be treated and addressed before hitting “rock bottom” through the intervention of family, friends, clergy, and employers, he founded the Johnson Institute in 1966 to promote early detection and treatment for “chemical dependencies.” By 1968, funded by Irene and Wheelock Whitney, Johnson established a chemical dependecy program at St. Mary’s Hospital in Minneapolis and set up over 30 by 1980. More than actual medical treatment though, Johnson focused on training the public to do interventions. The Institute became heavily involved in workplace Employee-Assistance Programs (EAPs) that allowed employers to refer employees for medical help if they suspected performance issues were related to health issues like substance abuse rather than just outright firing them. Through these early intervention and detection approaches, Johnson was funneling the public into the entry points for Minnesota Model programs, many of which were implemented by Hazelden alumni.
I’ll discuss the Johnson Institute and the intervention literature in more depth elsewhere, but for now you should know that studies and scholars have not backed up the idea of confrontational interventions being a consistently effective method to restore someone to sobriety or treatment. Remember that Johnson had no scientific or statistical background when he set up the Institute. Since then, we have more scientifically validated intervention methods like Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT) which tries to work with the idea of gradual reinforcement of change rather than abrupt disruptions that can provoke fear and hostility. Studies show up to 70% of families engaged with CRAFT manage to engage their loved ones with treatment within a year while other intervention methods clocked in around 20% at best.
Nevertheless, with Hazelden alumni spreading across US hospitals looking to fill empty beds for the promise of federal funding, Anderson creating a highly publicized political controversy around scientific critiques, and Johnson promoting interventions from employers and families to funnel the chemically dependent into Minnesota Model treatment programs, all the pieces were there for standardization and institutionalization. In the 1970s, the private hospital lobby operated under an independent non-profit called the JCAH, consisting of:


The American Medical Association (AMA)


The American Hospital Association (AHS)


The American College of Surgeons (ACS)


The American College of Physicians (ACP)


The JCAH was not a government agency or a body of researchers. It was a trade organization for medical professionals and providers which maintained internal standards to avoid external regulation and inspection from the state. The 1970 Hughes Act gave the JCAH a legal monopoly on approving hospitals for accreditation and thus becoming eligible for Medicare/Medicaid reimbursements. The same Act was responsible for creating the National Institute on Alcohol, Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) that we discussed above, which was not incentivized to monopolize the gatekeeping of treatment protocols the way JCAH was.
The JCAH feared that either the federal government would step in to regulate the health sector more aggressively or alternative accreditation agencies would emerge that challenged their monopoly based on NIAAA’s alternative research projects. To address that fear, the JCAH created an Accreditation Council for Psychiatric Facilities. It was staffed with representatives of the American Psychiatric Association (which uses Benjamin Rush’s silhouette in the logo for being one of the first American psychiatrists; he pushed for a disease model of addiction centuries ago).
Together they came up with the 1972 Accreditation Manual for Psychiatric Facilities and established 28 components that had to be demonstrated in order for mental health programs to receive accreditation. By 1974, the NIAAA had begun contracting with the JCAH to create standards that medical insurance providers would cover. As the decade went on, insurance companies began offering coverage for alcoholism at the same time that hospitals were suddenly finding themselves with lots of empty beds.
Note: I am still searching for a version of the 1972 manual to reference and share. Frustratingly, many of the sources are paywalled, but that’s not that surprising given everything we’ve seen so far and will continue to see. Apparenty it’s still under copyright despite being an accreditation guideline that we’re supposed to trust in and that has been cited in court cases about patient rights.
Now let’s revisit the book I mentioned at the top, Broadening the Base of Treatment for Alcohol Problems (1990):
Although treatment programs continue to vary along ideological lines, the field has seen in recent years the evolution and emergence of hybrid programs that claim to reflect the biopsychosocial model.
Notice the wording “claim to reflect.” I would interpret that as suggesting that the values of a biopsychosocial model are recognized in the field but still bound to the ingrained institutional practices of the Minnesota Model.
The major hybrid is the Minnesota Model of Chemical Dependence Intervention and Treatment (Laundergan, 1982), a treatment strategy that blends AA and professional concepts and practices. It is widely believed that today the vast majority of U.S. treatment programs, both in the public and private sectors, subscribes to the philosophy and organization of treatment services that has become known simply as the Minnesota model (Anderson, 1981; Laundergan, 1982; Hoffmann et al., 1987b).
Notice the authors being cited and the dates? Laundergan and Anderson from the early 1980s. Notice that they’re only being cited for the proposal and adoption of the Minnesota Model, not its efficacy?
To understand the current status of treatment in this country, it is important to understand the evolution of Minnesota model inpatient treatment programs, a standardized specialist treatment system that has been criticized as emphasizing an overly expensive, inpatient-focused medical model (e.g., Miller and Hester, 1987; Yahr, 1988).
“Overly expensive” is an interesting critique for a program that was tacitly manualized and operationalized by a private trade organization that deals mostly through an “inpatient-focused medical model” and was aware of taxpayer-funded reimbursements coming through the federal government. Also, this Miller was involved in the studies about CRAFT’s efficacy from before, so there’s a pattern of some addiction researchers repeatedly refuting the claims made by private individuals and organizations who rush past evidence into dogma.
The standardized treatment program typically delivered to persons in treatment in the course of a four week inpatient stay, either in a hospital or in a freestanding facility, consists of detoxification, education (based on the disease concept) about the harmful medical and psychosocial effects of excessive alcohol consumption, confrontation, attendance at AA meetings and use of AA materials in developing a recovery plan (“stepwork”), and disulfiram therapy.
Insurance companies grew to love the Minnesota Model because it was very predictable in terms of costs: the length of stay, structure of treatment, staffing, billing codes, documentation of medical necessity, etc. For hospitals and insurers alike, it became really easy to make calculations like estimating the costs and profits of keeping 25 beds in a rotation for 4 weeks per person. You can’t do it that easily with cancer, heart failure, stroke, clot, amputation, infection, or another vector of illness. It also explains why certain therapeutic modalities form the basis for psychoeducation topics, like CBT/DBT that are focused on worksheets and short-term skills development.
This isn’t to say those modalities are inherently wrong or unhelpful, but the incentive behind promoting them as a “gold standard” or “one-size-fits-all” curriculum has to do with how easy it is to operationalize. Even the “evidence-based” marketing around CBT/DBT is heavily rooted in how easy they are to run experiments for compared to psychodynamic/psychoanalytic approaches. You can very easily create a skills module consisting of a certain number of classes and worksheets just like K-12 education, and then claim treatment is done because the patient completed those modules. Continued suffering from symptoms means another set of classes and worksheets under an unfalsifiable presumption that they simply didn’t internalize the tools to challenge cognitive distortions well enough for them to be effective.
Often the metric we use to measure effectiveness depends on numerical self-reporting, like saying that your depression went from an 8 to a 7, or that your sleep went from “Quite a bit” disrupted to “Moderately” disrupted which is one severity category down. It’s much harder to evaluate someone who might want to say “I feel just as hopeless as I did last week, but I’m more aware of it as a temporary state, so I can apply some of the coping skills we went over to get me through the day instead of ruminating, but I’d be lying if I said I was at all more optimistic for the future.” Does that sound like an 8 to a 7? Do we even know if this is a good thing, whether someone is becoming more dissociated from their daily experiences or applying a metacognitive perspective while self-regulating? I have no clue.
Therapists don’t even really have a chance to build a relationship or get a picture of someone’s life in just 4 weeks. Good therapists will be upfront about how difficult it would be to address trauma or something meaningful within that time frame. It can take months of conversations to even begin discovering what your traumas might be. Yet, studies increasingly show that for those with co-occurring disorders like PTSD and substance abuse at the same, addressing the two simultaneously rather than waiting for long-term stabilization can be more effective. Common factor studies strongly suggest that a successful and sustained relationship with a therapist makes a bigger difference in your mental health outcomes than the modality they choose. Recovery capital framework studies suggest that community recovery capital in the form of a couple of highly supportive relationships and access to healthcare can do more to improve sustained abstinence and quality of life than individual recovery capital in the form of more coping skills or spirituality.
Unfortunately, as soon as a monopoly attempts to put uniform standards on something, we add costs on the side of liability and lost innovation. Treatment facilities have to adhere to all kinds of guidelines that were not designed with the patients’ outcomes as a priority. Remember that the JCHA was composed of professional organizations in the private hospital industry, not patient advocacy groups or scientific communities. If a facility has to account for justifying a treatment plan, setting up diverse programming like family counseling sessions, hiring qualified staff that are trained in diverse programming, measuring outcomes in a comparable way, securing physical clinical space, maintaining patient privacy, handling medications and adverse reactions, and preparing for inspections or reports to several different groups for accountability, then “experimenting with a brand new state-of-the-art approach” is a borderline implausible task. Not impossible, but certainly a risk that I wouldn’t blame any facility or professional for considering unreasonable compared to iterating on the Minnesota Model.
Personally, I would say Housing First is probably the most viable alternative pathway to the existing standardized model, mostly because it just keeps someone in one safe and stable place long enough to meaningfully engage with treatments and find out what works for them. It was initially proposed to address the issue of homelessness, but I would argue it’s an ideal first step towards addressing any debilitating mental health condition. It becomes much easier to apply CRA/CRAFT approaches or therapeutic community approaches that have substantial evidence of their effectiveness but rely on providing a stable network to engage with. For many people, substance abuse is not the most destabilizing factor in their daily life or long-term goals.
Although one could trace a number of early precursors of this approach, the efforts begun in Minnesota at the Willmar State Hospital, the Hazelden Foundation, and the Johnson Foundation were particularly influential in the development and spread of this program model and in its adoption as the standard treatment regimen.
Indeed, we are still attempting to recover from being under their influence.

recovery/treatment/models/moral-model.title: The Moral Models of Addiction
recovery/treatment/models/moral-model.content:
I don’t think I can do better than the succint summary included in this link:
The moral model rests on a straightforward premise: using drugs is wrong, and people who become addicted have made immoral choices. Substance use is rooted in immorality, and the person using substances bears complete blame for their situation. There is no disease, no brain malfunction, no genetic vulnerability in this framework. There is only a person who chose badly.
This view assumes that willpower alone is sufficient to stop using substances. If someone cannot quit, it reflects a deficiency in their character, not a change in their biology. Recovery, under this model, is essentially a matter of deciding to be a better person. And failure to recover is further proof of moral weakness.
Although the scientific and medical communities have roundly rejected this model for decades, the moral model has remained embedded in policy, media, and public perception of addiction. Courts have ruled that suffering from addiction can’t alone be the justification for a penalty, but we still criminalize the behaviors around addiction, like possession of addictive substances or public drunkenness. Whether or not someone has an addiction, we expect that at some point they would leave their house, so arresting them for public intoxication is arguably arresting them for displaying a symptom in public. The very definition of addiction is that it compels one to compromise everything for a substance that compromises them further, which is obviously going to include rules.
That doesn’t mean we can’t hold someone with the disease accountable for trying to address it to the best of their abilities. If someone makes the decision to go to a bar sober and knows they’re going to drive back drunk, only to crash and kill some kids playing in their front yard, then we can obviously hold that person accountable in a very serious way. They made an extremely reckless decision from a clear state of mind that led to pain and death. If that same person made a plan not to use any kind of substance as a designated driver, but someone new they just met thought it would be funny to give everyone edibles without their knowledge, I would have a hard time blaming the person with a substance use disorder for ending up in a fatal crash instead of the person who drugs people without consent. I’ve certainly met people who find that kind of thing funny. As with almost everything, the context matters a lot, but we can hopefully see there are times when addiction can cause damage without being an open-and-shut case in terms of morality.
Of course, individuals may benefit from making amends by admitting wrongdoing or feel motivated by the call to be better, but modern science has evidence of structural changes in the brain of those who use substances long-term. If we consider addiction to be a type of Traumatic Brain Injury or at least something comparable, then it may not make sense to approach their healing and treatment through morality. In fact, it can veer into religion very quickly. If someone stops going to church and then relapses, it’s very easy to blame them for destroying their connection to God’s will in favor of egoistic self-will, but people stop going to church all the time without suffering immediate or noticeable negative consequences. The focus on morality might cause us to look past something underlying the decision to stop going to church, like a depressive episode, a new reminder of old traumas, tension in the church community, additional stress and fatigue from work, or just changes in one’s preferred mode of experiencing a spiritual connection to their God. At least for me, I can’t just see any of that as immoral or weak-willed.
So I’m not the biggest fan of the moral model, or moralizing any disease or illness as a blanket policy. Individuals can be judged once we know their context, but a categorical judgment is harder for me to stomach.

recovery/treatment/models/temperance-mod.title: The Temperance Model of Addiction
recovery/treatment/models/temperance-mod.content:
Temperance movements and organizations have been around since alcoholic drinks were manufactured at scale. In the 19th century, in the lead up to Prohibition in America, arguments to ban alcohol centered less on the need to morally reform “habitual drunks” and more on the substance itself being the root of evil. “Habitual drunks” were merely those who had submitted to a temptation like any sin because of a flawed human body, but the substance tightened its grip and drove the drinkers to sin. By banning alcohol to take it out of the hands of everyone, the “habitual drunks” could then pursue God from a sober state of mind to repent for falling into temptations.
Prohibition was a disaster, and the policies were quickly rolled back after a great expansion of wealth for organized crime. It turns out that everyday people will still seek alcohol despite what the law says, because people like to drink. Lots of people can drink in a way that doesn’t seriously derail their life or sanity. Even if you lock up a bunch of poor drunks and shut down back-alley breweries, wealthy families will still hold lavish parties with illicit substances that they could easily still procure. The focus after this returned to the drinker rather than the drink.

Commentary
In theory, CBT sounds right up my alley. I love the idea of leaning on rationality as a tool to navigate daily life successfully. I love challenging ideas that sound irrational, subjective, outdated, or just too-good-to-be-true. Navigating the world gets so much more comfortable for me when I believe that I can prepare a rationality toolkit that will slice through the parade of bullshit we’re all subjected to on a nonstop basis.
In practice, CBT seems to have become a gold standard or a silver bullet, and it’s impacted the culture of mental health in a way that has little, if anything, to do with the theory.
By the early 1990s, CBT had become the dominant approach to psychotherapy for depression. While there’s a strong base of evidence that supports that CBT itself has positive outcomes, there hasn’t been evidence to suggest that challenging cognitive distortions or correcting cognitive dysfunction was the reason. In short, we knew it helped but didn’t know how or why.
In 1996, Niel S. Jacobson ran an experiment that isolated components of CBT and studied their impacts. The first group would undergo behavioral action, the second group combined it identifying automatic thoughts, and the third group received the complete CBT protocol that involved cognitive restructuring. All three groups showed substantial improvement, and the third group was not meaningfully better than the first group. Many researchers at this point stepped into Behavioral Activation as its own modality independent of the rest of CBT. Other researchers moved away from examining its underlying mechanisms and into analyzing its effectiveness.
Steven D. Hollon and Robert J. DeRubeis continued studying CBT mechanisms, but it became difficult to find consistent patterns in those suffering from depressive symptoms undergoing CBT. Sometimes cognitive changes came before improvement in symptoms, but sometimes the symptoms improved before cognitive changes, and sometimes they both changed at the same time. This made it difficult to claim that challenging cognitive distortions was consistently improving depression.
Nevertheless, there grew an industry of CBT manuals targeting all kinds of mental health illnesses and disorders: panic disorders, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, PTSD, OCD, substance use, etc. Research had empirically validated many of these models, but the problem of excessive manualization emerged. CBT is really easy to study compared to other treatments, which meant it had more evidence, which meant it attracted more funding, which meant it had more evidence, which meant it attracted more funding… so on and so forth. However, having more evidence doesn’t mean other therapies are less evidence-based if the evidence is still high quality, such as peer-reviewed publications.
Ronald Kessler and colleagues in the research space ran the National Comorbidity Survey (NCS) which found that people with one mental health disorder very frequently presented with others. This presented some complications, since the manuals had mapped treatment protocols to individual diagnoses as presented by the DSM. If a patient came in with multiple co-occurring diagnoses, a therapist might find themselves combining multiple manuals instead of applying the fundamentals that worked across them all. Barlow sought to create a Unified Protocol in 2004 that did exactly that, and while it didn’t stick in the long run, other approaches to CBT that transcended diagnoses and manuals kept developing.
Jacobson and Dimidjan led studies into Behavioral Activation separate from Cognitive Therapy as a treatment protocol. In a 2006 publication, on patients with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), BA did as well if not better than CT especially for the severely depressed subgroups. In fact, BA was comparable to antidepressant medication in how effective it was.
The same year, Hayes et al published a review of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), which challenged the conventional thinking about changing cognition by arguing for an expansion of the concept of cognition. Rather than rational or irrational beliefs related to cognitive distortions that required restructuring, ACT was aimed at rigid internal organization around a belief regardless of its rationality or truth value. A patient with improve mental flexibility and a firm value system might be able to accept unwanted experiences or feelings that were previously avoided. Empirical results again showed that it was comparable in effectiveness to CBT, underscoring that changing the content of thoughts was not the primary mechanism for improvement.
In 2009, Hollon & DeRubeis reviewed the literature around CBT and found that, although its efficacy was still established, there was weak evidence to identify the mechanisms of CBT that lead to improved outcomes. They found lots of methodological issues in studies that were trying to pinpoint those drivers. The year after, we see some sparks fly. Lynch, Laws, & McKenna (2010) featured sharp criticisms of the literature up to that point as being overly reliant on comparing CBT to weak control groups like patients on waitlists. They argued that any intervention can look impressive relative to nothing instead of a comparison to established psychotherapy, and they pointed out that meta-studies had conflated both types of controls when describing the significance of CBT’s outcomes.
Specifically, they found a statistically significant difference between blinded and non-blinded studies for CBT for schizophrenia, implying that observer bias from researchers was substantially inflating the results. There was a small improvement in acute depression symptoms from CBT rather than the moderate-to-large effects some studies claimed, but the main benefits were in preventing relapses into depressive episodes. They found no statistically significant evidence that it was effective for those with schizophrenia or preventing episodes from bipolar disorder.
To be clear, Lynch et al were not trying to say that CBT is ineffective. They were clarifying that the literature so far can give the impression it’s far more effective than it really is given how heavily manualized and institutionalized it was becoming. Farchione et al 2012 gives us an empirical attempt at Barlow’s 2004 proposal for a transdiagnostic unified protocol of CBT that set aside the DSM’s diagnoses as a starting point for manuals and interventions.
The last two decades have featured a lot of debate over this, and I’m still in the process of sorting through the avalanche of studies and the consensus around them. Part of the problem is that studies try to answer very specific questions while the debate about protocols demands generalization. It is true that CBT is one of the most evidence-backed therapies, but it is also true that CBT’s effectiveness has been overstated when other therapy modes seem just as effective if not more so depending on the patient. It is true that CBT studies have had lots of issues in methodology, but it’s also true that CBT has generally held up as improving a patient’s outcomes in the follow-up studies with better methodologies.
One of the most vocal critics of the dominance of CBT over other therapies is Jonathan Shelder. A 2018 paper hosted on his website (and included in the links below) has some incisive critiques about the research and therapeutic communities. It’s a paper written in plain enough language for non-academics and non-professionals to read. Shelder is very opinionated on how CBT gets marketed as “evidence-based” or a “gold standard” when we also have evidence for psychodynamic therapies that are excluded from those labels. He doesn’t go as far as to say CBT is wrong or bad as theory in this paper, but he does criticize the widespread use of manualized therapy for short-term symptom reduction method as convenient for institutions rather than the outcome of good science and health policy.
Even ardent CBT advocates have acknowledged that manualized CBT offers lasting help to few. Writing in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, eminent CBT researcher Steven Hollon noted “Only about half of all patients respond to any given intervention, and only about a third eventually meet the criteria for remission… . More over, most patients will not stay well once they get better unless they receive ongoing treatment.”2 Ironically, this was written by the same researcher who declared other forms of psychotherapy “inadequate.” Sadly, such information reaches few clinicians and fewer patients. I wonder what the public and policy makes would think if they knew these are the same treatments described publicly as “evidence-based,” “scientifically proven,” and “the gold standard.”
Lest the reader think this a misrepresentation or caricature, consider that prominent proponents of manualized therapy advocate treatment by minimally trained paraprofessionals. The journal Psycho logical Science in the Public Interest, the house organ of the Association for Psychological Science, published the following: “Many of these [evidence-based] interventions can be disseminated without highly trained and expensive personnel… . CBT is effective even when delivered by nondoctoral ther apists or by health educators with little or no prior experience with CBT who received only a modest level of training … manuals and workbooks are available on user-friendly websites.”22 The devaluation of clinical expertise inherent in these statements requires no interpretation
The researchers examined studies that claimed to compare an “evidence-based” therapy with an alternative form of psychotherapy. The researchers examined more than 2500 abstracts. After closer examination, they winnowed that down to 149 studies that looked like they might actually compare an “evidence-based” therapy with another legitimate form of therapy. But when they finished, there were only 14 studies that compared “evidence based” therapy with a control group that received anything resembling bona fide psychotherapy. These studies showed no advantages whatever for “evidence based” therapies.
From 2500 to 14 actual comparisons between “evidence based” manualized therapy and other psychotherapy. That speaks to how easy it is to run a CBT study compared to a psychotherapeutic alternative. In fact, Shelder proposes that one of the reasons CBT can lead to improvements is the implementation of techniques that come from the domain of psychodynamic therapy. Another argument proposes that the consistent effectiveness of most psychotherapies has less to do with a particular mode. Instead, there are common factors shared by all therapeutic interventions that explain more of the variation in outcomes than a particular modality.
One of these is the therapeutic relationship that forms the shared understanding between the patient and therapist, and forming a trusted relationship can’t be standardized and commodified. There is no manual to relationships. Yet, achieving that relationship can be a more significant factor in the outcome of therapy than whether a CBT or alternative psychodynamic framework was used. Shelder points out that means therapists should be trained like apprentices who learn from experienced professionals modeling successful relationships rather than mass produced through manualized training modules.
What was even more telling than the numbers was this footnote:
Lest the reader think this a misrepresentation or caricature, consider that prominent proponents of manualized therapy advocate treatment by minimally trained paraprofessionals. The journal Psychological Science in the Public Interest, the house organ of the Association for Psychological Science, published the following: “Many of these [evidence-based] interventions can be disseminated without highly trained and expensive personnel… . CBT is effective even when delivered by nondoctoral therapists or by health educators with little or no prior experience with CBT who received only a modest level of training … manuals and workbooks are available on user-friendly websites.”22 The devaluation of clinical expertise inherent in these statements requires no interpretation
As a patient, you may not want to see that CBT can be delivered by people with “little or no prior experience with CBT who received only a modest level of training” or that you received a worksheet from materials “available on user-friendly websites.” So we can surmise that this benefit is being marketed to institutions looking to cut the costs of “highly trained and expensive personnel.” Whether Shelder is too harsh on CBT and the literature supporting its efficacy, it’s not hard to see that there are incentives within the system that are not necessarily aligned with optimizing patient outcomes.
So let’s do a quick recap of the state of CBT research we’ve touched on so far. Shelder challenges us to look at the institutions that adopt therapeutic models to see the influence of their incentives in the quality and delivery of healthcare. Wampold stepped back from the specifics of modalities to study the common factors across all therapies that contribute to success more than the choice of treatment. Cuijpers compares CBT to other credible and evidence-back psychotherapies like the psychodynamic talk therapy Shelder defends. Hayes and Hofmann consider the merits of CBT moving towards processes and away from diagnostic labels from the DSM. Hollon and DeRubeis attempt to figure out the specific mechanisms within CBT that accounts for successful improvements, particularly in exposure therapy where it has some of the biggest effects on patients.
You might be thinking, “Wait, Mank, what’s the actual problem? If CBT can genuinely help people to some extent, can be tried quickly through a standardized intervention, and has a lot of material easily accessible, it sounds like a great first line treatment that institutions can quickly roll out. If it doesn’t work, a therapist can use the relationship formed with the client in the process of CBT to try something else, right?”
Right, much of the time that is exactly the case. Not all of the time. One thing that gets swept under the rug when discussing average metrics is that some people get worse, just like with any treatment.
Michael Lambert conducted research into this in the 1990s and 2000s and found that continuous monitoring of deterioration in patients undergoing active treatment can help therapists adjust to slow or reverse it. This showed two things: deterioration is a detectable pattern, and deterioration can be addressed if caught. Lambert’s work estimated that 5-10% of a population of clinical patients in active therapy were deteriorating, but that could be halved if the therapist was aware of it. Interestingly, in randomized controlled trials by researchers, only 6% reported deterioration at all and the median rate was 4%. This suggests some more support for Shelder’s claim that many studies toss out complex cases that clinicians meet in the real world. Unfortunately, this is still not studied enough for us to have more evidence-based or data-driven insight into the types of populations at highest risk for deterioration, but we have some clues we can look at.
Marsha Linehan developed DBT in response to the observation that CBT could lead chronically suicidal patients with borderline personality disorder into more negative outcomes. Discussing cognitive restructuring or distortions with these patients could inadvertently lead to the message that their experiences with strong emotions is fundamentally wrong. This could lead to feelings of shame and self-blame that impacts engagement in treatment, dropout rates, ruptures in therapeutic relationships, and more emotions that prove difficult to regulate, which forms a kind of vicious cycle. Linehan specifically included validation as a foundational premise for DBT to address that.
In 2007, Scott Lilienfield published Psychological Treatments That Cause Harm which discussed the historical reluctance from the psych research community to examine adverse consequences of therapeutic interventions instead of assuming evidence-based treatments with appreciable improvements in the average case are neutral at worst.

recovery/treatment/procedures/therapies/.title: Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT)
recovery/treatment/procedures/therapies/.content:
The intuition behind CRAFT is that loved ones know a lot about the person in their life who is struggling in ways that professionals never will, but they may not know how to apply that into encouraging a reduction in substance use, treatment that explores abstinence, or setting up boundaries that respect everyone’s needs. Professionals can teach those skills in the abstract when someone enters their clinic or classroom, but loved ones have the ability to assess someone in the context of their unique lived experiences together.
CRAFT can change someone’s environment while they’re still deliberating about their substance use and treatment options; invitations to talk are considered more welcoming than confrontations with ultimatums. At the same time, CRAFT also helps loved ones assess and respect their own needs in order to be a long-term sustainable supporter, including setting boundaries around enabling the consequences of drug use without punity.
A 1999 study showed only 1 out of 10 Al-Anon attendees succeeded at introducing their loved one to treatment. That’s arguably not the goal of Al-Anon, but it is one of the most recommended venues to have these conversations. Other notable points of comparison include no overt spiritual or religious frameworks, so no emphasis on higher powers, powerlessness, or stepwork that can turn off those outside the AA Buchmanist umbrella.
